AL-001.topic: Systemic reaction to an insect sting
AL-001.stem_html:
A 42-year-old man comes to the office 1 week after an emergency department visit. While gardening he was stung on the hand by a yellow jacket. Within 10 minutes he developed generalized hives, throat tightness, wheezing and lightheadedness. Paramedics gave intramuscular epinephrine, and he recovered fully after observation. He had local swelling after a bee sting as a child. He has hypertension treated with amlodipine.

Examination today is normal.
AL-001.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.A: Advise avoidance of outdoor activity; no prescription is needed
choices.B: Prescribe an epinephrine autoinjector and refer for venom skin testing and immunotherapy
choices.C: Prescribe an epinephrine autoinjector only; no further evaluation is needed
choices.D: Prescribe an oral antihistamine to take after any future sting
choices.E: Prescribe daily oral prednisone during the summer months

AL-001.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Systemic reaction to an insect sting

He had anaphylaxis from a hymenoptera sting: skin involvement plus respiratory and cardiovascular symptoms within minutes. Without treatment, the chance of a similar or worse reaction to a future sting is about 30%–60% in adults.

Two steps protect him:

  1. Epinephrine autoinjector (two devices), with training to use it immediately for any systemic reaction and then call emergency services.
  2. Referral to an allergist for venom-specific IgE or skin testing and venom immunotherapy (VIT). VIT reduces the risk of a future systemic reaction to under 5% and is usually continued for 3–5 years.
Reaction to a sting Venom testing & immunotherapy?
Large local reaction (swelling >10 cm, contiguous) Not routinely
Cutaneous-only systemic reaction (adults) Consider (shared decision)
Anaphylaxis (respiratory or cardiovascular) Yes

Why not the others

  • (A) Advise avoidance of outdoor activity; no prescription is needed — Avoidance is advised but not reliable, and he needs epinephrine available.
  • (C) Prescribe an epinephrine autoinjector only; no further evaluation is needed — An autoinjector alone leaves him at high risk; immunotherapy is the only treatment that changes the natural history.
  • (D) Prescribe an oral antihistamine to take after any future sting — Antihistamines treat itching and hives but do not reverse airway edema or hypotension; they are never a substitute for epinephrine.
  • (E) Prescribe daily oral prednisone during the summer months — Prophylactic glucocorticoids do not prevent sting anaphylaxis and cause harm.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Beta-blockers can make anaphylaxis harder to treat (epinephrine resistance — give glucagon); ACE inhibitors may worsen reactions during venom immunotherapy. Review his medications before VIT.

🎯 Educational objective

After a systemic (anaphylactic) reaction to an insect sting, prescribe an epinephrine autoinjector and refer for venom testing and venom immunotherapy.

AL-002.stem_html:
A 35-year-old woman develops diffuse hives, throat tightness, wheezing and lightheadedness 10 minutes after receiving intravenous cefazolin in the preoperative area.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 82/48 mm Hg, pulse rate is 128/min, and respiration rate is 26/min. Oxygen saturation is 91% breathing ambient air. There is diffuse urticaria, lip swelling and expiratory wheezing.

The cefazolin infusion has been stopped, and she has been placed supine with legs elevated.
AL-002.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

choices.A: Intramuscular epinephrine, 0.5 mg, into the anterolateral thigh

AL-002.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Anaphylaxis — first-line treatment

Anaphylaxis — acute skin/mucosal involvement plus respiratory compromise and hypotension — after a drug exposure.

Intramuscular epinephrine is the first and most important treatment, and delay is the main cause of death:

  • 0.01 mg/kg of 1 mg/mL (1:1,000) solution, maximum 0.5 mg in adults, IM into the anterolateral thigh (vastus lateralis — faster, higher peak levels than deltoid or subcutaneous)
  • Repeat every 5–15 minutes as needed

Epinephrine's α₁ effect reverses vasodilation and mucosal edema; β₁ increases cardiac output; β₂ bronchodilates and stabilizes mast cells.

Then: oxygen, IV fluid bolus (1–2 L), airway support, and adjuncts — H₁/H₂ antihistamines, albuterol, glucocorticoids (which do not prevent biphasic reactions). Refractory hypotension → epinephrine infusion; patients on β-blockers → glucagon. Observe and prescribe an epinephrine autoinjector if exposure could recur.

Why not the others

  • (B) Intravenous diphenhydramine — Antihistamines help hives and itching but do not treat airway obstruction or shock.
  • (C) Intravenous methylprednisolone — Glucocorticoids act over hours and do not reverse acute anaphylaxis.
  • (D) Nebulized albuterol — Albuterol treats bronchospasm but not hypotension or upper airway edema.
  • (E) Subcutaneous epinephrine, 1 mg — Subcutaneous absorption is slower and less reliable, and 1 mg is twice the maximum IM dose.
🧠 Mnemonic

Anaphylaxis = "Epi, IM, thigh, now."

🎯 Educational objective

Treat anaphylaxis immediately with intramuscular epinephrine 0.5 mg (1 mg/mL) in the anterolateral thigh, repeated every 5–15 minutes as needed.

AL-003.stem_html: A 46-year-old woman with recurrent streptococcal pharyngitis has a penicillin allergy listed in her chart. When asked, she says that as a child, more than 20 years ago, she had an itchy rash after taking amoxicillin for an ear infection. She had no swelling, breathing difficulty, blistering, mucosal involvement, organ involvement or hospitalization. She has not taken a penicillin since.
AL-003.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

choices.B: Direct oral amoxicillin challenge under observation
choices.C: Penicillin skin testing is required before any challenge
choices.D: Prescribe azithromycin and keep the allergy label

AL-003.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Low-risk penicillin allergy label

About 10% of people report a penicillin allergy, but >95% are not allergic when tested. A penicillin allergy label leads to broader-spectrum, less effective and more expensive antibiotics, more C. difficile and MRSA infections, and more surgical site infections.

Her history is low risk by PEN-FAST and AAAAI/ACAAI 2022 criteria: a remote (>5–10 years) benign rash (maculopapular or urticaria without other features) and no anaphylaxis, angioedema, SCAR (SJS/TEN, DRESS) or organ involvement. The 2022 practice parameter recommends a direct oral amoxicillin challenge (single dose with 30–60 minutes of observation) without prior skin testing for low-risk histories (PALACE trial). If tolerated, remove the allergy label.

Skin testing first is recommended for higher-risk histories (recent anaphylaxis, urticaria within 5 years). Never rechallenge after SJS/TEN or DRESS.

Why not the others

  • (A) Avoid all β-lactams for life — Lifelong β-lactam avoidance is unnecessary for a low-risk history and causes harm.
  • (C) Penicillin skin testing is required before any challenge — Skin testing is not required for low-risk histories; direct oral challenge is safe and effective.
  • (D) Prescribe azithromycin and keep the allergy label — Keeping the label leads to inferior antibiotic choices; macrolide-resistant streptococci are common.
  • (E) Serum penicillin-specific IgE testing — Serum specific IgE tests have poor sensitivity and should not be used to clear or confirm allergy.
🎯 Educational objective

Delabel low-risk penicillin allergy (remote benign rash) with a direct oral amoxicillin challenge without prior skin testing.

AL-004.stem_html:
A 28-year-old woman is evaluated for recurrent episodes of swelling of her lips, hands and once her throat, lasting 2–4 days each. Some episodes are accompanied by severe abdominal pain and vomiting. Episodes began in adolescence and worsened after she started an estrogen-containing oral contraceptive. Her father has similar episodes. She never has hives, and antihistamines and steroids have not helped. She takes no ACE inhibitors.

C4low
C1 esterase inhibitor levellow
C1 esterase inhibitor functionlow
C1qnormal
AL-004.lead: Which of the following mediators is primarily responsible for her symptoms?
AL-004.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Angioedema without urticaria — bradykinin

Recurrent angioedema without urticaria, abdominal attacks, onset in youth, a family history (autosomal dominant), worsening with estrogen, no response to antihistamines or steroids, low C4 and low C1 inhibitor level and function with normal C1q → hereditary angioedema (HAE) type 1.

C1 inhibitor normally regulates the contact (kallikrein–kinin) system. Without it, plasma kallikrein cleaves high-molecular-weight kininogen and produces excess bradykinin, which increases vascular permeability via B2 receptors.

This is why mast-cell treatments (epinephrine, antihistamines, steroids) do not work. Acute attacks: C1 inhibitor concentrate, icatibant (B2 receptor antagonist) or ecallantide (kallikrein inhibitor). Prophylaxis: lanadelumab, berotralstat, C1 inhibitor, garadacimab. Avoid estrogens and ACE inhibitors.

Histamine angioedema Bradykinin angioedema
Hives, itch Yes No
Causes Allergy, idiopathic HAE, ACE inhibitors, acquired C1-INH deficiency
Responds to epinephrine/antihistamines Yes No
C4 Normal Low in HAE (normal with ACE inhibitors)

Acquired C1-INH deficiency (older patient, lymphoma, MGUS) has a low C1q.

Why not the others

  • (B) Histamine — Histamine-mediated angioedema is accompanied by urticaria and responds to antihistamines and epinephrine.
  • (C) Leukotriene C₄ — Leukotrienes contribute to asthma and aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease.
  • (D) Prostaglandin D₂ — Prostaglandin D₂ is a mast-cell mediator involved in allergic reactions and flushing.
  • (E) Tryptase — Tryptase is released by mast cells in anaphylaxis and is a marker of mast-cell activation, not a driver of HAE.
🎯 Educational objective

Hereditary angioedema is a bradykinin-mediated disorder caused by C1 inhibitor deficiency, presenting as angioedema without urticaria and unresponsive to antihistamines and epinephrine.

AL-005.stem_html:
A 39-year-old woman is evaluated for daily itchy hives for 10 weeks. Individual wheals last less than 24 hours and resolve without bruising. She has no fever, joint pain or weight loss. She cannot identify any triggers. Cetirizine, 10 mg daily, helps only a little.

On physical examination, there are several raised erythematous wheals on her trunk and arms. The remainder of the examination is normal.

Complete blood count with differentialnormal
C-reactive proteinnormal
AL-005.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Extensive allergy testing for foods and environmental allergens
choices.B: Increase cetirizine up to 4 times the standard dose

AL-005.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Chronic spontaneous urticaria

Chronic spontaneous urticaria (CSU): hives (± angioedema) on most days for >6 weeks, without an identifiable external trigger. It is an autoimmune mast-cell disorder in many patients (IgG against IgE or its receptor). Wheals that each last <24 hours and leave no bruising argue against urticarial vasculitis.

Extensive testing is not recommended — only a CBC and ESR or CRP (international guideline), with more tests only if clinical clues are present.

Stepwise treatment (EAACI/GA²LEN/WAO 2022):

  1. Second-generation H₁ antihistamine at standard dose
  2. Increase up to 4-fold (e.g., cetirizine 40 mg/d) if not controlled after 2–4 weeks
  3. Add omalizumab (anti-IgE); dupilumab and remibrutinib are newer options
  4. Cyclosporine for refractory disease

Avoid long-term systemic steroids (short bursts only for severe flares). NSAIDs can worsen CSU. Most patients remit within 1–5 years.

Why not the others

  • (A) Extensive allergy testing for foods and environmental allergens — CSU is not caused by allergens; allergy testing has a very low yield and leads to unnecessary diet restrictions.
  • (C) Oral prednisone for 3 months — Prolonged systemic glucocorticoids have major toxicity and are not recommended for CSU.
  • (D) Skin biopsy — Skin biopsy is reserved for suspected urticarial vasculitis (wheals >24 hours, burning, bruising, systemic symptoms).
  • (E) Start cyclosporine — Cyclosporine is a fourth-step option for disease refractory to high-dose antihistamines and omalizumab.
🎯 Educational objective

Treat chronic spontaneous urticaria with a second-generation H₁ antihistamine, increasing to up to 4 times the standard dose before adding omalizumab.

CV-036.topic: AF rate control in decompensated HFrEF
CV-036.stem_html:
A 68-year-old man is admitted with 5 days of worsening dyspnea and orthopnea. He has heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (left ventricular ejection fraction 25% on echocardiography 3 months ago) due to nonischemic cardiomyopathy. Medications are furosemide, metoprolol succinate, sacubitril-valsartan, spironolactone and empagliflozin.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 102/68 mm Hg, pulse rate is 134/min and irregularly irregular, and respiration rate is 24/min. Oxygen saturation is 92% breathing ambient air. Jugular venous pressure is 14 cm H₂O. Crackles are heard at both lung bases, and there is 2+ bilateral leg edema. Extremities are warm.

Electrocardiogram shows atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of 132/min and no ST-segment changes. Intravenous furosemide is started.

Potassium4.4 mEq/L
Creatinine1.2 mg/dL
High-sensitivity troponin Imildly elevated and flat on repeat
CV-036.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate additional treatment?
CV-036.explain_html:
Correct answer: A AF rate control in decompensated HFrEF

He has atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response during acute decompensated HFrEF with borderline blood pressure. The fast rate worsens filling and congestion, so rate control helps — but the drug must not depress contractility further.

In decompensated HFrEF, the 2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS AF guideline favors intravenous digoxin or intravenous amiodarone for acute rate control. Digoxin slows AV-nodal conduction through vagal effects and has mild positive inotropy; it does not lower blood pressure. His beta-blocker can be continued at the home dose if tolerated, but escalating beta-blockade during active congestion and soft pressure risks shock.

Acute rate control HFrEF, decompensated Preserved EF
Beta-blocker IV Caution (negative inotrope) ✅
Diltiazem / verapamil ❌ Avoid ✅
Digoxin IV ✅ Add-on
Amiodarone IV ✅ (also may convert — anticoagulation rules apply) Selected

Why not the others

  • (B) Intravenous diltiazem — Nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers are negative inotropes and are contraindicated in HFrEF (LVEF <40%), especially during decompensation.
  • (C) Intravenous esmolol infusion — A beta-blocker infusion during active congestion with a systolic pressure near 100 mm Hg can precipitate cardiogenic shock.
  • (D) Oral dronedarone — Dronedarone increases mortality in patients with recent decompensated heart failure or NYHA class IV symptoms.
  • (E) Oral flecainide — Flecainide (class IC) is contraindicated in structural heart disease and reduced ejection fraction because it increases proarrhythmic death.
🧠 Mnemonic

"Weak heart? Dig or Amio." Diltiazem is out when the EF is low.

🎓 ABIM pearl

Before chasing the rate, ask whether the tachycardia is causing the decompensation or compensating for it (sepsis, hypovolemia, anemia). Treat the cause first when AF is a response, not the driver.

🎯 Educational objective

In atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response and decompensated HFrEF, use intravenous digoxin or amiodarone for rate control; avoid nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers.

CV-037.topic: Early rhythm control in recent-onset AF
CV-037.stem_html:
A 58-year-old woman is evaluated in follow-up for atrial fibrillation diagnosed 4 months ago. She has persistent episodes of palpitations, reduced exercise tolerance and fatigue despite metoprolol succinate, which keeps her resting ventricular rate near 75/min. She has hypertension controlled with lisinopril. She takes apixaban. She does not smoke and drinks alcohol rarely.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 128/78 mm Hg and pulse rate is 76/min and irregular. BMI is 26 kg/m². Cardiac examination shows an irregular rhythm without murmurs.

Echocardiogram shows normal left ventricular size and function, a mildly enlarged left atrium and no significant valve disease. Thyroid-stimulating hormone level is normal. Sleep study is negative for sleep apnea.
CV-037.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.E: Stop apixaban if sinus rhythm is restored

CV-037.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Early rhythm control in recent-onset AF

She has symptomatic atrial fibrillation diagnosed less than 1 year ago, with risk factors already addressed (blood pressure, weight, alcohol, sleep apnea). Good rate control has not relieved her symptoms.

Two lines of evidence favor rhythm control now:

  • EAST-AFNET 4: early rhythm control (within 1 year of diagnosis) reduced cardiovascular death, stroke and heart failure hospitalization compared with usual care.
  • Catheter ablation is more effective than antiarrhythmic drugs at maintaining sinus rhythm and improving quality of life; the 2023 guideline gives it a Class 1 recommendation as first-line therapy in selected symptomatic patients (paroxysmal AF; younger patients with few comorbidities).

An antiarrhythmic drug (for example flecainide with a nodal blocker, since she has a structurally normal heart) would also be reasonable; of the options shown, ablation is the best choice.

Why not the others

  • (A) Add digoxin — Adding digoxin further slows the rate, but her rate is already controlled; symptoms come from the loss of atrial contraction and irregularity, not from tachycardia.
  • (B) Add diltiazem — Diltiazem added to metoprolol adds more AV-nodal blockade (risk of bradycardia) without restoring sinus rhythm.
  • (C) Continue current therapy unchanged — Continuing rate control alone leaves a symptomatic patient untreated and forfeits the benefit of early rhythm control.
  • (E) Stop apixaban if sinus rhythm is restored — Anticoagulation is based on stroke risk (CHA₂DS₂-VASc), not on the rhythm. Restoring sinus rhythm — even by ablation — is not a reason to stop anticoagulation.
🎓 ABIM pearl

The "time is atrium" concept: the longer AF persists, the more the atria remodel and the harder sinus rhythm becomes to keep. Rhythm control works best early.

🎯 Educational objective

Offer early rhythm control, including catheter ablation, to patients with symptomatic atrial fibrillation diagnosed within the past year; continue anticoagulation according to stroke risk regardless of rhythm.

CV-038.topic: AF with female sex as the only risk factor
CV-038.stem_html:
A 52-year-old woman is evaluated after an episode of palpitations that lasted 6 hours and resolved spontaneously. An electrocardiogram obtained by her smartwatch and confirmed by a 14-day patch monitor shows paroxysmal atrial fibrillation. She has no history of hypertension, diabetes, heart failure, stroke, transient ischemic attack or vascular disease. She takes no medications.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg and pulse rate is 68/min and regular. The remainder of the examination is normal. Echocardiogram shows normal ventricular function and no valve disease. Thyroid function is normal.
CV-038.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate stroke-prevention strategy?

choices.E: Warfarin with a target INR of 2.0 to 3.0

CV-038.explain_html:
Correct answer: D AF with female sex as the only risk factor

Her CHA₂DS₂-VASc score is 1, and the only point is female sex. Female sex is a risk modifier, not an independent risk factor: it raises stroke risk only in women who also have other risk factors. A woman whose only point is sex has the same low annual stroke risk as a man with a score of 0 (well under 1% per year).

The 2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS guideline recommends anticoagulation when estimated annual stroke risk is ≥2% (CHA₂DS₂-VASc ≥2 in men, ≥3 in women) and considers it reasonable at 1%–2%. With a score of 1 from sex alone, no antithrombotic therapy is recommended. The 2024 ESC guideline went further and dropped sex from the score (CHA₂DS₂-VA).

CHA₂DS₂-VASc Men Women Anticoagulate?
0 ✔ — No
1 ✔ (sex only) Men: consider · Women with 1: No
≥2 men / ≥3 women ✔ ✔ Yes (DOAC preferred)

Reassess the score yearly — new hypertension or diabetes changes the answer.

Why not the others

  • (A) Apixaban — A DOAC is indicated only when stroke risk outweighs bleeding risk; her risk is low.
  • (B) Aspirin — Aspirin is not recommended for stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation; it adds bleeding with little or no stroke benefit.
  • (C) Aspirin plus clopidogrel — Dual antiplatelet therapy causes nearly as much bleeding as anticoagulation and is less effective; it has no role here.
  • (E) Warfarin with a target INR of 2.0 to 3.0 — Warfarin carries the same bleeding risk as DOACs without a benefit at this low stroke risk.
🎓 ABIM pearl

The "Sc" in CHA₂DS₂-VASc only counts when another letter is present. On test day, a woman with lone AF and no other points does not need anticoagulation.

🎯 Educational objective

In atrial fibrillation, female sex alone (CHA₂DS₂-VASc of 1 from sex) does not warrant antithrombotic therapy; reassess stroke risk periodically.

CV-039.topic: Cardioversion of AF of unknown duration
CV-039.stem_html:
A 66-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of fatigue and palpitations. He cannot say when the palpitations started; he thinks they began sometime in the past week. He has hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. He takes metformin and amlodipine. He has never taken an anticoagulant.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 138/84 mm Hg, pulse rate is 112/min and irregularly irregular, and respiration rate is 16/min. Oxygen saturation is 97% breathing ambient air. The lungs are clear, and there is no edema.

Electrocardiogram shows atrial fibrillation. After intravenous metoprolol, the ventricular rate is 88/min. Transthoracic echocardiogram shows normal left ventricular function and a mildly enlarged left atrium. He would like to restore sinus rhythm as soon as possible.
CV-039.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.A: Anticoagulate for 1 week, then perform electrical cardioversion
choices.B: Perform electrical cardioversion now without anticoagulation
choices.C: Perform electrical cardioversion now, then anticoagulate for 48 hours
choices.D: Perform electrical cardioversion now, then start daily aspirin
choices.E: Start anticoagulation and perform transesophageal echocardiography–guided cardioversion

CV-039.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Cardioversion of AF of unknown duration

When atrial fibrillation has lasted ≥48 hours or for an unknown time, thrombus may already be present in the left atrial appendage, and cardioversion — electrical or pharmacologic — can dislodge it. There are two safe paths:

  1. Therapeutic anticoagulation for at least 3 weeks, then cardioversion; or
  2. Start anticoagulation and perform transesophageal echocardiography (TEE); if no thrombus is seen, cardiovert now.

With either path, continue anticoagulation for at least 4 weeks after cardioversion, because the atria are "stunned" and mechanically weak for weeks after sinus rhythm returns. Long-term anticoagulation then depends on CHA₂DS₂-VASc — his score is 2 (hypertension, diabetes), so he will need it indefinitely.

:::flow Q: AF ≥48 h or unknown duration, stable? Y: 3 weeks anticoagulation OR TEE-guided cardioversion → anticoagulate ≥4 weeks after N: <48 h with low CHA₂DS₂-VASc: may cardiovert; still consider anticoagulation :::

Why not the others

  • (A) Anticoagulate for 1 week, then perform electrical cardioversion — One week of anticoagulation is not enough time for an existing thrombus to organize or resolve; the standard is at least 3 weeks.
  • (B) Perform electrical cardioversion now without anticoagulation — Cardioversion without anticoagulation after an unknown duration of AF carries a high risk of stroke.
  • (C) Perform electrical cardioversion now, then anticoagulate for 48 hours — Forty-eight hours of anticoagulation after cardioversion does not cover the period of atrial stunning; at least 4 weeks is required.
  • (D) Perform electrical cardioversion now, then start daily aspirin — Aspirin does not prevent cardioembolic stroke after cardioversion.
🎓 ABIM pearl

"Unknown duration" is treated as "≥48 hours." Hemodynamically unstable AF is the exception: cardiovert immediately and start anticoagulation as soon as possible.

🎯 Educational objective

Before cardioverting atrial fibrillation of ≥48 hours or unknown duration, either anticoagulate for 3 weeks or exclude left atrial thrombus with TEE; continue anticoagulation for at least 4 weeks afterward.

CV-040.topic: AF with a mechanical mitral valve
CV-040.stem_html:
A 61-year-old woman comes to the office for a routine visit. She underwent mitral valve replacement with a bileaflet mechanical prosthesis 9 years ago for rheumatic mitral stenosis. She has had permanent atrial fibrillation since then. She takes warfarin and metoprolol. Her INR values have been stable but she dislikes frequent INR checks and asks to switch to apixaban, which her sister takes for atrial fibrillation.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 124/76 mm Hg and pulse rate is 72/min and irregular. A crisp mechanical closing click is heard. There is no murmur suggesting valve dysfunction.

INR2.9
Hemoglobin13.1 g/dL
CV-040.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate anticoagulation management?

choices.A: Continue warfarin with a target INR of 3.0 (range 2.5–3.5)
choices.B: Reduce warfarin to a target INR of 1.5 to 2.0 and add aspirin

CV-040.explain_html:
Correct answer: A AF with a mechanical mitral valve

Mechanical heart valves require a vitamin K antagonist. DOACs are contraindicated:

  • RE-ALIGN (dabigatran vs warfarin) was stopped early for more valve thrombosis, stroke and bleeding with dabigatran.
  • PROACT Xa (apixaban vs warfarin with the On-X aortic valve) was stopped early for excess thromboembolism with apixaban.

For a mechanical mitral valve (or a mechanical aortic valve with risk factors such as atrial fibrillation), the target INR is 3.0 (2.5–3.5). Mitral prostheses are more thrombogenic than aortic ones because of low-velocity flow across the mitral position. Low-dose aspirin may be added only if there is another indication or a low bleeding risk.

Valve Anticoagulant INR target
Mechanical aortic, no risk factors Warfarin 2.5 (2.0–3.0)
Mechanical aortic + AF/LV dysfunction/prior emboli, or On-X after 3 months Warfarin 3.0 or 1.5–2.0 for On-X
Mechanical mitral Warfarin 3.0 (2.5–3.5)
Bioprosthetic valve + AF DOAC acceptable —

Why not the others

  • (B) Reduce warfarin to a target INR of 1.5 to 2.0 and add aspirin — The lower INR target (1.5–2.0) applies only to the On-X mechanical aortic valve without risk factors, not to a mechanical mitral valve.
  • (C) Switch to apixaban — Apixaban was inferior to warfarin for mechanical valves and is contraindicated.
  • (D) Switch to aspirin plus clopidogrel — Antiplatelet therapy alone does not prevent mechanical valve thrombosis.
  • (E) Switch to dabigatran — Dabigatran caused more thromboembolic and bleeding events than warfarin in patients with mechanical valves.
🧠 Mnemonic

"Metal = warfarin." Mitral metal aims higher (3).

🎓 ABIM pearl

The "valvular AF" exclusion for DOACs means two things only: a mechanical valve or moderate–severe rheumatic mitral stenosis. AF with other valve disease (including bioprosthetic valves and aortic stenosis) can be treated with a DOAC.

🎯 Educational objective

Patients with a mechanical mitral valve require warfarin with a target INR of 3.0 (2.5–3.5); DOACs are contraindicated with mechanical heart valves.

CV-041.stem_html:
An 82-year-old woman is evaluated for newly diagnosed persistent atrial fibrillation found during a preoperative visit. She has hypertension and osteoarthritis. She takes amlodipine and acetaminophen. She has no history of bleeding or falls and lives independently.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 134/80 mm Hg and pulse rate is 84/min and irregular. Weight is 57 kg (125.7 lb). The remainder of the examination is normal.

Her CHA₂DS₂-VASc score is 4. Anticoagulation with apixaban is planned.

Hemoglobin12.8 g/dL
Platelet count236000/µL
Creatinine1.1 mg/dL
Estimated creatinine clearance (Cockcroft-Gault)36 mL/min
CV-041.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate apixaban dose?
CV-041.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Apixaban dose selection

The standard dose of apixaban for atrial fibrillation is 5 mg twice daily. The dose is reduced to 2.5 mg twice daily when a patient meets at least 2 of 3 criteria (the "ABC" rule):

Criterion This patient
Age ≥80 years ✅ 82
Body weight ≤60 kg ✅ 57 kg
Creatinine ≥1.5 mg/dL ❌ 1.1

She meets 2 criteria, so 2.5 mg twice daily is correct. Note that apixaban dosing uses serum creatinine, not creatinine clearance — unlike dabigatran, rivaroxaban and edoxaban, which are adjusted by creatinine clearance.

Underdosing DOACs is common and is associated with more strokes without less bleeding. Use the label criteria, not a general impression of frailty.

Why not the others

  • (A) 2.5 mg once daily — Once-daily dosing is not used for apixaban in atrial fibrillation; its half-life (about 12 hours) requires twice-daily dosing.
  • (C) 5 mg once daily — Once-daily dosing is not used for apixaban in atrial fibrillation.
  • (D) 5 mg twice daily — The full dose would be appropriate if she met fewer than 2 dose-reduction criteria.
  • (E) 10 mg twice daily — Ten milligrams twice daily is the initial 7-day loading regimen for acute venous thromboembolism, not a dose for atrial fibrillation.
🧠 Mnemonic

Apixaban "ABC — 2 of 3": Age ≥80, Body weight ≤60 kg, Creatinine ≥1.5 → 2.5 mg twice daily.

🎯 Educational objective

Reduce apixaban to 2.5 mg twice daily for atrial fibrillation only when at least 2 of the following are present: age ≥80 years, weight ≤60 kg, serum creatinine ≥1.5 mg/dL.

CV-042.topic: Catheter ablation for AF with HFrEF
CV-042.stem_html:
A 61-year-old man is evaluated for persistent fatigue and dyspnea on exertion. He has had persistent atrial fibrillation for 10 months and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction for 8 months. Coronary angiography showed no coronary artery disease. Despite 6 months of guideline-directed therapy with metoprolol succinate, sacubitril-valsartan, spironolactone and dapagliflozin, plus apixaban, he has NYHA class II–III symptoms. Resting ventricular rate has been controlled at 70–80/min.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 116/72 mm Hg and pulse rate is 78/min and irregularly irregular. Jugular venous pressure is normal, the lungs are clear, and there is no edema.

Echocardiogram shows left ventricular ejection fraction of 30% (unchanged from diagnosis) and a moderately dilated left atrium.
CV-042.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.B: Atrioventricular node ablation with biventricular pacing

CV-042.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Catheter ablation for AF with HFrEF

In patients with HFrEF and atrial fibrillation, restoring sinus rhythm with catheter ablation improves outcomes. In CASTLE-AF, ablation reduced the composite of death or heart failure hospitalization compared with medical therapy, and LVEF improved. CASTLE-HTx showed benefit even in end-stage heart failure. The 2023 AF guideline gives ablation a Class 1 recommendation in selected patients with HFrEF who are on GDMT.

Ventricular rate is already controlled, so the remaining problem is the loss of atrial contraction and the irregular rhythm. A component of AF-mediated cardiomyopathy may be present, which ablation can reverse.

Antiarrhythmic in HFrEF Use?
Amiodarone, dofetilide ✅ Safe options
Sotalol With caution (QT, negative inotropy)
Flecainide, propafenone ❌ Structural disease
Dronedarone ❌ NYHA III–IV or recent decompensation

Why not the others

  • (A) Add digoxin — The resting rate is already controlled; more rate control will not relieve symptoms caused by AF itself.
  • (B) Atrioventricular node ablation with biventricular pacing — AV-node ablation with pacing ("ablate and pace") is a last resort when rhythm control fails and rate control cannot be achieved; it commits the patient to lifelong pacing.
  • (D) Start dronedarone — Dronedarone increases mortality in patients with advanced or recently decompensated heart failure and in permanent AF.
  • (E) Start flecainide — Class IC drugs increase mortality in patients with structural heart disease or reduced ejection fraction.
🎓 ABIM pearl

A patient with new cardiomyopathy and AF may have tachycardia- or AF-mediated cardiomyopathy. Restoring sinus rhythm (or strict rate control) followed by a repeat echo in 2–3 months is how you tell.

🎯 Educational objective

In patients with HFrEF and symptomatic atrial fibrillation despite GDMT, catheter ablation reduces mortality and heart failure hospitalization.

CV-043.stem_html:
A 78-year-old man is evaluated after his third hospitalization in 12 months for gastrointestinal bleeding requiring transfusion. Capsule endoscopy and double-balloon enteroscopy showed multiple small-bowel angiodysplasias, which were treated with argon plasma coagulation; bleeding recurred despite treatment and a trial of octreotide. He has permanent atrial fibrillation, hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus and a prior ischemic stroke 3 years ago. Apixaban was stopped at his last admission. Other medications are amlodipine, metformin and atorvastatin.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 132/76 mm Hg and pulse rate is 76/min and irregular. Examination is otherwise unremarkable.

Hemoglobin9.8 g/dL
Creatinine1.0 mg/dL
CV-043.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate stroke-prevention strategy?

choices.D: Restart apixaban at a reduced dose of 2.5 mg twice daily
choices.E: Switch to warfarin with a target INR of 2.0 to 3.0

CV-043.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Left atrial appendage occlusion

His stroke risk is very high (CHA₂DS₂-VASc 6: age ≥75 = 2, hypertension, diabetes, prior stroke = 2) but he has a contraindication to long-term anticoagulation: recurrent, transfusion-dependent bleeding from a cause that cannot be fixed.

Percutaneous left atrial appendage occlusion (LAAO) removes the main source of thrombus in nonvalvular AF (>90% of atrial thrombi form in the appendage). After implantation, patients take short-term antithrombotic therapy (a few weeks to months, depending on device and bleeding risk), then aspirin alone or nothing. The 2023 guideline gives LAAO a Class 2a recommendation for patients with a contraindication to long-term oral anticoagulation due to a nonreversible cause.

Why not the others

  • (A) Aspirin alone — Aspirin offers little or no stroke protection in atrial fibrillation and still increases gastrointestinal bleeding.
  • (B) No further stroke-prevention therapy — Leaving a patient with a prior stroke and CHA₂DS₂-VASc of 6 unprotected accepts an annual stroke risk near 10%.
  • (D) Restart apixaban at a reduced dose of 2.5 mg twice daily — Off-label dose reduction lowers stroke protection and does not remove the bleeding risk from angiodysplasia; he does not meet dose-reduction criteria.
  • (E) Switch to warfarin with a target INR of 2.0 to 3.0 — Warfarin causes as much or more gastrointestinal bleeding than apixaban.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Anticoagulation-associated GI bleeding is not automatically a reason to stop anticoagulation forever — find and fix the source first. LAAO is for recurrent or nonreversible bleeding risk.

🎯 Educational objective

Consider percutaneous left atrial appendage occlusion for patients with atrial fibrillation at high stroke risk who cannot take long-term anticoagulation because of a nonreversible bleeding risk.

CV-044.stem_html:
A 76-year-old woman comes for routine pacemaker follow-up. A dual-chamber pacemaker was implanted 2 years ago for sinus node dysfunction. She has hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. She has had no palpitations, stroke or transient ischemic attack. Medications are lisinopril and metformin.

Device interrogation shows 14 episodes of atrial high-rate events over the past 6 months, with electrograms confirming atrial fibrillation. The longest episode lasted 4 hours; total burden is 0.3%. No atrial fibrillation has been seen on any electrocardiogram.

Her CHA₂DS₂-VASc score is 5. She has no history of bleeding.
CV-044.lead: Which of the following is the most accurate statement to guide her decision about anticoagulation?

choices.A: Anticoagulation is not indicated because episodes shorter than 24 hours carry no stroke risk
choices.B: Aspirin provides the same stroke protection as apixaban for device-detected episodes
choices.C: Her stroke risk is lower than with clinical atrial fibrillation; anticoagulation lowers it further but increases major bleeding
choices.D: Her stroke risk is the same as with clinical atrial fibrillation, so anticoagulation is required
choices.E: Stroke risk with device-detected episodes depends only on total burden, not on clinical risk factors

CV-044.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Device-detected subclinical AF

Subclinical, device-detected atrial fibrillation (atrial high-rate episodes confirmed as AF on device electrograms) is common in pacemaker and ICD patients. Two randomized trials clarified its risk:

  • ARTESIA (apixaban vs aspirin; episodes 6 minutes–24 hours): apixaban reduced stroke and systemic embolism (about 1.2% → 0.8% per year) but increased major bleeding.
  • NOAH-AFNET 6 (edoxaban vs placebo): no significant reduction in the composite outcome; more bleeding.

Together they show that stroke risk with short device-detected episodes is about 1% per year — lower than clinical AF with the same risk score (often 3%–5%) — and that anticoagulation trades a modest stroke reduction for more bleeding. The 2023 guideline suggests anticoagulation is reasonable for episodes ≥24 hours with CHA₂DS₂-VASc ≥2, and may be considered for shorter episodes with a higher risk score, through shared decision-making.

Device-detected AF episode Approach (with CHA₂DS₂-VASc ≥2–3)
<5–6 minutes No anticoagulation; keep monitoring
6 minutes–24 hours Shared decision — higher scores favor a DOAC
≥24 hours Anticoagulation reasonable

Why not the others

  • (A) Anticoagulation is not indicated because episodes shorter than 24 hours carry no stroke risk — Episodes of minutes to hours do carry some stroke risk (about 1% per year in ARTESIA), and apixaban reduced that risk.
  • (B) Aspirin provides the same stroke protection as apixaban for device-detected episodes — In ARTESIA, apixaban was superior to aspirin in preventing stroke.
  • (D) Her stroke risk is the same as with clinical atrial fibrillation, so anticoagulation is required — Stroke risk with short device-detected episodes is substantially lower than with clinical AF; anticoagulation is optional, not required.
  • (E) Stroke risk with device-detected episodes depends only on total burden, not on clinical risk factors — Clinical risk factors (CHA₂DS₂-VASc) remain the main determinant of stroke risk; burden adds information but does not replace them.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Progression is common: subclinical AF often becomes clinical AF. Continue device follow-up and reassess when episodes lengthen.

🎯 Educational objective

Device-detected subclinical atrial fibrillation carries a lower stroke risk than clinical atrial fibrillation; decide about anticoagulation through shared decision-making based on episode duration, stroke risk and bleeding risk.

CV-045.stem_html:
A 34-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of 3 weeks of palpitations, heat intolerance, tremor and a 4-kg (8.8-lb) weight loss. She has no other medical history and takes no medications.

On physical examination, temperature is 37.4 °C (99.3 °F), blood pressure is 136/62 mm Hg, pulse rate is 128/min and irregularly irregular, and respiration rate is 18/min. She is alert and oriented. There is lid lag, a diffusely enlarged nontender thyroid with a bruit, and a fine tremor of the outstretched hands. The lungs are clear.

Electrocardiogram shows atrial fibrillation without ischemic changes.

Thyroid-stimulating hormone<0.01 µU/mL
Free thyroxine (T₄)4.8 ng/dL (reference 0.8–1.8)
Potassium4.0 mEq/L
CV-045.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?
CV-045.explain_html:
Correct answer: D AF in thyrotoxicosis

She has Graves disease (diffuse goiter with bruit, lid lag, suppressed TSH, high free T₄) with atrial fibrillation, which occurs in 10%–15% of patients with thyrotoxicosis.

A beta-blocker is the first treatment: it controls the ventricular rate and relieves adrenergic symptoms (tremor, palpitations, anxiety). Propranolol also blocks peripheral T₄-to-T₃ conversion at higher doses. Start a thionamide (methimazole) at the same time. Most patients revert to sinus rhythm spontaneously within 2–3 months of becoming euthyroid, so cardioversion is deferred until then.

Anticoagulation follows the usual CHA₂DS₂-VASc rules — thyrotoxicosis itself is not counted. Her score is 1 (female sex only), so anticoagulation is not indicated.

Why not the others

  • (A) Amiodarone — Amiodarone contains large amounts of iodine and can worsen thyrotoxicosis; it is reserved for refractory cases.
  • (B) Digoxin — Digoxin works poorly in thyrotoxicosis because of increased clearance and high sympathetic tone; larger doses are needed and toxicity is more likely.
  • (C) Immediate electrical cardioversion — Cardioversion while she is still thyrotoxic usually fails or AF quickly recurs; it is not needed in a stable patient.
  • (E) Radioactive iodine ablation today — Radioactive iodine can cause a transient release of thyroid hormone (worsening thyrotoxicosis) and is given after beta-blockade and usually after thionamide pretreatment; it is not an emergency rate-control treatment.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Check TSH in every new case of atrial fibrillation — subclinical hyperthyroidism (low TSH, normal T₄) also triples AF risk in older adults.

🎯 Educational objective

Treat atrial fibrillation caused by thyrotoxicosis with a beta-blocker and antithyroid therapy; most patients return to sinus rhythm once euthyroid.

CV-046.stem_html:
An 84-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her daughter because of 3 days of nausea, vomiting, poor appetite and confusion. She says that lights look yellow and blurry. She has permanent atrial fibrillation, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction and chronic kidney disease. Ten days ago her furosemide dose was increased and clarithromycin was started for sinusitis. Other medications are digoxin, metoprolol and apixaban.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 104/62 mm Hg, pulse rate is 44/min and regular, and respiration rate is 16/min. She is oriented to person only. Mucous membranes are dry.

Electrocardiogram shows atrial fibrillation with a slow regular junctional rhythm at 44/min, frequent premature ventricular complexes, and scooped ST-segment depression.

Sodium134 mEq/L
Potassium6.0 mEq/L
Creatinine2.3 mg/dL (baseline 1.4 mg/dL)
Digoxin (drawn 10 hours after the last dose)4.1 ng/mL
CV-046.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
CV-046.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Digoxin toxicity

She has digoxin toxicity: GI symptoms, confusion, xanthopsia (yellow vision), bradyarrhythmia with ventricular ectopy, hyperkalemia and a high level. Two precipitants are typical: acute kidney injury (digoxin is renally cleared) and clarithromycin (inhibits P-glycoprotein, raising digoxin levels).

Digoxin immune fab (digoxin-specific antibody fragments) is the treatment. Indications include:

  • Life-threatening arrhythmia (ventricular arrhythmia, high-grade AV block, severe bradycardia)
  • Potassium >5.0 mEq/L in acute toxicity
  • End-organ dysfunction (altered mental status, AKI) from toxicity
  • Level >10 ng/mL steady-state, or >15 ng/mL at any time

Hyperkalemia reflects poisoning of the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase and is a marker of severity; it corrects as fab binds digoxin. Check potassium afterward, as it can fall quickly.

Classic arrhythmias of digoxin toxicity
Atrial tachycardia with block
Accelerated junctional rhythm, "regularized" AF
Frequent PVCs, ventricular bigeminy
Bidirectional ventricular tachycardia (near-specific)

Why not the others

  • (B) Hemodialysis — Digoxin has a large volume of distribution and is extensively tissue-bound; hemodialysis removes very little.
  • (C) Intravenous calcium gluconate — Calcium does not treat digoxin toxicity, and the hyperkalemia resolves with fab; most experts avoid relying on calcium here (historical concern for "stone heart" is unproven, but it is not the definitive treatment).
  • (D) Intravenous lidocaine — Lidocaine may be used for ventricular arrhythmias if fab is unavailable, but fab treats the cause and is first-line.
  • (E) Transcutaneous pacing alone — Pacing does not reverse toxicity, and pacing wires can trigger ventricular arrhythmias in the digoxin-sensitized myocardium; fab is preferred.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Digoxin levels drawn earlier than 6 hours after a dose are falsely high (distribution phase). Interactions to remember: amiodarone, verapamil, macrolides, quinidine and cyclosporine raise levels; hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia and hypercalcemia increase toxicity at any level.

🎯 Educational objective

Treat digoxin toxicity with life-threatening arrhythmia, hyperkalemia or end-organ dysfunction with digoxin immune fab; digoxin is not dialyzable.

CV-047.stem_html:
A 72-year-old man is evaluated for 2 months of progressive dyspnea on exertion and a dry cough. He has no fever, chest pain or orthopnea. He has paroxysmal atrial fibrillation and coronary artery disease with preserved left ventricular function. Amiodarone, 400 mg daily, was started 8 months ago after recurrent episodes on sotalol. Other medications are apixaban, atorvastatin and metoprolol. He does not smoke and keeps no birds.

On physical examination, temperature is 37.2 °C (99.0 °F), blood pressure is 128/74 mm Hg, pulse rate is 62/min and regular, and respiration rate is 20/min. Oxygen saturation is 91% breathing ambient air, falling to 85% with walking. Fine bibasilar crackles are heard. Jugular venous pressure is normal, and there is no edema.

High-resolution CT of the chest shows bilateral, predominantly peripheral ground-glass and reticular opacities with areas of high attenuation in the consolidated lung. There is no pleural effusion.

Leukocyte count8200/µL
B-type natriuretic peptide48 pg/mL
Pulmonary functionrestrictive pattern; DLCO 48% of predicted (68% one year ago)
CV-047.lead: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
CV-047.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Amiodarone pulmonary toxicity

Amiodarone pulmonary toxicity fits: subacute dyspnea and dry cough months after starting amiodarone (risk rises with doses ≥400 mg/day and older age), new interstitial infiltrates, a fall in DLCO, and a normal BNP excluding heart failure.

High-attenuation lung opacities (and a high-attenuation liver or thyroid) are a clue: amiodarone contains iodine, which makes affected tissue bright on CT.

Management: stop amiodarone; give glucocorticoids for significant hypoxemia. Recovery is slow because amiodarone's half-life is about 50–100 days.

Amiodarone toxicity Monitoring
Lung — pneumonitis, fibrosis Baseline chest radiograph and PFTs with DLCO; evaluate new symptoms
Thyroid — hypo- or hyperthyroidism TSH at baseline and every 6 months
Liver — transaminase elevation LFTs at baseline and every 6 months
Eyes — corneal deposits, optic neuropathy Exam if visual symptoms
Skin — blue-gray discoloration, photosensitivity —
Heart — bradycardia, QT prolongation ECG
Interactions — ↑ warfarin, digoxin, some statins Adjust doses

Why not the others

  • (A) Acute decompensated heart failure — A normal BNP, normal jugular venous pressure and no edema argue strongly against heart failure.
  • (C) Hypersensitivity pneumonitis — He has no exposure (birds, molds, hot tubs), and hypersensitivity pneumonitis typically shows upper-lobe centrilobular nodules and air trapping rather than high-attenuation peripheral opacities.
  • (D) Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis — Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis progresses over years and shows basal subpleural honeycombing; this 2-month course after a new drug points to drug toxicity.
  • (E) Pulmonary embolism — He is anticoagulated, and pulmonary embolism does not cause bilateral interstitial opacities with a restrictive pattern.
🧠 Mnemonic

Amiodarone's toxicities are the "organs you check for thyroid and liver labs — plus lungs, eyes and skin." Think "PFTs, LFTs, TFTs."

🎯 Educational objective

Recognize amiodarone pulmonary toxicity (subacute interstitial infiltrates, falling DLCO) and treat by stopping the drug, with glucocorticoids for severe disease.

CV-048.stem_html:
A 64-year-old man is evaluated after his second electrical cardioversion in 5 months for atrial flutter. Each episode caused palpitations and fatigue with a ventricular rate near 150/min. He has hypertension and obstructive sleep apnea treated with CPAP. Medications are apixaban, metoprolol succinate and amlodipine.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 130/78 mm Hg and pulse rate is 64/min and regular. Examination is normal.

Electrocardiogram today shows sinus rhythm. An electrocardiogram from the last episode showed negative sawtooth flutter waves in leads II, III and aVF at an atrial rate of 300/min with 2:1 conduction. Echocardiogram shows normal left ventricular function and a mildly enlarged right atrium.
CV-048.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Atrioventricular node ablation with pacemaker implantation
choices.C: Increase metoprolol and continue current strategy
choices.E: Start flecainide without an atrioventricular nodal blocker

CV-048.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Typical atrial flutter — long-term management

The ECG shows typical (counterclockwise) atrial flutter: a macro-reentrant circuit around the tricuspid annulus that must pass through the cavotricuspid isthmus (CTI). Burning a line across the isthmus breaks the circuit.

CTI ablation succeeds in more than 90% of patients with a very low complication rate, and it is more effective than antiarrhythmic drugs. The 2023 guideline recommends it (Class 1) for symptomatic or recurrent typical flutter — it is reasonable as first-line therapy.

Remember: about 30%–50% of patients develop atrial fibrillation in the years after flutter ablation, so anticoagulation decisions follow CHA₂DS₂-VASc, not the success of the ablation.

Why not the others

  • (A) Atrioventricular node ablation with pacemaker implantation — AV-node ablation with pacing is reserved for refractory rate control when rhythm control fails; it is never preferred over a curative flutter ablation.
  • (C) Increase metoprolol and continue current strategy — Rate control in flutter is difficult (rates jump between 2:1 and 1:1), and recurrent episodes despite beta-blockade call for a definitive treatment.
  • (D) Start digoxin — Digoxin adds little rate control during exertion and does not prevent recurrence.
  • (E) Start flecainide without an atrioventricular nodal blocker — Class IC drugs can slow the flutter circuit enough to allow 1:1 AV conduction with a very fast ventricular rate; they must always be given with an AV-nodal blocker — and they are inferior to ablation.
🎓 ABIM pearl

A regular narrow-complex tachycardia at almost exactly 150/min is 2:1 atrial flutter until proven otherwise. Look for the second flutter wave hiding in the T wave or QRS.

🎯 Educational objective

Treat recurrent typical atrial flutter with cavotricuspid isthmus ablation; continue anticoagulation according to CHA₂DS₂-VASc.

CV-049.stem_html:
A 74-year-old woman is hospitalized with an exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. She is receiving nebulized albuterol and ipratropium every 4 hours, prednisone and azithromycin. On the second hospital day the nurse reports an irregular pulse.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 138/82 mm Hg, pulse rate is 118/min and irregular, and respiration rate is 24/min. Oxygen saturation is 89% on 2 L/min of oxygen by nasal cannula. She has diffuse expiratory wheezes.

Electrocardiogram shows an irregular narrow-complex rhythm at 118/min. Every QRS complex is preceded by a P wave; the P waves have four different morphologies, and the PR and R-R intervals vary.

Potassium3.2 mEq/L
Magnesium1.5 mg/dL
CV-049.lead: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.D: Sinus tachycardia with frequent premature atrial complexes

CV-049.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Multifocal atrial tachycardia

Multifocal atrial tachycardia (MAT) has three ECG features:

  1. Atrial rate >100/min
  2. At least three distinct P-wave morphologies in the same lead
  3. Varying P-P, PR and R-R intervals (irregular rhythm), with an isoelectric baseline between P waves

MAT is strongly associated with severe lung disease (COPD exacerbation, hypoxemia, hypercapnia), beta-agonist and theophylline use, and hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia — all present here.

Treatment is aimed at the cause: treat the exacerbation, correct oxygenation, replace potassium and magnesium, and reduce theophylline or beta-agonist exposure where possible. If rate control is needed, a nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker (verapamil, diltiazem) or a cardioselective beta-blocker (if bronchospasm allows) can be used. Cardioversion and anticoagulation do not help — there is no reentry circuit and no single focus.

Why not the others

  • (A) Atrial fibrillation — Atrial fibrillation has no discrete P waves — only fibrillatory baseline activity.
  • (B) Atrial flutter with variable block — Flutter has uniform sawtooth waves at about 300/min, not discrete P waves of varying shape.
  • (D) Sinus tachycardia with frequent premature atrial complexes — Sinus tachycardia with ectopy has one dominant P-wave morphology, interrupted by occasional premature beats.
  • (E) Wandering atrial pacemaker — Wandering atrial pacemaker has the same multiple P-wave morphologies but a rate below 100/min.
🧠 Mnemonic

MAT = "Many Atrial Types" — 3 or more P-wave shapes, rate >100, sick lungs.

🎯 Educational objective

Recognize multifocal atrial tachycardia (≥3 P-wave morphologies, rate >100/min) in severe lung disease and treat the underlying cause and electrolyte deficits.

CV-050.stem_html:
A 29-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of palpitations that began suddenly 40 minutes ago while she was climbing stairs. She has had similar brief episodes in the past that stopped on their own. She has no other medical history and takes no medications.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg, pulse rate is 186/min and regular, and respiration rate is 18/min. She is alert and comfortable aside from palpitations. The lungs are clear.

Electrocardiogram shows a regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 186/min with no visible P waves and a small terminal positive deflection in lead V1 (pseudo-r′). A modified Valsalva maneuver (strain followed by leg elevation) was performed twice without effect.
CV-050.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Adenosine, 6 mg by rapid intravenous push

CV-050.explain_html:
Correct answer: A AVNRT — acute termination

She has a regular narrow-complex tachycardia with no visible P waves and a pseudo-r′ in V1 — the retrograde P wave buried at the end of the QRS — typical of AV nodal reentrant tachycardia (AVNRT), the most common paroxysmal SVT in young women.

Both AVNRT and orthodromic AVRT use the AV node as part of the circuit, so transiently blocking the node terminates them. The stepwise approach (2015 SVT guideline, AHA ACLS):

  1. Vagal maneuvers — the modified Valsalva with passive leg raise converts about 40%.
  2. Adenosine 6 mg rapid IV push with a saline flush; repeat with 12 mg if needed. Warn her about a brief sense of doom, flushing and chest tightness.
  3. If adenosine fails or the arrhythmia recurs: IV verapamil/diltiazem or a beta-blocker.
  4. Synchronized cardioversion if hemodynamically unstable or if drugs fail.

Record a rhythm strip during adenosine — what happens tells you the diagnosis (termination = AV-node–dependent; flutter waves unmasked = atrial flutter).

Why not the others

  • (B) Intravenous amiodarone — Amiodarone is not a first-line drug for stable AV-node–dependent SVT; it acts slowly and has more adverse effects.
  • (C) Intravenous digoxin — Digoxin acts slowly and is not used for acute termination of SVT.
  • (D) Intravenous procainamide — Procainamide is used for stable wide-complex tachycardia and pre-excited AF, not for narrow-complex AVNRT.
  • (E) Synchronized electrical cardioversion — Electrical cardioversion is reserved for hemodynamic instability or failure of vagal maneuvers and adenosine.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Use a lower adenosine dose (3 mg) through a central line or in heart transplant recipients and patients on dipyridamole; higher doses may be needed with caffeine or theophylline. Avoid adenosine in severe bronchospastic asthma.

🎯 Educational objective

For stable AV-node–dependent SVT, use vagal maneuvers first, then rapid intravenous adenosine.

CV-051.stem_html:
A 36-year-old man is evaluated after his fourth emergency department visit this year for palpitations. Each episode was documented as a regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 190–200/min that terminated with adenosine; an electrophysiology consultant reviewed the tracings and diagnosed typical AV nodal reentrant tachycardia. He works as a firefighter and wants to avoid taking daily medication. He has no other medical history.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 122/76 mm Hg and pulse rate is 66/min and regular. Examination is normal.

Electrocardiogram in sinus rhythm is normal, with no pre-excitation. Echocardiogram is normal.
CV-051.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.B: Catheter ablation of the slow pathway

CV-051.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Recurrent SVT — definitive therapy

For recurrent symptomatic AVNRT, catheter ablation of the slow pathway is first-line (Class 1). It cures about 95% of patients with a risk of complete heart block requiring a pacemaker under 1%. It is the best choice for someone who wants no daily medication and works in a job where sudden incapacitation is dangerous.

Drug options (beta-blockers, diltiazem, verapamil) are reasonable for patients who prefer them, but they reduce rather than eliminate episodes and must be taken indefinitely.

Recurrent SVT option Comment
Catheter ablation Curative, Class 1 for AVNRT and AVRT
Beta-blocker, diltiazem, verapamil Reasonable if ablation declined
Flecainide, propafenone If no structural heart disease and nodal drugs fail
"Pill in the pocket" diltiazem + propranolol For infrequent, well-tolerated episodes
Amiodarone Rarely, when others fail or are contraindicated

Why not the others

  • (A) Amiodarone — Amiodarone's long-term toxicity is unjustified for a young patient with a curable arrhythmia.
  • (C) Daily diltiazem — Daily diltiazem reduces episodes but does not cure the arrhythmia, and he wants to avoid daily medication.
  • (D) Implantable loop recorder — The diagnosis is already documented; a loop recorder adds no information.
  • (E) Pill-in-the-pocket flecainide — A single-dose drug strategy suits infrequent, well-tolerated episodes; he has frequent episodes needing ED care and a safety-sensitive job.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Occupations in which sudden incapacitation endangers others (pilots, drivers, firefighters) push the decision toward curative ablation for SVT.

🎯 Educational objective

Offer catheter ablation as first-line therapy for recurrent symptomatic AV nodal reentrant tachycardia.

CV-052.stem_html:
A 26-year-old woman is referred after a preemployment electrocardiogram. She has never had palpitations, presyncope or syncope. She exercises regularly. There is no family history of sudden death. She takes no medications.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 112/70 mm Hg and pulse rate is 64/min and regular. Examination is normal.

Electrocardiogram shows sinus rhythm with a PR interval of 0.10 second, a slurred upstroke of the QRS complex (delta wave) and a QRS duration of 0.13 second. Echocardiogram is normal.
CV-052.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in evaluation?
CV-052.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Asymptomatic WPW pattern

She has an asymptomatic Wolff-Parkinson-White pattern (pre-excitation without arrhythmia). The main risk is sudden death, which happens when atrial fibrillation conducts rapidly down an accessory pathway with a short refractory period and degenerates to ventricular fibrillation. The risk is low (about 1–2 per 1,000 patient-years) but not zero.

Risk stratification is recommended:

  • Exercise test (noninvasive): abrupt, complete loss of the delta wave as heart rate rises means the pathway cannot conduct fast → low risk; no further testing needed.
  • If pre-excitation persists, or the pattern is intermittent but unclear → electrophysiology study, which can measure pathway refractoriness and ablate a high-risk pathway in the same session.

Patients in high-risk occupations or competitive athletes often go straight to EP study.

Low-risk features High-risk features
Intermittent pre-excitation on resting ECG Shortest pre-excited R-R in AF ≤250 ms
Abrupt loss with exercise Multiple pathways
Inducible AVRT or AF at EP study

Why not the others

  • (A) 30-day ambulatory event monitor — An event monitor records symptoms and arrhythmias; it does not assess whether the pathway can conduct dangerously fast.
  • (C) Reassurance with no further evaluation — Reassurance alone is reasonable only after risk stratification shows a low-risk pathway.
  • (D) Start flecainide — Antiarrhythmic drugs are not used in asymptomatic pre-excitation.
  • (E) Start metoprolol — Beta-blockers do not prevent rapid conduction over the accessory pathway, and they are not indicated without arrhythmia.
🎓 ABIM pearl

WPW pattern = pre-excitation without symptoms. WPW syndrome = pre-excitation plus arrhythmia. Symptomatic patients go straight to ablation.

🎯 Educational objective

Risk-stratify asymptomatic pre-excitation with exercise testing (abrupt loss of pre-excitation = low risk) or electrophysiology study.

CV-053.stem_html:
A 68-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of 1 hour of palpitations and lightheadedness. He had an anterior myocardial infarction 4 years ago and has ischemic cardiomyopathy with a left ventricular ejection fraction of 30%. Medications are aspirin, atorvastatin, metoprolol succinate, sacubitril-valsartan, spironolactone and dapagliflozin.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 112/70 mm Hg, pulse rate is 158/min and regular, and respiration rate is 18/min. He is alert. Intermittent cannon a waves are seen in the jugular venous pulse.

Electrocardiogram shows a regular wide-complex tachycardia at 158/min with a QRS duration of 0.18 second, extreme (northwest) axis deviation, and occasional P waves that bear no fixed relation to the QRS complexes. Two narrower complexes that look intermediate between sinus and tachycardia beats are seen.
CV-053.lead: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.C: Sinus tachycardia with preexisting bundle branch block

CV-053.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Wide-complex tachycardia after myocardial infarction

In a patient with structural heart disease (prior MI), a regular wide-complex tachycardia is ventricular tachycardia (VT) in more than 80%–90% of cases — history alone is the strongest predictor.

This ECG also shows features that are specific for VT:

  • AV dissociation — independent P waves (and cannon a waves at the bedside)
  • Fusion beats — a sinus impulse and a ventricular impulse activate the ventricles together, giving an intermediate QRS
  • Capture beats (a sinus beat briefly conducts normally) — not seen here but equally specific
  • Northwest axis and very wide QRS (>0.16 s)
Favors VT Favors SVT with aberrancy
Prior MI, cardiomyopathy, age >35 Young, no structural disease
AV dissociation, fusion and capture beats Typical RBBB or LBBB morphology
Northwest axis, QRS >0.16 s Same QRS as baseline ECG in sinus rhythm
Concordance across precordial leads Terminates with adenosine (usually)

Hemodynamic stability does not distinguish VT from SVT. When in doubt, treat as VT.

Why not the others

  • (A) Antidromic atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia — Antidromic AVRT is rare, occurs in patients with known pre-excitation, and does not produce AV dissociation.
  • (B) Atrial flutter with aberrant conduction — Flutter with aberrancy has a 1:1 or 2:1 relationship between atrial and ventricular activity; AV dissociation excludes it.
  • (C) Sinus tachycardia with preexisting bundle branch block — Sinus tachycardia has a P wave before every QRS complex.
  • (D) Supraventricular tachycardia with aberrancy — AV dissociation and fusion beats exclude a supraventricular origin.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Never give verapamil or diltiazem to a wide-complex tachycardia of uncertain origin — if it is VT, the patient can collapse.

🎯 Educational objective

In a patient with prior myocardial infarction, assume a regular wide-complex tachycardia is ventricular tachycardia; AV dissociation and fusion or capture beats confirm it.

CV-054.stem_html:
A 71-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by ambulance with chest pressure and near-syncope that began 30 minutes ago. She has ischemic cardiomyopathy.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 76/42 mm Hg, pulse rate is 182/min and regular, and respiration rate is 26/min. Oxygen saturation is 90% breathing ambient air. She is confused and diaphoretic, with cool, mottled extremities. A carotid pulse is palpable.

The monitor shows a regular monomorphic wide-complex tachycardia at 182/min. Intravenous access is in place.
CV-054.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

choices.A: Adenosine, 6 mg by rapid intravenous push

CV-054.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Unstable VT with a pulse

She has monomorphic ventricular tachycardia with a pulse and signs of instability: hypotension, altered mental status, signs of shock and chest pain. The AHA adult ACLS algorithm calls for immediate synchronized cardioversion (with sedation if time allows), escalating the energy if the first shock is unsuccessful.

Synchronization times the shock to the R wave and avoids delivering energy during the vulnerable T wave, which could cause ventricular fibrillation.

Tachycardia with a pulse Unstable Stable
Narrow regular Synchronized cardioversion Vagal → adenosine
Wide regular (monomorphic) Synchronized cardioversion Amiodarone or procainamide; adenosine only if SVT suspected
Polymorphic Defibrillation (cannot synchronize) Find the cause (ischemia, long QT)

Why not the others

  • (A) Adenosine, 6 mg by rapid intravenous push — Adenosine is not appropriate in unstable VT and would delay definitive treatment.
  • (B) Intravenous amiodarone, 150 mg over 10 minutes — Antiarrhythmic drugs act too slowly for a patient in shock; amiodarone is for stable VT or after cardioversion to prevent recurrence.
  • (C) Intravenous procainamide — Procainamide is reasonable for stable monomorphic VT, but it causes hypotension and is too slow here.
  • (E) Unsynchronized defibrillation — Unsynchronized shocks are for pulseless VT, ventricular fibrillation or polymorphic VT; synchronized cardioversion is preferred when an organized rhythm with a pulse is present.
🎓 ABIM pearl

If the defibrillator cannot sense the QRS well enough to synchronize and the patient is deteriorating, deliver an unsynchronized shock rather than wait.

🎯 Educational objective

Treat unstable monomorphic ventricular tachycardia with a pulse by immediate synchronized cardioversion.

She is confused and diaphoretic, with cool, mottled extremities. A carotid pulse is palpable. The monitor shows a regular monomorphic wide-complex tachycardia at 182/min. Intravenous access is in place. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate

CV-055.stem_html:
A 31-year-old woman is evaluated for palpitations that occur during exercise and after drinking coffee. She has had no syncope. There is no family history of sudden death or cardiomyopathy. She takes no medications.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 114/70 mm Hg and pulse rate is 72/min with occasional extra beats. Examination is otherwise normal.

A 24-hour ambulatory monitor shows frequent premature ventricular complexes (8% of beats) and three runs of nonsustained ventricular tachycardia during exercise, all with the same morphology: left bundle branch block pattern with an inferior axis (tall R waves in II, III and aVF). The resting electrocardiogram in sinus rhythm is normal, with no T-wave inversion in V1 through V3 and no epsilon waves.

Echocardiogram is normal. Cardiac MRI shows normal right and left ventricular size and function, and no late gadolinium enhancement.
CV-055.lead: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
CV-055.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Idiopathic RVOT ventricular tachycardia

Idiopathic outflow tract VT is the most common ventricular arrhythmia in a structurally normal heart. Its features:

  • LBBB morphology with inferior axis (the impulse starts high in the right ventricular outflow tract and travels down)
  • Triggered by exercise, stress, caffeine — catecholamine-sensitive, cAMP-mediated triggered activity
  • Normal ECG in sinus rhythm and normal cardiac MRI
  • Excellent prognosis

Treatment for symptoms: beta-blockers or nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers; catheter ablation is highly effective (>80%–90%). A very high PVC burden (>10%–15%) can cause cardiomyopathy, so follow ventricular function.

The key board task is to exclude ARVC, which can produce the same VT morphology — that is why the normal MRI and normal sinus-rhythm ECG matter.

Why not the others

  • (A) Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy — ARVC causes T-wave inversion in V1–V3, epsilon waves and right ventricular dilation, fatty-fibrous replacement or dysfunction on MRI; all are absent.
  • (B) Brugada syndrome — Brugada syndrome shows coved ST elevation in V1–V2 and causes polymorphic VT or VF, typically at rest or during sleep.
  • (C) Cardiac sarcoidosis — Sarcoidosis usually produces AV block, VT from scar, and late gadolinium enhancement on MRI.
  • (D) Catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia — CPVT causes exercise-induced bidirectional or polymorphic VT, not repetitive monomorphic VT from one focus.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Idiopathic VT that responds to verapamil is a different entity: fascicular VT from the left ventricle (RBBB pattern, superior axis).

🎯 Educational objective

Recognize idiopathic right ventricular outflow tract VT (LBBB, inferior axis, normal heart) after excluding ARVC with ECG and cardiac MRI.

CV-056.stem_html:
A 38-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after he lost consciousness while lying on the couch. His wife says he was unresponsive for about 30 seconds and then woke without confusion. He has had 2 days of fever, cough and myalgia; a rapid test is positive for influenza A. His brother died suddenly in his sleep at age 41. He takes no medications and does not use drugs.

On physical examination, temperature is 39.3 °C (102.7 °F), blood pressure is 124/76 mm Hg, pulse rate is 96/min and regular, and respiration rate is 18/min. Oxygen saturation is 97% breathing ambient air. Examination is otherwise normal.

Electrocardiogram shows sinus rhythm with 3-mm coved ST-segment elevation followed by a negative T wave in leads V1 and V2. There are no reciprocal ST depressions. An electrocardiogram from 1 year ago showed only incomplete right bundle branch block.

Potassium4.1 mEq/L
High-sensitivity troponin Ibelow the 99th percentile on two measurements 1 hour apart
CV-056.lead: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
CV-056.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Brugada pattern unmasked by fever

This is a type 1 Brugada pattern: coved ST elevation ≥2 mm with a negative T wave in V1–V2, appearing during fever. Combined with arrhythmic syncope and a family history of sudden nocturnal death, it establishes Brugada syndrome.

Brugada syndrome is usually caused by loss-of-function variants in SCN5A (cardiac sodium channel). Fever, sodium channel blockers (flecainide, procainamide, tricyclic antidepressants, cocaine), alcohol and high vagal tone (sleep, large meals) unmask the pattern and trigger polymorphic VT/VF, often at rest or during sleep.

Management:

  • Treat fever aggressively (acetaminophen), monitor on telemetry
  • Avoid triggering drugs (see brugadadrugs.org)
  • ICD for patients with arrhythmic syncope or aborted sudden death (Class 1) — this patient qualifies
  • Quinidine or catheter ablation of the RV outflow epicardium for recurrent shocks or electrical storm (isoproterenol acutely)

Why not the others

  • (A) Acute anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction — The ST elevation is confined to V1–V2 with a coved shape, there is no reciprocal depression, and serial troponins are normal.
  • (B) Acute pericarditis — Pericarditis causes diffuse concave ST elevation with PR depression, not localized coved elevation in V1–V2.
  • (C) Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy — ARVC shows T-wave inversion and epsilon waves in V1–V3 without coved ST elevation, and is triggered by exertion rather than fever.
  • (E) Hyperkalemia — Hyperkalemia can mimic a Brugada pattern, but his potassium is normal.
🧠 Mnemonic

Brugada: "Fever, Flecainide, Fast asleep" — the three F's that unmask it.

🎓 ABIM pearl

Only the type 1 (coved) pattern is diagnostic. A saddleback (type 2) pattern needs a drug challenge (ajmaline or procainamide) or high-lead ECG (V1–V2 in the 2nd–3rd intercostal spaces) to confirm.

🎯 Educational objective

Recognize a fever-induced type 1 Brugada pattern with arrhythmic syncope; treat fever, avoid sodium channel blockers and implant an ICD.

CV-057.stem_html:
A 19-year-old woman is evaluated after losing consciousness when her alarm clock rang early this morning. She fell back onto the bed and recovered within a minute. She had a similar episode at age 15 when a fire alarm went off at school. Her maternal uncle drowned at age 23 while being a strong swimmer. She takes no medications.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 112/68 mm Hg and pulse rate is 62/min and regular. Examination is normal.

Electrocardiogram shows sinus rhythm with a corrected QT interval (QTc) of 520 msec and broad, notched T waves. Electrocardiograms from two earlier visits show QTc values of 500 and 510 msec. Echocardiogram is normal.

Potassium4.3 mEq/L
Magnesium2.1 mg/dL
Calcium9.4 mg/dL
CV-057.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?
CV-057.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Congenital long QT syndrome

She has congenital long QT syndrome (LQTS): persistently prolonged QTc (≥480–500 msec) without a reversible cause, syncope triggered by a sudden loud noise and a family history of sudden death in a young relative. Auditory triggers and notched T waves point to LQT2 (KCNH2, the hERG potassium channel).

Beta-blockers are first-line for all symptomatic patients and for most asymptomatic patients with a prolonged QTc. Nadolol (or propranolol) is preferred over metoprolol. Other steps:

  • Avoid QT-prolonging drugs (crediblemeds.org) and hypokalemia/hypomagnesemia (vomiting, diuretics)
  • Genetic testing and cascade screening of first-degree relatives
  • ICD if cardiac arrest, or syncope recurs despite beta-blockade; left cardiac sympathetic denervation for breakthrough events
  • Avoid alarm clocks with jarring tones and abrupt noise exposures (LQT2)
Type Gene (channel) Typical trigger Notes
LQT1 KCNQ1 (I_Ks) Exercise, swimming Beta-blockers work best
LQT2 KCNH2 (I_Kr) Sudden noise, emotion, postpartum Notched T waves
LQT3 SCN5A (I_Na) Sleep/rest Mexiletine adjunct

Why not the others

  • (A) Intravenous isoproterenol — Isoproterenol shortens the QT in acquired, pause-dependent torsades; in congenital adrenergic-triggered LQTS it can provoke arrhythmias.
  • (B) Mexiletine — Mexiletine (sodium channel blocker) is an adjunct for LQT3, which is triggered during sleep; it is not first-line for LQT2.
  • (D) Permanent pacemaker — Pacing is an adjunct for pause-dependent or bradycardia-related torsades, not initial therapy.
  • (E) Verapamil — Verapamil has no role in long QT syndrome.
🧠 Mnemonic

LQT1 = Swimming (one lap), LQT2 = Two loud sounds (alarm, phone), LQT3 = Three a.m. (sleep).

🎯 Educational objective

Treat congenital long QT syndrome with a nonselective beta-blocker (nadolol or propranolol), avoid QT-prolonging drugs and electrolyte deficits, and screen relatives.
