CV-058.stem_html:
A 24-year-old man who runs marathons is evaluated after an episode of palpitations and near-syncope during a race. His father died suddenly at age 45. He takes no medications or supplements.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 118/70 mm Hg and pulse rate is 54/min and regular. Examination is normal.

Electrocardiogram in sinus rhythm shows T-wave inversion in leads V1 through V4 and a small low-amplitude deflection at the end of the QRS complex in V1. Exercise testing provoked sustained ventricular tachycardia with left bundle branch block morphology and a superior axis, which terminated with cardioversion.

Cardiac MRI shows a dilated right ventricle with regional akinesia of the free wall and a right ventricular ejection fraction of 38%. Left ventricular size and function are normal.
CV-058.lead: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.E: Idiopathic right ventricular outflow tract tachycardia

CV-058.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy

Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (ARVC) is an inherited (usually desmosomal, for example PKP2) disease in which right ventricular myocardium is replaced by fibrofatty tissue. It is a leading cause of sudden death in young athletes. Endurance exercise accelerates the disease.

His findings meet major Task Force criteria:

  • T-wave inversion V1–V3 (or beyond) in someone older than 14 without RBBB
  • Epsilon wave — a small deflection after the QRS in V1–V3 (delayed activation of RV free wall)
  • VT with LBBB morphology and superior axis (from the RV body or apex, not the outflow tract)
  • RV dilation with regional akinesia and reduced RV ejection fraction on MRI
  • Family history of premature sudden death

Management: stop competitive and endurance sport, beta-blocker, ICD for sustained VT or aborted arrest (this patient), genetic testing and cascade screening of relatives.

Why not the others

  • (B) Athlete's heart — Athlete's heart may enlarge the right ventricle but preserves function without regional wall motion abnormalities, and does not cause VT.
  • (C) Brugada syndrome — Brugada syndrome causes coved ST elevation in V1–V2 with a structurally normal heart, and events occur at rest or with fever rather than exercise.
  • (D) Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy — Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy causes left ventricular hypertrophy; the left ventricle is normal here.
  • (E) Idiopathic right ventricular outflow tract tachycardia — Idiopathic outflow tract VT has an inferior axis, a normal sinus-rhythm ECG and a normal MRI.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Distinguish ARVC VT from benign RVOT VT by three things: sinus-rhythm ECG (T inversion, epsilon waves), MRI (RV structural disease) and axis (superior axis points away from the outflow tract).

🎯 Educational objective

Recognize ARVC (T-wave inversion V1–V3, epsilon wave, LBBB-pattern VT, RV dysfunction) and treat with exercise restriction, beta-blockade and an ICD when high risk.

CV-059.stem_html:
A 59-year-old man is hospitalized after an out-of-hospital cardiac arrest. He collapsed while gardening; a bystander started CPR, and paramedics found ventricular fibrillation, which was terminated with one shock. He now has full neurologic recovery. He has hypertension and hyperlipidemia.

Initial electrocardiogram after resuscitation showed no ST-segment elevation. Coronary angiography showed a chronic total occlusion of the right coronary artery with collaterals and no acute thrombotic lesion. Cardiac MRI shows an inferior wall scar with late gadolinium enhancement and a left ventricular ejection fraction of 45%.

Potassium on arrival4.0 mEq/L
Magnesium2.0 mg/dL
High-sensitivity troponin Ipeak modestly elevated after resuscitationconsistent with defibrillation and CPR
Urine drug screennegative
CV-059.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.B: Beta-blocker therapy and repeat echocardiography in 3 months
choices.D: Percutaneous coronary intervention of the chronic total occlusion alone
choices.E: Wearable cardioverter-defibrillator for 90 days, then reassess

CV-059.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Secondary-prevention ICD

He survived ventricular fibrillation that was not caused by a reversible problem — no acute MI, no electrolyte disturbance, no drug. Myocardial scar from an old inferior infarction provides a substrate for reentrant VT/VF that will persist.

For secondary prevention after VF or hemodynamically unstable VT without a completely reversible cause, an ICD is recommended (Class 1) when meaningful survival over 1 year is expected — regardless of ejection fraction. Trials (AVID, CIDS, CASH) showed lower mortality with an ICD than with antiarrhythmic drugs.

Situation ICD timing
VF/unstable VT, no reversible cause ICD now (secondary prevention)
VF within 48 h of acute MI Revascularize; ICD usually not needed for this event
LVEF ≤35% within 40 days after MI or <90 days after revascularization Wait, reassess; wearable defibrillator may bridge
LVEF ≤35%, NYHA II–III on GDMT ≥3 months Primary-prevention ICD

Why not the others

  • (A) Amiodarone without device therapy — Antiarrhythmic drugs are inferior to an ICD for preventing sudden death after cardiac arrest and are adjuncts at most.
  • (B) Beta-blocker therapy and repeat echocardiography in 3 months — Waiting for improvement in ejection fraction applies to primary prevention; secondary prevention does not depend on ejection fraction.
  • (D) Percutaneous coronary intervention of the chronic total occlusion alone — Revascularizing a chronic occlusion does not remove the scar substrate that caused VF and does not replace an ICD.
  • (E) Wearable cardioverter-defibrillator for 90 days, then reassess — A wearable defibrillator is a bridge for patients with temporary or uncertain risk (early after MI or new cardiomyopathy), not for a survivor of scar-related VF.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Primary prevention = no arrhythmia yet, high risk (low EF). Secondary prevention = already survived VT/VF — EF does not matter.

🎯 Educational objective

Implant an ICD for secondary prevention in survivors of ventricular fibrillation or unstable VT without a completely reversible cause, regardless of ejection fraction.

CV-060.stem_html:
A 46-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of 3 days of vomiting from viral gastroenteritis, with leg cramps and weakness. She has hypertension treated with hydrochlorothiazide.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 104/66 mm Hg and pulse rate is 98/min and regular. Mucous membranes are dry. Muscle strength is 4/5 in the proximal lower extremities.

Sodium136 mEq/L
Potassium2.4 mEq/L
Chloride88 mEq/L
Bicarbonate34 mEq/L
Magnesium1.4 mg/dL
CV-060.lead: Which of the following electrocardiographic findings is most likely?

choices.A: Delta waves with a short PR interval and wide QRS
choices.C: Peaked T waves with a widened QRS complex
choices.D: Prominent U waves and ST-segment depression
choices.E: Shortened QT interval with a short ST segment

CV-060.explain_html:
Correct answer: D ECG of hypokalemia

She has severe hypokalemia with a metabolic alkalosis (vomiting plus a thiazide) and hypomagnesemia.

Low extracellular potassium slows and prolongs ventricular repolarization (reduced I_Kr current) and increases automaticity. On the ECG this appears as:

  • T-wave flattening and ST-segment depression
  • Prominent U waves (best seen in V2–V3), often taller than the T wave at K <2.5 mEq/L
  • An apparent long QT (really a long QU interval) → risk of torsades de pointes, PVCs and VT, especially with digoxin

Replace magnesium too — hypomagnesemia increases renal potassium wasting and makes hypokalemia refractory.

Electrolyte ECG
Hypokalemia Flat T, ST depression, U waves, long QU
Hyperkalemia Peaked T → wide QRS → sine wave
Hypocalcemia Long QT (long ST segment)
Hypercalcemia Short QT
Hypothermia Osborn (J) waves

Why not the others

  • (A) Delta waves with a short PR interval and wide QRS — Delta waves and a short PR interval indicate ventricular pre-excitation (WPW), not an electrolyte disturbance.
  • (B) J-point (Osborn) waves with sinus bradycardia — Osborn waves are characteristic of hypothermia.
  • (C) Peaked T waves with a widened QRS complex — Peaked T waves and QRS widening are signs of hyperkalemia.
  • (E) Shortened QT interval with a short ST segment — A short QT interval suggests hypercalcemia or digoxin effect; hypokalemia prolongs repolarization.
🎯 Educational objective

Recognize the ECG effects of hypokalemia (T-wave flattening, ST depression, prominent U waves) and replete magnesium along with potassium.

  2. Diercks DB, et al. Electrocardiographic manifestations: electrolyte abnormalities. J Emerg Med 2004;27:153.

CV-061.stem_html:
A 21-year-old college basketball player is referred after a preparticipation electrocardiogram showed high QRS voltage. He has no symptoms with intense training. There is no family history of cardiomyopathy or sudden death.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 118/68 mm Hg and pulse rate is 48/min and regular. A soft midsystolic murmur does not change with Valsalva maneuver or standing. Examination is otherwise normal.

Electrocardiogram shows sinus bradycardia and isolated voltage criteria for left ventricular hypertrophy; there is no T-wave inversion, ST depression or pathologic Q waves.

Echocardiogram shows a maximal left ventricular wall thickness of 13 mm (symmetric), no left ventricular outflow obstruction, normal mitral valve motion and normal ejection fraction.
CV-061.lead: Which of the following additional findings would most strongly support athlete's heart rather than hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?

choices.A: Diastolic dysfunction with reduced tissue Doppler e′ velocity
choices.B: Late gadolinium enhancement in the septum on cardiac MRI
choices.C: Left ventricular end-diastolic diameter of 42 mm
choices.D: Left ventricular end-diastolic diameter of 58 mm
choices.E: Peak oxygen consumption of 70% of predicted on exercise testing

CV-061.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Athlete's heart vs HCM

A wall thickness of 13–15 mm is the "gray zone" where physiologic athletic remodeling and mild hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) overlap. The features that separate them:

Favors athlete's heart Favors HCM
Enlarged LV cavity (>55 mm) Small LV cavity (<45 mm)
Normal diastolic function (normal e′) Impaired relaxation, low e′
Symmetric, mild thickening Asymmetric septal hypertrophy, SAM
No late gadolinium enhancement LGE (fibrosis) on MRI
High peak VO₂ (>110% predicted) Reduced peak VO₂
Wall thickness regresses after 3 months of detraining No regression
No family history Family history, sarcomere gene variant
Isolated QRS voltage T inversion, deep Q waves, ST depression

Endurance and mixed sports (basketball, rowing, cycling) produce eccentric hypertrophy — a big cavity with proportionally thick walls. A large chamber with normal relaxation is the athlete's pattern.

Why not the others

  • (A) Diastolic dysfunction with reduced tissue Doppler e′ velocity — Impaired relaxation is typical of HCM; athletes have normal or supranormal diastolic function.
  • (B) Late gadolinium enhancement in the septum on cardiac MRI — Late gadolinium enhancement indicates myocardial fibrosis and favors cardiomyopathy.
  • (C) Left ventricular end-diastolic diameter of 42 mm — A small left ventricular cavity with thick walls suggests HCM, not training adaptation.
  • (E) Peak oxygen consumption of 70% of predicted on exercise testing — Reduced exercise capacity favors disease; trained athletes exceed predicted values.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Isolated QRS voltage criteria are normal in athletes (2017 International Criteria). T-wave inversion beyond V2 (in non-Black athletes), ST depression and pathologic Q waves are not — they require evaluation.

🎯 Educational objective

Distinguish athlete's heart from HCM: an enlarged LV cavity, normal diastolic function, no fibrosis and regression with detraining favor physiologic remodeling.

CV-062.topic: Recurrent polymorphic VT during acute ischemia
CV-062.stem_html:
A 63-year-old man is admitted to the cardiac care unit with a non–ST-elevation myocardial infarction. He received aspirin, ticagrelor and heparin, and coronary angiography is planned for the next morning. Overnight he has three episodes of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, each terminated with defibrillation, despite an amiodarone bolus and infusion. Between episodes he reports ongoing chest pressure.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 108/68 mm Hg and pulse rate is 92/min and regular. The lungs have bibasilar crackles.

Electrocardiogram in sinus rhythm shows 2-mm ST-segment depression in leads V4 through V6. The QTc interval is 430 msec. The episodes of ventricular tachycardia begin without a preceding pause.

Potassium4.5 mEq/L
Magnesium2.2 mg/dL
High-sensitivity troponin Irising
CV-062.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
CV-062.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Recurrent polymorphic VT during acute ischemia

Polymorphic VT with a normal QT interval in a patient with an acute coronary syndrome is almost always caused by active myocardial ischemia. Recurrent ventricular arrhythmias and refractory angina are very-high-risk features that call for an immediate invasive strategy (<2 hours) rather than waiting for the next day.

Removing the ischemic trigger is the most effective antiarrhythmic. Meanwhile: beta-blockade if blood pressure allows, amiodarone, correction of electrolytes and treatment of heart failure.

Polymorphic VT Normal QT Long QT (torsades)
Usual cause Ischemia Drugs, low K/Mg, bradycardia, congenital
Pattern No pause needed Short–long–short "pause-dependent" onset
Treatment Revascularize, beta-blocker, amiodarone IV magnesium, stop drug, pace or isoproterenol to raise the rate

Why not the others

  • (A) Immediate implantable cardioverter-defibrillator placement — An ICD is not indicated for ventricular arrhythmias caused by acute ischemia within the first 48 hours; it does not prevent the episodes and revascularization addresses the cause.
  • (B) Intravenous isoproterenol — Isoproterenol raises heart rate to treat pause-dependent torsades with a long QT; in ischemic VT it worsens ischemia.
  • (C) Intravenous magnesium sulfate — Magnesium treats torsades de pointes with a long QT; his QT is normal and his magnesium level is normal.
  • (D) Temporary transvenous overdrive pacing — Overdrive pacing helps pause-dependent torsades; it does not address ischemia.
🎓 ABIM pearl

The 2025 ACC/AHA ACS guideline lists electrical storm or recurrent VT/VF, hemodynamic instability, cardiogenic shock and refractory chest pain as indications for an immediate (<2 h) invasive strategy in NSTE-ACS.

🎯 Educational objective

Treat recurrent polymorphic VT with a normal QT in acute coronary syndrome as ischemia-driven, with urgent coronary angiography and revascularization.

CV-063.stem_html:
A 77-year-old woman is evaluated for episodes of lightheadedness and one near-syncopal spell over the past 2 months. She also notices occasional rapid palpitations. She has hypertension. Medications are losartan and apixaban, which was started 6 months ago for paroxysmal atrial fibrillation. Metoprolol was stopped 3 weeks ago because of dizziness, but her symptoms have continued.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 138/76 mm Hg and pulse rate is 52/min and regular. Examination is otherwise normal.

A 14-day ambulatory monitor shows paroxysms of atrial fibrillation at 130–150/min. Each episode ends with a sinus pause of 4 to 6 seconds, which correlate with her symptoms of lightheadedness. Between episodes there is sinus bradycardia at 45–55/min.

Thyroid-stimulating hormone1.8 µU/mL
Potassium4.3 mEq/L
CV-063.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.E: Restart metoprolol at a lower dose

CV-063.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Tachy-brady syndrome

This is tachy-brady syndrome, a form of sinus node dysfunction: paroxysmal atrial tachyarrhythmias alternate with sinus bradycardia, and when the tachycardia stops, the "sick" sinus node takes seconds to recover (post-conversion pauses).

Symptoms correlate with documented pauses, and the bradycardia persists off AV-nodal blockers, so the problem is intrinsic. A permanent pacemaker (dual-chamber or atrial-based) is indicated (Class 1). Pacing also makes it safe to give the beta-blocker or antiarrhythmic needed to control the tachycardia.

Catheter ablation of AF is an alternative in selected patients because removing AF can remove the pauses — but of these options, pacing is correct.

Sinus node dysfunction pacing — Class 1
Symptoms clearly related to bradycardia or pauses
Symptomatic bradycardia caused by a drug that is essential (e.g., beta-blocker for AF)

Why not the others

  • (A) Electrophysiology study — The diagnosis is already established by symptom–rhythm correlation; an EP study adds nothing.
  • (B) Implantable loop recorder — A loop recorder is for infrequent symptoms not yet captured; her events are already documented.
  • (C) Oral theophylline — Theophylline can raise the sinus rate modestly but is poorly tolerated, proarrhythmic and not a substitute for pacing in symptomatic sinus node dysfunction.
  • (E) Restart metoprolol at a lower dose — Restarting a beta-blocker without pacing support would worsen the pauses.
🧠 Mnemonic

Tachy-brady: "the sprinter who faints at the finish line" — the pause comes when the tachycardia stops.

🎯 Educational objective

Treat symptomatic sinus node dysfunction, including tachy-brady syndrome with post-conversion pauses, with a permanent pacemaker.

CV-064.stem_html:
A 72-year-old man is evaluated for 2 weeks of exertional fatigue and two episodes of lightheadedness. He has hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. Medications are amlodipine, metformin and atorvastatin. He takes no AV-nodal blocking drugs.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 142/74 mm Hg and pulse rate is 54/min and irregular. Examination is otherwise normal.

Electrocardiogram shows sinus rhythm at 76/min with a constant PR interval of 0.18 second and right bundle branch block. Intermittently, a P wave is not followed by a QRS complex, without any preceding PR prolongation; the PR interval after the dropped beat is unchanged.

Potassium4.6 mEq/L
Thyroid-stimulating hormone2.4 µU/mL
High-sensitivity troponin Ibelow the 99th percentile
CV-064.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.C: Observation with repeat ECG in 3 months

CV-064.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Mobitz II AV block

This is Mobitz type II second-degree AV block: sudden dropped beats with a constant PR interval before and after. With a bundle branch block, the block is almost always infranodal (His-Purkinje system) — unpredictable and prone to progress abruptly to complete heart block with a slow, unreliable escape rhythm.

A permanent pacemaker is indicated for Mobitz II, high-grade AV block or third-degree AV block not due to a reversible cause — even without symptoms (Class 1). He also has symptoms.

Mobitz I (Wenckebach) Mobitz II
PR before drop Progressively lengthens Constant
Level AV node (usually) His–Purkinje
QRS Usually narrow Often wide (BBB)
Atropine/exercise Improves May worsen (more P waves arrive at a diseased system)
Pacemaker Only if symptomatic or infranodal Yes

Why not the others

  • (A) Atropine as needed — Atropine acts on the AV node; in infranodal block it may increase the sinus rate and worsen the conduction ratio. It is not long-term therapy.
  • (B) Exercise treadmill test — Exercise testing is sometimes used to localize block in unclear cases, but Mobitz II with bundle branch block already indicates pacing.
  • (C) Observation with repeat ECG in 3 months — Waiting exposes him to sudden complete heart block and syncope.
  • (E) Stop amlodipine and observe — Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers such as amlodipine do not affect AV conduction.
🎯 Educational objective

Implant a permanent pacemaker for Mobitz type II second-degree AV block without a reversible cause, regardless of symptoms.

CV-065.topic: Mobitz I in a young athlete
CV-065.stem_html:
A 23-year-old man who is a competitive rower comes for a preparticipation evaluation. He has no symptoms, including during maximal training. He takes no medications or supplements.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 114/66 mm Hg and pulse rate is 44/min. Examination is normal.

Resting electrocardiogram shows sinus bradycardia with progressive PR prolongation until a P wave fails to conduct, then a shorter PR interval after the pause; QRS duration is 0.09 second. During an exercise test, the heart rate rises to 186/min with 1:1 AV conduction and a normal PR interval.
CV-065.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
CV-065.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Mobitz I in a young athlete

This is Mobitz I (Wenckebach) second-degree AV block — progressive PR prolongation before a dropped beat — in a well-trained endurance athlete. It reflects high vagal tone acting on the AV node, is benign, and resolves with exercise (sympathetic activation), as shown here.

The 2017 International Criteria for ECG interpretation in athletes list sinus bradycardia, first-degree AV block and Mobitz I as normal training-related findings that need no further testing in an asymptomatic athlete.

Red flags that would change management: symptoms (syncope, exercise intolerance), Mobitz II or complete heart block, a wide QRS, or failure to conduct 1:1 with exercise.

Why not the others

  • (A) Cardiac MRI — Cardiac MRI would be appropriate for findings suggesting structural disease (pathologic Q waves, T-wave inversion), which are absent.
  • (B) Electrophysiology study — An EP study is reserved for unclear level of block or symptoms; this is clearly nodal and resolves with exercise.
  • (C) Permanent pacemaker implantation — Pacing is not indicated for asymptomatic Mobitz I at the AV-node level.
  • (E) Restriction from competitive sports — Training-related Mobitz I does not warrant sports restriction.
🎓 ABIM pearl

In athletes, "normal" ECG findings include sinus bradycardia (≥30/min), first-degree AV block, Mobitz I, incomplete RBBB, isolated QRS voltage and early repolarization. "Abnormal" includes T-wave inversion beyond V2 (non-Black athletes), ST depression, pathologic Q waves, LBBB and Mobitz II.

🎯 Educational objective

Mobitz I AV block in an asymptomatic athlete with a narrow QRS that resolves with exercise is benign and needs no treatment or restriction.

CV-066.stem_html:
A 74-year-old man is evaluated after an episode of sudden loss of consciousness while seated at dinner, without prodrome; he recovered fully within seconds and injured his face. He has hypertension and hyperlipidemia. Medications are chlorthalidone and rosuvastatin.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 136/80 mm Hg sitting and 134/78 mm Hg standing, and pulse rate is 70/min and regular. There is a facial abrasion. Cardiac and neurologic examinations are normal.

Electrocardiogram shows sinus rhythm, PR interval 0.20 second, right bundle branch block and left anterior fascicular block. Echocardiogram shows normal left ventricular function and no valve disease. Telemetry for 24 hours in the hospital shows no arrhythmia.

Potassium4.0 mEq/L
Hemoglobin13.9 g/dL
CV-066.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in evaluation?
CV-066.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Bifascicular block with unexplained syncope

Sudden syncope without prodrome, with injury, in an older patient with bifascicular block (RBBB + left anterior fascicular block), strongly suggests intermittent high-grade AV block — the third fascicle failing intermittently.

The 2017 syncope and 2018 bradycardia guidelines support:

  • Electrophysiology study — an HV interval ≥70 ms, or infranodal block induced by atrial pacing, supports pacemaker implantation (and can be done right away in a patient with injurious syncope); or
  • an implantable loop recorder if the EP study is nondiagnostic — long-term rhythm monitoring to capture the event.

Some experts implant a pacemaker empirically in this setting (B4 study); the key ABIM point is that conduction disease plus unexplained arrhythmic-type syncope needs a rhythm diagnosis, not reassurance or a neurologic workup.

Why not the others

  • (A) Carotid duplex ultrasonography — Carotid imaging does not explain transient global loss of consciousness and is not part of syncope evaluation without focal symptoms.
  • (B) Electroencephalography — EEG is for suspected seizure; abrupt brief syncope with immediate recovery is not suggestive of seizure.
  • (D) Reassurance without further testing — Bifascicular block with syncope carries a significant risk of complete heart block; it needs evaluation.
  • (E) Tilt-table testing — Tilt testing evaluates reflex syncope, which usually has a prodrome and a trigger; his history suggests an arrhythmia.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Asymptomatic bifascicular block (even with first-degree AV block) does not need a pacemaker. Syncope changes everything.

🎯 Educational objective

Evaluate unexplained syncope in a patient with bifascicular block with an electrophysiology study (or an implantable loop recorder if nondiagnostic) to detect intermittent high-grade AV block.

CV-067.stem_html:
A 28-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of 3 days of fatigue and lightheadedness. Three weeks ago, after a hiking trip in Connecticut in July, he noticed an expanding red rash on his thigh that cleared on its own. He has had migratory joint aches. He takes no medications.

On physical examination, temperature is 37.6 °C (99.7 °F), blood pressure is 112/68 mm Hg, and pulse rate is 40/min and regular. He is alert. There is no rash now. Cardiac examination shows a regular slow rhythm. Neurologic examination is normal.

Electrocardiogram shows complete heart block with a narrow-complex junctional escape rhythm at 40/min.

Potassium4.2 mEq/L
Thyroid-stimulating hormone1.6 µU/mL
High-sensitivity troponin Imildly elevated
Lyme serology (ELISA with confirmatory immunoblot)pending
CV-067.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.A: Admission for intravenous ceftriaxone and cardiac monitoring
choices.C: Outpatient oral doxycycline after serology results return
choices.E: Repeat Lyme serology in 4 weeks before antibiotics

CV-067.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Lyme carditis

Lyme carditis occurs weeks after infection (often after erythema migrans) and most often causes AV block at the level of the AV node, which can fluctuate rapidly between degrees. Use the SILC score (Suspicious Index in Lyme Carditis) to raise suspicion in young patients with unexplained AV block from endemic areas.

Management (IDSA/AAN/ACR 2020):

  • Hospitalize with continuous monitoring for symptomatic patients, PR >300 msec, or second- or third-degree block.
  • IV ceftriaxone initially; switch to oral doxycycline (or amoxicillin) once high-grade block resolves, to complete 14–21 days.
  • Temporary pacing if needed — not a permanent pacemaker, because block almost always resolves (often within 1 week).
  • Treat empirically without waiting for serology when suspicion is high.

Why not the others

  • (B) Oral prednisone with outpatient follow-up — Glucocorticoids are not standard therapy for Lyme carditis.
  • (C) Outpatient oral doxycycline after serology results return — Outpatient oral therapy is appropriate only for mild first-degree block (PR <300 msec) in an asymptomatic patient; complete heart block requires admission and monitoring.
  • (D) Permanent dual-chamber pacemaker implantation now — Lyme-related AV block usually resolves with antibiotics; permanent pacing is premature.
  • (E) Repeat Lyme serology in 4 weeks before antibiotics — Delaying treatment risks progression and sudden death; treat on clinical suspicion.
🧠 Mnemonic

Lyme heart = "BAN"-ish block: Block at the AV Node — and it goes away with antibiotics.

🎯 Educational objective

Treat Lyme carditis with high-grade AV block with hospitalization, IV ceftriaxone and temporary pacing if needed; permanent pacing is rarely required.

CV-068.topic: Cardiac sarcoidosis presenting as AV block
CV-068.stem_html:
A 44-year-old woman is evaluated after an episode of syncope. Two years ago she had erythema nodosum and bilateral ankle arthritis that resolved without treatment. She has no tick exposure and lives in Arizona. She takes no medications.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 124/76 mm Hg and pulse rate is 42/min and regular. Examination is otherwise normal.

Electrocardiogram shows complete heart block with a narrow-complex escape rhythm. Chest radiograph shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. Echocardiogram shows a left ventricular ejection fraction of 45% with thinning and akinesis of the basal anteroseptum. Coronary CT angiography shows no coronary artery disease.

Lyme serologynegative
Thyroid-stimulating hormonenormal
Serum calcium10.6 mg/dL
CV-068.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next diagnostic test?

choices.C: Endomyocardial biopsy as the first test

CV-068.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Cardiac sarcoidosis presenting as AV block

Unexplained AV block in a patient younger than 60 should raise suspicion of cardiac sarcoidosis, especially with prior erythema nodosum and arthritis (Löfgren syndrome), bilateral hilar adenopathy, mild hypercalcemia, and basal septal thinning without coronary disease.

Cardiac sarcoidosis is diagnosed with advanced imaging:

  • Cardiac MRI: patchy late gadolinium enhancement, typically basal septal and subepicardial (non-coronary distribution)
  • FDG-PET (after a high-fat, low-carbohydrate prep): active inflammation, guides and monitors immunosuppression

Tissue confirmation is best obtained from an extracardiac site (EBUS-guided lymph node biopsy here) because endomyocardial biopsy is patchy and has low sensitivity (~25%).

Treatment: glucocorticoids (± methotrexate), and given AV block and reduced EF, an ICD-capable device rather than a simple pacemaker.

Why not the others

  • (B) Coronary angiography — CT angiography has already excluded coronary disease as the cause of the wall-motion abnormality.
  • (C) Endomyocardial biopsy as the first test — Endomyocardial biopsy misses patchy granulomas in most cases; imaging and an accessible extracardiac biopsy site come first.
  • (D) Serum angiotensin-converting enzyme level — Serum ACE is neither sensitive nor specific and does not establish cardiac involvement.
  • (E) Tilt-table testing — Tilt testing evaluates reflex syncope; her syncope is explained by complete heart block.
🎓 ABIM pearl

In cardiac sarcoid with an indication for pacing, choose an ICD — sudden death from VT is the leading cause of death in cardiac sarcoidosis.

🎯 Educational objective

Suspect cardiac sarcoidosis in adults younger than 60 with unexplained AV block; evaluate with cardiac MRI and FDG-PET and biopsy an extracardiac site.

CV-069.stem_html:
An 81-year-old woman is evaluated for fatigue, dizziness, a pulsating sensation in the neck and dyspnea that began 2 weeks after implantation of a single-chamber ventricular (VVI) pacemaker for intermittent complete heart block. She is in sinus rhythm most of the time.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 102/60 mm Hg (it was 138/78 mm Hg before the implant), and pulse rate is 60/min and regular. Prominent cannon a waves are visible in the neck with every beat. Lungs have faint bibasilar crackles.

Electrocardiogram shows ventricular paced rhythm at 60/min with P waves occurring after each paced QRS complex. Device interrogation shows normal lead function and 98% ventricular pacing.
CV-069.lead: Which of the following best explains her symptoms?
CV-069.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Pacemaker syndrome

Pacemaker syndrome occurs when single-chamber ventricular pacing breaks the normal AV synchrony:

  • Atria contract against closed AV valves → cannon a waves, a pulsating neck, raised atrial pressure, pulmonary congestion
  • Loss of the atrial "kick" (up to 20%–30% of ventricular filling) → lower stroke volume, hypotension, fatigue, dizziness
  • Atrial stretch releases natriuretic peptides and triggers vasodilatory reflexes

Retrograde ventriculoatrial (VA) conduction — P waves after each paced QRS — is common and makes the syndrome worse.

Treatment: upgrade to dual-chamber (DDD) pacing to restore AV synchrony. Patients in sinus rhythm with AV block should receive a dual-chamber device from the start.

Why not the others

  • (A) Lead perforation causing pericardial tamponade — Tamponade causes hypotension and dyspnea but not beat-to-beat cannon a waves; lead function is normal and the onset with pacing points to AV dyssynchrony.
  • (C) Pacemaker-mediated tachycardia from retrograde conduction — Pacemaker-mediated tachycardia requires a dual-chamber device that tracks retrograde P waves; this is a single-chamber device at the lower rate.
  • (D) Right ventricular pacing–induced cardiomyopathy — Pacing-induced cardiomyopathy develops over months to years of high RV pacing burden, not within 2 weeks.
  • (E) Undersensing of intrinsic ventricular activity — Undersensing causes competitive pacing; interrogation shows normal function.
🎯 Educational objective

Recognize pacemaker syndrome (loss of AV synchrony with VVI pacing) and treat by upgrading to dual-chamber pacing.

CV-070.stem_html:
A 66-year-old man comes to the emergency department after receiving three shocks from his implantable cardioverter-defibrillator over the past hour while he was awake and walking around his house. He felt palpitations before each shock but did not lose consciousness. He has ischemic cardiomyopathy with a left ventricular ejection fraction of 30% and paroxysmal atrial fibrillation. Medications are metoprolol succinate, sacubitril-valsartan, spironolactone, empagliflozin and apixaban; he stopped metoprolol 5 days ago because of fatigue.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg and pulse rate is 142/min and irregularly irregular. He is alert and comfortable.

Electrocardiogram shows atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of 140/min and narrow QRS complexes.

Potassium4.3 mEq/L
Magnesium2.0 mg/dL
CV-070.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in evaluation?

choices.C: Electrophysiology study for ventricular tachycardia ablation

CV-070.explain_html:
Correct answer: B ICD shocks during AF

ICD shocks while the patient is conscious, preceded by palpitations, in someone with AF with a fast ventricular rate (after stopping a beta-blocker), suggest inappropriate shocks: the device counted rapid AF as ventricular tachycardia.

Device interrogation comes first — the stored electrograms show what the device saw and whether each shock was appropriate (VT/VF) or inappropriate (AF, sinus tachycardia, lead noise, T-wave oversensing).

If inappropriate: control the AF rate (restart beta-blocker), adjust detection zones and SVT discriminators, and consider rhythm control. If appropriate: look for triggers (ischemia, electrolytes, heart failure) and consider antiarrhythmics or VT ablation.

Causes of inappropriate ICD shocks
AF or flutter with rapid ventricular rate (most common)
Sinus tachycardia above the VT detection rate
Lead fracture — noise on the electrogram
T-wave or P-wave oversensing

Why not the others

  • (A) Coronary angiography — Ischemia may trigger VT, but first establish whether the shocks treated VT at all.
  • (C) Electrophysiology study for ventricular tachycardia ablation — VT ablation is considered only after interrogation confirms recurrent appropriate shocks for VT.
  • (D) Exercise stress test — Stress testing is not useful until the rhythm behind the shocks is known.
  • (E) Transthoracic echocardiography — Echocardiography will not show which rhythm the device detected.
🎓 ABIM pearl

A patient receiving repeated shocks in clinic can have therapies suspended temporarily by placing a magnet over an ICD — it inhibits tachycardia therapies but does not change bradycardia pacing.

🎯 Educational objective

Evaluate ICD shocks with device interrogation to distinguish appropriate therapy for VT/VF from inappropriate shocks, most often caused by rapid atrial fibrillation.

CV-071.stem_html:
A 63-year-old woman is evaluated for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction due to nonischemic cardiomyopathy diagnosed 8 months ago. She has dyspnea walking one block (NYHA class III). She takes optimized doses of metoprolol succinate, sacubitril-valsartan, spironolactone and dapagliflozin and has had no hospitalizations in 4 months.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 108/66 mm Hg and pulse rate is 68/min and regular. Jugular venous pressure is normal, and there is no edema.

Electrocardiogram shows sinus rhythm with left bundle branch block and a QRS duration of 0.16 second. Echocardiogram today shows left ventricular ejection fraction of 25%.
CV-071.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.C: Implant a cardiac resynchronization therapy defibrillator

CV-071.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Cardiac resynchronization therapy

She has symptomatic HFrEF with LVEF ≤35%, sinus rhythm, LBBB with QRS ≥150 ms, and NYHA class II–IV symptoms despite at least 3 months of GDMT. This is the strongest (Class 1) indication for cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT).

LBBB activates the left ventricular lateral wall late, so the ventricle contracts in an uncoordinated way. Pacing both ventricles (biventricular pacing) restores synchronous contraction, improving EF, symptoms, hospitalizations and survival (CARE-HF, MADIT-CRT, RAFT). Because she also meets primary-prevention ICD criteria, a CRT-D is chosen.

CRT indication (LVEF ≤35%, GDMT ≥3 months, sinus rhythm) Class
LBBB, QRS ≥150 ms, NYHA II–IV 1
LBBB, QRS 120–149 ms 2a
Non-LBBB, QRS ≥150 ms 2a
Non-LBBB, QRS 120–149 ms 2b
QRS <120 ms Not indicated (harm)

Why not the others

  • (A) Add digoxin — Digoxin reduces heart failure hospitalizations modestly but does not improve survival or correct dyssynchrony.
  • (B) Add ivabradine — Ivabradine requires sinus rhythm with a resting rate ≥70/min on maximally tolerated beta-blocker; her rate is 68/min.
  • (D) Implant a single-chamber implantable cardioverter-defibrillator — An ICD alone prevents sudden death but does not address dyssynchrony; CRT-D adds the benefits of resynchronization.
  • (E) Refer for heart transplantation evaluation — She is not in advanced (stage D) heart failure; CRT is the next evidence-based step.
🎯 Educational objective

Implant CRT (with defibrillator when indicated) in patients with LVEF ≤35%, LBBB with QRS ≥150 ms and NYHA class II–IV symptoms despite GDMT.

CV-072.stem_html:
A 66-year-old man is admitted after primary percutaneous coronary intervention of the right coronary artery for an inferior ST-elevation myocardial infarction. Six hours later, the telemetry shows sinus rhythm at 64/min with progressive PR prolongation and a dropped QRS every fourth beat. QRS complexes are narrow. He has no symptoms.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg and pulse rate is 56/min and irregular. Lungs are clear.
CV-072.lead: Which of the following best explains this conduction abnormality?

choices.A: Ischemia of the atrioventricular node supplied by the right coronary artery, with increased vagal tone
choices.B: Ischemia of the His bundle and bundle branches from left anterior descending artery occlusion
choices.C: Necrosis of the interventricular septum from septal perforator occlusion
choices.D: Reperfusion injury of the sinus node from circumflex artery occlusion
choices.E: Ventricular septal rupture causing conduction delay

CV-072.explain_html:
Correct answer: A AV block in inferior MI

He has Mobitz I (Wenckebach) AV block with narrow QRS complexes after an inferior MI. In about 90% of people the AV nodal artery arises from the right coronary artery. Inferior infarction causes:

  • AV nodal ischemia and adenosine release
  • Increased vagal tone (Bezold-Jarisch reflex from inferior wall receptors)

The block is at the AV node — usually transient, with a narrow, reliable junctional escape, responsive to atropine, and rarely needs permanent pacing.

Anterior MI is the opposite: AV block arises from infranodal necrosis of the bundle branches (septal branches of the LAD), comes with wide QRS and new bundle branch block, signals a large infarct, and often requires pacing.

Inferior MI block Anterior MI block
Artery RCA (AV nodal artery) LAD (septal perforators)
Level AV node His–Purkinje
Escape Narrow, 40–60/min Wide, <40/min
Prognosis Transient Poor (large infarct)

Why not the others

  • (B) Ischemia of the His bundle and bundle branches from left anterior descending artery occlusion — LAD occlusion produces infranodal block with wide QRS complexes; this infarct was inferior with narrow complexes.
  • (C) Necrosis of the interventricular septum from septal perforator occlusion — Septal necrosis from anterior MI causes bundle branch block and infranodal AV block.
  • (D) Reperfusion injury of the sinus node from circumflex artery occlusion — Sinus node dysfunction produces sinus pauses or bradycardia, not progressive PR prolongation; the sinus node artery usually arises from the RCA.
  • (E) Ventricular septal rupture causing conduction delay — Ventricular septal rupture causes a new holosystolic murmur and shock, not isolated Wenckebach block.
🎯 Educational objective

AV block after inferior MI is usually nodal (RCA supply to the AV node plus vagal tone), transient and atropine-responsive; block after anterior MI is infranodal and ominous.

CV-073.stem_html:
A 79-year-old man is evaluated after he fainted while getting out of bed at night to urinate. He felt lightheaded and his vision dimmed for a few seconds before he fell; he woke immediately. He has had several similar near-episodes on standing over the past month. One month ago, tamsulosin was added for benign prostatic hyperplasia. Other medications are lisinopril, hydrochlorothiazide and atorvastatin. He has no chest pain or palpitations.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 138/78 mm Hg and pulse rate is 72/min supine; after 3 minutes standing, blood pressure is 108/66 mm Hg and pulse rate is 88/min, and he reports lightheadedness. Cardiac examination shows no murmurs. Neurologic examination is normal.

Electrocardiogram shows sinus rhythm with no conduction abnormalities.

Hemoglobin13.8 g/dL
Sodium136 mEq/L
Creatinine1.1 mg/dL
Glucose104 mg/dL
CV-073.lead: Which of the following is the most likely cause of his syncope?
CV-073.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Drug-induced orthostatic hypotension

Orthostatic hypotension = a fall in systolic pressure ≥20 mm Hg (or diastolic ≥10 mm Hg) within 3 minutes of standing. His fall from 138 to 108 mm Hg reproduced the symptoms.

The timing points to the alpha-1 blocker tamsulosin, added a month ago, on top of a thiazide and an ACE inhibitor. Nocturia, standing up from bed and a warm bladder emptying (micturition) add up. The pulse rose by 16/min, showing that the baroreflex works — a clue that the cause is drugs or volume, not autonomic failure (in neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, the heart rate rises <15/min).

Management: review and reduce alpha-blockers, diuretics, nitrates, tricyclics; advise rising slowly, hydration, sitting to urinate at night; consider an alternative BPH treatment (5-alpha-reductase inhibitor) or a more uroselective timing (dose at bedtime with caution).

Why not the others

  • (A) Autonomic failure from Parkinson disease — He has no parkinsonian features, and the compensatory rise in pulse argues against neurogenic autonomic failure.
  • (B) Carotid sinus hypersensitivity — Carotid sinus hypersensitivity is triggered by neck pressure or head turning, not by standing.
  • (C) Intermittent complete heart block — His ECG shows no conduction disease, and symptoms are reproduced by standing.
  • (E) Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome — POTS causes a heart-rate rise ≥30/min without hypotension, usually in young women.
🎓 ABIM pearl

The ΔHR/ΔSBP ratio <0.5 bpm/mm Hg suggests neurogenic orthostatic hypotension (Parkinson disease, multiple system atrophy, diabetic or amyloid neuropathy).

🎯 Educational objective

Recognize orthostatic hypotension caused by medications (especially alpha-blockers and diuretics) as a common cause of syncope in older adults and deprescribe.

CV-074.stem_html:
A 67-year-old man is evaluated in the emergency department after losing consciousness while jogging uphill. He felt a fluttering in his chest a few seconds before he collapsed and recovered within a minute, with no confusion. He has hypertension and had a myocardial infarction 6 years ago. Medications are lisinopril, metoprolol, aspirin and atorvastatin.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 128/80 mm Hg and pulse rate is 68/min and regular, without orthostatic change. There is a forehead laceration. Cardiac examination shows no murmurs. Neurologic examination is normal.

Electrocardiogram shows sinus rhythm with Q waves in leads V1 through V4 and a QRS duration of 0.11 second.

Hemoglobin14.2 g/dL
High-sensitivity troponin Ibelow the 99th percentile
CV-074.lead: Which of the following features of this patient's presentation most strongly indicates a high risk of an adverse outcome?

choices.C: Exertional onset with prior myocardial infarction

CV-074.explain_html:
Correct answer: C High-risk syncope features

The job in syncope is to separate reflex/orthostatic causes (benign) from cardiac causes (which predict sudden death). The 2017 ACC/AHA/HRS guideline lists high-risk features:

High-risk (suggests cardiac syncope) Low-risk (suggests reflex)
Syncope during exertion or supine Prodrome of nausea, warmth, sweating
Palpitations before the event Trigger: pain, emotion, standing, micturition
Known structural heart disease or prior MI, low EF Young age, no heart disease
Abnormal ECG (Q waves, BBB, long QT, Brugada, WPW) Normal ECG
Family history of sudden death <50 y Long history of similar episodes
Injury without warning

This man has several — exertional syncope, palpitations, prior MI with an anterior scar. Exertional syncope with an old infarct suggests scar-related ventricular tachycardia. He should be admitted with telemetry, echocardiography and likely EP evaluation.

Why not the others

  • (A) Age older than 60 years — Age adds some risk but is much weaker than exertional syncope in a patient with structural heart disease.
  • (B) Brief duration of unconsciousness — Short duration is typical of both cardiac and reflex syncope and does not lower risk.
  • (D) Normal hemoglobin level — A normal hemoglobin rules out hemorrhage as a cause but does not indicate risk.
  • (E) Prompt full recovery without confusion — Rapid full recovery distinguishes syncope from seizure; it does not distinguish benign from cardiac causes.
🧠 Mnemonic

Syncope red flags: "Exercise, Palpitations, a Bad heart, a Bad ECG, a Bad family history."

🎯 Educational objective

Exertional syncope, palpitations before syncope and known structural heart disease are high-risk features that warrant admission and cardiac evaluation.

CV-075.stem_html:
A 78-year-old man is evaluated for three episodes of syncope in 6 months. One occurred while he was shaving, another when he turned his head quickly to back out of his driveway, and the third while he was buttoning a tight shirt collar. Each episode was brief, with prompt recovery. He has hypertension and coronary artery disease. Medications are amlodipine, aspirin and atorvastatin.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 142/80 mm Hg and pulse rate is 70/min and regular, with no orthostatic change. There are no carotid bruits. Cardiac and neurologic examinations are normal.

Electrocardiogram and echocardiogram are normal. A 14-day ambulatory monitor recorded no arrhythmia; he had no episodes during the monitoring period.
CV-075.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnostic test?
CV-075.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Carotid sinus hypersensitivity

Syncope triggered by head turning, shaving and a tight collar in an older man points to carotid sinus hypersensitivity — exaggerated baroreceptor response to mechanical pressure on the carotid sinus.

The diagnostic test is carotid sinus massage (5–10 seconds, one side at a time, supine and upright), with continuous ECG and blood pressure monitoring:

  • Cardioinhibitory: asystole ≥3 seconds
  • Vasodepressor: systolic fall ≥50 mm Hg
  • Mixed

A diagnosis requires reproduction of symptoms. Avoid massage in patients with a carotid bruit, stroke or TIA in the past 3 months, or known significant carotid stenosis.

Treatment: avoid triggers (loose collars, turn the whole body); dual-chamber pacing is reasonable for the cardioinhibitory form with recurrent syncope (Class 2a).

Why not the others

  • (A) Electroencephalography — EEG is for suspected seizures, which this history does not suggest.
  • (B) Exercise treadmill test — Exercise testing evaluates exertional syncope or ischemia; his episodes are triggered by neck movement and pressure.
  • (D) MRI of the brain — Brain imaging is not indicated for syncope without focal neurologic signs.
  • (E) Tilt-table testing — Tilt testing evaluates vasovagal syncope with orthostatic triggers; his triggers are mechanical neck stimulation.
🎯 Educational objective

Diagnose carotid sinus hypersensitivity with monitored carotid sinus massage in older patients whose syncope is triggered by head turning or neck pressure.

CV-076.stem_html:
A 24-year-old woman is evaluated for 8 months of lightheadedness, palpitations, fatigue and "brain fog" when she stands, especially in the morning and after hot showers. Symptoms began after a viral illness. She has had no syncope. She takes no medications. She drinks about 1 liter of fluid daily.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 112/70 mm Hg and pulse rate is 74/min supine. After 10 minutes of standing, blood pressure is 114/74 mm Hg and pulse rate is 118/min, with palpitations and acral discoloration of the legs. The remainder of the examination is normal.

Electrocardiogram shows sinus rhythm. Echocardiogram is normal.

Hemoglobin12.9 g/dL
Thyroid-stimulating hormone1.7 µU/mL
Morning cortisol14 µg/dL
CV-076.lead: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
CV-076.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome

Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS):

  • Sustained heart-rate rise ≥30/min within 10 minutes of standing (≥40/min if age 12–19)
  • No orthostatic hypotension
  • Chronic (≥3 months) orthostatic symptoms, relieved by lying down

It most often affects young women, frequently after a viral illness, and overlaps with deconditioning, joint hypermobility and mast-cell disorders.

First-line management is nonpharmacologic: fluids 2–3 L/day, salt 6–10 g/day (if no hypertension), compression garments, and a graduated recumbent exercise program (rowing, recumbent bike, swimming). Drugs for refractory symptoms: low-dose propranolol, fludrocortisone, midodrine, ivabradine or pyridostigmine.

Why not the others

  • (A) Inappropriate sinus tachycardia — Inappropriate sinus tachycardia causes a fast resting rate (>100/min) even when supine; her supine rate is normal.
  • (B) Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension — Orthostatic hypotension requires a fall in blood pressure on standing; hers is unchanged.
  • (C) Pheochromocytoma — Pheochromocytoma causes paroxysmal hypertension, headaches and sweating, not a reproducible postural heart-rate rise without hypertension.
  • (E) Vasovagal syncope — Vasovagal syncope causes episodic hypotension and bradycardia with loss of consciousness, not sustained orthostatic tachycardia.
🎯 Educational objective

Diagnose POTS by a sustained heart-rate rise ≥30/min within 10 minutes of standing without orthostatic hypotension; treat first with fluids, salt, compression and recumbent exercise.

CV-077.topic: Recurrent unexplained syncope — implantable loop recorder
CV-077.stem_html:
A 69-year-old woman is evaluated for three episodes of sudden syncope over 18 months, each without prodrome and lasting less than a minute. The last episode caused a wrist fracture. She has hypertension treated with amlodipine.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 134/78 mm Hg and pulse rate is 72/min and regular, with no orthostatic change. Cardiac and neurologic examinations are normal.

Electrocardiogram is normal. Echocardiogram shows normal ventricular and valve function. Two 14-day ambulatory patch monitors captured no symptoms and no significant arrhythmias. Exercise testing was normal.
CV-077.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in evaluation?
CV-077.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Recurrent unexplained syncope — implantable loop recorder

She has recurrent, infrequent, unexplained syncope with injury and a sudden onset suggesting an arrhythmia, but a normal structural evaluation. Short-term monitors failed because events occur only every few months.

An implantable loop recorder (ILR) monitors the rhythm continuously for up to 3–5 years and records automatically or when activated. It gives a diagnosis in about 30%–50% of such patients — most often paroxysmal AV block or sinus pauses — and guides specific therapy such as pacing.

Event frequency Monitor
Daily 24–48-hour Holter
Every few days to weeks 2–4-week patch or event monitor
Less often than monthly Implantable loop recorder

Why not the others

  • (A) Coronary angiography — She has no symptoms or findings suggesting ischemia, and exercise testing was normal.
  • (B) Electroencephalography — Sudden syncope with prompt recovery does not suggest seizure.
  • (C) Empiric permanent pacemaker implantation — Empiric pacing without documented bradycardia is not recommended for unexplained syncope with a normal ECG.
  • (E) Repeat 14-day patch monitor — Repeating a short-term monitor is unlikely to capture events that occur every few months.
🎯 Educational objective

Use an implantable loop recorder for recurrent, infrequent, unexplained syncope suspected to be arrhythmic after a nondiagnostic initial evaluation.

CV-078.stem_html:
A 58-year-old man comes to the emergency department of a rural hospital 90 minutes after the onset of crushing substernal chest pain. He has hypertension and smokes cigarettes. He has no history of bleeding, stroke or recent surgery.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 146/88 mm Hg, pulse rate is 92/min, and respiration rate is 18/min. Oxygen saturation is 97% breathing ambient air. The lungs are clear.

Electrocardiogram shows 4-mm ST-segment elevation in leads V1 through V5. The hospital has no catheterization laboratory. Because of weather, the estimated time from first medical contact to balloon inflation at the nearest PCI-capable center is 150 minutes. He has received aspirin, 325 mg.
CV-078.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.A: Fibrinolytic therapy with angiography only if symptoms recur
choices.B: Fibrinolytic therapy with transfer for angiography within 2 to 24 hours
choices.C: Heparin infusion and observation in the local hospital
choices.D: Heparin infusion and transfer for primary PCI
choices.E: Transfer for primary PCI with a glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitor

CV-078.explain_html:
Correct answer: B STEMI at a non-PCI hospital

Primary PCI is the preferred reperfusion strategy only if it can be performed within 120 minutes of first medical contact. When the expected delay is longer, and symptoms began <12 hours ago with no contraindication, give fibrinolytic therapy within 30 minutes of arrival (door-to-needle).

After fibrinolysis, use a pharmacoinvasive strategy: transfer every patient to a PCI-capable center —

  • Immediately for failed reperfusion (<50% ST resolution at 60–90 minutes, ongoing pain) → rescue PCI
  • Otherwise for routine angiography within 2–24 hours (STREAM, TRANSFER-AMI)

Adjuncts with fibrinolysis: aspirin, clopidogrel (300-mg load if age ≤75; 75 mg if >75), and an anticoagulant (enoxaparin preferred).

Why not the others

  • (A) Fibrinolytic therapy with angiography only if symptoms recur — An ischemia-guided approach after fibrinolysis is inferior to routine early angiography, which reduces reinfarction and recurrent ischemia.
  • (C) Heparin infusion and observation in the local hospital — Anticoagulation alone does not reperfuse an occluded artery.
  • (D) Heparin infusion and transfer for primary PCI — A 150-minute delay to PCI exceeds the 120-minute window; immediate fibrinolysis restores flow sooner and saves myocardium.
  • (E) Transfer for primary PCI with a glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitor — Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors do not reperfuse the vessel and do not overcome the delay to PCI.
🧠 Mnemonic

STEMI clock: "30 to needle, 90 to balloon, 120 to transfer."

🎯 Educational objective

In STEMI when primary PCI cannot be performed within 120 minutes of first medical contact, give fibrinolytic therapy within 30 minutes and transfer for routine angiography within 2–24 hours.

CV-079.stem_html:
A 74-year-old woman comes to a rural emergency department 2 hours after the onset of chest pain. Electrocardiogram shows ST-segment elevation in leads II, III and aVF. The nearest PCI-capable hospital is 3 hours away by ground, and air transport is unavailable. Fibrinolytic therapy is being considered.

She has hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus and a history of peptic ulcer disease 6 years ago that was treated. Ten weeks ago she had an ischemic stroke with mild residual left-hand weakness. She takes lisinopril, metformin, aspirin and atorvastatin.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 168/94 mm Hg and pulse rate is 64/min.
CV-079.lead: Which of the following findings is an absolute contraindication to fibrinolytic therapy in this patient?

choices.E: Treated peptic ulcer disease 6 years ago

CV-079.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Fibrinolysis contraindication

Ischemic stroke within the past 3 months is an absolute contraindication to fibrinolysis because of the high risk of intracranial hemorrhage. She should be transferred for primary PCI despite the delay.

Absolute contraindications Relative contraindications
Any prior intracranial hemorrhage Ischemic stroke >3 months ago
Ischemic stroke within 3 months (except acute stroke within 4.5 h) BP >180/110 on presentation
Known cerebral vascular lesion (AVM) or intracranial neoplasm Traumatic or prolonged (>10 min) CPR
Suspected aortic dissection Major surgery within 3 weeks
Active bleeding (not menses) or bleeding diathesis Internal bleeding within 2–4 weeks
Significant closed-head or facial trauma within 3 months Current oral anticoagulant therapy, pregnancy, active peptic ulcer
Intracranial or spinal surgery within 2 months Dementia

Why not the others

  • (A) Age older than 70 years — Older age increases bleeding risk but is not a contraindication; older patients benefit from reperfusion.
  • (B) Blood pressure of 168/94 mm Hg — Blood pressure above 180/110 mm Hg is a relative contraindication; hers is below that threshold.
  • (C) Daily aspirin use — Aspirin is given to every patient with STEMI, including those receiving fibrinolytics.
  • (E) Treated peptic ulcer disease 6 years ago — Only an active peptic ulcer is a relative contraindication; remote treated disease is not.
🎯 Educational objective

Recognize the absolute contraindications to fibrinolytic therapy in STEMI, including ischemic stroke within 3 months.

CV-080.stem_html:
A 62-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of 1 hour of substernal chest pressure radiating to his back, with diaphoresis. He has hypertension and hyperlipidemia.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 138/84 mm Hg in both arms, pulse rate is 82/min, and respiration rate is 18/min. The lungs are clear. Peripheral pulses are equal.

Electrocardiogram shows horizontal ST-segment depression of 3 mm in leads V1 through V3 with tall, broad R waves (R/S ratio >1 in V2) and upright T waves. There are no ST-segment changes in the inferior or lateral leads. Additional leads V7 through V9 show 1-mm ST-segment elevation. Bedside echocardiogram shows akinesis of the inferolateral wall and no pericardial effusion or aortic root dilation.

High-sensitivity troponin I210 ng/L (reference <20)
CV-080.lead: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
CV-080.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Posterior STEMI

ST depression in V1–V3 with tall R waves and upright T waves is the mirror image of ST elevation in the posterior (inferobasal) wall: the anterior leads look at the posterior wall from the front, so elevation and Q waves appear upside down as depression and tall R waves.

Posterior leads V7–V9 (left back, at the scapular line) confirm it: ≥0.5 mm ST elevation (≥1 mm in men <40) is diagnostic. The culprit is usually the left circumflex artery (or a dominant RCA).

This is a STEMI equivalent → emergent reperfusion. Posterior MI is often missed because it does not meet standard STEMI criteria — and these patients then receive delayed care.

STEMI equivalents
Posterior MI (ST depression V1–V3, tall R, positive posterior leads)
De Winter T waves (upsloping ST depression with tall T waves in precordial leads — proximal LAD)
LBBB or paced rhythm meeting Sgarbossa criteria
ST elevation in aVR with diffuse ST depression and ongoing ischemia (left main/multivessel)

Why not the others

  • (B) Anterior subendocardial ischemia (non–ST-elevation myocardial infarction) — Subendocardial ischemia produces ST depression, but not tall R waves in V1–V2, and does not cause ST elevation in posterior leads.
  • (C) Right ventricular myocardial infarction — Right ventricular infarction causes ST elevation in V1 and right-sided leads (V4R), usually with inferior ST elevation.
  • (D) Type A aortic dissection — Equal arm pressures and pulses, no root dilation, and a regional wall-motion abnormality favor MI; dissection remains a consideration in every patient with back pain.
  • (E) Wellens syndrome — Wellens syndrome shows deep T-wave inversions in V2–V3 after chest pain has resolved, not ST depression with tall R waves.
🎯 Educational objective

Recognize posterior STEMI (ST depression with tall R waves in V1–V3, ST elevation in V7–V9) as a STEMI equivalent requiring emergent reperfusion.

CV-081.stem_html:
A 52-year-old man comes to the emergency department because he had 40 minutes of substernal chest pressure last night while carrying groceries upstairs. The pain resolved with rest, and he has been pain-free since. He smokes cigarettes and has hyperlipidemia. He takes no medications.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 134/82 mm Hg and pulse rate is 76/min. Cardiac and pulmonary examinations are normal.

Electrocardiogram obtained while pain-free shows deep, symmetric T-wave inversions in leads V2 and V3, with preserved R waves, no Q waves and an isoelectric ST segment.

High-sensitivity troponin I48 ng/L at arrival and 61 ng/L at 1 hour (reference <20)
CV-081.lead: Which of the following is the most likely cause of this electrocardiogram pattern?
CV-081.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Wellens syndrome

Wellens syndrome is a pattern of deep symmetric (type B) or biphasic (type A) T-wave inversions in V2–V3 recorded during a pain-free period after angina, with preserved R waves and little or no ST elevation. It reflects reperfusion of the anterior wall after transient occlusion and indicates critical proximal LAD stenosis.

Without revascularization, about 75% of patients develop a large anterior MI within weeks. Management:

  • Treat as NSTE-ACS (antiplatelet, anticoagulant, statin)
  • Coronary angiography with revascularization — early invasive strategy
  • Avoid stress testing, which can precipitate infarction

Why not the others

  • (A) Acute pericarditis — Pericarditis causes diffuse ST elevation and PR depression; T-wave inversion appears only after the ST segments normalize and is diffuse.
  • (B) Apical hypertrophic cardiomyopathy — Apical HCM causes giant T-wave inversions across V2–V6 that are chronic and unchanged, without a story of new angina and rising troponin.
  • (D) Pulmonary embolism — PE may cause T inversions in V1–V4, but with dyspnea, tachycardia and right heart strain; his presentation is exertional angina.
  • (E) Stress (takotsubo) cardiomyopathy — Takotsubo may cause deep T inversions, but it typically follows an emotional or physical stressor in postmenopausal women and shows apical ballooning.
🧠 Mnemonic

Wellens = "Warning of the Widowmaker" — T waves in V2–V3 that are deep or biphasic after pain goes away.

🎯 Educational objective

Recognize Wellens syndrome (deep or biphasic T waves in V2–V3 after resolved angina) as a marker of critical proximal LAD stenosis; perform angiography and avoid stress testing.

CV-082.topic: Acute MI with left bundle branch block
CV-082.stem_html:
A 74-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of 45 minutes of severe substernal chest pressure with diaphoresis and nausea. She has hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus and known left bundle branch block on electrocardiograms over the past 3 years.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 136/80 mm Hg, pulse rate is 88/min, and respiration rate is 20/min. Oxygen saturation is 95% breathing ambient air. The lungs are clear.

Electrocardiogram shows sinus rhythm with left bundle branch block and 2 mm of ST-segment elevation in leads V5 and V6 in the same direction as the predominantly positive QRS complexes. A copy of her electrocardiogram from 6 months ago shows left bundle branch block without this finding.

High-sensitivity troponin Ipending
CV-082.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.C: Exercise stress test after troponin results
choices.D: Repeat electrocardiogram and troponin in 3 hours

CV-082.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Acute MI with left bundle branch block

LBBB distorts repolarization, so ST changes usually go in the opposite direction (discordant) to the QRS. Ischemic changes are recognized by the Sgarbossa criteria:

Sgarbossa criterion Points
Concordant ST elevation ≥1 mm (same direction as QRS) in any lead 5
Concordant ST depression ≥1 mm in V1–V3 3
Excessively discordant ST elevation (≥25% of the preceding S-wave depth — Smith-modified) Diagnostic

Concordant ST elevation in V5–V6 is highly specific for acute coronary occlusion. With ongoing ischemic symptoms, she has a STEMI equivalent and needs emergent reperfusion — primary PCI.

Note: the 2025 ACS guideline does not treat a new or presumed-new LBBB alone as a STEMI equivalent. Decisions rest on symptoms, hemodynamics, Sgarbossa findings and, when uncertain, urgent echocardiography or angiography.

Why not the others

  • (A) Coronary CT angiography — CT angiography is for stable low-to-intermediate risk chest pain, not for an ECG that meets criteria for acute coronary occlusion.
  • (C) Exercise stress test after troponin results — Stress testing is contraindicated in a patient with ongoing pain and an ECG showing acute injury.
  • (D) Repeat electrocardiogram and troponin in 3 hours — Waiting for troponin or serial ECGs delays reperfusion of an occluded artery; troponin is not required before primary PCI.
  • (E) Transthoracic echocardiography before deciding — Echocardiography may help when the ECG is equivocal, but here the ECG is diagnostic and should not delay angiography.
🎯 Educational objective

In a patient with LBBB and ischemic symptoms, concordant ST elevation (Sgarbossa) indicates acute coronary occlusion and requires emergent reperfusion.

CV-083.stem_html:
A 70-year-old man has sudden severe dyspnea on the third hospital day after an inferior ST-elevation myocardial infarction. He presented 20 hours after symptom onset and was treated medically; angiography is scheduled.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 84/52 mm Hg, pulse rate is 118/min, and respiration rate is 32/min. Oxygen saturation is 84% on 6 L/min of oxygen. He is diaphoretic, with cool extremities. A new grade 2/6 holosystolic murmur is heard at the apex, radiating to the axilla; there is no thrill. Crackles are heard throughout both lung fields. Jugular venous pressure is 12 cm H₂O.

Chest radiograph shows bilateral alveolar edema. A pulmonary artery catheter shows large v waves in the pulmonary capillary wedge pressure tracing, without an oxygen step-up between the right atrium and pulmonary artery.
CV-083.lead: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
CV-083.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Papillary muscle rupture

Acute severe mitral regurgitation from papillary muscle rupture typically occurs 2–7 days after MI, more often after inferior infarction, because the posteromedial papillary muscle has a single blood supply (posterior descending artery). The anterolateral muscle has dual supply (LAD and circumflex) and rarely ruptures.

Clues:

  • Sudden flash pulmonary edema and cardiogenic shock
  • A new apical murmur that may be soft or even absent — with very high left atrial pressure, the pressure gradient falls quickly, so the murmur is short and quiet
  • Large v waves in the wedge tracing (regurgitant volume into a small, noncompliant left atrium)
  • No oxygen step-up (excludes a left-to-right shunt)

Treatment: afterload reduction (nitroprusside if BP allows), mechanical circulatory support (IABP or microaxial pump) as a bridge, and emergency surgery.

Mechanical complication Timing Clue
Papillary muscle rupture 2–7 d (inferior) Apical murmur, pulmonary edema, large v waves
Ventricular septal rupture 3–5 d Harsh murmur + thrill at LSB, O₂ step-up RA→PA
Free wall rupture 1–14 d Sudden tamponade, PEA
LV aneurysm Weeks–months Persistent ST elevation, HF, VT, thrombus

Why not the others

  • (A) Free wall rupture — Free wall rupture causes hemopericardium with tamponade or sudden pulseless electrical activity, not a new mitral murmur with v waves.
  • (B) Left ventricular aneurysm — Aneurysm develops weeks later and causes persistent ST elevation, heart failure or ventricular arrhythmias.
  • (D) Recurrent myocardial infarction — Reinfarction can cause ischemic MR, but the abrupt onset, new murmur and giant v waves on day 3 point to mechanical rupture.
  • (E) Ventricular septal rupture — Septal rupture causes a harsh murmur with a thrill at the left sternal border and an oxygen step-up from right atrium to pulmonary artery.
🎯 Educational objective

Recognize posteromedial papillary muscle rupture after inferior MI (sudden pulmonary edema, shock, new apical murmur, large v waves) and arrange emergency surgery.

CV-084.stem_html:
A 76-year-old woman develops hypotension and worsening dyspnea 4 days after an anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction. She presented late, 30 hours after symptom onset, and was managed medically.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 88/58 mm Hg, pulse rate is 112/min, and respiration rate is 26/min. A new loud, harsh grade 4/6 holosystolic murmur is heard best at the left lower sternal border, with a palpable thrill. Jugular venous pressure is 15 cm H₂O. Bibasilar crackles are present.

A pulmonary artery catheter is placed.

Oxygen saturationright atrium58%
Oxygen saturationpulmonary artery82%
Pulmonary capillary wedge pressure22 mm Hg without prominent v waves
CV-084.lead: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
CV-084.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Ventricular septal rupture

Ventricular septal rupture after MI:

  • 3–5 days after infarction (now rare, ~0.2%), more likely with late presentation, no reperfusion, older age, female sex and anterior MI (apical septum)
  • Loud harsh holosystolic murmur at the left sternal border with a thrill (high-velocity left-to-right jet across a defect that keeps a large gradient)
  • Oxygen step-up of ≥7%–8% from right atrium to pulmonary artery — oxygenated LV blood enters the right ventricle. Here it rises from 58% to 82%.
  • Biventricular failure (high JVP and pulmonary congestion)

Echocardiography with color Doppler confirms the defect. Treatment: afterload reduction and mechanical circulatory support as a bridge to surgical or transcatheter closure. Mortality without repair exceeds 90%.

Why not the others

  • (A) Acute aortic regurgitation — Acute aortic regurgitation causes a diastolic murmur and is not a complication of MI.
  • (B) Free wall rupture with tamponade — Free wall rupture causes hemopericardium with tamponade physiology (equalized diastolic pressures), not a loud murmur with an oxygen step-up.
  • (C) Papillary muscle rupture — Papillary muscle rupture causes a softer apical murmur, large v waves in the wedge tracing and no oxygen step-up.
  • (D) Right ventricular infarction — Right ventricular infarction causes hypotension with clear lungs and high right-sided pressures, without a new murmur or step-up.
🎓 ABIM pearl

The louder murmur with a thrill belongs to the septum (big gradient); the softer apical murmur with pulmonary edema belongs to the papillary muscle.

🎯 Educational objective

Diagnose post-infarction ventricular septal rupture by a new harsh murmur with thrill and an oxygen saturation step-up between the right atrium and pulmonary artery.

She presented late, 30 hours after symptom onset, and was managed medically. On physical examination, blood pressure is 88/58 mm Hg, pulse rate is 112/min, and respiration rate is 26/min. A new loud, harsh grade 4/6 holosystolic murmur is heard best at the left lower sternal border, with a palpable thrill. Jugular venous pressure is 15 cm H₂O. Bibasilar crackles are present. A pulmonary artery catheter is placed. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

CV-085.stem_html:
A 61-year-old man is evaluated on day 4 after an anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction treated with primary PCI and a drug-eluting stent in the proximal left anterior descending artery. He feels well. Medications are aspirin, 81 mg daily, ticagrelor, metoprolol succinate, lisinopril and atorvastatin.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg and pulse rate is 66/min. Examination is unremarkable.

Echocardiogram shows left ventricular ejection fraction of 35%, apical akinesis, and a 1.6-cm mobile, protruding apical thrombus, confirmed by contrast echocardiography.

Hemoglobin14.0 g/dL
Platelet count248000/µL
Creatinine0.9 mg/dL
CV-085.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate antithrombotic regimen?

choices.A: Add an anticoagulant for 3 months and change ticagrelor to clopidogrel
choices.B: Add an anticoagulant indefinitely to aspirin plus ticagrelor
choices.C: Continue aspirin plus ticagrelor without changes
choices.E: Stop aspirin and ticagrelor and start an anticoagulant alone

CV-085.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Left ventricular thrombus after MI

Left ventricular thrombus develops in about 5%–15% of large anterior MIs with apical akinesis, mostly within the first 2 weeks. It carries a high risk of stroke and systemic embolism, especially when mobile or protruding.

Treatment is oral anticoagulation for 3 to 6 months (warfarin or a DOAC — DOACs appear comparable in observational data and small trials), with repeat imaging to confirm resolution.

He also needs antiplatelet therapy for a new stent, so he will be on triple therapy briefly. To limit bleeding:

  • Use clopidogrel as the P2Y12 inhibitor (not ticagrelor or prasugrel) with an anticoagulant
  • Keep aspirin only as long as needed (often 1–4 weeks), then continue anticoagulant + clopidogrel
  • Add a proton pump inhibitor

Why not the others

  • (B) Add an anticoagulant indefinitely to aspirin plus ticagrelor — Triple therapy with ticagrelor has a high bleeding risk, and anticoagulation for LV thrombus is time-limited, not indefinite.
  • (C) Continue aspirin plus ticagrelor without changes — Antiplatelet therapy alone does not treat LV thrombus or prevent embolization.
  • (D) Refer for surgical thrombectomy — Surgical removal is rarely needed and carries more risk than anticoagulation.
  • (E) Stop aspirin and ticagrelor and start an anticoagulant alone — Stopping all antiplatelet therapy 4 days after a drug-eluting stent risks stent thrombosis.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Prophylactic anticoagulation for every large anterior MI is not recommended — image first (contrast echo or cardiac MRI are more sensitive than standard echo), and anticoagulate when thrombus is found.

🎯 Educational objective

Treat post-MI left ventricular thrombus with 3–6 months of anticoagulation, using clopidogrel as the P2Y12 inhibitor and limiting the duration of aspirin when a recent stent requires antiplatelet therapy.
