CV-086.stem_html:
A 63-year-old man is evaluated for 3 days of sharp chest pain that worsens when he lies down and improves when he leans forward, with low-grade fever. Three weeks ago he had an inferior myocardial infarction treated with a drug-eluting stent. Medications are aspirin, 81 mg daily, clopidogrel, metoprolol succinate, lisinopril and atorvastatin.

On physical examination, temperature is 38.0 °C (100.4 °F), blood pressure is 128/78 mm Hg, and pulse rate is 88/min. A three-component friction rub is heard. There is no pulsus paradoxus.

Electrocardiogram shows diffuse concave ST-segment elevation with PR-segment depression; inferior Q waves are unchanged. Echocardiogram shows a small circumferential pericardial effusion without tamponade physiology and no new wall-motion abnormality.

Leukocyte count11800/µL
C-reactive protein64 mg/L
High-sensitivity troponin Iunchanged from discharge level
CV-086.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
CV-086.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Pericarditis after myocardial infarction

This is post–myocardial infarction (Dressler) syndrome, an immune-mediated pericarditis occurring 1–6 weeks after MI (or cardiac surgery), with fever, pleuritic positional pain, a rub, diffuse ST elevation with PR depression, elevated inflammatory markers and an effusion. Troponin is stable and there is no new wall-motion abnormality, so this is not reinfarction.

Aspirin at anti-inflammatory doses (650–1,000 mg every 6–8 hours, then tapered) is preferred after MI, together with colchicine for about 3 months to reduce recurrence.

Why not other NSAIDs or glucocorticoids early after MI? They impair myocardial scar healing and have been linked to infarct thinning and rupture, and nonaspirin NSAIDs increase cardiovascular events.

Why not the others

  • (B) Ibuprofen plus colchicine — Nonaspirin NSAIDs such as ibuprofen are avoided after recent MI because they may impair healing and raise ischemic risk; they also blunt aspirin's antiplatelet effect.
  • (C) Indomethacin — Indomethacin reduces coronary blood flow and impairs scar formation; it should be avoided after MI.
  • (D) Prednisone, 1 mg/kg daily — Glucocorticoids are reserved for refractory cases; early after MI they impair healing, and they increase recurrence risk of pericarditis.
  • (E) Urgent coronary angiography — Stable troponin and no new wall-motion abnormality argue against recurrent ischemia; angiography is not needed.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Early infarct-associated pericarditis (days 1–3, over a transmural infarct) is managed supportively; Dressler syndrome (weeks later) is the immune version. Both are rarer today because of rapid reperfusion.

🎯 Educational objective

Treat post–myocardial infarction pericarditis with high-dose aspirin plus colchicine; avoid nonaspirin NSAIDs and glucocorticoids early after MI.

CV-087.stem_html:
A 67-year-old man is brought to the catheterization laboratory with an anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction that began 3 hours ago. He is hypotensive and confused.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 82/56 mm Hg on norepinephrine, pulse rate is 112/min, and respiration rate is 28/min. Extremities are cold. Lactate is 5.2 mmol/L.

Coronary angiography shows an acute thrombotic occlusion of the proximal left anterior descending artery, an 80% stenosis of the mid right coronary artery and a 75% stenosis of the obtuse marginal branch. All lesions are suitable for PCI.
CV-087.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate revascularization strategy?

choices.A: Emergency bypass grafting of all three vessels
choices.C: Immediate PCI of all three lesions
choices.E: PCI of the culprit artery only

CV-087.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Cardiogenic shock with multivessel disease

In cardiogenic shock complicating MI, emergency revascularization of the culprit artery is the single most important intervention (SHOCK trial: survival benefit with early revascularization).

For multivessel disease in shock, CULPRIT-SHOCK showed that culprit-only PCI (with staged revascularization of other lesions later, if needed) reduced death or dialysis at 30 days compared with immediate multivessel PCI. The extra contrast, time and procedural risk of treating bystander lesions harms an unstable patient.

This differs from hemodynamically stable STEMI, where complete revascularization (immediate or staged) is recommended (COMPLETE trial).

Hemodynamic support: in selected patients with STEMI shock, a microaxial flow pump reduced mortality in DanGer Shock; routine IABP did not (IABP-SHOCK II).

Why not the others

  • (A) Emergency bypass grafting of all three vessels — CABG is reserved for anatomy unsuitable for PCI or a mechanical complication; PCI of the culprit is faster here.
  • (B) Fibrinolytic therapy, then delayed angiography — Fibrinolysis is much less effective in shock (poor coronary perfusion pressure) and delays mechanical reperfusion that is immediately available.
  • (C) Immediate PCI of all three lesions — Immediate multivessel PCI in shock increased death or renal failure compared with culprit-only PCI.
  • (D) Intra-aortic balloon pump without PCI — Routine IABP does not reduce mortality in infarct-related shock, and withholding revascularization is harmful.
🎯 Educational objective

In cardiogenic shock with multivessel disease, perform PCI of the culprit lesion only, with staged revascularization of nonculprit lesions if needed.

CV-088.stem_html:
A 41-year-old woman comes to the emergency department with 1 hour of substernal chest pain that began during an intense spin class. She delivered her second child 4 months ago and is breastfeeding. She has migraine headaches. She does not smoke and has no hypertension, diabetes or hyperlipidemia. She takes no medications and denies drug use.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 122/74 mm Hg and pulse rate is 84/min. Examination is normal.

Electrocardiogram shows 1-mm ST-segment depression in leads V4 through V6. High-sensitivity troponin I rises from 64 to 380 ng/L. Coronary angiography shows a long, smooth, diffuse narrowing of the mid-to-distal left anterior descending artery with abrupt change in caliber and TIMI 3 flow; the other arteries are smooth without atherosclerosis. Her pain has resolved.
CV-088.lead: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
CV-088.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Spontaneous coronary artery dissection

Spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD) causes up to a third of MIs in women younger than 50 and is the most common cause of pregnancy-associated MI. A tear or intramural hematoma separates the arterial wall and compresses the lumen.

Typical setting: young or middle-aged women, few traditional risk factors, postpartum state, intense exercise or emotional stress, and associated fibromuscular dysplasia (FMD) (migraine is common).

Angiography usually shows a long, smooth narrowing (type 2, intramural hematoma) rather than the classic double lumen. Intracoronary imaging confirms it when unclear.

Management differs from atherosclerotic MI:

  • Conservative therapy if stable with preserved flow — most dissections heal in weeks; PCI has a high complication rate (propagation)
  • Beta-blocker (reduces recurrence); aspirin is commonly used; statins only for usual indications
  • Screen for FMD with CT angiography from head to pelvis
  • Avoid future pregnancy counseling and extreme exertion; cardiac rehabilitation

Why not the others

  • (A) Atherosclerotic plaque rupture — She has no atherosclerosis elsewhere in the coronary tree and few risk factors; the long smooth tapering lesion is typical of SCAD.
  • (B) Coronary artery embolism — Embolism produces an abrupt cutoff, usually in a distal vessel, with a source such as AF or endocarditis.
  • (C) Coronary vasospasm — Vasospasm resolves with intracoronary nitroglycerin and usually causes transient ST elevation at rest, often early morning.
  • (E) Stress (takotsubo) cardiomyopathy — Takotsubo causes a typical wall-motion pattern (apical ballooning) with normal coronary arteries, not a focal narrowing.
🎯 Educational objective

Recognize spontaneous coronary artery dissection in young women (often postpartum or after exertion) and manage conservatively with screening for fibromuscular dysplasia.

CV-089.stem_html:
A 68-year-old woman comes to the emergency department with chest pressure and dyspnea that began 2 hours after she learned of her husband's sudden death. She has hypertension treated with amlodipine.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 112/70 mm Hg, pulse rate is 98/min, and respiration rate is 20/min. Oxygen saturation is 95% breathing ambient air. A soft systolic murmur is heard at the left sternal border. Bibasilar crackles are present.

Electrocardiogram shows 2-mm ST-segment elevation in leads V2 through V5. High-sensitivity troponin I is 820 ng/L. Emergency coronary angiography shows no obstructive coronary disease. Left ventriculography shows akinesis of the mid and apical segments with hyperkinesis of the base, extending beyond the territory of any single coronary artery.
CV-089.lead: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.B: Anterior myocardial infarction with spontaneous reperfusion

CV-089.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Takotsubo cardiomyopathy

Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy: transient left ventricular dysfunction triggered by emotional or physical stress, mostly in postmenopausal women. A surge of catecholamines stuns the myocardium (apical myocardium has more beta-receptors), causing apical ballooning with basal hyperkinesis — the shape of a Japanese octopus trap (takotsubo).

Diagnostic features (Mayo criteria):

  • Transient wall-motion abnormality beyond a single coronary territory
  • No obstructive CAD or acute plaque rupture
  • New ECG changes (ST elevation or T inversion) or modest troponin rise (out of proportion small for the wall motion)
  • No pheochromocytoma or myocarditis

Management: supportive HF care, beta-blocker if no LVOT obstruction, ACE inhibitor; anticoagulation if apical thrombus. Watch for dynamic LVOT obstruction (the new murmur) — avoid inotropes and nitrates if present. EF usually recovers in weeks, but recurrence occurs in about 5%–10%.

Why not the others

  • (A) Acute myocarditis — Myocarditis usually follows a viral illness and causes patchy, non-territorial dysfunction without a sudden emotional trigger or this classic apical pattern; cardiac MRI would show late gadolinium enhancement.
  • (B) Anterior myocardial infarction with spontaneous reperfusion — An LAD infarct is limited to the LAD territory and shows a culprit lesion or residual thrombus on angiography.
  • (C) Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy — HCM causes chronic ventricular hypertrophy, not acute apical akinesis.
  • (D) Pheochromocytoma crisis — Pheochromocytoma can cause catecholamine cardiomyopathy but presents with paroxysmal hypertension, headache and sweating; it should be excluded if suspected, but her trigger and presentation point to takotsubo.
🎯 Educational objective

Diagnose takotsubo cardiomyopathy by transient apical ballooning beyond one coronary territory with nonobstructive coronaries after an emotional or physical stressor.

CV-090.stem_html:
A 34-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of chest pressure and anxiety that began 1 hour after he snorted cocaine. He has no other medical history.

On physical examination, temperature is 37.6 °C (99.7 °F), blood pressure is 172/104 mm Hg, pulse rate is 118/min, and respiration rate is 22/min. He is diaphoretic and agitated, with dilated pupils. Cardiac and pulmonary examinations are otherwise normal. Pulses are equal in all extremities.

Electrocardiogram shows sinus tachycardia without ST-segment elevation. Chest radiograph is normal. He has received aspirin, 325 mg, and sublingual nitroglycerin, with partial relief.

High-sensitivity troponin Ibelow the 99th percentile
CV-090.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
CV-090.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Cocaine-associated chest pain

Cocaine causes chest pain through alpha-adrenergic coronary vasoconstriction, increased myocardial oxygen demand (tachycardia, hypertension), platelet activation and accelerated atherosclerosis.

First-line therapy:

  • Benzodiazepines (lorazepam, diazepam) — reduce central sympathetic outflow, lowering heart rate, blood pressure and agitation
  • Aspirin and nitroglycerin (coronary vasodilation)
  • Calcium channel blocker or phentolamine for persistent hypertension or vasospasm

Avoid beta-blockers during acute intoxication: blocking β₂ vasodilation leaves alpha stimulation unopposed, which can worsen coronary vasospasm and hypertension. (The 2025 ACS guideline still advises against them in patients with signs of acute intoxication; once the intoxication resolves, beta-blockers can be used for usual indications.)

Why not the others

  • (A) Fibrinolytic therapy — Fibrinolysis is not indicated without ST elevation, and severe hypertension raises the risk of intracranial hemorrhage.
  • (B) Intravenous haloperidol — Haloperidol lowers the seizure threshold, impairs heat dissipation and can prolong the QT; benzodiazepines are preferred for agitation in stimulant toxicity.
  • (D) Intravenous metoprolol — Beta-blockers during acute cocaine intoxication may cause unopposed alpha-adrenergic vasoconstriction.
  • (E) Physostigmine — Physostigmine reverses anticholinergic toxicity, not sympathomimetic toxicity.
🎯 Educational objective

Treat cocaine-associated chest pain with benzodiazepines, aspirin and nitrates; avoid beta-blockers during acute intoxication.

CV-091.stem_html:
A 46-year-old woman is evaluated for recurrent episodes of chest pressure that wake her between 4 and 6 AM and last 5 to 15 minutes. The episodes are not related to exertion; she exercises daily without symptoms. She smokes one pack of cigarettes daily and has migraine headaches and Raynaud phenomenon. She takes sumatriptan as needed.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 124/78 mm Hg and pulse rate is 72/min. Examination is normal.

During an episode recorded on an ambulatory monitor, the electrocardiogram showed transient 2-mm ST-segment elevation in the inferior leads that resolved completely when the pain stopped. Coronary angiography showed no obstructive coronary artery disease; intracoronary acetylcholine reproduced her pain with severe focal spasm of the right coronary artery.
CV-091.lead: In addition to smoking cessation, which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

choices.D: PCI of the right coronary artery

CV-091.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Vasospastic angina

Vasospastic (Prinzmetal, variant) angina causes angina at rest, often early morning, with transient ST elevation, normal or nonobstructive coronaries, and spasm provoked by acetylcholine or ergonovine. It is associated with smoking, migraine, Raynaud phenomenon, cocaine and triptans.

Treatment:

  • Calcium channel blockers (diltiazem, verapamil, amlodipine, nifedipine) — first-line, often at bedtime; prevent spasm in about 90%
  • Long-acting nitrates as add-on; sublingual nitroglycerin for attacks
  • Stop smoking; avoid triggers (triptans, cocaine, amphetamines, ergots)
  • Avoid nonselective beta-blockers: unopposed alpha-mediated vasoconstriction can worsen spasm

Why not the others

  • (A) Clopidogrel — Antiplatelet therapy treats atherosclerotic plaque, not vasomotor spasm.
  • (C) Metoprolol — Beta-blockers can aggravate coronary spasm by leaving alpha-adrenergic tone unopposed.
  • (D) PCI of the right coronary artery — There is no fixed stenosis to stent; spasm resolves without intervention.
  • (E) Ranolazine — Ranolazine treats demand ischemia from fixed disease and has no proven role in vasospasm.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Ask about triptans in any patient with vasospastic angina — this patient's sumatriptan should be stopped.

🎯 Educational objective

Treat vasospastic angina with calcium channel blockers and nitrates, eliminate triggers such as smoking and triptans, and avoid beta-blockers.

CV-092.topic: DAPT after PCI with high bleeding risk
CV-092.stem_html:
An 80-year-old man is being discharged after a non–ST-elevation myocardial infarction treated with a drug-eluting stent in the circumflex artery. One year ago he was hospitalized for a bleeding duodenal ulcer requiring transfusion. He has chronic kidney disease and hypertension. He is not taking an anticoagulant.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 126/72 mm Hg and pulse rate is 64/min. Examination is unremarkable.

Hemoglobin10.8 g/dL
Platelet count168000/µL
Estimated glomerular filtration rate28 mL/min/1.73 m²
CV-092.lead: In addition to a proton pump inhibitor, which of the following is the most appropriate antiplatelet regimen?

choices.B: Aspirin plus clopidogrel for 1 month, then clopidogrel alone

CV-092.explain_html:
Correct answer: B DAPT after PCI with high bleeding risk

He is at high bleeding risk (HBR) by Academic Research Consortium criteria: age ≥75, prior major GI bleeding requiring transfusion, anemia (Hb <11 g/dL) and eGFR <30.

The default after ACS is 12 months of DAPT, but in high-bleeding-risk patients the 2025 ACC/AHA ACS guideline supports shortening DAPT to 1–3 months, then continuing P2Y12 inhibitor monotherapy (MASTER DAPT, STOPDAPT-2 ACS, TWILIGHT). Clopidogrel is preferred over potent agents because it causes less bleeding. Modern stents make short DAPT safe.

Patient DAPT strategy after PCI for ACS
Not high bleeding risk Aspirin + ticagrelor or prasugrel × 12 months (option to drop aspirin after ≥1 month)
High bleeding risk 1–3 months DAPT → P2Y12 monotherapy (clopidogrel)
Needs oral anticoagulation OAC + clopidogrel; aspirin ≤1–4 weeks

Why not the others

  • (A) Aspirin alone starting at discharge — Aspirin alone immediately after a new stent increases the risk of stent thrombosis.
  • (C) Aspirin plus prasugrel for 12 months — Prasugrel is not recommended for patients ≥75 years (more bleeding, no net benefit) and 12 months of potent DAPT is excessive here.
  • (D) Aspirin plus ticagrelor for 12 months — Twelve months of aspirin plus ticagrelor causes substantially more bleeding in a high-bleeding-risk patient.
  • (E) Aspirin plus ticagrelor indefinitely — Indefinite potent DAPT is for selected low-bleeding-risk patients with very high ischemic risk, not for him.
🎯 Educational objective

In patients at high bleeding risk after PCI for ACS, shorten DAPT to 1–3 months followed by P2Y12 inhibitor monotherapy, preferably clopidogrel.

CV-093.stem_html:
A 62-year-old man is evaluated for 2 months of substernal chest tightness when he walks briskly uphill, relieved within 3 minutes by rest. He has hypertension and hyperlipidemia. Medications are aspirin, atorvastatin, 80 mg daily, and lisinopril. He has no asthma.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 136/82 mm Hg and pulse rate is 84/min. Examination is normal.

Resting electrocardiogram is normal. Stress echocardiography shows inducible hypokinesis of the inferior wall at a high workload, with normal resting function and no high-risk features.
CV-093.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
CV-093.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Chronic stable angina — first antianginal

He has chronic stable angina with low-to-intermediate-risk ischemia at a high workload, already on aspirin, high-intensity statin and an ACE inhibitor.

The 2023 AHA/ACC chronic coronary disease guideline recommends beta-blockers or calcium channel blockers as first-line antianginal therapy. A beta-blocker is a natural choice here: his resting heart rate of 84/min leaves room to lower demand. Titrate to a resting rate of about 55–60/min. Long-acting nitrates and ranolazine are add-ons when symptoms persist.

Revascularization is reserved for symptoms refractory to medical therapy or high-risk anatomy — it relieves angina but, in stable disease, does not reduce death or MI (ISCHEMIA).

Everyone also gets: sublingual nitroglycerin, risk-factor control, exercise and cardiac rehabilitation where available.

Why not the others

  • (A) Coronary angiography with PCI — With low-to-intermediate risk ischemia and no medical therapy for angina yet, angiography and PCI are not first-line.
  • (B) Isosorbide mononitrate — Long-acting nitrates are second-line and require a nitrate-free interval to avoid tolerance.
  • (C) Ivabradine — Ivabradine is used in HFrEF with sinus rhythm and a high resting rate; it is not a first-line antianginal in the United States.
  • (E) Ranolazine — Ranolazine is an add-on for persistent angina despite first-line agents.
🎯 Educational objective

Start a beta-blocker or calcium channel blocker as first-line antianginal therapy in chronic stable angina; add nitrates or ranolazine for persistent symptoms.

CV-094.topic: Revascularization vs medical therapy in stable CAD
CV-094.stem_html:
A 66-year-old man with chronic stable angina asks whether he should undergo coronary angiography and stenting. He has angina about twice a week with heavy exertion despite metoprolol and amlodipine. He takes aspirin and rosuvastatin. He has type 2 diabetes mellitus with HbA₁c of 7.0%.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 124/74 mm Hg and pulse rate is 58/min. Examination is normal.

Stress myocardial perfusion imaging shows moderate inducible ischemia (12% of the myocardium) in the right coronary territory. Left ventricular ejection fraction is 58%. Coronary CT angiography shows no left main stenosis.
CV-094.lead: Compared with continued optimal medical therapy, a routine invasive strategy with revascularization is most likely to provide which of the following benefits?

choices.E: Lower risk of myocardial infarction over 4 years

CV-094.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Revascularization vs medical therapy in stable CAD

The ISCHEMIA trial randomized more than 5,000 patients with stable coronary disease and moderate-to-severe ischemia (excluding left main disease, low EF and recent ACS) to a routine invasive strategy or optimal medical therapy. Over about 3–4 years:

  • No reduction in cardiovascular death, MI, resuscitated arrest or hospitalization for unstable angina or heart failure
  • No reduction in all-cause mortality
  • Better angina control and quality of life with the invasive strategy, especially in patients with frequent angina

So the decision rests mainly on symptoms and patient preference — revascularization is reasonable for angina limiting his life despite medicines. It is recommended to improve survival only in selected anatomy (significant left main disease, multivessel disease with reduced EF; and CABG for multivessel disease with diabetes).

Why not the others

  • (A) Fewer heart failure hospitalizations — Heart failure hospitalization was not reduced in patients with preserved ejection fraction.
  • (B) Fewer strokes — Revascularization does not reduce stroke; CABG carries a periprocedural stroke risk.
  • (D) Lower all-cause mortality — All-cause mortality was similar between strategies in ISCHEMIA.
  • (E) Lower risk of myocardial infarction over 4 years — Over the follow-up period, MI rates were not reduced overall; procedural MIs early offset fewer spontaneous MIs later.
🎯 Educational objective

In stable coronary disease with moderate-to-severe ischemia but no left main disease, routine revascularization improves angina and quality of life but does not reduce death or MI compared with optimal medical therapy.

CV-095.topic: Stress testing with left bundle branch block
CV-095.stem_html:
A 72-year-old woman is evaluated for 3 months of exertional dyspnea and occasional chest heaviness when climbing two flights of stairs. She has hypertension and hyperlipidemia. She walks 2 miles daily. Medications are losartan and rosuvastatin.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 138/80 mm Hg and pulse rate is 72/min. Examination is normal.

Resting electrocardiogram shows sinus rhythm with left bundle branch block, unchanged from 2 years ago. A coronary artery calcium score obtained 1 year ago was 920 Agatston units. Echocardiogram shows normal left ventricular function and no valve disease.
CV-095.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnostic test?
CV-095.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Stress testing with left bundle branch block

She has symptoms suggestive of stable ischemic heart disease and needs a functional test. Two details steer the choice:

  1. Left bundle branch block makes the exercise ECG uninterpretable (ST changes are always abnormal). With exercise perfusion imaging, LBBB causes false-positive septal perfusion defects, because septal relaxation is delayed and septal flow falls at high heart rates. Vasodilator stress (regadenoson, adenosine, dipyridamole) does not raise the heart rate much and avoids this artifact. Pacing creates the same problem.
  2. Heavy coronary calcium (CAC >400) blooms on CT and makes stenosis grading inaccurate, so stress imaging is preferred over CCTA.
Baseline problem Best stress test
Normal ECG, can exercise Exercise ECG (or stress imaging)
LBBB or ventricular pacing Vasodilator perfusion imaging (or dobutamine echo)
Digoxin, LVH with strain, WPW, ST depression ≥1 mm Exercise imaging
Cannot exercise Pharmacologic stress (vasodilator MPI or dobutamine echo)

Why not the others

  • (A) Coronary CT angiography — Extensive calcification limits CCTA's ability to grade stenoses; a functional test is preferred.
  • (B) Exercise electrocardiographic stress test — LBBB makes ST-segment interpretation impossible.
  • (C) Exercise SPECT myocardial perfusion imaging — Exercise perfusion imaging with LBBB often shows false septal defects.
  • (D) Invasive coronary angiography — Invasive angiography is reserved for high-risk noninvasive findings or refractory symptoms.
🎯 Educational objective

In patients with LBBB or ventricular pacing, use vasodilator myocardial perfusion imaging (not exercise imaging) to avoid false-positive septal defects.

CV-096.stem_html:
A 45-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of 30 minutes of left-sided chest discomfort that started 5 hours ago while he was sitting at work and resolved on its own. He has no shortness of breath, diaphoresis or syncope. He has no known heart disease, does not smoke and takes no medications. His father had a myocardial infarction at age 72.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 128/80 mm Hg, pulse rate is 70/min, and respiration rate is 14/min. Examination is normal.

Electrocardiogram is normal. Chest radiograph is normal.

High-sensitivity troponin T (arrival)<5 ng/L (limit of detection 5 ng/L)
CV-096.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Coronary CT angiography in the emergency department

CV-096.explain_html:
Correct answer: B High-sensitivity troponin rapid rule-out

High-sensitivity troponin assays allow rapid rule-out of myocardial infarction. A single hs-troponin below the limit of detection in a patient whose symptoms began more than 3 hours before the blood draw, with a nonischemic ECG, has a negative predictive value above 99.5% for MI and identifies a low-risk patient (2021 AHA/ACC chest pain guideline).

His 30-day risk of death or MI is <1%. Low-risk patients need no further urgent testing — admission or stress testing adds cost and false positives without benefit. Arrange outpatient follow-up and risk-factor assessment.

:::flow Q: hs-troponin at arrival below limit of detection and symptoms >3 h ago, normal ECG? Y: MI ruled out → low risk → discharge N: Repeat at 1–3 h per assay algorithm (0/1-h or 0/2-h); delta decides rule-in, observe or rule-out :::

Why not the others

  • (A) Coronary CT angiography in the emergency department — Coronary CT angiography is reasonable for intermediate-risk patients; it is not needed after a low-risk rule-out.
  • (C) Hospital admission for stress testing — Admission for stress testing in a low-risk patient does not improve outcomes.
  • (D) Invasive coronary angiography — Invasive angiography is for confirmed ACS or high-risk features.
  • (E) Repeat high-sensitivity troponin in 6 hours — The single undetectable value with symptom onset >3 hours earlier is sufficient; serial testing is required only if symptoms began within 3 hours or the value is detectable.
🎯 Educational objective

A single high-sensitivity troponin below the limit of detection more than 3 hours after symptom onset, with a nonischemic ECG, rules out MI and identifies a low-risk patient who can be discharged.

CV-097.stem_html:
A 76-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of 2 days of black stools and lightheadedness. Since this morning she has had chest pressure at rest. She has osteoarthritis and takes naproxen daily. She has no history of coronary artery disease.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 98/60 mm Hg, pulse rate is 118/min, and respiration rate is 20/min. Conjunctivae are pale. Rectal examination shows black, tarry stool.

Electrocardiogram shows sinus tachycardia with 1-mm horizontal ST-segment depression in leads V4 through V6, II and aVF, without ST-segment elevation.

Hemoglobin6.6 g/dL (baseline 12.8 g/dL)
Blood urea nitrogen52 mg/dL
Creatinine1.0 mg/dL
High-sensitivity troponin I64 ng/Lrising to 182 ng/L at 3 hours (reference <20)
CV-097.lead: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
CV-097.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Type 2 myocardial infarction

The Fourth Universal Definition of MI separates:

  • Type 1 MI — atherosclerotic plaque rupture or erosion with thrombus
  • Type 2 MI — supply–demand mismatch without acute plaque disruption: anemia, hypotension, tachyarrhythmia, hypoxemia, severe hypertension, coronary spasm
  • Myocardial injury — troponin rise without ischemic symptoms or signs (sepsis, CKD, PE, myocarditis); called acute if rising or falling

She has ischemic symptoms, ischemic ECG changes and a rising troponin caused by acute blood loss anemia and tachycardia from an NSAID-related upper GI bleed — a type 2 MI.

Treat the cause: transfuse (a restrictive threshold is less safe in MI; many target Hb ≥8–10 g/dL — MINT trial suggested a liberal strategy may be better), stop the NSAID, proton pump inhibitor, endoscopy. Do not give antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy for a type 2 MI caused by bleeding. Evaluate for underlying CAD once stable.

Why not the others

  • (A) Acute aortic dissection — She has no tearing back pain, pulse deficit or mediastinal widening, and her drop in hemoglobin explains the ischemia.
  • (B) Nonischemic myocardial injury — Nonischemic injury applies when troponin rises without ischemic symptoms or ECG changes; she has both.
  • (C) Stress (takotsubo) cardiomyopathy — Takotsubo follows an emotional or physical stressor with a typical wall-motion pattern; this is better explained by anemia and tachycardia.
  • (D) Type 1 non–ST-elevation myocardial infarction — Type 1 MI involves plaque rupture; ischemia here is explained by a demand–supply mismatch, and antithrombotic treatment would be harmful.
🎯 Educational objective

Recognize type 2 myocardial infarction (supply–demand mismatch, e.g., acute anemia) and treat the precipitating cause rather than with antithrombotic therapy.

CV-098.stem_html:
A 61-year-old man comes for a follow-up visit 3 weeks after a non–ST-elevation myocardial infarction treated with a drug-eluting stent. He has had no chest pain since discharge. He used to golf but is afraid that exercise will cause another heart attack, and he has gained 2 kg (4.4 lb) since discharge. Medications are aspirin, ticagrelor, metoprolol succinate, lisinopril and atorvastatin, 80 mg daily. He quit smoking in the hospital.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 124/76 mm Hg and pulse rate is 62/min. BMI is 31 kg/m². Examination is otherwise normal. Echocardiogram before discharge showed left ventricular ejection fraction of 55%.
CV-098.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to reduce his risk of future cardiovascular events?

choices.A: Advise him to avoid exercise for 3 months
choices.B: Begin an unsupervised running program at home
choices.C: Obtain a coronary CT angiogram before any exercise
choices.D: Prescribe a benzodiazepine for exercise-related anxiety
choices.E: Refer him to a cardiac rehabilitation program

CV-098.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Cardiac rehabilitation after MI

Cardiac rehabilitation is a Class 1 recommendation after ACS, PCI, CABG, stable angina, HFrEF and valve surgery. A comprehensive program includes supervised exercise training, risk-factor management (lipids, BP, diabetes, weight), smoking cessation support, nutrition counseling and psychosocial care (depression and anxiety are common after MI).

Participation reduces cardiovascular mortality and rehospitalization and improves exercise capacity and quality of life — yet fewer than a third of eligible patients enroll. Physician referral is the strongest predictor of participation. Home-based or hybrid programs are acceptable alternatives when center-based programs are not accessible.

Why not the others

  • (A) Advise him to avoid exercise for 3 months — Prolonged inactivity after MI worsens deconditioning and risk; supervised exercise is safe and beneficial.
  • (B) Begin an unsupervised running program at home — A sudden unsupervised high-intensity program in a fearful, deconditioned patient lacks the individualized prescription, monitoring and education that rehabilitation provides.
  • (C) Obtain a coronary CT angiogram before any exercise — Routine imaging after successful revascularization in an asymptomatic patient is not indicated.
  • (D) Prescribe a benzodiazepine for exercise-related anxiety — Benzodiazepines do not address deconditioning or risk; anxiety is better addressed through rehabilitation's psychosocial support and, if needed, therapy or an SSRI.
🎯 Educational objective

Refer all eligible patients to cardiac rehabilitation after myocardial infarction; it reduces mortality and rehospitalization.

CV-099.stem_html:
A 56-year-old woman is evaluated for 1 year of exertional chest pressure and dyspnea that limit her daily walks and sometimes last 20 minutes after she stops. Nitroglycerin gives only partial relief. She has hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. Medications are losartan, metformin, aspirin and atorvastatin.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 132/80 mm Hg and pulse rate is 76/min. Examination is normal.

Exercise stress echocardiography reproduced her symptoms with 2-mm ST-segment depression but no wall-motion abnormality. Invasive coronary angiography showed mild luminal irregularities without stenosis greater than 30%. Echocardiogram shows normal ventricular function, normal valves and no left ventricular hypertrophy.
CV-099.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next diagnostic step?

choices.D: Reassurance that her symptoms are not cardiac

CV-099.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Ischemia with nonobstructive coronary arteries

She has ischemia with no obstructive coronary arteries (INOCA): angina, objective evidence of ischemia and no stenosis ≥50%. INOCA is common, especially in women, and is not benign — it carries higher rates of MI, heart failure and poor quality of life.

The main mechanisms are:

  • Coronary microvascular dysfunction — impaired vasodilation of small vessels (low coronary flow reserve <2.0–2.5, high index of microcirculatory resistance)
  • Epicardial or microvascular vasospasm

Invasive coronary function testing (adenosine for flow reserve and resistance; acetylcholine for spasm) defines the endotype and directs therapy — the CorMicA trial showed that stratified therapy improved angina. PET myocardial blood flow quantification is a noninvasive alternative.

Endotype Treatment
Microvascular dysfunction Beta-blocker, ACE inhibitor/ARB, statin, ranolazine
Vasospasm Calcium channel blocker, nitrate

Why not the others

  • (A) Coronary CT angiography — She already had invasive angiography that excluded obstructive disease; CCTA would add no functional information.
  • (B) Esophageal manometry — Esophageal testing might be considered if cardiac causes are excluded, but she has objective ischemia.
  • (D) Reassurance that her symptoms are not cardiac — Objective ischemia with typical symptoms is a cardiac problem; reassurance alone leaves treatable disease untreated.
  • (E) Repeat coronary angiography in 6 months — Repeat anatomic imaging does not assess microvascular function or spasm.
🎯 Educational objective

Evaluate ischemia with nonobstructive coronary arteries with coronary function testing (flow reserve, microvascular resistance, acetylcholine provocation) to guide therapy.

CV-100.topic: Acute chest pain — coronary CT angiography
CV-100.stem_html:
A 48-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of 2 hours of intermittent substernal chest pressure that began while he was walking his dog. The pressure lasts several minutes and resolves with rest. He has hypertension and hyperlipidemia and smokes cigarettes. Medications are lisinopril and simvastatin. He has never had a cardiac evaluation.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 142/86 mm Hg and pulse rate is 78/min. Examination is normal.

Electrocardiogram shows no ischemic changes. High-sensitivity troponin I measurements at 0 and 2 hours are both below the 99th percentile without a significant change. He is now pain-free. His HEART score is 5 (intermediate risk).
CV-100.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in evaluation?
CV-100.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Acute chest pain — coronary CT angiography

Acute MI has been ruled out by serial hs-troponin, but his symptoms are typical and he has several risk factors — he is intermediate risk (HEART score 4–6). The 2021 AHA/ACC chest pain guideline recommends further testing for intermediate-risk patients without known CAD:

  • Coronary CT angiography (CCTA) — excellent negative predictive value; finds nonobstructive plaque that should change prevention (statin intensity, aspirin); it can be done before discharge or within days
  • Stress testing with imaging is an alternative

CCTA is preferred for patients <65 years who are not on optimal preventive therapy; stress imaging is preferred for known CAD or extensive calcification.

Why not the others

  • (A) Coronary artery calcium scoring — Calcium scoring alone is for asymptomatic risk assessment and does not detect noncalcified plaque or stenosis in a symptomatic patient.
  • (C) Discharge home without further testing — Intermediate-risk patients with typical symptoms benefit from further evaluation; discharge without testing is appropriate only for low-risk patients.
  • (D) Invasive coronary angiography — Invasive angiography is for high-risk patients or confirmed ACS; noninvasive testing comes first here.
  • (E) Repeat troponin measurement in 24 hours — Serial troponins have already excluded MI; more measurements add nothing.
🎯 Educational objective

In intermediate-risk patients with acute chest pain, no known CAD and MI excluded, coronary CT angiography is an appropriate next test.

CV-101.stem_html:
A 64-year-old man with chronic stable angina comes to the emergency department because of chest pressure that began 30 minutes ago. He took sildenafil 6 hours ago. He is given sublingual nitroglycerin, 0.4 mg, before this history is obtained.

Within 10 minutes, he becomes lightheaded. Blood pressure falls from 138/82 mm Hg to 72/40 mm Hg, and pulse rate rises from 84/min to 118/min.
CV-101.lead: Which of the following best explains the hypotension?

choices.A: Alpha-1 adrenergic receptor blockade in vascular smooth muscle
choices.B: Beta-adrenergic receptor blockade in the myocardium
choices.E: Synergistic increase in cyclic GMP in vascular smooth muscle

CV-101.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Nitrate–PDE-5 inhibitor interaction

Nitrates release nitric oxide (NO), which activates soluble guanylate cyclase and raises cyclic GMP (cGMP) in vascular smooth muscle → relaxation (venodilation more than arteriolar dilation).

Phosphodiesterase-5 (PDE-5) inhibitors (sildenafil, vardenafil, tadalafil, avanafil) block the breakdown of cGMP.

Together, one increases production and the other blocks degradation → profound, prolonged vasodilation and hypotension, which can cause syncope, MI and death. Nitrates are contraindicated within 24 hours of sildenafil or vardenafil and 48 hours of tadalafil.

Treatment of the interaction: supine position, IV fluids, and an alpha-agonist (phenylephrine) if needed.

Why not the others

  • (A) Alpha-1 adrenergic receptor blockade in vascular smooth muscle — Alpha-1 blockers (such as tamsulosin or doxazosin) also cause hypotension with PDE-5 inhibitors, but neither drug here acts by alpha blockade.
  • (B) Beta-adrenergic receptor blockade in the myocardium — Beta blockade causes bradycardia; his heart rate rose reflexively.
  • (C) Histamine release from mast cells — Histamine release causes flushing, urticaria and bronchospasm; it is not the mechanism of this interaction.
  • (D) Inhibition of the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system — RAAS inhibition lowers blood pressure gradually; it does not explain abrupt collapse after nitroglycerin.
🎯 Educational objective

Nitrates and PDE-5 inhibitors cause severe hypotension by synergistically increasing vascular smooth-muscle cGMP; avoid nitrates within 24–48 hours of a PDE-5 inhibitor.

CV-102.stem_html:
A 57-year-old man comes for a follow-up visit 1 week after discharge for a non–ST-elevation myocardial infarction treated with a drug-eluting stent in the left anterior descending artery. He has no bleeding or chest pain. He reports occasional mild dyspnea at rest that does not limit him. At discharge he was prescribed aspirin, 81 mg daily, and ticagrelor, 90 mg twice daily, but he has been taking aspirin, 325 mg daily, because he thought it would protect him more. Other medications are metoprolol succinate, lisinopril and atorvastatin.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 122/74 mm Hg and pulse rate is 64/min. Lungs are clear. Examination is normal.
CV-102.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate change in his antiplatelet regimen?

choices.A: Continue aspirin, 325 mg daily, with ticagrelor
choices.B: Reduce aspirin to 81 mg daily and continue ticagrelor
choices.C: Stop aspirin and continue ticagrelor alone
choices.D: Stop ticagrelor and continue aspirin, 325 mg daily
choices.E: Switch ticagrelor to prasugrel and continue aspirin, 325 mg daily

CV-102.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Aspirin dose with ticagrelor

With ticagrelor, aspirin must be 75–100 mg daily. In the PLATO trial, ticagrelor was less effective in North American patients, an effect explained by the higher aspirin doses used there (≥300 mg). High-dose aspirin may blunt ticagrelor's benefit and increases GI bleeding. The ticagrelor label carries a boxed warning about aspirin doses above 100 mg.

The mild dyspnea is a common, usually benign adverse effect of ticagrelor (adenosine-mediated); it is not a reason to stop the drug if mild and the lungs and examination are normal.

In patients without high bleeding risk, the 2025 ACS guideline allows dropping aspirin to ticagrelor monotherapy after at least 1 month of DAPT (TWILIGHT, TICO, ULTIMATE-DAPT) — but not 1 week after PCI.

Why not the others

  • (A) Continue aspirin, 325 mg daily, with ticagrelor — Aspirin doses above 100 mg with ticagrelor reduce its effectiveness and increase bleeding.
  • (C) Stop aspirin and continue ticagrelor alone — Dropping aspirin 1 week after PCI is too early; monotherapy is considered after at least 1 month.
  • (D) Stop ticagrelor and continue aspirin, 325 mg daily — Aspirin alone 1 week after a drug-eluting stent for ACS raises the risk of stent thrombosis and recurrent MI.
  • (E) Switch ticagrelor to prasugrel and continue aspirin, 325 mg daily — Changing P2Y12 inhibitors is not needed, and the aspirin dose would still be too high.
🧠 Mnemonic

Ticagrelor loves "baby aspirin" — 81, not 325.

🎯 Educational objective

Use aspirin 75–100 mg daily with ticagrelor; higher aspirin doses reduce ticagrelor's efficacy.

CV-103.stem_html:
A 71-year-old woman comes for an annual visit. She has hypertension and hyperlipidemia treated with amlodipine and atorvastatin. She has no history of myocardial infarction, stroke, peripheral artery disease or coronary revascularization. She does not smoke. Her neighbor told her to start taking a daily aspirin "for her heart," and she asks whether she should.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 128/76 mm Hg. Examination is normal.

LDL cholesterol82 mg/dL
Estimated glomerular filtration rate64 mL/min/1.73 m²
10-year ASCVD risk (PREVENT-ASCVD)9%
CV-103.lead: Compared with no aspirin, starting daily low-dose aspirin is most likely to have which of the following effects in this patient?

choices.A: A net reduction in all-cause mortality
choices.B: A reduction in cancer deaths within 5 years
choices.C: A reduction in ischemic stroke without an increase in bleeding
choices.D: A small reduction in nonfatal MI offset by more major bleeding

CV-103.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Aspirin for primary prevention

Contemporary trials of aspirin for primary prevention — ASPREE (age ≥70), ARRIVE (moderate risk) and ASCEND (diabetes) — showed that aspirin causes major bleeding (GI and intracranial) about as often as it prevents nonfatal ischemic events. In ASPREE, all-cause mortality was slightly higher with aspirin.

Current recommendations:

  • USPSTF 2022: do not start aspirin for primary prevention at age ≥60; for ages 40–59 with 10-year risk ≥10%, the decision is individual (small net benefit).
  • ACC/AHA: low-dose aspirin may be considered only in selected adults 40–70 at higher ASCVD risk and low bleeding risk; not routinely for adults >70.

Secondary prevention (after MI, stroke, revascularization or with PAD) is different — aspirin clearly helps there.

Why not the others

  • (A) A net reduction in all-cause mortality — Aspirin did not reduce all-cause mortality in primary prevention trials; ASPREE showed slightly higher mortality.
  • (B) A reduction in cancer deaths within 5 years — Long-term colorectal cancer benefit seen in older studies was not confirmed in ASPREE, which found more cancer deaths with aspirin in older adults.
  • (C) A reduction in ischemic stroke without an increase in bleeding — Aspirin increases major bleeding, including intracranial hemorrhage.
  • (E) No effect on gastrointestinal bleeding — Gastrointestinal bleeding increases by about 50%–60% with daily aspirin.
🎓 ABIM pearl

The aspirin question on boards usually hinges on one word: primary (no established ASCVD → usually no) versus secondary (established ASCVD → yes).

🎯 Educational objective

In older adults without ASCVD, aspirin for primary prevention increases major bleeding about as much as it reduces nonfatal ischemic events and should not be started routinely at age ≥60–70.

CV-104.stem_html:
A 66-year-old woman comes for follow-up 1 year after a myocardial infarction treated with a drug-eluting stent. She developed disabling thigh and shoulder myalgia with atorvastatin, 40 mg, then with rosuvastatin, 5 mg, and finally with pravastatin, 10 mg every other day; symptoms resolved within 2 weeks of stopping each drug and recurred on rechallenge. Creatine kinase was normal each time. She takes aspirin, metoprolol, lisinopril and ezetimibe. She declines injectable medications.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 122/72 mm Hg. Examination is normal.

LDL cholesterol128 mg/dL (on ezetimibe)
Thyroid-stimulating hormone2.0 µU/mL
ALT22 U/L
CV-104.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate addition to her therapy?
CV-104.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Statin intolerance with ASCVD

She has statin intolerance: symptoms with three statins, including a low-intensity dose, that resolve on stopping and recur on rechallenge, with no hypothyroidism or other cause. She has very-high-risk ASCVD, and her LDL is far above the 2026 ACC/AHA goal of <55 mg/dL despite ezetimibe.

Bempedoic acid inhibits ATP-citrate lyase, upstream of HMG-CoA reductase. It is a prodrug activated only in the liver (not skeletal muscle), so it rarely causes myalgia. In CLEAR Outcomes (statin-intolerant patients), it lowered LDL by about 21% and reduced major adverse cardiovascular events by 13%. It comes alone or combined with ezetimibe.

If she later accepts injections, a PCSK9 monoclonal antibody (evolocumab, alirocumab) lowers LDL by about 60% and has outcome data.

Adverse effects of bempedoic acid: higher uric acid (gout), small rise in creatinine, tendon rupture (rare), cholelithiasis.

Why not the others

  • (B) Coenzyme Q10 — Coenzyme Q10 has not been shown to prevent or treat statin-associated muscle symptoms or to lower LDL.
  • (C) Fenofibrate — Fenofibrate lowers triglycerides and has not reduced cardiovascular events in statin-era trials; it does little for LDL.
  • (D) Niacin — Niacin causes flushing and hyperglycemia and failed to reduce events when added to LDL-lowering therapy (AIM-HIGH, HPS2-THRIVE).
  • (E) Over-the-counter fish oil — Over-the-counter fish oil does not lower LDL or cardiovascular events.
🎯 Educational objective

In statin-intolerant patients with ASCVD above their LDL goal, add bempedoic acid (oral) or a PCSK9 monoclonal antibody, both of which reduce cardiovascular events.

A 48-year-old man comes for follow-up of lipid results. He has type 2 diabetes mellitus and drinks 4 to 6 beers daily. He has no abdominal pain. Medications are metformin and atorvastatin, 20 mg daily.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 134/84 mm Hg. BMI is 32 kg/m². There are eruptive yellow papules on the buttocks and extensor surfaces of the arms. The abdomen is nontender. Fundoscopic examination shows creamy-white retinal vessels.

Triglycerides (fasting)2140 mg/dL
Total cholesterol412 mg/dL
Hemoglobin A₁c9.6%
Lipase38 U/L (normal)
Thyroid-stimulating hormone2.1 µU/mL
Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio18 mg/g
CV-105.lead: In addition to stopping alcohol, a very-low-fat diet and improving glycemic control, which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
CV-105.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Severe hypertriglyceridemia

Triglycerides ≥1,000 mg/dL (some sources use ≥500–880) put him at high risk of acute pancreatitis. He shows signs of chylomicronemia: eruptive xanthomas and lipemia retinalis.

Priorities:

  1. Remove secondary causes: alcohol, uncontrolled diabetes (insulin lowers triglycerides quickly), estrogen, thiazides, beta-blockers, glucocorticoids, retinoids, protease inhibitors, hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome
  2. Very-low-fat diet (<15% of calories when chylomicronemic)
  3. A fibrate — fenofibrate lowers triglycerides by 30%–50% (PPAR-α agonist: more lipoprotein lipase activity)
  4. High-dose prescription omega-3 fatty acids as an additional option

Once triglycerides fall below about 500 mg/dL, focus returns to ASCVD risk (statin, LDL and non-HDL goals). Statins remain the foundation for long-term risk reduction.

Why not the others

  • (A) Ezetimibe — Ezetimibe lowers LDL, with little effect on triglycerides at this level.
  • (C) Gemfibrozil — Gemfibrozil with a statin markedly increases the risk of rhabdomyolysis (it inhibits statin glucuronidation); fenofibrate is the fibrate to combine with a statin.
  • (D) Increase atorvastatin to 80 mg daily — Higher-dose statins lower triglycerides by only 20%–30%, not enough to prevent pancreatitis at this level.
  • (E) Niacin — Niacin worsens glycemic control and has no outcome benefit.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Severe hypertriglyceridemia falsely lowers measured sodium (pseudohyponatremia with some methods) and can make amylase unreliable — order lipase when you suspect pancreatitis.

🎯 Educational objective

Treat triglycerides ≥1,000 mg/dL with removal of secondary causes, a very-low-fat diet and fenofibrate to prevent pancreatitis.

CV-106.stem_html:
A 62-year-old man with coronary artery disease comes for a routine visit. He had a myocardial infarction 3 years ago. He follows a Mediterranean diet, exercises 150 minutes per week and does not drink alcohol. Medications are aspirin, metoprolol, lisinopril, atorvastatin, 80 mg daily, and ezetimibe.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 124/74 mm Hg. BMI is 28 kg/m². Examination is normal.

LDL cholesterol52 mg/dL
Triglycerides (fasting)238 mg/dL
HDL cholesterol38 mg/dL
Hemoglobin A₁c5.8%
Thyroid-stimulating hormone1.8 µU/mL
CV-106.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate addition to his therapy to reduce cardiovascular events?
CV-106.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Icosapent ethyl

His LDL is at goal (<55 mg/dL) on a high-intensity statin plus ezetimibe, but he has persistent hypertriglyceridemia (150–499 mg/dL), a marker of residual risk from triglyceride-rich lipoproteins.

Icosapent ethyl (purified EPA ethyl ester, 2 g twice daily) reduced major adverse cardiovascular events by 25% in REDUCE-IT, in statin-treated patients with ASCVD (or diabetes plus risk factors) and triglycerides 135–499 mg/dL. Watch for atrial fibrillation and bleeding, both slightly increased.

Other triglyceride-lowering drugs have not reduced events on top of statins:

  • Mixed EPA + DHA (STRENGTH, OMEMI) — no benefit
  • Fenofibrate (ACCORD-Lipid) and pemafibrate (PROMINENT) — no benefit
  • Niacin (AIM-HIGH, HPS2-THRIVE) — no benefit, more harm
  • Dietary-supplement fish oil — unregulated, low doses, no outcome data

Why not the others

  • (A) Fenofibrate — Fibrates lower triglycerides but did not reduce cardiovascular events in statin-treated patients.
  • (C) Niacin — Niacin did not reduce events when added to a statin and increased adverse effects.
  • (D) Omega-3 carboxylic acids (EPA plus DHA) — EPA + DHA combinations did not reduce events in STRENGTH, despite lowering triglycerides.
  • (E) Over-the-counter fish oil capsules — Supplement-grade fish oil provides low, variable doses without proven benefit.
🎯 Educational objective

In statin-treated patients with ASCVD and triglycerides 150–499 mg/dL, icosapent ethyl reduces cardiovascular events; other triglyceride-lowering drugs do not.

CV-107.stem_html:
A 42-year-old man asks about his heart disease risk. His father had a myocardial infarction at age 49, and his paternal uncle had coronary bypass surgery at age 52. He does not smoke, exercises regularly and has no hypertension or diabetes. He takes no medications.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg. BMI is 24 kg/m². Examination is normal; there are no xanthomas.

Total cholesterol196 mg/dL
LDL cholesterol118 mg/dL
HDL cholesterol52 mg/dL
Triglycerides130 mg/dL
10-year ASCVD risk (PREVENT-ASCVD)1.6%
CV-107.lead: Which of the following laboratory tests is most appropriate to refine his cardiovascular risk?
CV-107.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Lipoprotein(a)

Lipoprotein(a) is an LDL-like particle with an attached apolipoprotein(a). It is atherogenic, proinflammatory and prothrombotic, and an independent, causal risk factor for MI, stroke and calcific aortic stenosis. Levels are about 90% genetically determined, stable through life and barely changed by diet or exercise.

The 2026 ACC/AHA dyslipidemia guideline recommends measuring Lp(a) at least once in every adult — and it is especially useful in people with a family history of premature ASCVD and otherwise unremarkable risk factors, as here. A level ≥50 mg/dL (≥125 nmol/L) is a risk enhancer that favors earlier and more intensive LDL lowering. About 20% of people have elevated Lp(a).

Specific Lp(a)-lowering drugs (antisense and siRNA agents such as pelacarsen, olpasiran, lepodisiran) are in outcome trials. PCSK9 antibodies lower Lp(a) by about 25%; statins do not lower it.

Why not the others

  • (A) Apolipoprotein E genotype — APOE genotyping is not used for cardiovascular risk assessment in clinical practice.
  • (B) Fasting insulin level — Fasting insulin is not a recommended cardiovascular risk marker.
  • (C) Homocysteine level — Lowering homocysteine with B vitamins did not reduce cardiovascular events, so measuring it does not change management.
  • (E) Serum uric acid — Uric acid is not a recommended tool for refining ASCVD risk.
🎓 ABIM pearl

A patient with premature ASCVD and "normal" lipids — or with a family history like this — should have Lp(a) checked. Elevated Lp(a) also justifies cascade testing of relatives.

🎯 Educational objective

Measure lipoprotein(a) at least once in adulthood, especially with a family history of premature ASCVD; an elevated level is a risk enhancer.

CV-108.stem_html:
A 68-year-old woman is evaluated for 2 months of diffuse muscle aching and stiffness in her thighs and shoulders, with fatigue, constipation and a 3-kg (6.6-lb) weight gain. She started atorvastatin, 40 mg daily, 8 months ago after a transient ischemic attack and initially felt well. Other medications are aspirin and amlodipine.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 136/84 mm Hg and pulse rate is 56/min. Skin is dry. Muscle strength is normal, with mild tenderness of the proximal muscles. Ankle reflexes show delayed relaxation.

Creatine kinase420 U/L (reference 30–170)
ALT28 U/L
Creatinine0.9 mg/dL
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate14 mm/h
CV-108.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in evaluation?
CV-108.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Statin-associated muscle symptoms

Her muscle symptoms began months after a statin was started, but she also has fatigue, constipation, weight gain, bradycardia, dry skin and delayed relaxation of the ankle reflexes — features of hypothyroidism.

Hypothyroidism causes myalgia and a raised CK by itself, and it increases the risk of statin myopathy (reduced statin clearance). Guidelines recommend checking TSH in anyone with statin-associated muscle symptoms, along with CK, vitamin D status and interacting drugs (amlodipine and atorvastatin share CYP3A4 but the interaction is minor; diltiazem, verapamil, macrolides, azole antifungals, cyclosporine, gemfibrozil and grapefruit matter more).

Treating hypothyroidism often relieves symptoms and allows the statin to continue — important after a TIA.

CK Muscle symptoms on a statin
Normal Myalgia — stop, let resolve, rechallenge (different statin or lower dose)
<10× ULN Look for causes (TSH, exercise, drugs); temporary hold
>10× ULN Myositis/rhabdomyolysis → stop statin, check kidney function
Persistent weakness + high CK after stopping Anti-HMGCR immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy

Why not the others

  • (A) Electromyography — Electromyography is used to evaluate weakness and myopathy after common reversible causes are excluded; she has normal strength.
  • (B) Muscle biopsy — Biopsy is reserved for persistent weakness and high CK after the statin is stopped, suggesting inflammatory or necrotizing myopathy.
  • (C) Serum aldolase — Aldolase adds little to CK and does not identify the cause.
  • (D) Serum anti-HMG-CoA reductase antibodies — Anti-HMGCR antibodies are tested when weakness and a markedly elevated CK persist despite stopping the statin.
🎯 Educational objective

In patients with statin-associated muscle symptoms, check TSH because hypothyroidism causes myalgia and raises the risk of statin myopathy.

CV-109.stem_html:
A 52-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus diagnosed 2 years ago comes for a routine visit. She has no history of cardiovascular disease and does not smoke. She has no diabetic retinopathy, neuropathy or albuminuria. Medications are metformin and semaglutide.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 124/76 mm Hg. BMI is 31 kg/m². Examination is normal.

Hemoglobin A₁c6.8%
LDL cholesterol112 mg/dL
HDL cholesterol48 mg/dL
Triglycerides168 mg/dL
Estimated glomerular filtration rate88 mL/min/1.73 m²
Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio10 mg/g
CV-109.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate lipid management?

choices.B: Lifestyle changes alone, with repeat lipids in 5 years

CV-109.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Statin therapy in diabetes

Diabetes at age ≥40 is one of the conditions for which the 2026 ACC/AHA dyslipidemia guideline (like the ADA Standards of Care) recommends starting lipid-lowering therapy regardless of LDL level or calculated risk. A statin is first-line; at least moderate intensity, and high intensity when there are additional risk factors or diabetes-specific risk enhancers (long duration, albuminuria, eGFR <60, retinopathy, neuropathy, ankle-brachial index <0.9).

Rationale: diabetes multiplies ASCVD risk and the 10-year score underestimates lifetime risk. Statins reduce cardiovascular events in people with diabetes by about 20%–25% per 39 mg/dL LDL reduction (CTT meta-analysis), even with "normal" LDL.

The same "start at 40 regardless" rule now also applies to CKD stage ≥3 and HIV.

Why not the others

  • (A) Fenofibrate — Fenofibrate did not reduce cardiovascular events in diabetes on top of statins (ACCORD-Lipid, FIELD) and is used mainly for severe hypertriglyceridemia.
  • (B) Lifestyle changes alone, with repeat lipids in 5 years — Waiting 5 years leaves a high-risk patient untreated; lifestyle change is necessary but not sufficient.
  • (C) Omega-3 fatty acid supplement — Omega-3 supplements do not reduce cardiovascular events in primary prevention of diabetes (ASCEND, VITAL).
  • (E) Start ezetimibe alone — Ezetimibe is an add-on to statins, not first-line monotherapy, unless statins are not tolerated.
🎯 Educational objective

Start statin therapy in adults with diabetes aged 40 or older, regardless of LDL level; intensify with additional risk factors.

CV-110.stem_html: A 58-year-old man with prior coronary artery bypass grafting has an LDL cholesterol of 96 mg/dL despite atorvastatin, 80 mg daily, and ezetimibe. Evolocumab is started, and 8 weeks later his LDL cholesterol is 34 mg/dL.
CV-110.lead: Which of the following best explains the reduction in his LDL cholesterol?

choices.A: Activation of peroxisome proliferator–activated receptor alpha
choices.B: Blockade of intestinal cholesterol absorption by NPC1L1
choices.C: Increased recycling of hepatic LDL receptors to the cell surface
choices.D: Inhibition of ATP-citrate lyase in the liver
choices.E: Inhibition of microsomal triglyceride transfer protein

CV-110.explain_html:
Correct answer: C PCSK9 inhibitor mechanism

PCSK9 (proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9) is secreted by the liver and binds the LDL receptor. When the LDL receptor–LDL complex is internalized, bound PCSK9 directs the receptor to the lysosome for degradation instead of recycling to the cell surface.

Evolocumab and alirocumab (monoclonal antibodies) bind circulating PCSK9, so more LDL receptors recycle to the hepatocyte surface and clear LDL from the blood. LDL falls by about 60% on top of a statin; FOURIER and ODYSSEY OUTCOMES showed fewer cardiovascular events. Inclisiran (siRNA) blocks PCSK9 synthesis.

Statins add to the effect because they upregulate LDL-receptor synthesis (via SREBP-2) — but also upregulate PCSK9, which limits their own efficacy.

Drug Mechanism
Statins HMG-CoA reductase inhibition → more LDL receptors
PCSK9 antibodies / inclisiran Less LDL-receptor degradation
Ezetimibe NPC1L1 blockade → less intestinal absorption
Bempedoic acid ATP-citrate lyase inhibition (liver only)
Fibrates PPAR-α activation → more lipoprotein lipase
Lomitapide MTP inhibition (homozygous FH)

Why not the others

  • (A) Activation of peroxisome proliferator–activated receptor alpha — PPAR-α activation is the mechanism of fibrates, which mainly lower triglycerides.
  • (B) Blockade of intestinal cholesterol absorption by NPC1L1 — NPC1L1 blockade is the mechanism of ezetimibe.
  • (D) Inhibition of ATP-citrate lyase in the liver — ATP-citrate lyase inhibition is the mechanism of bempedoic acid.
  • (E) Inhibition of microsomal triglyceride transfer protein — MTP inhibition is the mechanism of lomitapide, used for homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia.
🎯 Educational objective

PCSK9 inhibitors lower LDL by preventing lysosomal degradation of hepatic LDL receptors, allowing more receptors to recycle to the cell surface.

CV-111.stem_html:
A 59-year-old man comes for follow-up 1 year after a myocardial infarction. He has tried supervised diet and exercise programs for 9 months, losing 2 kg (4.4 lb). He does not have diabetes. He has no history of pancreatitis or medullary thyroid carcinoma and no family history of multiple endocrine neoplasia. Medications are aspirin, metoprolol, lisinopril and atorvastatin, 80 mg daily.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 128/80 mm Hg. BMI is 34 kg/m². Examination is otherwise normal.

Hemoglobin A₁c5.9%
LDL cholesterol50 mg/dL
Estimated glomerular filtration rate82 mL/min/1.73 m²
CV-111.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate addition to reduce his risk of future cardiovascular events?
CV-111.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Obesity with established ASCVD

In SELECT, adults with established cardiovascular disease and overweight or obesity (BMI ≥27) without diabetes who received weekly semaglutide 2.4 mg had a 20% reduction in major adverse cardiovascular events (cardiovascular death, MI, stroke) over about 3 years, along with about 9% weight loss. The benefit appeared early and was partly independent of weight loss.

Semaglutide is now FDA-approved to reduce MACE in this population. Common adverse effects are GI (nausea, vomiting, constipation); avoid with a personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or MEN2, and use caution with prior pancreatitis or gallbladder disease.

Tirzepatide also produces large weight loss and is being studied for cardiovascular outcomes.

Why not the others

  • (A) Metformin — Metformin is not approved for obesity, causes little weight loss without diabetes, and has no proven cardiovascular benefit in this population.
  • (B) Orlistat — Orlistat causes modest weight loss with GI side effects and has no cardiovascular outcome benefit.
  • (C) Phentermine — Phentermine is a sympathomimetic that raises heart rate and blood pressure and is generally avoided in patients with cardiovascular disease.
  • (E) Topiramate — Topiramate alone is not an approved obesity treatment and has no cardiovascular outcome data.
🎯 Educational objective

In patients with established ASCVD and BMI ≥27 without diabetes, semaglutide reduces major adverse cardiovascular events.

CV-112.stem_html:
A 54-year-old man is hospitalized with a non–ST-elevation myocardial infarction treated with a drug-eluting stent. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 35 years and says he wants to quit; two previous attempts with nicotine gum failed within a week. He has no history of seizures, eating disorders or depression and does not drink alcohol.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 126/78 mm Hg and pulse rate is 68/min. Examination is normal.
CV-112.lead: In addition to counseling, which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy for smoking cessation?

choices.A: Avoid all pharmacotherapy until 3 months after the myocardial infarction
choices.B: Electronic cigarettes as the primary method
choices.C: Nicotine gum alone at a higher dose

CV-112.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Smoking cessation after ACS

Stopping smoking after MI reduces mortality by about a third — as much as any drug he will take. Smokers hospitalized with ACS should receive counseling plus pharmacotherapy started in the hospital, with follow-up for at least a month after discharge.

Varenicline (partial agonist at the α4β2 nicotinic receptor) is the most effective single agent. It is safe in stable cardiovascular disease — EAGLES and EVITA found no increase in cardiovascular events, and EAGLES found no excess of neuropsychiatric events.

Alternatives: combination nicotine replacement (patch plus a short-acting form such as gum or lozenge), which is more effective than a single NRT product and is safe after ACS; or bupropion. Varenicline plus a nicotine patch is more effective than varenicline alone.

Why not the others

  • (A) Avoid all pharmacotherapy until 3 months after the myocardial infarction — Delaying treatment loses the window of motivation created by the hospitalization; pharmacotherapy is safe early after ACS.
  • (B) Electronic cigarettes as the primary method — E-cigarettes are not FDA-approved cessation aids, and long-term cardiovascular safety is uncertain.
  • (C) Nicotine gum alone at a higher dose — A single short-acting nicotine product is less effective than varenicline or combination NRT, and it already failed.
  • (D) Nortriptyline — Nortriptyline is a second-line option with anticholinergic and arrhythmic adverse effects, undesirable after MI.
🎯 Educational objective

Start varenicline (or combination nicotine replacement) with counseling for smokers hospitalized with ACS; it is safe in cardiovascular disease.

CV-113.stem_html:
A 64-year-old man is ready for discharge after 5 days of treatment for newly diagnosed acute decompensated heart failure. Echocardiogram showed left ventricular ejection fraction of 25%; coronary angiography showed no significant coronary disease. With intravenous furosemide he lost 6 kg (13.2 lb) and is now euvolemic. Metoprolol succinate, 25 mg daily, was started yesterday. He takes oral furosemide, 40 mg daily.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 114/72 mm Hg and pulse rate is 86/min. Jugular venous pressure is normal, the lungs are clear, and there is no edema.

Sodium138 mEq/L
Potassium4.1 mEq/L
Creatinine1.1 mg/dL
Estimated glomerular filtration rate70 mL/min/1.73 m²
CV-113.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate management at discharge?

choices.A: Add digoxin and ivabradine before discharge
choices.B: Add one new class of drug every 3 months as an outpatient
choices.C: Continue metoprolol only until a repeat echocardiogram in 3 months
choices.D: Start sacubitril-valsartan, spironolactone and dapagliflozin now
choices.E: Stop metoprolol until he has been stable for 4 weeks

CV-113.explain_html:
Correct answer: D GDMT initiation before discharge

The four pillars of guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) for HFrEF each reduce death and hospitalization, and their benefits add up (about a 60%–70% relative mortality reduction combined):

Pillar Example Starts working
ARNI (or ACEi/ARB) Sacubitril-valsartan Weeks
Beta-blocker Metoprolol succinate, carvedilol, bisoprolol Weeks–months
MRA Spironolactone, eplerenone Weeks
SGLT2 inhibitor Dapagliflozin, empagliflozin Days

Current practice is rapid, simultaneous initiation in the hospital at low doses and up-titration within weeks, not one drug at a time over months. In STRONG-HF, rapid initiation and up-titration within 2 weeks of discharge, with close follow-up of blood pressure, potassium, creatinine and natriuretic peptides, reduced death or HF readmission at 180 days. Patients started on GDMT in the hospital are much more likely to be on it later.

He has adequate blood pressure, potassium and kidney function to start all classes now, with a follow-up visit and labs in 1–2 weeks.

Why not the others

  • (A) Add digoxin and ivabradine before discharge — Digoxin and ivabradine are add-ons for persistent symptoms on full GDMT; they do not replace the core pillars.
  • (B) Add one new class of drug every 3 months as an outpatient — Sequential titration over many months leaves patients undertreated during the highest-risk period after discharge.
  • (C) Continue metoprolol only until a repeat echocardiogram in 3 months — Waiting for an echocardiogram before starting proven therapy delays treatment; EF improvement is the result of GDMT, not a requirement for it.
  • (E) Stop metoprolol until he has been stable for 4 weeks — Beta-blockers can be started once the patient is euvolemic and stable; stopping it would delay benefit.
🎯 Educational objective

Start all four pillars of HFrEF therapy (ARNI, beta-blocker, MRA, SGLT2 inhibitor) during hospitalization when tolerated, with rapid outpatient up-titration.

CV-114.topic: Switching from ACE inhibitor to ARNI
CV-114.stem_html:
A 59-year-old woman with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (left ventricular ejection fraction 30%) comes for a follow-up visit. She has NYHA class II symptoms. Medications are lisinopril, 20 mg daily, carvedilol, spironolactone, empagliflozin and furosemide. She has never had angioedema.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 118/70 mm Hg and pulse rate is 64/min. She is euvolemic.

Potassium4.4 mEq/L
Estimated glomerular filtration rate58 mL/min/1.73 m²
CV-114.lead: Her physician plans to replace lisinopril with sacubitril-valsartan. Which of the following is the most appropriate way to make this change?

choices.A: Start sacubitril-valsartan after a 2-week washout off lisinopril
choices.B: Start sacubitril-valsartan the same day lisinopril is stopped
choices.C: Start sacubitril-valsartan today and stop lisinopril in 1 week
choices.D: Stop lisinopril and start sacubitril-valsartan 36 hours later
choices.E: Take both drugs together at reduced doses

CV-114.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Switching from ACE inhibitor to ARNI

Sacubitril inhibits neprilysin, which degrades natriuretic peptides — and also bradykinin. ACE also breaks down bradykinin. Blocking both at the same time causes high bradykinin levels and a high rate of angioedema (seen with omapatrilat, an earlier combined ACE–neprilysin inhibitor).

Therefore:

  • Stop the ACE inhibitor at least 36 hours before the first dose of sacubitril-valsartan (about 5 half-lives of the ACE inhibitor)
  • Never combine an ARNI with an ACE inhibitor
  • Do not use an ARNI in anyone with a history of angioedema
  • No washout is needed when switching from an ARB

PARADIGM-HF showed that sacubitril-valsartan reduces cardiovascular death and HF hospitalization by about 20% compared with enalapril, so the switch is recommended for patients like her who tolerate an ACE inhibitor.

Why not the others

  • (A) Start sacubitril-valsartan after a 2-week washout off lisinopril — A 2-week washout is unnecessary and leaves her without RAAS blockade.
  • (B) Start sacubitril-valsartan the same day lisinopril is stopped — Same-day switching does not allow the ACE inhibitor to clear and raises the risk of angioedema.
  • (C) Start sacubitril-valsartan today and stop lisinopril in 1 week — Overlapping the two drugs for a week is contraindicated.
  • (E) Take both drugs together at reduced doses — Combination therapy is contraindicated at any dose.
🧠 Mnemonic

"ACE to ARNI: wait 36 (hours)." ARB to ARNI: no wait.

🎯 Educational objective

When switching from an ACE inhibitor to sacubitril-valsartan, stop the ACE inhibitor at least 36 hours before the first dose to avoid angioedema.

CV-115.stem_html:
A 58-year-old Black woman with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction due to hypertensive cardiomyopathy comes for follow-up. She has dyspnea when walking one block (NYHA class III). She takes sacubitril-valsartan, 97/103 mg twice daily, metoprolol succinate, 200 mg daily, spironolactone, 25 mg daily, dapagliflozin and furosemide; she has taken these doses for 4 months.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 126/78 mm Hg and pulse rate is 62/min. Jugular venous pressure is normal, the lungs are clear, and there is no edema.

Echocardiogram shows left ventricular ejection fraction of 30%. Electrocardiogram shows sinus rhythm with a QRS duration of 0.10 second.

Potassium4.6 mEq/L
Estimated glomerular filtration rate64 mL/min/1.73 m²
CV-115.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate addition to her therapy?

choices.E: Torsemide in place of furosemide at a higher dose

CV-115.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Hydralazine–isosorbide dinitrate

In A-HeFT, adding a fixed-dose combination of hydralazine and isosorbide dinitrate (H-ISDN) to standard therapy in self-identified Black patients with NYHA class III–IV HFrEF reduced mortality by 43% and also reduced HF hospitalizations. The 2022 guideline gives this a Class 1 recommendation for Black patients with persistent NYHA III–IV symptoms on optimal GDMT.

H-ISDN is also used in any patient with HFrEF who cannot take an ACE inhibitor, ARB or ARNI (angioedema, severe kidney dysfunction, hyperkalemia).

Mechanism: hydralazine is an arteriolar dilator (lowers afterload) that also reduces nitrate tolerance; isosorbide dinitrate is a venodilator and NO donor (lowers preload and improves NO bioavailability).

Why not the others

  • (A) Digoxin — Digoxin reduces hospitalizations modestly but does not reduce mortality; H-ISDN has a mortality benefit in this population.
  • (B) Diltiazem — Nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers worsen outcomes in HFrEF.
  • (D) Ivabradine — Ivabradine requires a resting sinus rate of at least 70/min on maximal beta-blocker; her rate is 62/min.
  • (E) Torsemide in place of furosemide at a higher dose — She is euvolemic; more diuretic would not improve outcomes and risks volume depletion.
🎯 Educational objective

Add hydralazine–isosorbide dinitrate for self-identified Black patients with NYHA class III–IV HFrEF despite optimal GDMT.

CV-116.stem_html:
A 67-year-old man with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (left ventricular ejection fraction 30%) comes for follow-up. He has fatigue and dyspnea with moderate exertion (NYHA class II–III) despite optimized doses of sacubitril-valsartan, carvedilol, eplerenone and empagliflozin. Colonoscopy 1 year ago was normal.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 112/68 mm Hg and pulse rate is 64/min. He is euvolemic.

Hemoglobin12.6 g/dL
Mean corpuscular volume86 fL
Ferritin74 ng/mL
Transferrin saturation14%
Estimated glomerular filtration rate56 mL/min/1.73 m²
CV-116.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

choices.C: No treatment because he is not anemic

CV-116.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Iron deficiency in heart failure

Iron deficiency is present in about half of patients with heart failure, with or without anemia, and worsens exercise capacity and outcomes. In heart failure it is defined as:

  • Ferritin <100 ng/mL, or
  • Ferritin 100–299 ng/mL with transferrin saturation <20%

He meets the definition. Intravenous iron (ferric carboxymaltose or ferric derisomaltose) improves symptoms, exercise capacity and quality of life (FAIR-HF, CONFIRM-HF) and reduces HF hospitalizations (AFFIRM-AHF, IRONMAN; HEART-FID showed no clear benefit on its hierarchical endpoint). The 2022 guideline gives it a Class 2a recommendation in NYHA II–III HFrEF.

Oral iron is poorly absorbed in heart failure (gut edema, high hepcidin) and did not improve exercise capacity in IRONOUT-HF.

Why not the others

  • (A) Darbepoetin alfa — Erythropoiesis-stimulating agents did not improve outcomes in HF and increased thromboembolic events (RED-HF).
  • (C) No treatment because he is not anemic — Iron deficiency harms patients with heart failure even when hemoglobin is normal; treating it improves symptoms.
  • (D) Oral ferrous sulfate — Oral iron does not replete iron stores effectively in heart failure.
  • (E) Red blood cell transfusion — Transfusion is not indicated for a hemoglobin of 12.6 g/dL.
🎯 Educational objective

Treat iron deficiency (ferritin <100 ng/mL, or 100–299 ng/mL with transferrin saturation <20%) in symptomatic HFrEF with intravenous iron, even without anemia.
