CV-117.stem_html:
A 72-year-old man with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction is seen 1 week after his spironolactone dose was increased from 12.5 mg to 25 mg daily. He feels well. Other medications are sacubitril-valsartan, metoprolol succinate, dapagliflozin and furosemide. He started ibuprofen 5 days ago for knee pain.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 116/70 mm Hg and pulse rate is 60/min. He is euvolemic. Muscle strength is normal.

Potassium (nonhemolyzedrepeated)6.1 mEq/L (2 weeks ago 4.9 mEq/L)
Creatinine1.7 mg/dL (2 weeks ago 1.4 mg/dL)
Bicarbonate22 mEq/L
CV-117.lead: An electrocardiogram shows no hyperkalemic changes. In addition to stopping ibuprofen, which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.A: Continue spironolactone and recheck potassium in 3 months
choices.B: Hold spironolactone and recheck potassium and creatinine within a few days
choices.D: Replace spironolactone with eplerenone at an equivalent dose

CV-117.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Hyperkalemia on mineralocorticoid antagonist

Hyperkalemia is the main barrier to keeping patients on mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (MRAs). Guidance for an MRA in HFrEF:

Potassium (mEq/L) Action
≤5.0 Continue, titrate
5.1–5.5 Do not up-titrate; consider dose reduction or a potassium binder
>5.5 Hold the MRA, look for causes, recheck in days
>6.0 or ECG changes Treat hyperkalemia urgently

Here, potassium is >5.5 soon after an MRA dose increase plus a new NSAID (which reduces renal potassium excretion and worsens kidney function). Hold spironolactone, stop ibuprofen, recheck potassium and creatinine in 2–3 days, and restart at a lower dose (12.5 mg daily or every other day) once potassium is <5.0. Potassium binders (patiromer, sodium zirconium cyclosilicate) can help keep patients on RAAS inhibitors and MRAs when hyperkalemia recurs.

Why not the others

  • (A) Continue spironolactone and recheck potassium in 3 months — Continuing the full dose with a potassium of 6.1 mEq/L risks life-threatening hyperkalemia.
  • (C) Permanently stop sacubitril-valsartan and spironolactone — Permanently stopping two mortality-reducing drugs is premature; the cause is reversible.
  • (D) Replace spironolactone with eplerenone at an equivalent dose — Eplerenone also raises potassium; switching does not solve the problem.
  • (E) Stop dapagliflozin — SGLT2 inhibitors do not raise potassium — they slightly lower the risk of hyperkalemia — and should be continued.
🎓 ABIM pearl

SGLT2 inhibitors reduce hyperkalemia risk and make it easier to stay on MRAs. Always ask about NSAIDs, potassium supplements, salt substitutes (KCl) and trimethoprim when potassium rises.

🎯 Educational objective

Hold a mineralocorticoid antagonist when potassium exceeds 5.5 mEq/L, correct precipitating causes, and restart at a lower dose when potassium normalizes.

CV-118.stem_html:
A 71-year-old woman with ischemic cardiomyopathy (left ventricular ejection fraction 20%) is admitted with 1 week of worsening dyspnea, orthopnea, nausea and confusion. Over 2 days of intravenous furosemide, urine output has been poor and creatinine has risen.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 86/62 mm Hg (narrow pulse pressure), pulse rate is 108/min, and respiration rate is 24/min. She is drowsy. Extremities are cool and mottled, with delayed capillary refill. Jugular venous pressure is 16 cm H₂O. There are bibasilar crackles and 2+ leg edema.

A pulmonary artery catheter is placed.

Creatinine2.4 mg/dL (baseline 1.3 mg/dL)
Lactate3.4 mmol/L
Cardiac index1.6 L/min/m²
Pulmonary capillary wedge pressure30 mm Hg
Systemic vascular resistance1900 dyn·s/cm⁵
CV-118.lead: Which of the following best describes her hemodynamic profile?

choices.A: Cold and dry (low output, normal filling pressures)
choices.B: Cold and wet (low output, high filling pressures)
choices.D: Warm and dry (normal output, normal filling pressures)
choices.E: Warm and wet (normal output, high filling pressures)

CV-118.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Cold and wet hemodynamic profile

The Stevenson profiles classify acute heart failure by perfusion (warm vs cold) and congestion (dry vs wet):

Dry (no congestion) Wet (congested)
Warm (adequate perfusion) Compensated Most common → diuretics, vasodilators
Cold (hypoperfused) Volume-depleted or end-stage → cautious fluids, reassess Worst prognosis → inotropes, mechanical support

She has signs of hypoperfusion (cool mottled extremities, narrow pulse pressure, confusion, rising creatinine and lactate, cardiac index <2.2) and congestion (high JVP, crackles, edema, PCWP 30). This is cold and wet — cardiogenic shock (SCAI stage C).

Management: an inotrope (dobutamine or milrinone; norepinephrine if needed for blood pressure), continued diuresis once perfusion improves, and early consideration of mechanical circulatory support and an advanced heart failure team.

Why not the others

  • (A) Cold and dry (low output, normal filling pressures) — High JVP, edema and a PCWP of 30 mm Hg show she is congested.
  • (C) Distributive shock (high output, low resistance) — Distributive shock has warm extremities with a high cardiac index and low systemic vascular resistance; hers is the reverse.
  • (D) Warm and dry (normal output, normal filling pressures) — She is neither adequately perfused nor free of congestion.
  • (E) Warm and wet (normal output, high filling pressures) — Cool, mottled extremities, rising lactate and a low cardiac index show she is hypoperfused, not warm.
🧠 Mnemonic

"Cold and wet → add the pump (inotrope)." Warm and wet → just drain it (diuretic).

🎯 Educational objective

Classify acute heart failure by perfusion and congestion; the cold-and-wet profile (low output, high filling pressures) requires inotropic support.

CV-119.stem_html:
A 58-year-old woman is evaluated for 4 months of progressive exertional dyspnea and leg swelling. She has hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus and obstructive sleep apnea. Medications are lisinopril, metformin and semaglutide.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 148/88 mm Hg, pulse rate is 82/min, and respiration rate is 18/min. Oxygen saturation is 95% breathing ambient air. BMI is 46 kg/m². Jugular venous pressure is difficult to assess. Heart sounds are distant. There is 2+ pitting edema of both legs to the knees.

B-type natriuretic peptide58 pg/mL
Hemoglobin13.2 g/dL
Creatinine0.9 mg/dL
Thyroid-stimulating hormone2.2 µU/mL
CV-119.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in evaluation?

choices.A: Conclude that heart failure has been excluded
choices.B: Measure NT-proBNP to confirm the BNP result
choices.D: Start an empiric trial of furosemide without testing

CV-119.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Natriuretic peptides in obesity

Natriuretic peptides are excellent for ruling out heart failure in most patients — but obesity lowers BNP and NT-proBNP levels, by about 30%–50% at BMI ≥35. Mechanisms include greater clearance by natriuretic peptide clearance receptors in adipose tissue, reduced synthesis and the effect of neprilysin activity in fat.

With her symptoms, edema and strong risk factors for HFpEF (obesity, hypertension, diabetes, sleep apnea), a "normal" BNP does not exclude heart failure. Echocardiography is needed to assess ejection fraction, LV hypertrophy, diastolic function (E/e′), left atrial size and pulmonary pressures. Scores such as H₂FPEF combine these features (heavy, hypertensive, AF, pulmonary hypertension, elder, filling pressure). Invasive exercise hemodynamics settle unclear cases.

Lower natriuretic peptides Higher natriuretic peptides
Obesity Older age, female sex
Flash pulmonary edema (early) Kidney dysfunction
Constrictive pericarditis, mitral stenosis Atrial fibrillation, PE, sepsis
Sacubitril-valsartan raises BNP (not NT-proBNP)

Why not the others

  • (A) Conclude that heart failure has been excluded — A low BNP in severe obesity does not exclude heart failure.
  • (B) Measure NT-proBNP to confirm the BNP result — NT-proBNP is lowered by obesity as well and would not resolve the uncertainty.
  • (C) Repeat BNP in 3 months — Waiting 3 months delays diagnosis of a treatable condition.
  • (D) Start an empiric trial of furosemide without testing — Diuretics may relieve edema but will not establish a diagnosis or guide disease-modifying therapy.
🎯 Educational objective

Obesity lowers natriuretic peptide levels; a normal BNP does not exclude heart failure in an obese patient with symptoms, so obtain echocardiography.

CV-120.topic: Heart failure with improved ejection fraction
CV-120.stem_html:
A 47-year-old woman comes for follow-up of nonischemic dilated cardiomyopathy diagnosed 2 years ago, when her left ventricular ejection fraction was 25%. She has no symptoms and runs 3 miles twice a week. She takes sacubitril-valsartan, metoprolol succinate, spironolactone and dapagliflozin. She asks whether she can stop her medications now that her "heart has healed."

On physical examination, blood pressure is 112/70 mm Hg and pulse rate is 62/min. Examination is normal.

Echocardiogram shows left ventricular ejection fraction of 56% with normal left ventricular size. NT-proBNP is 90 pg/mL.
CV-120.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.A: Continue all current heart failure medications
choices.C: Stop all medications and repeat echocardiography in 6 months
choices.D: Stop dapagliflozin and spironolactone, and continue the others
choices.E: Stop metoprolol succinate, and continue the others

CV-120.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Heart failure with improved ejection fraction

She has heart failure with improved ejection fraction (HFimpEF): previous LVEF ≤40%, now >40% with an increase of ≥10 points. Improvement means the disease is in remission, not cured.

In TRED-HF, patients with recovered dilated cardiomyopathy who stopped their medications had a relapse rate of about 44% within 6 months (LVEF fall, LV enlargement or NT-proBNP rise), versus none in those who continued. The 2022 guideline recommends continuing GDMT in HFimpEF (Class 1).

Why not the others

  • (B) Stop all heart failure medications — Stopping all drugs led to relapse in nearly half of patients in TRED-HF.
  • (C) Stop all medications and repeat echocardiography in 6 months — Repeat imaging after stopping would only document relapse after it happens.
  • (D) Stop dapagliflozin and spironolactone, and continue the others — Stopping any GDMT component may trigger relapse; there are no data showing which drugs can be safely removed.
  • (E) Stop metoprolol succinate, and continue the others — Beta-blocker withdrawal is linked to recurrence of LV dysfunction.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Report the trajectory, not just the number: an LVEF of 56% after 25% is HFimpEF, not HFpEF — the treatment is different.

🎯 Educational objective

Continue guideline-directed medical therapy in heart failure with improved ejection fraction; stopping it frequently causes relapse.

CV-121.stem_html:
A 69-year-old man with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (left ventricular ejection fraction 32%) and type 2 diabetes mellitus is admitted with 2 weeks of progressive dyspnea, orthopnea and a 5-kg (11-lb) weight gain. He has been adherent to his medications and to a low-sodium diet. Six weeks ago, his primary care clinician added a new drug because his hemoglobin A₁c was 8.4% on metformin. Other medications are sacubitril-valsartan, carvedilol, spironolactone, empagliflozin and furosemide.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 128/78 mm Hg and pulse rate is 84/min and regular. Jugular venous pressure is 14 cm H₂O. There are crackles at both lung bases and 3+ leg edema.

Electrocardiogram shows sinus rhythm without ischemic changes. High-sensitivity troponin is unchanged from baseline.
CV-121.lead: Which of the following newly added drugs most likely contributed to his decompensation?
CV-121.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Drugs that worsen HFrEF

Thiazolidinediones (pioglitazone, rosiglitazone) activate PPAR-γ in the renal collecting duct, increasing sodium and water reabsorption (via ENaC) and causing fluid retention and edema. They increase the risk of heart failure hospitalization and are contraindicated in NYHA class III–IV heart failure and should be avoided in symptomatic HF.

Drugs to avoid or use with caution in HFrEF Why
Thiazolidinediones Fluid retention
Nondihydropyridine CCBs (diltiazem, verapamil) Negative inotropy
NSAIDs Sodium retention, kidney dysfunction, blunt diuretics
Saxagliptin, alogliptin Increased HF hospitalization (SAVOR-TIMI 53)
Class I antiarrhythmics (flecainide), dronedarone Proarrhythmia, mortality
Cilostazol Mortality in HFrEF
Some chemotherapies (anthracyclines, trastuzumab) Cardiotoxicity
Pregabalin, itraconazole, TNF inhibitors (high dose), minoxidil Fluid retention or LV depression

Why not the others

  • (A) Dulaglutide — GLP-1 receptor agonists are neutral for heart failure outcomes and reduce ASCVD events in diabetes.
  • (B) Insulin glargine — Insulin is neutral for heart failure outcomes in randomized trials (ORIGIN), although it can cause mild fluid retention.
  • (C) Linagliptin — Linagliptin was neutral for heart failure hospitalization in CARMELINA.
  • (E) Sitagliptin — Sitagliptin did not increase heart failure hospitalization in TECOS.
🎯 Educational objective

Recognize thiazolidinediones (and other drugs such as nondihydropyridine CCBs, NSAIDs and saxagliptin) as precipitants of heart failure decompensation.

CV-122.stem_html:
A 74-year-old woman is evaluated for exertional dyspnea that limits her to walking about one block (NYHA class II–III). She was hospitalized for heart failure 3 months ago. She has hypertension and obesity. Medications are amlodipine, losartan and furosemide, 20 mg daily. She does not have diabetes.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 128/74 mm Hg and pulse rate is 72/min and regular. BMI is 33 kg/m². Jugular venous pressure is normal. There is trace ankle edema.

Echocardiogram shows left ventricular ejection fraction of 60%, concentric left ventricular hypertrophy, a dilated left atrium and an E/e′ ratio of 16. NT-proBNP is 640 pg/mL.

Estimated glomerular filtration rate52 mL/min/1.73 m²
Potassium4.3 mEq/L
CV-122.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate addition to her therapy?
CV-122.explain_html:
Correct answer: B SGLT2 inhibitor in HFpEF

She has heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF): symptoms, LVEF ≥50%, structural heart disease (LVH, enlarged left atrium), elevated filling pressures (E/e′ >14) and high NT-proBNP.

SGLT2 inhibitors are the first therapy proven to improve outcomes across the full EF range: EMPEROR-Preserved (empagliflozin) and DELIVER (dapagliflozin) showed about a 20% reduction in cardiovascular death or HF hospitalization, mostly driven by fewer hospitalizations, plus better quality of life. They are Class 2a in the 2022 guideline and first-line in the 2023 ACC HFpEF pathway — with or without diabetes.

Other HFpEF pillars: diuretics for congestion; blood pressure control; weight loss (semaglutide improved symptoms in STEP-HFpEF; tirzepatide reduced HF events in SUMMIT); an MRA (spironolactone or finerenone — FINEARTS-HF) and an ARNI in selected patients, particularly with LVEF toward the lower end of normal.

Why not the others

  • (A) Digoxin — Digoxin has no proven benefit in HFpEF and is used mainly for rate control in AF.
  • (C) Isosorbide mononitrate — Isosorbide mononitrate reduced activity levels in HFpEF (NEAT-HFpEF) and is not recommended.
  • (D) Ivabradine — Ivabradine has no outcome benefit in HFpEF and may worsen symptoms by limiting heart rate reserve.
  • (E) Sildenafil — Sildenafil did not improve exercise capacity in HFpEF (RELAX).
🎯 Educational objective

Add an SGLT2 inhibitor for patients with HFpEF to reduce heart failure hospitalization and cardiovascular death.

CV-123.stem_html: A 61-year-old man with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (left ventricular ejection fraction 30%) and NYHA class II symptoms remains in sinus rhythm with a resting pulse rate of 78/min on carvedilol, 25 mg twice daily; higher doses caused symptomatic hypotension. He also takes sacubitril-valsartan, eplerenone and dapagliflozin. Ivabradine is started, and 4 weeks later his resting pulse rate is 64/min with no change in blood pressure.
CV-123.lead: Which of the following best describes the mechanism of action of ivabradine?

choices.A: Blockade of beta-1 adrenergic receptors in the sinoatrial node
choices.B: Blockade of L-type calcium channels in the atrioventricular node
choices.C: Inhibition of sodium–potassium ATPase in myocytes
choices.D: Inhibition of the delayed rectifier potassium current in ventricular myocytes
choices.E: Inhibition of the If ("funny") current in the sinoatrial node

CV-123.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Ivabradine

Ivabradine selectively inhibits the I_f ("funny") current, carried through HCN4 channels in sinoatrial node pacemaker cells. I_f produces the slow diastolic (phase 4) depolarization that sets the sinus rate. Blocking it slows the sinus rate without affecting contractility, AV conduction or blood pressure.

In SHIFT, ivabradine reduced HF hospitalization in HFrEF (LVEF ≤35%) with sinus rhythm and a resting rate ≥70/min despite maximally tolerated beta-blockade. It does not work in atrial fibrillation (no sinus node driving the rate).

Adverse effects: phosphenes (luminous visual flashes, because related HCN channels exist in the retina), bradycardia and atrial fibrillation; avoid in pregnancy.

Why not the others

  • (A) Blockade of beta-1 adrenergic receptors in the sinoatrial node — Beta-1 blockade (carvedilol, metoprolol) lowers heart rate but also reduces contractility and blood pressure; it is not ivabradine's action.
  • (B) Blockade of L-type calcium channels in the atrioventricular node — L-type calcium channel blockade is the action of verapamil and diltiazem, which slow AV conduction and depress contractility.
  • (C) Inhibition of sodium–potassium ATPase in myocytes — Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase inhibition is the mechanism of digoxin.
  • (D) Inhibition of the delayed rectifier potassium current in ventricular myocytes — Delayed rectifier potassium-current blockade (class III drugs such as dofetilide) prolongs repolarization and the QT interval.
🎯 Educational objective

Ivabradine slows the sinus rate by inhibiting the I_f current in the sinoatrial node, without negative inotropic or hypotensive effects; it requires sinus rhythm.

CV-124.stem_html:
A 66-year-old man with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction and chronic kidney disease is seen 2 weeks after dapagliflozin, 10 mg daily, was added. He feels well, with no dizziness. Other medications are sacubitril-valsartan, metoprolol succinate, spironolactone and furosemide.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 118/70 mm Hg and pulse rate is 66/min, with no orthostatic change. He is euvolemic.

Estimated glomerular filtration rate47 mL/min/1.73 m² (54 mL/min/1.73 m² before dapagliflozin)
Potassium4.5 mEq/L
Urinalysisnormal
CV-124.lead: Which of the following best explains the change in his estimated glomerular filtration rate?

choices.A: Acute interstitial nephritis from the new drug
choices.B: Afferent arteriolar constriction via tubuloglomerular feedback
choices.C: Efferent arteriolar vasodilation from RAAS blockade
choices.D: Euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis with volume loss
choices.E: Renal artery stenosis unmasked by the new drug

CV-124.explain_html:
Correct answer: B eGFR dip after SGLT2 inhibitor

SGLT2 inhibitors block glucose and sodium reabsorption in the proximal tubule, so more sodium chloride reaches the macula densa. The macula densa senses this and, through tubuloglomerular feedback (adenosine release), constricts the afferent arteriole. Intraglomerular pressure and GFR fall.

This early, modest dip (usually 3–6 mL/min/1.73 m², sometimes up to ~10%–30%) is hemodynamic and reversible and reflects lower glomerular hyperfiltration — the same mechanism that protects the kidney long term. In DAPA-CKD, EMPA-KIDNEY and the heart failure trials, eGFR then declined more slowly than with placebo.

Continue the drug. Reassess volume status and diuretic dose if the dip is larger than about 30%.

Why not the others

  • (A) Acute interstitial nephritis from the new drug — Interstitial nephritis would cause pyuria, leukocyte casts or eosinophiluria and a progressive decline; his urinalysis is normal.
  • (C) Efferent arteriolar vasodilation from RAAS blockade — Efferent arteriolar dilation is the mechanism of the eGFR dip seen with ACE inhibitors, ARBs and ARNI, not SGLT2 inhibitors.
  • (D) Euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis with volume loss — Euglycemic ketoacidosis presents with nausea, malaise and an anion-gap acidosis; he is well and his eGFR change is expected.
  • (E) Renal artery stenosis unmasked by the new drug — Renal artery stenosis causes a large eGFR drop after RAAS blockade (efferent dilation), not after SGLT2 inhibitors.
🧠 Mnemonic

SGLT2: "Afferent squeeze." ACEi/ARB: "Efferent release." Both lower glomerular pressure — both protect the kidney.

🎯 Educational objective

The early eGFR dip after starting an SGLT2 inhibitor results from afferent arteriolar vasoconstriction via tubuloglomerular feedback; it is expected and the drug should be continued.

CV-125.stem_html:
A 52-year-old man is evaluated for 3 months of fatigue and exertional dyspnea. He has had palpitations "on and off" for about 4 months. He drinks one glass of wine weekly and does not use drugs. There is no family history of cardiomyopathy. He takes no medications.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 118/78 mm Hg, pulse rate is 134/min and irregularly irregular. Jugular venous pressure is mildly elevated, and there is trace ankle edema.

Electrocardiogram shows atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of 132/min. Echocardiogram shows a mildly dilated left ventricle with global hypokinesis and an ejection fraction of 30%, and no valve disease. Coronary CT angiography shows no coronary artery disease. Cardiac MRI shows no late gadolinium enhancement. Thyroid function is normal.
CV-125.lead: Which of the following is the most likely cause of his cardiomyopathy?
CV-125.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Tachycardia-mediated cardiomyopathy

Tachycardia-mediated (tachycardia-induced) cardiomyopathy is LV dysfunction caused by persistently fast heart rates — AF, atrial flutter, atrial tachycardia, frequent PVCs (>10%–15% burden) or incessant SVT. Clues:

  • Weeks to months of uncontrolled tachycardia preceding symptoms
  • Global dysfunction, mild LV dilation
  • No late gadolinium enhancement (no scar) on MRI — a favorable sign for recovery
  • No other cause (normal coronaries, no alcohol excess, normal thyroid, no family history)

The diagnosis is confirmed in retrospect: LVEF improves substantially within 1–6 months of strict rate or rhythm control (often rhythm control by catheter ablation). Continue GDMT while EF recovers; recurrence of the tachycardia can cause rapid relapse.

Why not the others

  • (A) Alcoholic cardiomyopathy — He drinks very little alcohol; alcoholic cardiomyopathy requires heavy use over years.
  • (B) Familial dilated cardiomyopathy — There is no family history, and the clear temporal link with uncontrolled AF points to a reversible cause.
  • (C) Ischemic cardiomyopathy — Coronary CT angiography excluded coronary artery disease.
  • (E) Viral myocarditis — Myocarditis typically follows a viral illness and shows late gadolinium enhancement or edema on MRI.
🎯 Educational objective

Suspect tachycardia-mediated cardiomyopathy in new LV dysfunction with persistent tachyarrhythmia and no scar on MRI; EF recovers with rate or rhythm control.

CV-126.stem_html: A 38-year-old man was diagnosed 6 months ago with dilated cardiomyopathy (left ventricular ejection fraction 28%). Coronary angiography was normal, thyroid function and iron studies were normal, he does not drink alcohol or use drugs, and cardiac MRI showed midwall septal fibrosis without edema. His father died suddenly at age 50, and a paternal aunt had a "weak heart." He is doing well on GDMT. He has two children, ages 10 and 14, and a 41-year-old sister.
CV-126.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation for his first-degree relatives?

choices.A: Cardiac MRI only for relatives older than 40 years
choices.B: Clinical screening with ECG and echocardiography, plus genetic testing of the patient
choices.C: No screening unless relatives develop symptoms
choices.D: Screening of relatives only if his ejection fraction fails to improve
choices.E: Screening with B-type natriuretic peptide levels only

CV-126.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Familial dilated cardiomyopathy

About 30%–40% of idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathies are genetic, most often autosomal dominant (TTN truncating variants, LMNA, FLNC, desmosomal genes, MYH7, RBM20). His family history of sudden death and heart failure and midwall fibrosis make an inherited cause likely.

Recommendations (HFSA/ACMG, 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA, ESC 2023):

  • Genetic counseling and testing of the patient (the proband) — a pathogenic variant allows cascade testing of relatives
  • Clinical screening of all first-degree relatives (parents, siblings, children) with ECG and echocardiography, beginning in childhood or adolescence, and repeated every 1–5 years depending on age and genotype, because the disease appears with age
  • LMNA, FLNC or desmosomal variants carry high arrhythmic risk and may warrant an ICD at higher EF than usual thresholds

Why not the others

  • (A) Cardiac MRI only for relatives older than 40 years — Familial DCM can appear in children and young adults; screening limited to older relatives and a single test misses many cases.
  • (C) No screening unless relatives develop symptoms — Waiting for symptoms forfeits the chance to treat early LV dysfunction and prevent sudden death.
  • (D) Screening of relatives only if his ejection fraction fails to improve — The need to screen relatives does not depend on whether his own ejection fraction recovers.
  • (E) Screening with B-type natriuretic peptide levels only — Natriuretic peptides are not sensitive enough to detect early cardiomyopathy.
🎯 Educational objective

In idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy, offer genetic testing to the patient and clinical screening with ECG and echocardiography to all first-degree relatives.

CV-127.stem_html:
A 61-year-old man with ischemic cardiomyopathy (left ventricular ejection fraction 18%) has had three hospitalizations for decompensated heart failure in the past 6 months. Sacubitril-valsartan and spironolactone were stopped because of symptomatic hypotension and rising creatinine, and carvedilol was reduced to 3.125 mg twice daily. He needs furosemide, 160 mg twice daily, to stay euvolemic. He has dyspnea while dressing. He has a CRT defibrillator, which has delivered two appropriate shocks for ventricular tachycardia in the past 3 months. He lives with his wife, has no substance use and wants to "do everything possible."

On physical examination, blood pressure is 86/58 mm Hg and pulse rate is 82/min. Extremities are cool.

Sodium130 mEq/L
Creatinine1.9 mg/dL
NT-proBNP8600 pg/mL
CV-127.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.B: Increase carvedilol to the target dose
choices.C: Refer to an advanced heart failure center
choices.D: Restart sacubitril-valsartan at the full dose

CV-127.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Advanced heart failure — referral

He has advanced (stage D) heart failure. Warning signs are summarized by the mnemonic "I NEED HELP":

Letter Marker
I Inotropes needed (prior or current)
N NYHA III–IV or persistently high Natriuretic peptides
E End-organ dysfunction (worsening kidney or liver function)
E EF ≤35%
D Defibrillator shocks
H Hospitalizations (>1 in 12 months)
E Edema despite escalating diuretics
L Low blood pressure (SBP <90), high heart rate
P Prognostic medication — intolerance or down-titration of GDMT

He has nearly all of them, and his 1-year mortality is high (>25%–50%). Timely referral to an advanced heart failure center allows evaluation for heart transplantation or durable LVAD before end-organ damage makes him ineligible. Palliative care should be involved in parallel.

Why not the others

  • (A) Add ivabradine — Ivabradine requires adequate blood pressure and a resting sinus rate ≥70/min, and would not change his trajectory.
  • (B) Increase carvedilol to the target dose — Hypotension and hypoperfusion prevent beta-blocker up-titration; forcing it could precipitate shock.
  • (D) Restart sacubitril-valsartan at the full dose — Sacubitril-valsartan was stopped for hypotension and worsening kidney function; restarting at a full dose would be unsafe.
  • (E) Start long-term outpatient milrinone — Chronic inotropes can bridge to advanced therapies or serve as palliation, but deciding on that requires advanced HF evaluation first.
🎯 Educational objective

Refer patients with markers of advanced heart failure (recurrent hospitalizations, GDMT intolerance, hypotension, end-organ dysfunction, escalating diuretics, ICD shocks) to an advanced HF center for transplant or LVAD evaluation.

CV-128.stem_html:
A 68-year-old man with a continuous-flow left ventricular assist device implanted 8 months ago as destination therapy is admitted with melena. He takes warfarin (target INR 2.0–2.5) and aspirin, 81 mg daily. He had a similar episode 3 months ago.

On physical examination, blood pressure (Doppler mean) is 74 mm Hg and pulse rate is 96/min. A continuous mechanical hum is heard over the precordium. Pulses are not palpable.

Endoscopy shows multiple bleeding angiodysplasias in the jejunum.

Hemoglobin7.2 g/dL
INR2.3
Platelet count212000/µL
Von Willebrand factor activity-to-antigen ratiolow; high-molecular-weight multimers absent
CV-128.lead: Which of the following best explains his tendency to bleed?

choices.A: Acquired von Willebrand syndrome from shear stress

CV-128.explain_html:
Correct answer: A GI bleeding with an LVAD

GI bleeding affects about 20%–30% of patients with continuous-flow LVADs. Two mechanisms work together:

  1. Acquired von Willebrand syndrome: the high shear stress in the pump unfolds large von Willebrand factor (VWF) multimers, which are then cleaved by ADAMTS13. Loss of high-molecular-weight multimers impairs platelet adhesion — the same mechanism seen in severe aortic stenosis (Heyde syndrome).
  2. Angiodysplasia formation: reduced pulsatility causes intestinal hypoperfusion and angiopoietin-2 release, leading to fragile arteriovenous malformations.

Plus warfarin and aspirin. Management: endoscopic therapy, adjust antithrombotics, and for recurrent bleeding octreotide (reduces splanchnic flow and angiogenesis) or other anti-angiogenic agents.

Why not the others

  • (B) Disseminated intravascular coagulation — DIC would cause thrombocytopenia, low fibrinogen and a prolonged INR beyond the warfarin effect.
  • (C) Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia — HIT causes thrombocytopenia and thrombosis; his platelet count is normal and he is not on heparin.
  • (D) Supratherapeutic anticoagulation — His INR is within the target range.
  • (E) Uremic platelet dysfunction — There is no kidney failure to explain uremic platelet dysfunction.
🎯 Educational objective

Continuous-flow LVADs cause acquired von Willebrand syndrome (shear-induced loss of large multimers) and angiodysplasia, explaining their high rate of GI bleeding.

CV-129.stem_html:
A 78-year-old man is evaluated for 6 months of exertional dyspnea and ankle swelling. He had bilateral carpal tunnel release 8 years ago and has lumbar spinal stenosis. He has hypertension that has become easier to control; his amlodipine was stopped last year because of lightheadedness.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 108/68 mm Hg and pulse rate is 72/min. Jugular venous pressure is 10 cm H₂O, and there is 1+ ankle edema.

Electrocardiogram shows low QRS voltage in the limb leads and a pseudoinfarct pattern in V1 through V3. Echocardiogram shows a left ventricular wall thickness of 17 mm, left ventricular ejection fraction of 52%, a granular "sparkling" myocardium and an apical-sparing pattern of longitudinal strain. Cardiac biomarkers are mildly elevated.

A technetium-99m pyrophosphate (PYP) scan is being considered.
CV-129.lead: Which of the following tests should be performed before the PYP scan result can be used to diagnose transthyretin amyloidosis?

choices.C: Serum free light chains and immunofixation

CV-129.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis

Everything points to cardiac amyloidosis: HFpEF in an older man, LV wall thickening with low ECG voltage (voltage–mass discordance), apical-sparing strain, intolerance of antihypertensives, and the classic extracardiac clues of transthyretin (ATTR) amyloid — bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome (often 5–10 years earlier) and lumbar spinal stenosis.

Two types cause nearly all cardiac amyloidosis:

  • AL (light-chain) — a plasma cell disorder; rapidly fatal without urgent chemotherapy
  • ATTR — wild-type (age-related) or hereditary (V122I common in Black Americans)

A PYP (or DPD/HMDP) scan with grade 2–3 myocardial uptake diagnoses ATTR without biopsy — but only if AL has been excluded, because some AL deposits also take up the tracer. So serum free light chains plus serum and urine immunofixation must be done first (or at the same time).

:::flow Q: Monoclonal protein present (abnormal κ/λ ratio or immunofixation)? Y: Possible AL → tissue biopsy (fat pad, bone marrow, endomyocardial) and hematology referral now N: PYP grade 2–3 → ATTR confirmed → TTR gene testing to separate hereditary from wild-type :::

Why not the others

  • (A) Cardiac MRI with gadolinium — Cardiac MRI supports amyloidosis (diffuse late gadolinium enhancement, high extracellular volume) but cannot distinguish AL from ATTR.
  • (B) Endomyocardial biopsy — Biopsy is needed only when a monoclonal protein is found or the noninvasive results are discordant.
  • (D) Transthyretin gene sequencing — TTR gene sequencing follows a confirmed ATTR diagnosis to separate hereditary from wild-type disease.
  • (E) Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio — Albuminuria may suggest renal AL involvement, but it does not exclude AL and is not part of the required pathway.
🎯 Educational objective

Before diagnosing ATTR cardiac amyloidosis by a positive PYP scan, exclude AL amyloidosis with serum free light chains and serum and urine immunofixation.

CV-130.stem_html:
A 79-year-old man was diagnosed 1 month ago with wild-type transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy: grade 3 myocardial uptake on technetium-99m pyrophosphate scan, normal serum free light chain ratio and negative serum and urine immunofixation, and no pathogenic TTR variant. He has dyspnea climbing one flight of stairs (NYHA class II). Medications are furosemide and apixaban for paroxysmal atrial fibrillation.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 106/66 mm Hg and pulse rate is 70/min. He is euvolemic.

Echocardiogram shows left ventricular ejection fraction of 50%.

Estimated glomerular filtration rate52 mL/min/1.73 m²
NT-proBNP2400 pg/mL
CV-130.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate disease-specific treatment?
CV-130.explain_html:
Correct answer: E ATTR cardiomyopathy treatment

Transthyretin is a tetramer made in the liver. In ATTR amyloidosis, the tetramer dissociates into monomers, which misfold and deposit as amyloid fibrils in the heart.

TTR stabilizers bind the tetramer and prevent dissociation:

  • Tafamidis — in ATTR-ACT, reduced all-cause mortality and cardiovascular hospitalization and slowed functional decline in NYHA I–III ATTR-CM
  • Acoramidis — reduced the composite of death and cardiovascular events (ATTRibute-CM)

TTR silencers (siRNA or antisense; vutrisiran reduced death and cardiovascular events in HELIOS-B) cut TTR production in the liver.

Benefit is greatest when started early (NYHA I–II). Supportive care: loop diuretics, anticoagulation for AF regardless of CHA₂DS₂-VASc; avoid drugs that patients with amyloid tolerate poorly.

Why not the others

  • (A) Bortezomib, cyclophosphamide and dexamethasone — Plasma cell–directed chemotherapy treats AL amyloidosis, which has been excluded.
  • (B) Digoxin — Digoxin binds amyloid fibrils and causes toxicity at normal serum levels; it is generally avoided and has no disease-modifying effect.
  • (C) Diltiazem — Nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers bind amyloid fibrils and can cause profound hypotension, heart block and worsening heart failure.
  • (D) Doxycycline plus ursodeoxycholic acid — Doxycycline–ursodiol was studied as a fibril disruptor but has not shown outcome benefit and is not standard therapy.
🎓 ABIM pearl

In cardiac amyloidosis, anticoagulate AF regardless of CHA₂DS₂-VASc — atrial thrombus is very common, even in sinus rhythm.

🎯 Educational objective

Treat transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy with a TTR stabilizer (tafamidis or acoramidis) or silencer (vutrisiran); avoid digoxin and nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers.

CV-131.stem_html:
A 62-year-old man is evaluated for 8 months of progressive abdominal swelling, leg edema and fatigue. He received mediastinal radiation for Hodgkin lymphoma at age 28 and underwent coronary artery bypass grafting 4 years ago. He does not drink alcohol.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 108/72 mm Hg and pulse rate is 92/min and regular. Jugular venous pressure is 18 cm H₂O, rises with inspiration, and shows a prominent y descent. An early diastolic sound is heard at the left sternal border. There is shifting dullness and 3+ leg edema. There are no stigmata of chronic liver disease.

Echocardiogram shows normal left ventricular size and ejection fraction (60%), normal wall thickness, an abnormal septal "bounce" with respiratory ventricular interdependence, more than 25% respiratory variation in mitral inflow, and a medial mitral annular e′ velocity higher than the lateral e′. Chest CT shows pericardial thickening (6 mm) with calcification.

Serum–ascites albumin gradient1.4 g/dL
Ascitic fluid total protein3.2 g/dL
NT-proBNP180 pg/mL
CV-131.lead: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
CV-131.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Constrictive pericarditis

Constrictive pericarditis: a stiff, fibrotic (often calcified) pericardium limits diastolic filling of both ventricles. Common causes in the United States: prior cardiac surgery, mediastinal radiation, idiopathic/viral pericarditis; tuberculosis worldwide.

Clues:

  • Right-sided failure out of proportion (ascites, edema, high JVP) with a normal LV
  • Kussmaul sign (JVP rises with inspiration) and a steep y descent
  • Pericardial knock — early diastolic sound as filling stops abruptly
  • Ventricular interdependence: septal bounce, exaggerated respiratory variation in inflow
  • Annulus reversus (medial e′ ≥ lateral e′) and preserved e′ — the myocardium relaxes normally
  • High-protein ascites with SAAG ≥1.1 (like cardiac ascites)
  • Low or mildly elevated natriuretic peptides (the constrained myocardium is not stretched)

Treatment: diuretics for symptoms; pericardiectomy for chronic constriction (transient/inflammatory constriction may respond to anti-inflammatory therapy).

Constriction Restrictive cardiomyopathy
Pericardium Thick, calcified Normal
Septal motion Bounce, respiratory shift Normal
Tissue Doppler e′ Normal, medial ≥ lateral Low
BNP Normal–mild High
Respiratory variation in inflow >25% <10%

Why not the others

  • (A) Cardiac amyloidosis — Amyloidosis is a restrictive cardiomyopathy with thick walls, low e′ velocities and high natriuretic peptides.
  • (B) Cardiac tamponade — Tamponade requires a pericardial effusion and shows pulsus paradoxus with an absent y descent.
  • (C) Cirrhosis — Cirrhosis does not raise the JVP or cause Kussmaul sign; ascitic protein is usually low (<2.5 g/dL) in cirrhosis.
  • (E) Right ventricular infarction — RV infarction is acute and associated with inferior MI.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Unexplained "cirrhosis" with high-protein ascites and a high JVP — look at the neck veins and the pericardium.

🎯 Educational objective

Recognize constrictive pericarditis (Kussmaul sign, pericardial knock, septal bounce, preserved e′ with annulus reversus, low BNP) after cardiac surgery or radiation, and distinguish it from restrictive cardiomyopathy.

  2. Adler Y, et al. 2015 ESC guidelines for the diagnosis and management of pericardial diseases. Eur Heart J 2015;36:2921.

CV-132.stem_html:
A 26-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of 1 day of constant substernal chest pain. Ten days ago he had fever, sore throat and myalgia that resolved. He takes no medications and does not use drugs.

On physical examination, temperature is 37.4 °C (99.3 °F), blood pressure is 124/76 mm Hg, pulse rate is 104/min, and respiration rate is 18/min. Oxygen saturation is 98% breathing ambient air. There is no friction rub. The lungs are clear.

Electrocardiogram shows sinus tachycardia with 1-mm ST-segment elevation in leads I, aVL and V4 through V6. Echocardiogram shows mild lateral wall hypokinesis with a left ventricular ejection fraction of 48% and no effusion. Coronary CT angiography shows normal coronary arteries.

High-sensitivity troponin I4200 ng/L (reference <20)
C-reactive protein38 mg/L
Leukocyte count9800/µL
CV-132.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next diagnostic test?
CV-132.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Acute myocarditis

A young adult with a recent viral illness, chest pain, high troponin, ST changes, a regional wall-motion abnormality and normal coronary arteries most likely has acute myocarditis (or myopericarditis).

Cardiac MRI is the key noninvasive test. The Lake Louise criteria require:

  • T2-based findings of myocardial edema, and
  • T1-based findings of injury: non-ischemic late gadolinium enhancement (subepicardial or midwall, not subendocardial), raised T1 or extracellular volume

Endomyocardial biopsy is reserved for fulminant or high-risk presentations: cardiogenic shock, new HF with a dilated LV unresponsive to treatment, sustained ventricular arrhythmias or high-grade AV block, or suspected giant cell or eosinophilic myocarditis.

Management of uncomplicated myocarditis: supportive care, GDMT if EF is reduced, avoid NSAIDs if LV function is impaired (debated), and restrict competitive sports and strenuous exercise for 3–6 months.

Why not the others

  • (B) Endomyocardial biopsy — Biopsy is invasive and reserved for fulminant illness, heart block, ventricular arrhythmias or failure to improve.
  • (C) Exercise stress testing — Exercise testing during acute myocarditis can precipitate arrhythmias and is contraindicated.
  • (D) Invasive coronary angiography — CT angiography has already excluded coronary disease.
  • (E) Viral serologic panel — Viral serologies rarely change management and do not establish myocardial involvement.
🎯 Educational objective

Use cardiac MRI (Lake Louise criteria) to diagnose suspected acute myocarditis after coronary disease is excluded; reserve endomyocardial biopsy for high-risk presentations.

CV-133.stem_html:
A 70-year-old man with metastatic melanoma comes to the emergency department because of 5 days of muscle aches, weakness, drooping eyelids, double vision and new dyspnea. He began combination therapy with nivolumab and ipilimumab 3 weeks ago.

On physical examination, temperature is 37.2 °C (99.0 °F), blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg, pulse rate is 48/min, and respiration rate is 20/min. Oxygen saturation is 95% breathing ambient air. There is bilateral ptosis and proximal muscle weakness with tenderness. The lungs are clear.

Electrocardiogram shows a new right bundle branch block and Mobitz type II second-degree AV block. Echocardiogram shows a left ventricular ejection fraction of 55%. Coronary angiography shows no obstructive coronary disease.

High-sensitivity troponin T1850 ng/L (reference <14)
Creatine kinase6400 U/L
Acetylcholine receptor antibodiespending
CV-133.lead: In addition to stopping immunotherapy and placing a temporary pacemaker, which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
CV-133.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Immune checkpoint inhibitor myocarditis

Immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) myocarditis is uncommon (about 1%) but has a mortality of up to 25%–50%. It occurs early — usually within the first 1–3 months — and is more frequent with combination PD-1 plus CTLA-4 therapy.

It often occurs as an overlap syndrome, the "triple M": myocarditis + myositis + myasthenia gravis–like illness (ptosis, diplopia, respiratory muscle weakness). A preserved ejection fraction does not mean mild disease — conduction disease, high troponin and arrhythmias predict death.

Treatment:

  • Stop the ICI permanently (for severe disease)
  • High-dose IV methylprednisolone (500–1,000 mg daily for 3–5 days), then oral taper — started without waiting for biopsy or MRI
  • Steroid-refractory disease: abatacept, mycophenolate, ATG, IVIG or plasma exchange (for myasthenic features); ruxolitinib in some protocols
  • Telemetry, temporary pacing, respiratory monitoring (negative inspiratory force)

Why not the others

  • (A) Continue nivolumab with close monitoring — Continuing the checkpoint inhibitor in severe myocarditis risks death.
  • (B) Intravenous immune globulin alone — IVIG may be added for myasthenic features or steroid-refractory disease, but it does not replace high-dose glucocorticoids.
  • (D) Oral prednisone, 10 mg daily — Low-dose oral prednisone is inadequate for life-threatening ICI myocarditis.
  • (E) Permanent pacemaker implantation without immunosuppression — Pacing treats the conduction block but not the underlying inflammation, which can progress to fatal arrhythmias or heart failure.
🎯 Educational objective

Treat immune checkpoint inhibitor myocarditis by stopping the drug and giving high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone promptly; watch for overlapping myositis and myasthenia.

CV-134.stem_html:
A 61-year-old woman with newly diagnosed HER2-negative breast cancer is referred before chemotherapy. Her oncologist plans doxorubicin and cyclophosphamide followed by paclitaxel, with a cumulative doxorubicin dose of 240 mg/m². She received left chest wall radiation for an earlier breast cancer 12 years ago. She has hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. She has no cardiac symptoms.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 142/86 mm Hg and pulse rate is 76/min. Examination is normal.

Electrocardiogram is normal.
CV-134.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate cardiovascular evaluation before chemotherapy begins?

choices.B: Coronary angiography before the first cycle
choices.C: Echocardiography with strain plus troponin and BNP
choices.D: Exercise stress testing before the first cycle
choices.E: No cardiac testing because she has no symptoms

CV-134.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Anthracycline cardiotoxicity

Anthracyclines cause dose-dependent, largely irreversible cardiomyopathy through topoisomerase-IIβ inhibition, mitochondrial damage and free radical formation in cardiomyocytes. Risk rises steeply with cumulative doxorubicin dose >250 mg/m² and with patient factors:

Risk factors for cancer therapy–related cardiac dysfunction
Cumulative doxorubicin ≥250 mg/m² (or prior anthracycline)
Prior chest radiation (especially with heart in the field)
Age ≥60 (or childhood)
Hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidemia, smoking, obesity
Pre-existing LV dysfunction, HF, CAD or valve disease
Elevated baseline troponin or natriuretic peptide
Subsequent trastuzumab

She is at high risk (prior left chest radiation, hypertension, diabetes, age). Guidelines recommend a baseline echocardiogram with LVEF and global longitudinal strain (GLS) plus troponin and natriuretic peptide, then surveillance during and after therapy. High-risk patients may benefit from cardioprotection (ACE inhibitor/ARB, beta-blocker, statin; dexrazoxane or liposomal doxorubicin in selected cases) and tight risk-factor control — not from avoiding effective cancer therapy.

Why not the others

  • (A) Changing to a non-anthracycline regimen — Treatment choice is driven by the cancer; the goal of cardio-oncology is to enable effective cancer therapy safely.
  • (B) Coronary angiography before the first cycle — Coronary angiography is not indicated without symptoms or abnormal noninvasive testing.
  • (D) Exercise stress testing before the first cycle — Stress testing assesses ischemia, not baseline ventricular function, which is the key parameter for anthracycline surveillance.
  • (E) No cardiac testing because she has no symptoms — Baseline imaging is recommended for all patients receiving anthracyclines, especially those with risk factors.
🎯 Educational objective

Before anthracycline therapy, obtain a baseline echocardiogram with global longitudinal strain and cardiac biomarkers, and identify risk factors such as prior chest radiation, hypertension, diabetes and cumulative dose >250 mg/m².

CV-135.stem_html:
A 52-year-old woman with HER2-positive breast cancer is evaluated after a routine surveillance echocardiogram during adjuvant trastuzumab. She has completed 4 months of a planned 12 months of therapy and received no anthracycline. She has no dyspnea, orthopnea or edema.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 122/76 mm Hg and pulse rate is 78/min. Examination is normal.

Echocardiogram shows left ventricular ejection fraction of 44% (62% at baseline) with a 20% relative reduction in global longitudinal strain.

NT-proBNP260 pg/mL
CV-135.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.A: Continue trastuzumab and repeat echocardiography in 3 months
choices.B: Hold trastuzumab, start heart failure therapy, and reassess soon
choices.C: Implant a primary-prevention ICD and continue trastuzumab
choices.E: Stop trastuzumab permanently and switch to doxorubicin

CV-135.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Trastuzumab-related LV dysfunction

Trastuzumab blocks HER2 (ErbB2) signaling, which cardiomyocytes use for stress-response and repair. Its cardiotoxicity differs from anthracyclines:

Anthracycline (type I) Trastuzumab (type II)
Dose relation Dose-dependent Not dose-dependent
Mechanism Cell death Myocardial stunning/dysfunction
Reversibility Mostly irreversible Usually reversible
Rechallenge Risky Often tolerated after recovery

She has moderate asymptomatic cancer therapy–related cardiac dysfunction (LVEF fall ≥10 points to 40%–49%). The 2022 ESC cardio-oncology guideline recommends temporarily interrupting HER2 therapy (or, in some cases, continuing under close cardio-oncology supervision), starting ACE inhibitor/ARB and beta-blocker, and repeating imaging in 2–3 weeks. Most patients recover and can resume trastuzumab to complete curative therapy.

Why not the others

  • (A) Continue trastuzumab and repeat echocardiography in 3 months — Continuing unchanged with an LVEF of 44% risks progression to symptomatic heart failure.
  • (C) Implant a primary-prevention ICD and continue trastuzumab — An ICD is not indicated for a potentially reversible, recently recognized LVEF reduction above 35%.
  • (D) Stop all HER2-directed therapy permanently — Permanently stopping HER2 therapy sacrifices oncologic benefit when the dysfunction is usually reversible.
  • (E) Stop trastuzumab permanently and switch to doxorubicin — Switching to an anthracycline adds a more toxic, irreversible cardiotoxic drug and removes effective HER2-targeted therapy.
🎯 Educational objective

Trastuzumab cardiotoxicity is usually reversible: hold the drug, start ACE inhibitor/ARB and beta-blocker, reassess LVEF in weeks, and resume after recovery.

CV-136.stem_html:
A 32-year-old woman comes for follow-up 18 months after she developed peripartum cardiomyopathy 3 weeks after the delivery of her first child. At diagnosis, her left ventricular ejection fraction was 25%. She has been treated with metoprolol succinate, sacubitril-valsartan, spironolactone and dapagliflozin, and she has no symptoms. She uses a levonorgestrel intrauterine device. She and her partner would like to have another child.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 106/68 mm Hg and pulse rate is 62/min. Examination is normal.

Echocardiogram today shows left ventricular ejection fraction of 40%, unchanged for the past 9 months.
CV-136.lead: Which of the following best describes the risk of another pregnancy for this patient?

choices.A: High risk of recurrent heart failure and death, so pregnancy is not advised
choices.B: Low risk because she has no symptoms
choices.C: Low risk if bromocriptine is started at conception
choices.D: Risk is acceptable if she continues her current medications throughout pregnancy
choices.E: Risk is the same as for women with no history of cardiomyopathy

CV-136.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Peripartum cardiomyopathy — future pregnancy

Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM): LVEF <45% presenting toward the end of pregnancy or within months after delivery, without another cause. About half of women recover LVEF to ≥50%.

Subsequent pregnancy risk depends on recovery:

LVEF before next pregnancy Risk with subsequent pregnancy
Recovered (≥50%) ~20% relapse of LV dysfunction; mortality low but not zero — counsel, monitor closely
Persistent dysfunction (<50%) ~40%–50% further LV deterioration, ~15%–20% mortality in older series

With a persistent LVEF of 40%, guidelines (ESC 2025 pregnancy guideline, AHA statement) advise against another pregnancy (modified WHO class IV if LVEF <30%; very high risk at 30%–45% after PPCM). Effective contraception is important; her levonorgestrel IUD is an excellent choice (avoid estrogen-containing methods).

Several of her drugs (ARNI, MRA, SGLT2 inhibitor) are teratogenic or not recommended in pregnancy.

Why not the others

  • (B) Low risk because she has no symptoms — Absence of symptoms does not predict tolerance of the hemodynamic load of pregnancy when LV dysfunction persists.
  • (C) Low risk if bromocriptine is started at conception — Bromocriptine has been studied for acute PPCM; it does not make pregnancy safe with persistent LV dysfunction.
  • (D) Risk is acceptable if she continues her current medications throughout pregnancy — ARNI, MRAs and SGLT2 inhibitors are contraindicated or not recommended in pregnancy.
  • (E) Risk is the same as for women with no history of cardiomyopathy — Women with prior PPCM have a much higher risk than the general population, especially without LV recovery.
🎯 Educational objective

After peripartum cardiomyopathy, persistent LV dysfunction (LVEF <50%) confers a high risk of deterioration and death with another pregnancy, which should be discouraged.

CV-137.stem_html:
A 48-year-old man is evaluated for palpitations and an episode of near-syncope. He grew up in a rural village in Bolivia, where his family lived in an adobe house with a thatched roof, and he moved to the United States 20 years ago. He has no history of hypertension, diabetes or coronary disease.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 112/70 mm Hg and pulse rate is 58/min with frequent extra beats. A soft holosystolic murmur is heard at the apex.

Electrocardiogram shows sinus bradycardia, right bundle branch block and left anterior fascicular block. A 24-hour monitor shows frequent multifocal premature ventricular complexes and runs of nonsustained ventricular tachycardia. Echocardiogram shows an apical left ventricular aneurysm with inferolateral hypokinesis and a left ventricular ejection fraction of 40%. Coronary CT angiography shows no coronary artery disease.
CV-137.lead: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
CV-137.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Chagas cardiomyopathy

Chagas disease is caused by Trypanosoma cruzi, transmitted by triatomine ("kissing") bugs that live in the walls and roofs of adobe and thatched houses in rural Latin America. About 300,000 people in the United States are infected. Chronic Chagas cardiomyopathy develops in 20%–30%, decades after infection.

Classic findings:

  • RBBB plus left anterior fascicular block (the earliest and most typical ECG pattern)
  • Sinus node dysfunction, AV block
  • Ventricular arrhythmias and sudden death
  • Apical aneurysm with segmental wall-motion abnormalities in a nonischemic pattern
  • Thromboembolism and heart failure

Diagnosis: two positive serologic tests using different antigens (ELISA, immunofluorescence or immunoblot); PCR is less useful in chronic disease. Treatment: GDMT, amiodarone or ICD for ventricular arrhythmias, pacing, anticoagulation for aneurysm with thrombus; benznidazole or nifurtimox for younger patients without advanced cardiomyopathy. Screen family members and offer testing to women of childbearing age (congenital transmission).

Why not the others

  • (A) Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy — ARVC affects the right ventricle with LBBB-pattern VT and T inversions in V1–V3, not RBBB with LAFB and an LV apical aneurysm.
  • (B) Cardiac sarcoidosis — Sarcoidosis can cause AV block and VT, but the epidemiologic exposure and apical aneurysm with RBBB/LAFB are classic for Chagas.
  • (D) Ischemic cardiomyopathy — CT angiography excluded coronary artery disease.
  • (E) Rheumatic heart disease — Rheumatic heart disease affects the valves (especially mitral stenosis), not the conduction system and apex.
🎯 Educational objective

Suspect Chagas cardiomyopathy in patients from rural Latin America with RBBB plus left anterior fascicular block, ventricular arrhythmias and an apical aneurysm; confirm with two serologic tests.

CV-138.stem_html:
A 54-year-old woman with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is evaluated for dyspnea and chest tightness when climbing one flight of stairs (NYHA class III), despite metoprolol succinate, 200 mg daily, for 6 months. She has no syncope or family history of sudden death. She takes no other medications.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg and pulse rate is 58/min. A grade 3/6 harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at the left sternal border increases with the Valsalva maneuver and standing.

Echocardiogram shows asymmetric septal hypertrophy (maximal thickness 21 mm), systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve, a resting left ventricular outflow tract gradient of 48 mm Hg rising to 86 mm Hg with Valsalva, and left ventricular ejection fraction of 70%.
CV-138.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate addition to her therapy?
CV-138.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Obstructive HCM — refractory symptoms

She has symptomatic obstructive HCM (LVOT gradient ≥30 mm Hg at rest, ≥50 mm Hg with provocation) despite a maximally tolerated beta-blocker. The 2024 AHA/ACC HCM guideline recommends one of three next steps:

  1. Mavacamten (or aficamten) — a cardiac myosin inhibitor that reduces actin–myosin cross-bridges, lowering hypercontractility and the LVOT gradient. In EXPLORER-HCM it improved exercise capacity and symptoms; in VALOR-HCM it reduced the need for septal reduction. Requires echo monitoring (hold if LVEF <50%), REMS program, and attention to CYP2C19/3A4 interactions.
  2. Disopyramide (negative inotrope, with an AV-nodal blocker)
  3. Septal reduction therapy — surgical myectomy or alcohol septal ablation at an experienced center
Worsens LVOT obstruction (avoid)
Vasodilators — nifedipine, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, nitrates, PDE-5 inhibitors
Volume depletion — high-dose diuretics, dehydration
Positive inotropes — digoxin, dobutamine

Why not the others

  • (A) Digoxin — Digoxin increases contractility and worsens dynamic outflow obstruction.
  • (B) Hydrochlorothiazide — Diuretics reduce preload and LV cavity size, increasing the gradient; use only cautiously for congestion.
  • (C) Lisinopril — ACE inhibitors are vasodilators that reduce afterload and worsen obstruction.
  • (E) Nifedipine — Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers cause vasodilation and can worsen obstruction and hypotension.
🎯 Educational objective

For symptomatic obstructive HCM despite beta-blockade, add a cardiac myosin inhibitor (mavacamten), disopyramide or refer for septal reduction; avoid vasodilators, inotropes and volume depletion.

CV-139.stem_html:
A 28-year-old man with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy diagnosed on a screening echocardiogram comes for risk assessment. He has no syncope, palpitations or chest pain. There is no family history of sudden death. He takes no medications.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 122/74 mm Hg and pulse rate is 64/min. A soft systolic murmur is heard.

A 48-hour ambulatory monitor shows no ventricular tachycardia. Echocardiogram shows asymmetric septal hypertrophy with a maximal wall thickness of 31 mm, a resting left ventricular outflow tract gradient of 20 mm Hg, mild mitral regurgitation, left atrial diameter of 42 mm and left ventricular ejection fraction of 68%. There is no apical aneurysm.
CV-139.lead: Which of the following findings most strongly supports implantation of a primary-prevention ICD?

choices.B: Left ventricular outflow tract gradient of 20 mm Hg
choices.C: Maximal left ventricular wall thickness of 31 mm

CV-139.explain_html:
Correct answer: C HCM sudden-death risk

HCM is a leading cause of sudden cardiac death in young people. The 2024 AHA/ACC guideline lists major risk factors; one or more makes a primary-prevention ICD reasonable (shared decision):

Major risk factors for sudden death in HCM
Massive LV hypertrophy ≥30 mm in any segment
Family history of sudden death from HCM in a first-degree or close relative ≤50 years
Unexplained syncope (likely arrhythmic) within 6 months
LV apical aneurysm
LVEF <50% (end-stage HCM)
Extensive late gadolinium enhancement (≥15% of LV mass) — tie-breaker
Nonsustained VT on monitoring — tie-breaker, especially in young patients

His septal thickness of 31 mm meets a major criterion. The HCM Risk-SCD calculator (ESC) can also estimate 5-year risk. Prior cardiac arrest or sustained VT is a Class 1 indication (secondary prevention).

Why not the others

  • (A) Left atrial diameter of 42 mm — Left atrial size enters the European risk calculator but is not a major independent indication.
  • (B) Left ventricular outflow tract gradient of 20 mm Hg — A modest outflow gradient is not a major risk factor for sudden death.
  • (D) Mild mitral regurgitation — Mild mitral regurgitation from systolic anterior motion does not predict sudden death.
  • (E) Patient age of 28 years — Younger age modifies the risk estimate but is not a stand-alone indication.
🎯 Educational objective

In HCM, major risk factors for sudden death — wall thickness ≥30 mm, family history of SCD, unexplained syncope, apical aneurysm, LVEF <50% — support a primary-prevention ICD.

CV-140.stem_html:
A 72-year-old man comes for follow-up of aortic stenosis. He walks 2 miles daily and plays golf without chest pain, dyspnea, lightheadedness or syncope. He has hypertension treated with amlodipine.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 134/78 mm Hg and pulse rate is 68/min. A grade 3/6 late-peaking crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur is heard at the right upper sternal border with radiation to the carotid arteries. The aortic component of S₂ is soft. Carotid upstrokes are delayed.

Echocardiogram shows a heavily calcified trileaflet aortic valve with a peak velocity of 4.6 m/s, a mean gradient of 52 mm Hg and an aortic valve area of 0.7 cm². Left ventricular ejection fraction is 45%, down from 60% 1 year ago; coronary CT angiography shows no significant coronary disease.
CV-140.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.C: Exercise stress testing to look for symptoms

CV-140.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Asymptomatic severe aortic stenosis

He has severe aortic stenosis (peak velocity ≥4 m/s, mean gradient ≥40 mm Hg, AVA ≤1.0 cm²) without symptoms, but with a fall in LVEF to <50% that has no other cause. This is stage C2 disease, and aortic valve replacement is recommended (Class 1) by both the 2020 ACC/AHA and 2025 ESC/EACTS guidelines.

Asymptomatic severe AS — AVR indications Class
LVEF <50% 1
Undergoing other cardiac surgery 1
Abnormal exercise test (symptoms, fall in BP) 2a
Very severe AS (velocity ≥5 m/s), rapid progression (≥0.3 m/s/yr), BNP >3× normal, LVEF falling on 3 serial studies to <60% 2a
Low procedural risk, otherwise (EARLY TAVR, AVATAR) Increasingly favored — heart team decision

Mode (TAVR or SAVR) depends on age, anatomy, risk and patient preference; at 72 with a trileaflet valve, either may be chosen by the heart team.

Why not the others

  • (B) Balloon aortic valvuloplasty — Balloon valvuloplasty gives only temporary relief and is used as a bridge in unstable patients, not as definitive therapy.
  • (C) Exercise stress testing to look for symptoms — Exercise testing is used to unmask symptoms when the decision is uncertain; LV dysfunction already establishes the indication.
  • (D) Repeat echocardiography in 6 months — Continued surveillance despite declining LV function risks irreversible myocardial damage and sudden death.
  • (E) Start lisinopril and continue surveillance — No medical therapy changes the natural history of severe AS; ACE inhibitors may treat hypertension but do not delay AVR.
🎯 Educational objective

Recommend aortic valve replacement for asymptomatic severe aortic stenosis when LVEF falls below 50%.

CV-141.topic: Valve replacement choice in a younger patient
CV-141.stem_html:
A 57-year-old man is evaluated for exertional dyspnea and chest tightness that began 4 months ago. He has hypertension and hyperlipidemia. He works as an electrician and has no other medical problems. His Society of Thoracic Surgeons predicted surgical mortality is 1.1%.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 128/76 mm Hg and pulse rate is 70/min. A grade 3/6 late-peaking systolic murmur is heard at the right upper sternal border.

Echocardiogram shows a trileaflet, heavily calcified aortic valve with a mean gradient of 48 mm Hg and an aortic valve area of 0.8 cm². Left ventricular ejection fraction is 60%. Coronary angiography shows no significant coronary disease. The ascending aorta measures 3.6 cm.
CV-141.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
CV-141.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Valve replacement choice in a younger patient

He has symptomatic severe aortic stenosis, so AVR is indicated (Class 1). The question is how.

The 2020 ACC/AHA guideline bases the choice largely on age and life expectancy, because the long-term durability of TAVR valves beyond 10 years is still being defined and younger patients may need a second procedure:

Age Preferred approach (low surgical risk, suitable anatomy)
<65 years (or life expectancy >20 years) SAVR (mechanical or bioprosthetic)
65–80 years Shared decision: SAVR or transfemoral TAVR
>80 years (or life expectancy <10 years) or high surgical risk TAVR

The 2025 ESC/EACTS guideline uses a threshold of age 70. Other factors favoring SAVR: bicuspid valve, aortic dilation needing repair, need for other cardiac surgery, unfavorable anatomy for TAVR.

At 57, the choice between a mechanical valve (durable, lifelong warfarin) and a bioprosthetic valve (no warfarin, likely redo valve-in-valve later) is a shared decision.

Why not the others

  • (A) Balloon aortic valvuloplasty — Balloon valvuloplasty is a temporizing measure with early restenosis.
  • (B) Medical therapy with close surveillance — Medical therapy does not change the course of symptomatic severe AS, which carries a high mortality without valve replacement.
  • (C) Repeat echocardiography in 6 months — Symptomatic severe AS requires prompt intervention, not more surveillance.
  • (E) Transcatheter aortic valve replacement — TAVR is an option for older patients; for a low-risk patient younger than 65, surgical replacement is preferred because of uncertain long-term TAVR durability.
🎯 Educational objective

For symptomatic severe aortic stenosis in a low-risk patient younger than 65, surgical aortic valve replacement is preferred over TAVR.

CV-142.stem_html:
A 74-year-old man is evaluated for 3 months of exertional dyspnea and fatigue. He had a myocardial infarction 5 years ago. Medications are aspirin, atorvastatin, metoprolol succinate, sacubitril-valsartan and dapagliflozin.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 108/70 mm Hg and pulse rate is 66/min. A grade 2/6 systolic ejection murmur is heard at the right upper sternal border. S₂ is single.

Echocardiogram shows a calcified aortic valve with reduced leaflet opening, an aortic valve area of 0.8 cm², a mean gradient of 26 mm Hg, a peak velocity of 3.3 m/s and a stroke volume index of 28 mL/m². Left ventricular ejection fraction is 30% with regional wall-motion abnormalities.
CV-142.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next diagnostic step?

choices.D: Noncontrast CT calcium scoring of the aortic valve as the first test

CV-142.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Low-flow low-gradient aortic stenosis

The echocardiogram is discordant: the valve area suggests severe AS (≤1.0 cm²), but the gradient is low (<40 mm Hg) because the weak ventricle cannot generate flow (stroke volume index <35 mL/m²). This is classical low-flow, low-gradient AS with reduced EF (stage D2).

Two possibilities:

  • True severe AS — the stenosis caused or worsened the LV dysfunction; AVR helps
  • Pseudosevere AS — moderate AS in a weak ventricle that cannot open the valve fully; AVR does not help

Low-dose dobutamine stress echocardiography (up to 20 µg/kg/min) separates them:

With dobutamine Interpretation
Gradient rises to ≥40 mm Hg, AVA stays ≤1.0 cm² True severe AS → AVR
AVA increases to >1.0 cm², gradient stays low Pseudosevere → treat the cardiomyopathy
Stroke volume does not rise ≥20% (no contractile reserve) Indeterminate → CT calcium score; higher operative risk, but TAVR may still help

CT aortic valve calcium scoring is the key test for low-flow, low-gradient AS with preserved EF (paradoxical, stage D3) or when there is no contractile reserve.

Why not the others

  • (A) Cardiac MRI — Cardiac MRI assesses scar and function but does not resolve whether the stenosis is truly severe.
  • (B) Exercise treadmill testing — Exercise testing does not reliably increase flow in patients with reduced EF and is not the standard test here.
  • (D) Noncontrast CT calcium scoring of the aortic valve as the first test — Calcium scoring is most useful for low-flow, low-gradient AS with preserved EF or when dobutamine testing is inconclusive.
  • (E) Repeat transthoracic echocardiography in 3 months — Waiting delays a decision in a symptomatic patient who may benefit from AVR.
🎯 Educational objective

In low-flow, low-gradient aortic stenosis with reduced LVEF, use low-dose dobutamine stress echocardiography to distinguish true severe from pseudosevere stenosis.

CV-143.stem_html:
A 34-year-old man is evaluated after a murmur was heard at a preemployment examination. He has no symptoms and runs regularly. There is no family history of aortic disease known to him. He takes no medications.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 126/74 mm Hg in both arms and pulse rate is 64/min. Femoral pulses are normal without delay. An early systolic ejection click is heard at the apex, followed by a grade 2/6 systolic ejection murmur at the right upper sternal border.

Echocardiogram shows a bicuspid aortic valve with fusion of the right and left coronary cusps, mild aortic stenosis (peak velocity 2.4 m/s) and trace aortic regurgitation. The aortic root measures 3.8 cm, and the ascending aorta measures 4.3 cm. Left ventricular size and function are normal.
CV-143.lead: In addition to periodic imaging of his valve and aorta, which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation?

choices.C: Echocardiographic screening of his first-degree relatives

CV-143.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Bicuspid aortic valve

A bicuspid aortic valve (BAV) is the most common congenital heart defect (about 1%–2% of people, men more than women). Two problems develop over time:

  • Valve disease — premature aortic stenosis (often by age 50–60) or aortic regurgitation; endocarditis
  • Aortopathy — dilation of the ascending aorta or root (about 30%–50%), with a risk of dissection

BAV clusters in families (autosomal dominant with variable penetrance; about 9% of first-degree relatives also have BAV or aortopathy). The guidelines therefore recommend screening echocardiography of first-degree relatives of patients with BAV and aortopathy (Class 2a, ACC/AHA).

Surveillance: echocardiogram every 3–5 years for mild disease, with imaging of the ascending aorta (CT or MRI if not well seen); yearly when the aorta is ≥4.5 cm. Surgery on the aorta at ≥5.5 cm (≥5.0 cm with risk factors or at an experienced center). Look for coarctation — about 5%–10% of BAV patients have it.

Why not the others

  • (A) Antibiotic prophylaxis before dental procedures — Endocarditis prophylaxis is reserved for prosthetic valves, prior endocarditis, certain congenital disease and cardiac transplant valvulopathy; uncomplicated BAV does not qualify.
  • (B) Coronary angiography — He has no symptoms or findings to suggest coronary disease.
  • (D) Genetic testing for fibrillin-1 mutations — Fibrillin-1 testing is for suspected Marfan syndrome; he has no systemic features.
  • (E) Restriction from all aerobic exercise — Aerobic exercise is encouraged; only heavy isometric exercise is limited when the aorta is markedly dilated.
🎯 Educational objective

In bicuspid aortic valve with aortopathy, monitor the valve and aorta and recommend echocardiographic screening of first-degree relatives.

CV-144.stem_html:
A 58-year-old woman with known mitral valve prolapse comes for follow-up. She has no dyspnea, fatigue or palpitations and swims 1 km three times a week.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 122/72 mm Hg and pulse rate is 70/min and regular. A grade 3/6 holosystolic murmur is heard at the apex, radiating to the axilla, with a mid-systolic click. An S₃ is heard.

Echocardiogram shows a flail posterior mitral leaflet (P2 segment) with severe mitral regurgitation (effective regurgitant orifice area 0.5 cm²), left ventricular end-systolic diameter of 42 mm (37 mm 1 year ago) and left ventricular ejection fraction of 58% (65% 1 year ago). Pulmonary artery systolic pressure is 34 mm Hg. The repair center estimates a >95% likelihood of successful repair.
CV-144.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.D: Start metoprolol and repeat echocardiography in 1 year

CV-144.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Chronic severe primary mitral regurgitation

In chronic primary (degenerative) mitral regurgitation, the ventricle compensates for years with a normal or high EF because it ejects into the low-pressure left atrium. An EF that looks "normal" can already reflect hidden LV dysfunction.

Surgery is indicated in asymptomatic severe primary MR when early signs of LV dysfunction appear (Class 1):

  • LVEF ≤60%, or
  • LV end-systolic diameter ≥40 mm

She has both, and they are progressing. Mitral valve repair (preferred to replacement) at a center with high repair success preserves the subvalvular apparatus and LV function and restores normal life expectancy.

Severe primary MR Intervention
Symptoms Surgery (Class 1)
Asymptomatic, LVEF ≤60% or LVESD ≥40 mm Surgery (Class 1)
Asymptomatic, normal LV, repair likelihood >95% at expert center Repair reasonable (2a)
New AF or PASP >50 mm Hg Repair reasonable (2a)
High or prohibitive surgical risk, symptomatic TEER

Why not the others

  • (B) Repeat echocardiography in 6 months — Waiting with an EF of 58% and an LVESD of 42 mm risks irreversible LV dysfunction and worse long-term survival.
  • (C) Start lisinopril to reduce afterload — Vasodilators do not delay surgery or improve outcomes in normotensive patients with chronic primary MR.
  • (D) Start metoprolol and repeat echocardiography in 1 year — Beta-blockers do not change the natural history of primary MR.
  • (E) Transcatheter edge-to-edge repair — Transcatheter edge-to-edge repair is for symptomatic patients at high or prohibitive surgical risk; surgical repair is more durable in a low-risk patient.
🧠 Mnemonic

Primary MR surgery triggers: "60–40" — EF ≤60%, LVESD ≥40 mm.

🎯 Educational objective

Refer asymptomatic patients with severe primary mitral regurgitation for mitral valve repair when LVEF falls to ≤60% or LV end-systolic diameter reaches ≥40 mm.

CV-145.stem_html:
A 70-year-old man with ischemic cardiomyopathy (left ventricular ejection fraction 30%) has dyspnea walking 50 yards (NYHA class III) and two heart failure hospitalizations in the past year. For more than 6 months he has taken optimized doses of sacubitril-valsartan, metoprolol succinate, spironolactone and dapagliflozin. He has a cardiac resynchronization therapy defibrillator. He is not a candidate for further coronary revascularization; his surgical risk is high.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 112/68 mm Hg and pulse rate is 70/min. A grade 3/6 holosystolic murmur is heard at the apex. Jugular venous pressure is normal on his current diuretic dose.

Echocardiogram shows severe secondary (functional) mitral regurgitation from apical tethering of structurally normal leaflets, a left ventricular end-systolic diameter of 58 mm and a pulmonary artery systolic pressure of 46 mm Hg.
CV-145.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.C: Refer for left ventricular assist device implantation

CV-145.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Secondary mitral regurgitation

Secondary MR is a disease of the ventricle, not the valve leaflets: LV dilation and wall-motion abnormalities pull the papillary muscles apart and tether the leaflets. First-line treatment is therefore GDMT and CRT (which often reduce MR).

For persistent severe secondary MR with NYHA II–IV symptoms despite optimal GDMT and CRT, transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (TEER, MitraClip) is recommended (Class 2a) when anatomy is suitable — LVEF 20%–50%, LVESD ≤70 mm, PASP ≤70 mm Hg. In COAPT, TEER reduced HF hospitalization by about 50% and all-cause mortality by about a third. (MITRA-FR, which enrolled patients with more dilated ventricles and less GDMT, was neutral — selection matters.)

Surgical treatment of secondary MR does not improve survival and is usually considered only during CABG or other cardiac surgery.

Why not the others

  • (A) Add hydralazine–isosorbide dinitrate — H-ISDN is indicated for self-identified Black patients with persistent NYHA III–IV symptoms or for those who cannot take RAAS inhibitors; it does not address severe MR.
  • (B) Increase the loop diuretic dose — He is euvolemic; more diuretic does not treat the regurgitation.
  • (C) Refer for left ventricular assist device implantation — LVAD is reserved for stage D heart failure after other therapies fail or are not possible; TEER is the next evidence-based step.
  • (D) Surgical mitral valve replacement — Isolated mitral surgery for secondary MR has high risk in this patient and has not shown a survival benefit.
🎯 Educational objective

For symptomatic severe secondary mitral regurgitation despite optimal GDMT and CRT, with suitable anatomy (LVEF 20%–50%, LVESD ≤70 mm), transcatheter edge-to-edge repair reduces hospitalization and mortality.
