CV-146.stem_html:
A 27-year-old woman is evaluated after her primary care clinician heard a murmur at a routine visit. She has occasional brief palpitations but no chest pain, dyspnea or syncope. She takes no medications. She is tall and thin but has no lens dislocation or family history of aortic disease.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 108/66 mm Hg and pulse rate is 68/min. A mid-systolic click is heard at the apex, followed by a grade 2/6 late systolic murmur. When she stands up from a squatting position, the click moves closer to S₁ and the murmur becomes longer. With squatting, the click moves later in systole and the murmur shortens.
CV-146.lead: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
CV-146.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Mitral valve prolapse

Mitral valve prolapse (MVP): one or both mitral leaflets bow >2 mm into the left atrium during systole (myxomatous degeneration). It affects about 2%–3% of people.

The mid-systolic click is the sudden tensing of the prolapsing leaflet and chordae; a late systolic murmur follows if regurgitation develops.

Maneuvers depend on LV volume:

  • Smaller LV (standing, Valsalva, amyl nitrite) → prolapse happens earlier → click moves toward S₁, murmur longer
  • Larger LV (squatting, leg raise, handgrip) → prolapse later → click moves toward S₂, murmur shorter

Prognosis is usually excellent. Follow with echocardiography every 3–5 years if MR is mild. No endocarditis prophylaxis. Watch for "arrhythmic MVP" (bileaflet prolapse, mitral annular disjunction, T inversion in inferior leads, frequent complex PVCs) — a rare cause of sudden death.

Maneuver MVP HCM AS, MR, VSD
Standing / Valsalva (↓ preload) Earlier click, longer murmur Louder Softer
Squatting / leg raise (↑ preload) Later click, shorter Softer Louder
Handgrip (↑ afterload) Later click Softer MR, VSD louder

Why not the others

  • (A) Aortic stenosis — Aortic stenosis causes a crescendo-decrescendo murmur at the right upper sternal border that becomes softer with standing, without a mid-systolic click.
  • (B) Atrial septal defect — ASD causes fixed splitting of S₂ and a pulmonary flow murmur.
  • (C) Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy — The HCM murmur becomes louder with standing and Valsalva, but there is no mid-systolic click and the murmur is harsh and crescendo-decrescendo at the left sternal border.
  • (E) Ventricular septal defect — A VSD murmur is holosystolic at the left lower sternal border and is not preceded by a click.
🎯 Educational objective

Recognize mitral valve prolapse by a mid-systolic click and late systolic murmur that occur earlier and longer with maneuvers that reduce LV volume.

CV-147.stem_html:
A 38-year-old woman who emigrated from Guatemala 5 years ago is evaluated for 6 months of progressive dyspnea when climbing one flight of stairs. She had "rheumatic fever" as a child. She is in sinus rhythm. She does not plan pregnancy. Her only medication is metoprolol, started 2 months ago with partial improvement.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 112/70 mm Hg and pulse rate is 72/min and regular. An opening snap is followed by a low-pitched diastolic rumble at the apex with presystolic accentuation. S₁ is loud.

Transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiography show rheumatic mitral stenosis with a mitral valve area of 1.1 cm², a mean gradient of 11 mm Hg, pliable noncalcified leaflets with commissural fusion, mild mitral regurgitation and no left atrial thrombus. Pulmonary artery systolic pressure is 52 mm Hg. The Wilkins score is 7.
CV-147.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.A: Continue metoprolol and repeat echocardiography in 1 year

CV-147.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Rheumatic mitral stenosis — intervention

She has symptomatic severe rheumatic mitral stenosis (MVA ≤1.5 cm²). In rheumatic MS the leaflets fuse at the commissures, so they can be split apart with a balloon.

Percutaneous mitral balloon commissurotomy (PMBC) is the treatment of choice (Class 1) when:

  • Favorable valve morphology (pliable leaflets, little calcification or subvalvular thickening; Wilkins score ≤8)
  • No more than mild MR
  • No left atrial thrombus (TEE required before the procedure)

Results match surgical commissurotomy, with lower risk. Surgery is for unfavorable anatomy, ≥moderate MR, persistent LA thrombus, or need for other cardiac surgery.

Anticoagulation in MS: warfarin (not DOAC) for AF, prior embolism or left atrial thrombus.

Why not the others

  • (A) Continue metoprolol and repeat echocardiography in 1 year — Symptomatic severe MS with pulmonary hypertension needs intervention; heart-rate control only lengthens diastolic filling time.
  • (C) Start warfarin — Anticoagulation is indicated for AF, prior embolism or LA thrombus, none of which she has.
  • (D) Surgical mitral valve replacement — Valve replacement is reserved for patients whose anatomy is unsuitable for balloon commissurotomy.
  • (E) Transcatheter edge-to-edge mitral repair — Edge-to-edge repair treats mitral regurgitation and would worsen stenosis.
🎯 Educational objective

Treat symptomatic severe rheumatic mitral stenosis with favorable anatomy, no more than mild MR and no left atrial thrombus with percutaneous mitral balloon commissurotomy.

CV-148.stem_html:
A 56-year-old man with a bileaflet mechanical mitral valve placed 6 years ago comes for a routine visit. He missed several warfarin doses over the past month while traveling. He feels well, with no dyspnea, neurologic symptoms or embolic events.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 126/76 mm Hg and pulse rate is 70/min and regular. Crisp mechanical valve clicks are heard. There are no new murmurs.

Transthoracic echocardiogram shows a normal transmitral gradient for his prosthesis. Transesophageal echocardiography shows normal leaflet motion and a small (0.6 cm²), nonobstructive thrombus on the atrial side of the sewing ring.

INR1.4 (target 3.0)
CV-148.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
CV-148.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Mechanical valve thrombosis

Mechanical valve thrombosis usually follows subtherapeutic anticoagulation. Management depends on whether the thrombus obstructs the valve and on its size:

Situation Management
Nonobstructive, small (<0.8 cm²), no embolism Optimize anticoagulation: IV unfractionated heparin, then warfarin at the therapeutic INR (± low-dose aspirin); serial imaging
Nonobstructive, large (≥0.8 cm²) or embolism Consider surgery or fibrinolysis
Obstructive (stuck leaflet, high gradient), especially with HF Urgent surgery or low-dose slow-infusion fibrinolysis, chosen by the heart team on surgical risk, thrombus size, NYHA class and fibrinolytic contraindications

His thrombus is small and nonobstructive, valve function is normal and he has no embolism — so intensify anticoagulation and image again in weeks to confirm resolution. Explore why doses were missed and arrange INR self-testing or closer monitoring.

Why not the others

  • (A) Emergency valve replacement — Surgery is for obstructive thrombosis, large thrombi, embolism, or failure of anticoagulation.
  • (C) Low-dose fibrinolytic therapy — Fibrinolysis carries risks of embolism and bleeding and is reserved for obstructive or larger thrombi.
  • (D) No change in therapy — A thrombus on a mechanical valve with a subtherapeutic INR requires intensified anticoagulation.
  • (E) Switch warfarin to apixaban — DOACs are contraindicated with mechanical heart valves.
🎯 Educational objective

Treat small nonobstructive mechanical valve thrombus with intravenous heparin and therapeutic warfarin; reserve surgery or fibrinolysis for obstructive or large thrombi.

CV-149.stem_html:
A 76-year-old woman is evaluated for newly diagnosed persistent atrial fibrillation. She underwent surgical aortic valve replacement with a bioprosthetic valve 4 years ago for severe aortic stenosis. She has hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. She has no history of bleeding. Medications are aspirin, 81 mg daily, lisinopril and metformin.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 132/78 mm Hg and pulse rate is 82/min and irregular. A soft systolic flow murmur is heard at the right upper sternal border.

Echocardiogram shows a normally functioning aortic bioprosthesis and no mitral stenosis.

Creatinine0.9 mg/dL
Hemoglobin13.4 g/dL
CV-149.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate stroke-prevention strategy?
CV-149.explain_html:
Correct answer: A AF with a bioprosthetic valve

Her CHA₂DS₂-VASc score is 5 (age ≥75 = 2, female, hypertension, diabetes), so she needs oral anticoagulation.

Bioprosthetic valves are not "valvular AF." The DOAC exclusion applies only to mechanical valves and moderate-to-severe rheumatic mitral stenosis. In RIVER, rivaroxaban was noninferior to warfarin in patients with AF and a bioprosthetic mitral valve, and DOACs performed similarly in bioprosthetic subgroups of the large AF trials. The 2023 AF guideline recommends a DOAC as an alternative to warfarin with a bioprosthetic valve (≥3 months after implantation).

Stop the aspirin when anticoagulation starts (unless she has another indication) to reduce bleeding.

Why not the others

  • (B) Aspirin plus clopidogrel — Dual antiplatelet therapy is less effective than anticoagulation for stroke prevention in AF and causes similar bleeding.
  • (C) Continue aspirin alone — Aspirin alone does not adequately prevent cardioembolic stroke.
  • (D) Left atrial appendage occlusion — LAAO is for patients who cannot take long-term anticoagulation; she has no contraindication.
  • (E) No antithrombotic therapy — Her stroke risk is high; withholding antithrombotic therapy is inappropriate.
🎯 Educational objective

Patients with atrial fibrillation and a bioprosthetic heart valve may be treated with a DOAC; only mechanical valves and moderate–severe rheumatic mitral stenosis require warfarin.

CV-150.stem_html: Several patients are scheduled for dental extractions with manipulation of the gingival tissue at a community dental clinic. The dentist asks which of them should receive antibiotic prophylaxis against infective endocarditis.
CV-150.lead: Which of the following patients should receive antibiotic prophylaxis before the procedure?

choices.B: A 52-year-old man with a bicuspid aortic valve and mild stenosis
choices.C: A 60-year-old man with a drug-eluting coronary stent
choices.D: A 64-year-old woman with mitral valve prolapse and moderate regurgitation
choices.E: A 78-year-old man who underwent transcatheter aortic valve replacement

CV-150.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Endocarditis prophylaxis

The 2021 AHA scientific statement (and 2023 ESC guideline) limit antibiotic prophylaxis before dental procedures that manipulate gingival tissue, the periapical region of teeth or perforate the oral mucosa to patients at highest risk of adverse outcomes from endocarditis:

Prophylaxis recommended
Prosthetic cardiac valve — surgical or transcatheter (TAVR, TEER device), or prosthetic material used for valve repair (annuloplasty rings, chords)
Previous infective endocarditis
Unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart disease, or repaired CHD with residual shunt or regurgitation at a prosthetic site; any repaired CHD with prosthetic material in the first 6 months
Cardiac transplant recipients with valvulopathy
Ventricular assist devices (ESC 2023)

Standard regimen: amoxicillin 2 g orally 30–60 minutes before the procedure (cephalexin, azithromycin or doxycycline for penicillin allergy; clindamycin is no longer recommended).

Prophylaxis is not recommended for most native valve disease, HCM, MVP, bicuspid valves, coronary stents, pacemakers/ICDs (in the AHA statement) or for GI/GU procedures. Good oral hygiene matters more.

Why not the others

  • (A) A 45-year-old woman with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy — Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is not a high-risk condition for endocarditis prophylaxis.
  • (B) A 52-year-old man with a bicuspid aortic valve and mild stenosis — Bicuspid aortic valve without prior endocarditis or prosthetic material does not require prophylaxis.
  • (C) A 60-year-old man with a drug-eluting coronary stent — Coronary stents do not require endocarditis prophylaxis.
  • (D) A 64-year-old woman with mitral valve prolapse and moderate regurgitation — Mitral valve prolapse, even with regurgitation, does not require prophylaxis.
🎯 Educational objective

Limit dental endocarditis prophylaxis to patients with prosthetic valves (including TAVR), prior endocarditis, certain congenital heart disease and transplant valvulopathy.

CV-151.stem_html:
A 67-year-old man is evaluated for 3 weeks of fevers, night sweats, fatigue and a 3-kg (6.6-lb) weight loss. He had dental cleaning 6 weeks ago. He has known mitral valve prolapse. He has taken no antibiotics.

On physical examination, temperature is 38.3 °C (100.9 °F), blood pressure is 128/72 mm Hg, pulse rate is 96/min, and respiration rate is 16/min. A new grade 3/6 holosystolic murmur is heard at the apex. There are splinter hemorrhages under two fingernails and small, painless macules on both palms. The spleen tip is palpable. He is alert and hemodynamically stable, with no neurologic deficits.

Leukocyte count11400/µL
Hemoglobin10.8 g/dL
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate78 mm/h
Urinalysis10–20 erythrocytes/hpf
CV-151.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Begin empiric vancomycin immediately, then obtain blood cultures
choices.B: CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis
choices.C: Obtain one set of blood cultures and start ceftriaxone
choices.D: Obtain three sets of blood cultures from separate sites, then perform echocardiography
choices.E: Perform transesophageal echocardiography before any blood cultures

CV-151.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Suspected endocarditis — initial evaluation

He likely has subacute infective endocarditis (viridans streptococci after dental work on a prolapsing valve): fever, a new regurgitant murmur, splinter hemorrhages, Janeway lesions (painless palmar macules), splenomegaly, anemia, high ESR and hematuria (immune complex glomerulonephritis).

In a stable patient with a subacute course, the priority is microbiologic diagnosis:

  • At least three sets of blood cultures from separate venipunctures, ideally spaced over time (≥1 hour between first and last), before antibiotics
  • Then transthoracic echocardiography, followed by TEE if TTE is negative and suspicion remains, or if complications (abscess) are suspected
  • Start empiric antibiotics after cultures — immediately if the patient is acutely ill or septic

Prior antibiotics are the most common cause of culture-negative endocarditis.

Modified Duke (2023 ISCVID) major criteria
Typical organism in ≥2 separate blood cultures (viridans strep, S. gallolyticus, HACEK, S. aureus, E. faecalis)
Echo/CT/PET evidence of endocardial involvement (vegetation, abscess, new regurgitation, prosthetic valve dehiscence)

Why not the others

  • (A) Begin empiric vancomycin immediately, then obtain blood cultures — Giving antibiotics before cultures in a stable patient may sterilize the blood and make the organism impossible to identify.
  • (B) CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis — Imaging for emboli may follow, but it does not replace blood cultures and echocardiography.
  • (C) Obtain one set of blood cultures and start ceftriaxone — A single set of cultures is insufficient to establish continuous bacteremia or to interpret skin contaminants.
  • (E) Perform transesophageal echocardiography before any blood cultures — Cultures should be drawn first; TEE is usually performed after TTE or when complications are suspected.
🎯 Educational objective

In a hemodynamically stable patient with suspected subacute endocarditis, obtain three sets of blood cultures before antibiotics, then echocardiography.

CV-152.stem_html:
A 63-year-old man is hospitalized with methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus native aortic valve endocarditis. He has received intravenous cefazolin for 5 days, and blood cultures became negative on day 3. He continues to have fevers.

On physical examination, temperature is 38.4 °C (101.1 °F), blood pressure is 118/58 mm Hg, and pulse rate is 64/min. A grade 2/6 early diastolic murmur is heard at the left sternal border. The lungs are clear.

Daily electrocardiograms show that the PR interval has lengthened from 0.18 second at admission to 0.28 second today. Transesophageal echocardiography shows a 9-mm aortic valve vegetation, moderate aortic regurgitation and a perivalvular aortic root abscess.
CV-152.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
CV-152.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Endocarditis with perivalvular abscess

A new conduction abnormality (PR prolongation or AV block) in aortic valve endocarditis signals extension of infection into the aortic root near the AV node and His bundle — a perivalvular abscess. Persistent fever despite sterile blood cultures is another clue.

Early surgery (during the initial hospitalization, before completing antibiotics) is indicated for:

Indications for early surgery in left-sided IE
Heart failure from valve dysfunction
Uncontrolled infection: abscess, heart block, fistula, enlarging vegetation; persistent bacteremia >5–7 days on appropriate therapy
Fungal or highly resistant organisms
Embolism prevention: vegetation >10 mm with embolism, or very large (>15–30 mm) mobile vegetations
Relapsing prosthetic valve infection

Antibiotics alone rarely sterilize an abscess.

Why not the others

  • (A) Add gentamicin to cefazolin — Gentamicin adds nephrotoxicity without benefit for native-valve S. aureus endocarditis and does not treat an abscess.
  • (B) Add rifampin to cefazolin — Rifampin is used for prosthetic valve staphylococcal infection; it does not replace surgical drainage of a root abscess.
  • (D) Extend intravenous antibiotics to 8 weeks — Longer antibiotic courses do not cure a perivalvular abscess.
  • (E) Implant a permanent pacemaker — Pacing may become necessary, but the infection that is destroying the conduction system must be treated surgically.
🎯 Educational objective

New AV conduction delay in aortic valve endocarditis suggests a perivalvular abscess; abscess and heart block are indications for early surgery.

CV-153.topic: Tricuspid endocarditis in a person who injects drugs
CV-153.stem_html:
A 29-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of 1 week of fever, pleuritic chest pain and cough with blood-streaked sputum. He injects heroin and fentanyl daily.

On physical examination, temperature is 39.4 °C (102.9 °F), blood pressure is 106/62 mm Hg, pulse rate is 118/min, and respiration rate is 26/min. Oxygen saturation is 92% breathing ambient air. There are track marks on both forearms. A grade 2/6 holosystolic murmur is heard at the left lower sternal border that increases with inspiration. Prominent v waves are seen in the jugular venous pulse.

CT of the chest shows multiple bilateral peripheral nodules of various sizes, several with cavitation, and some with a "feeding vessel" sign. Two of two sets of blood cultures grow gram-positive cocci in clusters.
CV-153.lead: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
CV-153.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Tricuspid endocarditis in a person who injects drugs

Right-sided (tricuspid) endocarditis is typical of people who inject drugs, most often caused by Staphylococcus aureus. The infected tricuspid valve showers septic emboli to the lungs, producing:

  • Multiple peripheral nodules, often cavitating, at different stages, with a feeding vessel sign
  • Pleuritic pain, cough, hemoptysis, sometimes empyema
  • A tricuspid regurgitation murmur that increases with inspiration (Carvallo sign) and large v waves

Systemic emboli (stroke, Janeway lesions) are uncommon unless there is left-sided involvement or a shunt (PFO).

Management: cultures, echocardiography, IV antistaphylococcal therapy (cefazolin or nafcillin for MSSA; vancomycin or daptomycin for MRSA), addiction treatment (start buprenorphine or methadone in the hospital), naloxone, and hepatitis C/HIV testing. Surgery for persistent sepsis, very large vegetations (>20 mm) with recurrent emboli, or right heart failure from severe TR.

Why not the others

  • (A) Aspiration lung abscess — Aspiration abscess usually forms a single cavity in dependent segments, not multiple peripheral nodules with staphylococcal bacteremia.
  • (B) Granulomatosis with polyangiitis — GPA can cause cavitary nodules, but not with staphylococcal bacteremia and a new tricuspid murmur.
  • (C) Metastatic malignancy — Metastases rarely cavitate this rapidly and do not cause fever with positive blood cultures.
  • (D) Reactivation pulmonary tuberculosis — TB typically causes upper-lobe cavitation with a subacute course and does not cause staphylococcal bacteremia.
🎯 Educational objective

In people who inject drugs, multiple cavitating peripheral lung nodules with S. aureus bacteremia and a tricuspid regurgitation murmur indicate tricuspid endocarditis with septic pulmonary emboli.

CV-154.stem_html:
A 71-year-old woman is admitted with 2 weeks of fevers and malaise. She underwent surgical aortic valve replacement with a bioprosthesis 4 months ago. She takes aspirin and atorvastatin.

On physical examination, temperature is 38.2 °C (100.8 °F), blood pressure is 124/66 mm Hg, and pulse rate is 92/min. A grade 2/6 systolic murmur is heard at the right upper sternal border. Neurologic examination is normal.

Four of four sets of blood cultures grow methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus epidermidis (vancomycin MIC 1 µg/mL, rifampin susceptible). Transesophageal echocardiography shows a 6-mm vegetation on the bioprosthesis without abscess, dehiscence or significant regurgitation.

Creatinine0.9 mg/dL
CV-154.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate antibiotic regimen?
CV-154.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Prosthetic valve staphylococcal endocarditis

Coagulase-negative staphylococci (especially S. epidermidis) are a leading cause of early prosthetic valve endocarditis (within 1 year of surgery), usually acquired at the time of surgery and methicillin-resistant.

Staphylococci form biofilm on prosthetic material. Rifampin penetrates biofilm and kills adherent organisms, but resistance emerges quickly if used alone. The AHA regimen for staphylococcal prosthetic valve endocarditis:

Organism Regimen
MRSA or methicillin-resistant CoNS Vancomycin + rifampin ≥6 weeks + gentamicin for the first 2 weeks
MSSA / methicillin-susceptible CoNS Nafcillin/oxacillin (or cefazolin) + rifampin ≥6 weeks + gentamicin 2 weeks

Start rifampin once blood cultures clear (some experts add it after 3–5 days of the other drugs) to limit resistance. Obtain early cardiac surgical consultation — many patients with staphylococcal PVE need surgery.

Why not the others

  • (A) Cefazolin plus gentamicin for 4 weeks — Cefazolin does not cover methicillin-resistant staphylococci, and 4 weeks without biofilm-active rifampin is inadequate for prosthetic valves.
  • (B) Daptomycin alone for 2 weeks — Two weeks of a single drug is far too short for prosthetic valve endocarditis.
  • (C) Oral linezolid alone for 4 weeks — Oral linezolid alone is not a standard regimen for prosthetic valve endocarditis and lacks the biofilm activity of rifampin combinations.
  • (D) Vancomycin alone for 4 weeks — Vancomycin alone without rifampin has higher failure rates on prosthetic material.
🎯 Educational objective

Treat methicillin-resistant staphylococcal prosthetic valve endocarditis with vancomycin plus rifampin for at least 6 weeks and gentamicin for the first 2 weeks, with early surgical evaluation.

CV-155.stem_html:
A 52-year-old man who has been experiencing homelessness for 3 years is admitted with 2 months of intermittent fevers, fatigue and weight loss. He has severe alcohol use disorder. He has had no recent antibiotics. He says he has "itchy bugs" in his clothes.

On physical examination, temperature is 38.1 °C (100.6 °F), blood pressure is 124/62 mm Hg, and pulse rate is 98/min. There are excoriations over the trunk, and lice are seen in the seams of his clothing. A grade 2/6 early diastolic murmur is heard at the left sternal border.

Transesophageal echocardiography shows a 12-mm vegetation on the aortic valve with moderate regurgitation. Three sets of blood cultures drawn before antibiotics show no growth after 5 days of incubation.

Leukocyte count9100/µL
Creatinine1.6 mg/dL
Urinalysis2+ protein10–20 erythrocytes/hpf
CV-155.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnostic test?

choices.E: Prolonged incubation of blood cultures for HACEK organisms

CV-155.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Culture-negative endocarditis

Culture-negative endocarditis is most often caused by prior antibiotics. When none were given, think of organisms that do not grow in routine blood cultures:

Organism Exposure clue Test
Bartonella quintana Homelessness, body lice, alcohol use disorder Serology (IgG ≥1:800), PCR of valve tissue
Bartonella henselae Cats (scratches, fleas) Serology, PCR
Coxiella burnetii (Q fever) Farm animals, unpasteurized milk, parturient animals Phase I IgG serology
Brucella Unpasteurized dairy, livestock, travel Serology, prolonged culture
Tropheryma whipplei Arthralgia, diarrhea Valve PCR
Fungi IV drug use, prosthetic valves, immunosuppression Fungal cultures, β-D-glucan

B. quintana (trench fever) is transmitted by body lice and is a classic cause of aortic valve endocarditis in people experiencing homelessness. Treatment: doxycycline plus gentamicin (or rifampin), often with valve surgery.

HACEK organisms now usually grow in standard automated blood culture systems within 5 days — prolonged incubation is no longer needed.

Why not the others

  • (B) Brucella serology — Brucella is linked to unpasteurized dairy or livestock exposure, which he lacks.
  • (C) Coxiella burnetii serology — Q fever is linked to farm animal exposure; body lice point instead to Bartonella quintana.
  • (D) Fungal blood cultures — Fungal endocarditis is more likely with prosthetic valves, injection drug use or immunosuppression.
  • (E) Prolonged incubation of blood cultures for HACEK organisms — Modern culture systems detect HACEK organisms within 5 days, and his exposures point to Bartonella.
🎯 Educational objective

In culture-negative endocarditis in a person experiencing homelessness with body lice, test for Bartonella quintana with serology.

CV-156.stem_html:
A 44-year-old man has received 12 days of intravenous ceftriaxone for native mitral valve endocarditis caused by penicillin-susceptible viridans group streptococci. Blood cultures became negative within 48 hours. He has been afebrile for 9 days. Transesophageal echocardiography shows a 7-mm vegetation without abscess, perforation or significant regurgitation. He has no heart failure or embolic events. He is reliable and wants to go home, but he has a history of injection drug use (in remission for 4 years on buprenorphine), and his team prefers to avoid a long-term central venous catheter.

On physical examination, temperature is 36.8 °C (98.2 °F), blood pressure is 122/74 mm Hg, and pulse rate is 72/min.

C-reactive protein12 mg/L (148 mg/L at admission)
Leukocyte count7200/µL
CV-156.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate way to complete his antibiotic therapy?

choices.A: Oral amoxicillin, 500 mg three times daily for 7 days
choices.C: Single dose of intramuscular benzathine penicillin
choices.E: Switch to an oral two-drug regimen to complete about 6 weeks

CV-156.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Oral step-down therapy for endocarditis

The POET trial randomized clinically stable patients with left-sided endocarditis (streptococci, E. faecalis, S. aureus or CoNS) who had received ≥10 days of IV therapy (≥7 days after valve surgery) to continued IV therapy or a switch to high-dose oral two-drug combinations (for streptococci, for example, amoxicillin plus rifampin, or linezolid plus rifampin). Oral step-down was noninferior for death, embolism, relapse and unplanned surgery — and remained so at 5 years.

The 2023 ESC guideline supports oral step-down (Class 2a) when the patient is stable, afebrile, has cleared bacteremia, has no abscess or need for surgery, and can take oral drugs reliably. It avoids prolonged hospitalization and central lines — especially helpful for people with a history of injection drug use.

Total duration for native valve streptococcal endocarditis remains about 4–6 weeks; doses are higher than usual outpatient doses.

Why not the others

  • (A) Oral amoxicillin, 500 mg three times daily for 7 days — Standard-dose amoxicillin for 7 days is far too short and too low a dose to complete treatment of endocarditis.
  • (B) Oral doxycycline alone for 4 weeks — Doxycycline alone is not an established regimen for streptococcal endocarditis.
  • (C) Single dose of intramuscular benzathine penicillin — A single intramuscular dose cannot complete therapy for endocarditis.
  • (D) Stop antibiotics now — Twelve days is too short for native valve endocarditis; stopping now risks relapse.
🎯 Educational objective

In stable patients with left-sided endocarditis who have received at least 10 days of IV therapy and have no complications, switching to a high-dose oral two-drug regimen is noninferior to continued IV therapy.

CV-157.stem_html:
A 61-year-old man is evaluated for 6 months of leg swelling and abdominal fullness. For 2 years he has had episodes of facial flushing and watery diarrhea several times a week. He does not drink alcohol.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg and pulse rate is 88/min. There is facial telangiectasia. Jugular venous pressure is 14 cm H₂O with large v waves. A holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border increases with inspiration, and a systolic ejection murmur is heard at the left upper sternal border. The liver is enlarged and pulsatile. There is 2+ leg edema.

Echocardiogram shows thickened, retracted and immobile tricuspid and pulmonic valve leaflets with severe tricuspid regurgitation and moderate pulmonic stenosis. Left-sided valves are normal. CT of the abdomen shows multiple liver masses and a small ileal mass with mesenteric fibrosis.
CV-157.lead: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
CV-157.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Carcinoid heart disease

Carcinoid syndrome occurs when a neuroendocrine (carcinoid) tumor — usually from the small bowel — metastasizes to the liver, so vasoactive substances (especially serotonin) bypass hepatic inactivation and reach the systemic circulation: flushing, diarrhea, bronchospasm, telangiectasia.

Carcinoid heart disease develops in up to 50% of patients with the syndrome. Serotonin stimulates fibroblasts to lay down plaque-like fibrous tissue on the valves of the right heart, causing tricuspid regurgitation (most common) and pulmonic stenosis/regurgitation. The lungs inactivate serotonin (monoamine oxidase), so left-sided valves are spared — unless there is a PFO, a bronchial carcinoid or a very high hormone burden.

Diagnosis: 24-hour urinary 5-HIAA or plasma 5-HIAA, NT-proBNP, echocardiography. Treatment: somatostatin analogs (octreotide, lanreotide), telotristat for diarrhea, tumor control, and valve replacement for severe disease.

Why not the others

  • (B) Ebstein anomaly — Ebstein anomaly is a congenital apical displacement of the tricuspid valve and does not cause flushing, diarrhea or liver masses.
  • (C) Ergot-derivative valvulopathy — Ergot derivatives (cabergoline at high doses, pergolide) and fenfluramine cause similar serotonergic valve lesions, but he takes no such drugs and has metastatic tumor.
  • (D) Rheumatic heart disease — Rheumatic heart disease primarily affects the mitral and aortic valves.
  • (E) Tricuspid valve endocarditis — Endocarditis causes fever and vegetations, not thickened, retracted leaflets with flushing and liver metastases.
🎯 Educational objective

Recognize carcinoid heart disease (right-sided valve fibrosis — TR and pulmonic stenosis — with flushing, diarrhea and liver metastases) and confirm with 5-HIAA.

CV-158.stem_html:
A 22-year-old woman who emigrated from Haiti 1 year ago comes to establish care. At age 16 she had acute rheumatic fever with carditis; echocardiography now shows mild mitral regurgitation and mild mitral leaflet thickening from rheumatic heart disease. She has had no recurrence since. She has no penicillin allergy. She is a teacher's aide at an elementary school.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 110/68 mm Hg and pulse rate is 70/min. A soft apical holosystolic murmur is heard.
CV-158.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation to prevent recurrent rheumatic fever?

choices.B: Intramuscular benzathine penicillin G every 4 weeks for 1 year
choices.C: Intramuscular benzathine penicillin G every 4 weeks until age 40
choices.D: No prophylaxis because she has had no recurrence
choices.E: Oral penicillin for 10 days whenever she has a sore throat

CV-158.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Secondary prevention of rheumatic fever

After acute rheumatic fever, recurrent group A streptococcal pharyngitis can trigger recurrences that worsen valve damage. Secondary prophylaxis with intramuscular benzathine penicillin G (every 4 weeks; every 3 weeks in high-incidence settings) is the most effective intervention.

Duration (AHA):

History Duration of prophylaxis
Rheumatic fever without carditis 5 years or until age 21, whichever is longer
Carditis without residual heart disease 10 years or until age 21, whichever is longer
Carditis with residual valve disease 10 years or until age 40, whichever is longer; sometimes lifelong

She had carditis with residual valve disease at 16: 10 years would end at age 26, but until age 40 is longer, so she should continue to age 40. Her job with frequent exposure to children also supports continued prophylaxis. Reassess at 40 — patients with moderate–severe disease or valve surgery may continue lifelong.

Why not the others

  • (A) Amoxicillin before dental procedures only — Dental prophylaxis prevents endocarditis, not rheumatic fever, and is not indicated for native rheumatic valve disease without other high-risk features.
  • (B) Intramuscular benzathine penicillin G every 4 weeks for 1 year — One year is far too short after rheumatic carditis.
  • (D) No prophylaxis because she has had no recurrence — Recurrence risk persists for years, particularly with exposure to school-aged children.
  • (E) Oral penicillin for 10 days whenever she has a sore throat — Treating each sore throat misses asymptomatic streptococcal infections, which can also trigger recurrences.
🎯 Educational objective

After rheumatic fever with carditis and residual valve disease, give benzathine penicillin G every 4 weeks for 10 years or until age 40, whichever is longer.

CV-159.stem_html:
A 38-year-old woman is evaluated for her third episode of pericarditis in 14 months. The first episode followed a viral illness and was treated with ibuprofen and colchicine for 3 months. Two months after stopping, pain recurred and she was given prednisone, 40 mg daily; each attempt to taper below 10 mg daily has caused recurrence despite continued colchicine. She now has sharp positional chest pain again. She has gained 8 kg (17.6 lb) and has new insomnia. Antinuclear antibody testing and tuberculosis screening are negative.

On physical examination, temperature is 37.6 °C (99.7 °F), blood pressure is 124/78 mm Hg, and pulse rate is 92/min. A pericardial friction rub is heard.

Electrocardiogram shows diffuse ST-segment elevation with PR depression. Echocardiogram shows a small effusion without tamponade. C-reactive protein is 42 mg/L.
CV-159.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Increase prednisone to 1 mg/kg daily long term
choices.D: Six weeks of empiric antituberculous therapy

CV-159.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Recurrent pericarditis

She has recurrent, glucocorticoid-dependent pericarditis with colchicine failure and signs of systemic inflammation (fever, high CRP) — an autoinflammatory phenotype driven by the NLRP3 inflammasome and interleukin-1.

IL-1 blockade is the recommended next step (2025 ESC pericardial guideline; ACC expert pathway):

  • Rilonacept (IL-1α/β trap, weekly subcutaneous) — in RHAPSODY, it rapidly resolved recurrences and reduced the risk of recurrence by about 96% versus placebo, allowing glucocorticoid withdrawal
  • Anakinra (IL-1 receptor antagonist) — AIRTRIP trial

Treatment is usually continued for months, with slow tapering. Pericardiectomy is reserved for refractory cases after medical options fail.

Pericarditis step Therapy
First episode NSAID/aspirin + colchicine 3 months
First recurrence NSAID + colchicine 6 months
Refractory / steroid-dependent IL-1 blocker (rilonacept, anakinra); low-dose glucocorticoid if needed
Failure of medical therapy Pericardiectomy

Why not the others

  • (A) Increase prednisone to 1 mg/kg daily long term — High-dose glucocorticoids increase recurrence risk and cause cumulative toxicity, which she already has.
  • (B) Pericardiectomy — Pericardiectomy is a last resort for refractory disease after IL-1 blockade, given its surgical risk.
  • (D) Six weeks of empiric antituberculous therapy — She has no evidence of tuberculosis; empiric therapy is not indicated.
  • (E) Stop colchicine — Colchicine reduces recurrences and should be continued with other therapy.
🎯 Educational objective

Treat recurrent glucocorticoid-dependent pericarditis that fails colchicine with an interleukin-1 blocker such as rilonacept.

CV-160.stem_html:
A 44-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of 2 days of sharp chest pain that is worse when he lies flat and better when he sits forward. He had an upper respiratory infection 1 week ago. He takes no medications and does not take anticoagulants.

On physical examination, temperature is 37.5 °C (99.5 °F), blood pressure is 128/80 mm Hg with a 6-mm Hg inspiratory decline, pulse rate is 96/min, and respiration rate is 18/min. A pericardial friction rub is heard. Jugular venous pressure is normal.

Electrocardiogram shows diffuse concave ST-segment elevation and PR-segment depression. Echocardiogram shows normal ventricular function and a circumferential pericardial effusion measuring 24 mm in diastole without chamber collapse.

High-sensitivity troponin Ibelow the 99th percentile
C-reactive protein38 mg/L
CV-160.lead: Which of the following findings most strongly indicates that he should be admitted to the hospital rather than treated as an outpatient?

choices.A: Concave ST-segment elevation with PR depression

CV-160.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Acute pericarditis — high-risk features

Most patients with acute pericarditis are low risk and can be treated as outpatients with an NSAID (or aspirin) plus colchicine. High-risk features predict complications (tamponade, constriction, specific causes such as bacterial, tuberculous or neoplastic disease) and call for admission and investigation:

Major predictors of poor prognosis Minor predictors
Fever >38 °C Myopericarditis (troponin rise)
Subacute onset (days to weeks) Immunosuppression
Large effusion (>20 mm) or tamponade Trauma
No response to NSAIDs after 1 week Oral anticoagulant therapy

His effusion of 24 mm is a major predictor — he should be hospitalized for monitoring and evaluation for a specific cause, even though there is no tamponade now.

Why not the others

  • (A) Concave ST-segment elevation with PR depression — Diffuse concave ST elevation with PR depression is the expected ECG pattern of pericarditis, not a sign of high risk.
  • (C) Pericardial friction rub — A friction rub is a diagnostic finding, not a marker of poor prognosis.
  • (D) Pleuritic, positional chest pain — Pleuritic, positional pain is typical of pericarditis and does not indicate high risk.
  • (E) Recent upper respiratory infection — A preceding viral infection suggests the common idiopathic/viral form, which usually has a benign course.
🎯 Educational objective

Admit patients with acute pericarditis who have high-risk features: fever >38 °C, subacute onset, large effusion (>20 mm) or tamponade, or failure of NSAID therapy.

CV-161.stem_html:
A 58-year-old man with end-stage kidney disease on hemodialysis three times weekly is evaluated for 3 days of pleuritic chest pain and low-grade fever. He has missed four of his last eight dialysis sessions.

On physical examination, temperature is 37.9 °C (100.2 °F), blood pressure is 152/86 mm Hg with a 7-mm Hg inspiratory decline, pulse rate is 98/min, and respiration rate is 18/min. A loud three-component pericardial friction rub is heard. Jugular venous pressure is 9 cm H₂O. There is 1+ leg edema.

Electrocardiogram shows sinus tachycardia without ST-segment elevation. Echocardiogram shows a moderate circumferential pericardial effusion without right atrial or right ventricular collapse.

Blood urea nitrogen128 mg/dL
Potassium5.4 mEq/L
Hemoglobin9.6 g/dL
CV-161.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
CV-161.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Uremic pericarditis

Uremic pericarditis develops in patients with advanced kidney failure before dialysis or with inadequate dialysis (missed sessions, here). Unlike viral pericarditis, the ECG often lacks diffuse ST elevation because the inflammation does not involve the epicardium.

Treatment is intensive dialysis — daily sessions for 1–2 weeks — which resolves most cases. Use heparin-free or minimal-heparin dialysis to reduce the risk of hemorrhagic effusion and tamponade. Watch for intradialytic hypotension, which can signal tamponade.

Pericardiocentesis is reserved for tamponade or for large effusions that do not respond to intensified dialysis.

Why not the others

  • (A) Colchicine at full dose — Colchicine is renally cleared and its dose must be greatly reduced or avoided in dialysis patients; it does not treat the cause.
  • (B) High-dose ibuprofen — NSAIDs have limited benefit in uremic pericarditis and cause GI bleeding and loss of residual kidney function.
  • (D) Pericardiocentesis — Pericardiocentesis is unnecessary without tamponade and carries procedural risk.
  • (E) Prednisone, 1 mg/kg daily — Glucocorticoids are not first-line and do not address the uremia that caused the pericarditis.
🎯 Educational objective

Treat uremic or dialysis-associated pericarditis with intensified (daily) heparin-free hemodialysis; reserve pericardiocentesis for tamponade or refractory effusion.

CV-162.stem_html:
A 20-year-old college soccer player is evaluated 2 weeks after hospitalization for myopericarditis that followed a viral illness. He presented with positional chest pain, diffuse ST-segment elevation and a troponin I peak of 2,400 ng/L. Cardiac MRI showed subepicardial late gadolinium enhancement of the lateral wall with a left ventricular ejection fraction of 54%. He was treated with ibuprofen and colchicine and now has no symptoms. He asks when he can return to training and competition.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 118/70 mm Hg and pulse rate is 60/min. Examination is normal.
CV-162.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation about return to competitive sports?

choices.B: Return after 1 week without any symptoms
choices.C: Return after 3–6 months if repeat testing is normal
choices.D: Return as soon as C-reactive protein normalizes
choices.E: Return once chest pain has been absent for 2 weeks

CV-162.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Myopericarditis — return to sport

Myocarditis (including myopericarditis with significant myocardial involvement) is a recognized cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes. Exercise during active inflammation increases viral replication, inflammation and arrhythmia risk.

AHA/ACC eligibility recommendations and the 2024 ACC myocarditis pathway:

  • No competitive sports or strenuous exercise for 3–6 months after diagnosis
  • Return only if all of the following are normal: LV systolic function, biomarkers (troponin, inflammatory markers), 24-hour Holter and exercise ECG without significant arrhythmias
  • Repeat cardiac MRI is reasonable; persistent extensive late gadolinium enhancement may warrant a longer restriction and closer follow-up

For isolated pericarditis without myocardial involvement, return is allowed once symptoms and inflammatory markers resolve, usually after at least 3 months for competitive athletes (shorter for non-athletes).

Why not the others

  • (A) Permanent disqualification from competitive sports — Most patients recover fully; permanent disqualification is reserved for persistent LV dysfunction or arrhythmias.
  • (B) Return after 1 week without any symptoms — One week is far too short; the risk of arrhythmia persists during healing.
  • (D) Return as soon as C-reactive protein normalizes — CRP normalization alone does not exclude ongoing myocardial inflammation or arrhythmic risk.
  • (E) Return once chest pain has been absent for 2 weeks — Absence of pain does not mean the myocardium has healed.
🎯 Educational objective

After myocarditis or myopericarditis, restrict competitive sports for 3–6 months and allow return only with normal ventricular function, biomarkers and arrhythmia evaluation.

CV-163.stem_html:
A 64-year-old man comes to the emergency department 1 hour after the sudden onset of severe, tearing chest pain radiating to his back. He has long-standing poorly controlled hypertension.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 178/96 mm Hg in the right arm and 142/84 mm Hg in the left arm, and pulse rate is 104/min. A grade 2/6 early diastolic murmur is heard at the right sternal border. The lungs are clear. Neurologic examination is normal.

Electrocardiogram shows left ventricular hypertrophy without acute ST-segment changes. CT angiography shows an intimal flap beginning in the ascending aorta just above the aortic valve and extending to the descending thoracic aorta. There is a small pericardial effusion.
CV-163.lead: In addition to intravenous blood pressure and heart-rate control, which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.A: Coronary angiography before any other intervention
choices.D: Medical therapy with repeat CT in 48 hours
choices.E: Thoracic endovascular aortic repair of the descending aorta

CV-163.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Type A aortic dissection

This is an acute type A (Stanford) aortic dissection — any dissection involving the ascending aorta. Without surgery, mortality rises by about 1%–2% per hour in the first 48 hours from aortic rupture into the pericardium (tamponade), acute aortic regurgitation (the new diastolic murmur), coronary malperfusion (usually the right coronary) and stroke.

Emergency open surgical repair (replacement of the ascending aorta, with valve resuspension or replacement as needed) is the treatment of choice (Class 1). Meanwhile, give an IV beta-blocker first (esmolol, labetalol) to a heart rate <60/min, then a vasodilator if needed to a systolic BP of about 100–120 mm Hg; provide analgesia.

Type A (ascending involved) Type B (descending only)
Treatment Emergency surgery Medical therapy (uncomplicated); TEVAR if complicated (malperfusion, rupture, refractory pain/HTN, rapid expansion)

Why not the others

  • (A) Coronary angiography before any other intervention — Routine coronary angiography delays life-saving surgery and can extend the dissection.
  • (C) Intravenous heparin — Anticoagulation can precipitate fatal hemorrhage and is contraindicated in acute dissection.
  • (D) Medical therapy with repeat CT in 48 hours — Medical therapy alone for type A dissection carries very high early mortality.
  • (E) Thoracic endovascular aortic repair of the descending aorta — Endovascular repair is used for complicated type B dissection; it does not treat ascending aortic dissection.
🎯 Educational objective

Acute type A aortic dissection requires emergency surgical repair, with IV beta-blockade first to control heart rate and blood pressure.

CV-164.stem_html:
A 59-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of sudden, severe pain between her shoulder blades that began 40 minutes ago while lifting a heavy box. She has hypertension. She describes the pain as "the worst ever" and "ripping."

On physical examination, blood pressure is 172/94 mm Hg in the right arm and 148/86 mm Hg in the left arm, and pulse rate is 98/min. The lungs are clear. There is no murmur. The left radial pulse is weaker than the right.

Electrocardiogram shows sinus rhythm with no ST-segment changes. Chest radiograph shows a widened mediastinum.

Creatinine0.9 mg/dL
High-sensitivity troponin Ibelow the 99th percentile
CV-164.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next diagnostic test?

choices.A: CT angiography of the chest, abdomen and pelvis
choices.B: D-dimer to decide whether imaging is needed

CV-164.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Suspected aortic dissection — imaging

She has a high pretest probability of acute aortic syndrome. The ADD-RS (aortic dissection detection risk score) has three categories, and she has features in all of them:

  • High-risk condition (e.g., Marfan, known aortic disease) — not present
  • High-risk pain: abrupt onset, severe, tearing/ripping — yes
  • High-risk examination: pulse deficit, BP differential >20 mm Hg between arms, new AR murmur, focal neuro deficit, hypotension — yes

With ADD-RS ≥2, go straight to imaging without a D-dimer. CT angiography of the chest, abdomen and pelvis is the test of choice in a stable patient: fast, widely available, ~100% sensitive, and shows the extent of dissection and branch-vessel malperfusion. TEE is preferred if the patient is unstable or cannot receive contrast; MRA for follow-up.

Start IV beta-blockade while imaging is arranged.

Why not the others

  • (B) D-dimer to decide whether imaging is needed — A negative D-dimer can help exclude dissection only in low-risk patients (ADD-RS 0–1); with high clinical probability, it should not delay imaging.
  • (C) Invasive coronary angiography — Coronary angiography delays diagnosis and does not image the aorta adequately; troponin and ECG are normal.
  • (D) Transthoracic echocardiography alone — Transthoracic echocardiography may show an ascending flap or effusion but cannot exclude dissection of the arch and descending aorta.
  • (E) Ventilation–perfusion lung scan — A V/Q scan evaluates pulmonary embolism and does not image the aorta.
🎯 Educational objective

In patients with high clinical probability of aortic dissection (ADD-RS ≥2), proceed directly to CT angiography without D-dimer testing.

(d) transthoracic echocardiography alone — transthoracic echocardiography may show an ascending flap or effusion but cannot exclude dissection of the arch and descending aorta. (e) ventilation–perfusion lung scan — a v/q scan evaluates pulmonary embolism and does not image the aorta. 🎯 educational objective in patients with high clinical probability of aortic dissection (add-rs ≥2), proceed directly to ct angiography without d-dimer testing. 📚 read more in wardology 🧵 acute aortic dissection → references isselbacher em, et al. 2022 acc/aha guideline for the diagnosis and management of aortic disease. circulation 2022;146:e334. nazerian p, et al. diagnostic accuracy of the aortic dissection detection risk score plus d-dimer for acute aortic syndromes (advised). circulation 2018;137:250.  suspected aortic dissection — imaging

CV-165.topic: Thoracic aortic aneurysm in Marfan syndrome
CV-165.stem_html:
A 29-year-old woman with Marfan syndrome (confirmed FBN1 variant) comes for preconception counseling. She has no symptoms. She takes losartan, 50 mg daily. She has lens subluxation and pectus excavatum. Her mother had an aortic dissection at age 42.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 112/68 mm Hg and pulse rate is 66/min. Examination is consistent with Marfan syndrome; there is no murmur.

Cardiac MRI shows an aortic root diameter at the sinuses of Valsalva of 4.6 cm (4.3 cm 1 year ago), normal valve function and mild mitral valve prolapse.
CV-165.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation?

choices.B: Pregnancy is safe if she takes a beta-blocker
choices.C: Pregnancy is safe once aortic growth slows
choices.D: Prophylactic aortic root replacement before pregnancy
choices.E: Repeat MRI annually; no other change is needed before pregnancy

CV-165.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Thoracic aortic aneurysm in Marfan syndrome

Marfan syndrome (fibrillin-1 defect) causes aortic root dilation and a high risk of dissection. Pregnancy increases risk — hormonal changes weaken the aortic wall, and cardiac output and volume rise — with most dissections occurring in the third trimester and early postpartum.

Risk depends on root size:

Aortic root (Marfan) Pregnancy risk / recommendation
<4.0 cm Low (~1% dissection) — proceed with surveillance and beta-blocker
4.0–4.5 cm Higher risk — consider repair, especially if growing or family history of dissection
>4.5 cm High risk — prophylactic root replacement before pregnancy (2022 ACC/AHA aortic; ESC 2025)

She has a 4.6-cm root, rapid growth (0.3 cm/yr) and a family history of dissection → recommend valve-sparing aortic root replacement before conception. Surgery is also indicated in nonpregnant Marfan patients at ≥5.0 cm (≥4.5 cm with risk factors).

During pregnancy: beta-blocker throughout, echocardiographic surveillance every 4–12 weeks, delivery at a center with cardiothoracic surgery. Losartan is contraindicated in pregnancy (fetotoxic).

Why not the others

  • (A) Continue losartan throughout pregnancy — ARBs cause fetal kidney injury and oligohydramnios and are contraindicated in pregnancy.
  • (B) Pregnancy is safe if she takes a beta-blocker — Beta-blockers reduce but do not eliminate dissection risk when the root exceeds 4.5 cm.
  • (C) Pregnancy is safe once aortic growth slows — Waiting for growth to slow does not reduce risk with a root already above 4.5 cm.
  • (E) Repeat MRI annually; no other change is needed before pregnancy — Surveillance alone leaves her at high risk of dissection during pregnancy.
🎯 Educational objective

In Marfan syndrome, an aortic root >4.5 cm (especially with growth or family history of dissection) warrants prophylactic root replacement before pregnancy.

CV-166.stem_html:
A 72-year-old man comes for follow-up of an abdominal aortic aneurysm found on screening ultrasonography 3 years ago. He has no abdominal or back pain. He smoked for 40 years and quit 5 years ago. He has hypertension and hyperlipidemia treated with amlodipine and atorvastatin. He walks 2 miles daily.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 132/78 mm Hg and pulse rate is 68/min. A pulsatile, nontender abdominal mass is palpable.

CT angiography shows an infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm with a maximal diameter of 5.7 cm (5.2 cm 1 year ago), with anatomy suitable for endovascular repair.
CV-166.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
CV-166.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Abdominal aortic aneurysm — repair threshold

Rupture risk of an AAA rises steeply with diameter. The 2022 ACC/AHA aortic guideline recommends elective repair for:

  • Men: diameter ≥5.5 cm
  • Women: diameter ≥5.0 cm (women rupture at smaller sizes)
  • Rapid growth ≥0.5 cm in 6 months (or ≥1 cm/yr), at any size
  • Symptomatic aneurysms (tenderness, back or abdominal pain) — urgent repair at any size

He meets both size and growth criteria. With suitable anatomy, endovascular repair (EVAR) has lower early mortality than open repair; long-term survival is similar, but EVAR requires lifelong imaging surveillance for endoleaks.

AAA size (men) Surveillance imaging
3.0–3.9 cm Every 3 years
4.0–4.9 cm Every 12 months
5.0–5.4 cm Every 6 months
≥5.5 cm Repair

Why not the others

  • (A) Doxycycline to slow aneurysm growth — Doxycycline did not slow AAA growth in randomized trials.
  • (C) Repeat CT in 1 year — Waiting a year with a 5.7-cm, rapidly growing aneurysm exposes him to a high rupture risk.
  • (D) Repeat ultrasonography in 6 months — Surveillance is appropriate for smaller aneurysms; he already meets repair criteria.
  • (E) Start metoprolol and continue surveillance — Beta-blockers do not reduce aneurysm growth or rupture.
🎯 Educational objective

Recommend elective AAA repair for diameter ≥5.5 cm in men (≥5.0 cm in women), rapid growth, or symptoms.

CV-167.stem_html:
A 74-year-old woman comes to the emergency department 3 hours after the sudden onset of pain and numbness in her right leg. She has atrial fibrillation; she stopped apixaban 2 weeks ago because of cost. She has hypertension. She had no previous leg symptoms.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 146/84 mm Hg and pulse rate is 96/min and irregularly irregular. The right leg is pale and cool below the knee. Right popliteal, dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are absent; the left leg pulses are normal. Light touch is reduced over the right toes, and toe dorsiflexion is mildly weak. Doppler signals are absent in the right pedal arteries.
CV-167.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Aspirin and cilostazol with outpatient vascular follow-up
choices.D: Restart apixaban and repeat the examination in 24 hours

CV-167.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Acute limb ischemia

Acute limb ischemia (ALI) is a sudden loss of limb perfusion that threatens viability. Here the cause is embolism from atrial fibrillation after stopping anticoagulation (sudden onset, no prior claudication, normal contralateral pulses).

The "6 Ps": pain, pallor, pulselessness, poikilothermia (cold), paresthesia, paralysis.

Rutherford classification guides urgency:

Class Sensory loss Motor weakness Doppler (arterial) Action
I viable None None Audible Urgent evaluation
IIa marginally threatened Minimal (toes) None Often inaudible Prompt revascularization
IIb immediately threatened More than toes Mild–moderate Inaudible Emergency revascularization
III irreversible Profound, anesthetic Paralysis, rigor Inaudible (arterial and venous) Amputation

She is class IIa–IIb. Give IV unfractionated heparin immediately (prevents clot propagation) and arrange emergency revascularization — surgical embolectomy or catheter-directed thrombolysis/thrombectomy — ideally within 6 hours. Watch for reperfusion injury and compartment syndrome (fasciotomy) afterward.

Why not the others

  • (A) Aspirin and cilostazol with outpatient vascular follow-up — Antiplatelet therapy and cilostazol treat chronic claudication, not a threatened limb.
  • (C) Primary below-knee amputation — Amputation is reserved for irreversible ischemia (profound sensory loss, paralysis, no venous Doppler signal); her limb is salvageable.
  • (D) Restart apixaban and repeat the examination in 24 hours — A DOAC alone and a 24-hour delay would likely result in limb loss.
  • (E) Supervised exercise therapy — Exercise therapy is for chronic stable claudication.
🎯 Educational objective

Treat acute limb ischemia with immediate intravenous heparin and emergency revascularization when the limb is viable or threatened.

CV-168.stem_html:
A 68-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus for 20 years and chronic kidney disease stage 4 is evaluated for cramping pain in both calves after walking two blocks, relieved by rest. He smokes cigarettes. He has peripheral neuropathy.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 148/76 mm Hg in both arms. Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are faint bilaterally. There are no ulcers. Monofilament sensation is reduced in both feet.

Resting ankle-brachial index is 1.52 on the right and 1.48 on the left; the arteries could not be fully compressed at 250 mm Hg.
CV-168.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next diagnostic test?

choices.A: CT angiography of the lower extremities
choices.C: No further testing; the ABI excludes PAD

CV-168.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Noncompressible arteries — toe-brachial index

An ankle-brachial index (ABI) >1.40 indicates noncompressible, calcified tibial arteries (medial calcinosis), common with long-standing diabetes and CKD. The ankle pressure is falsely high, so the ABI is uninterpretable — it can hide significant PAD.

The next test is the toe-brachial index (TBI): digital arteries are rarely calcified. A TBI ≤0.70 is abnormal and supports PAD. Toe pressure and transcutaneous oxygen measurements also help assess wound-healing potential.

Resting ABI Interpretation
>1.40 Noncompressible → obtain TBI
1.00–1.40 Normal (exercise ABI if symptoms suggest PAD)
0.91–0.99 Borderline
≤0.90 PAD

Anatomic imaging (duplex, CTA, MRA, angiography) is reserved for planning revascularization in patients with lifestyle-limiting claudication despite therapy or chronic limb-threatening ischemia.

Why not the others

  • (A) CT angiography of the lower extremities — Anatomic imaging is used when revascularization is being considered, not to establish the diagnosis.
  • (B) Exercise treadmill ankle-brachial index — Exercise ABI is useful when the resting ABI is normal but symptoms suggest PAD; with noncompressible arteries, ankle pressures remain unreliable.
  • (C) No further testing; the ABI excludes PAD — An ABI >1.40 does not exclude PAD; it is nondiagnostic.
  • (D) Repeat ankle-brachial index in 1 year — Waiting a year leaves a symptomatic, high-risk patient without a diagnosis.
🎯 Educational objective

When the ABI is >1.40 because of noncompressible arteries, obtain a toe-brachial index to diagnose peripheral artery disease.

CV-169.stem_html:
A 66-year-old man underwent endovascular revascularization of a right superficial femoral artery stenosis 2 weeks ago for lifestyle-limiting claudication. He has hypertension and hyperlipidemia and quit smoking 1 year ago. He has no history of bleeding, stroke or atrial fibrillation. Medications are aspirin, 81 mg daily, clopidogrel (started after the procedure), atorvastatin, 80 mg daily, and lisinopril.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 128/76 mm Hg and pulse rate is 70/min. The right leg has palpable pedal pulses.

Hemoglobin14.1 g/dL
Estimated glomerular filtration rate74 mL/min/1.73 m²
CV-169.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate long-term antithrombotic regimen after the short course of clopidogrel?

choices.B: Aspirin plus rivaroxaban, 2.5 mg twice daily
choices.E: Warfarin with a target INR of 2.0 to 3.0 plus aspirin

CV-169.explain_html:
Correct answer: B PAD — antithrombotic therapy

Patients with symptomatic PAD, especially after lower-extremity revascularization, are at high risk of both major adverse cardiovascular events and major adverse limb events (acute limb ischemia, amputation).

Low-dose ("vascular-dose") rivaroxaban, 2.5 mg twice daily, plus aspirin:

  • VOYAGER PAD (after revascularization): reduced acute limb ischemia, major amputation, MI, ischemic stroke and cardiovascular death, with more major bleeding but no increase in fatal or intracranial bleeding
  • COMPASS (stable PAD or CAD): reduced cardiovascular events and major limb events

The 2024 ACC/AHA PAD guideline recommends it (Class 1 after revascularization for patients without high bleeding risk). A short course of clopidogrel may be added after endovascular therapy.

Every patient with PAD also needs high-intensity statin, smoking cessation, BP and diabetes control, supervised exercise and foot care.

Why not the others

  • (A) Aspirin plus clopidogrel indefinitely — Long-term DAPT increases bleeding without the limb-event reduction shown with low-dose rivaroxaban plus aspirin.
  • (C) Rivaroxaban, 20 mg daily, alone — Full-dose rivaroxaban alone is the dose for AF or VTE, not for PAD, and has not been shown to be superior here.
  • (D) Ticagrelor alone — Ticagrelor monotherapy was not better than clopidogrel in PAD (EUCLID).
  • (E) Warfarin with a target INR of 2.0 to 3.0 plus aspirin — Warfarin plus aspirin increased life-threatening bleeding without benefit in PAD (WAVE).
🎯 Educational objective

After lower-extremity revascularization for PAD, add rivaroxaban 2.5 mg twice daily to aspirin to reduce limb and cardiovascular events in patients without high bleeding risk.

CV-170.stem_html:
A 71-year-old man is evaluated for rising creatinine and painful toes. Three weeks ago he underwent coronary angiography through the femoral artery with PCI of the left anterior descending artery. He has hypertension, hyperlipidemia and diffuse atherosclerosis. Medications are aspirin, clopidogrel, atorvastatin, metoprolol and lisinopril.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 158/88 mm Hg and pulse rate is 72/min. There is a mottled, reticular violaceous rash on both thighs and feet, and several toes are cyanotic and tender despite palpable pedal pulses. Fundoscopic examination shows bright yellow refractile plaques within retinal arterioles.

Creatinine2.6 mg/dL (1.2 mg/dL before the procedure; 1.5 mg/dL 1 week ago)
Leukocyte count9600/µL with 12% eosinophils
Complement C3low
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate64 mm/h
Urinalysistrace proteinfew leukocytes; no casts
CV-170.lead: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
CV-170.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Cholesterol crystal embolization

Cholesterol crystal (atheroembolic) embolization occurs when atherosclerotic plaque is disrupted — most often during arterial catheterization, vascular surgery, or after starting anticoagulants or thrombolytics. Cholesterol crystals shower small arteries, triggering inflammation.

Classic features:

  • Onset days to weeks after the procedure, with stepwise progressive AKI
  • Livedo reticularis, "blue toes" with intact pedal pulses
  • Hollenhorst plaques — refractile cholesterol emboli in retinal arterioles
  • Eosinophilia, eosinophiluria, low complement, high ESR
  • GI ischemia, pancreatitis, stroke in severe cases

Diagnosis: clinical; confirmed by biopsy of skin, kidney or muscle showing biconvex clefts (cholesterol crystals dissolve during fixation). Treatment is supportive: statin, BP control, avoid further vascular procedures and anticoagulation when possible; many patients have permanent kidney damage.

Why not the others

  • (A) Acute interstitial nephritis from clopidogrel — AIN causes AKI with rash, fever and eosinophilia, but not livedo, blue toes or Hollenhorst plaques; clopidogrel is an uncommon cause.
  • (B) Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody–associated vasculitis — ANCA vasculitis causes glomerulonephritis with hematuria and red cell casts; the timing after catheterization and the retinal plaques point to atheroemboli.
  • (D) Contrast-associated nephropathy — Contrast-associated AKI begins within 24–72 hours and recovers within 1–2 weeks, without eosinophilia or skin findings.
  • (E) Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia — HIT causes thrombocytopenia and thrombosis 5–10 days after heparin exposure; his presentation fits embolic cholesterol crystals.
🎯 Educational objective

Recognize cholesterol crystal embolization (delayed progressive AKI, livedo reticularis, blue toes with pulses, eosinophilia, low complement) after arterial catheterization.

CV-171.stem_html:
A 70-year-old man is referred after a carotid bruit was heard during a routine visit. He has never had a stroke, transient ischemic attack, amaurosis fugax or focal weakness. He has hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus and hyperlipidemia. Medications are atorvastatin, 40 mg daily, lisinopril, metformin and aspirin.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 134/78 mm Hg. A left carotid bruit is heard. Neurologic examination is normal.

Carotid duplex ultrasonography shows 75% stenosis of the left internal carotid artery and 30% stenosis on the right, confirmed by CT angiography. MRI of the brain shows no infarcts.

LDL cholesterol88 mg/dL
Hemoglobin A₁c7.4%
CV-171.lead: Which of the following statements about his risk and management is most accurate?

choices.A: Carotid endarterectomy clearly reduced stroke compared with intensive medical therapy in the most recent trial
choices.B: His annual risk of ipsilateral stroke on intensive medical therapy is about 10%
choices.C: His annual stroke risk with intensive medical therapy is about 1%–2%, and stenting may lower it further
choices.D: His stroke risk is low enough that statin and blood pressure therapy are unnecessary
choices.E: Stenosis of 75% requires urgent endarterectomy within 2 weeks

CV-171.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Asymptomatic carotid stenosis

With modern intensive medical therapy (high-intensity statin to LDL targets, BP <130/80 mm Hg, diabetes control, antiplatelet therapy, smoking cessation, exercise), the risk of stroke from asymptomatic high-grade carotid stenosis is low — about 1%–2% per year — much lower than in the older trials of the 1990s (ACAS, ACST).

CREST-2 (NEJM, published November 2025) randomized patients with ≥70% asymptomatic stenosis to intensive medical management with or without revascularization:

  • Stenting + medical therapy significantly reduced the 4-year risk of perioperative stroke/death or ipsilateral stroke compared with medical therapy alone
  • Endarterectomy + medical therapy did not significantly reduce it (3.7% vs 5.3%)
  • Neither improved cognition

So the first priority is intensifying medical therapy for him (his LDL of 88 mg/dL is above goal for his risk level); revascularization, particularly stenting at experienced centers with low complication rates, is a shared decision. This contrasts with symptomatic stenosis ≥50%–70%, where endarterectomy within 2 weeks of the event is clearly beneficial.

Why not the others

  • (A) Carotid endarterectomy clearly reduced stroke compared with intensive medical therapy in the most recent trial — In CREST-2, endarterectomy did not significantly reduce stroke compared with intensive medical therapy alone.
  • (B) His annual risk of ipsilateral stroke on intensive medical therapy is about 10% — An annual stroke risk of about 10% applies to recently symptomatic stenosis, not to asymptomatic stenosis on modern therapy.
  • (D) His stroke risk is low enough that statin and blood pressure therapy are unnecessary — Intensive risk-factor therapy is the foundation of treatment and the reason the risk is low.
  • (E) Stenosis of 75% requires urgent endarterectomy within 2 weeks — Urgent endarterectomy within 2 weeks is the standard for symptomatic carotid stenosis.
🎯 Educational objective

Asymptomatic high-grade carotid stenosis carries about a 1%–2% annual stroke risk with intensive medical therapy; in CREST-2, stenting but not endarterectomy reduced that risk further.

CV-172.stem_html:
A 68-year-old man is evaluated before elective total hip arthroplasty. He has hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus treated with metformin, and coronary artery disease treated with PCI 8 years ago. He has had no chest pain or dyspnea since. Despite his hip pain, he climbs two flights of stairs at home carrying laundry without stopping, and he gardens. Medications are aspirin, atorvastatin, metoprolol and lisinopril.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 132/78 mm Hg and pulse rate is 62/min. Cardiac examination is normal, and there is no edema.

Electrocardiogram shows sinus rhythm with no ischemic changes. His Revised Cardiac Risk Index score is 1.

Creatinine1.0 mg/dL
Hemoglobin A₁c6.9%
CV-172.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step before surgery?

choices.D: Proceed with surgery without further cardiac testing

CV-172.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Preoperative evaluation — functional capacity

The 2024 ACC/AHA perioperative guideline uses a stepwise approach:

  1. Emergency surgery? Proceed.
  2. Active cardiac condition (ACS, decompensated HF, significant arrhythmia, severe valve disease)? Evaluate and treat first.
  3. Estimate risk (RCRI or other calculator): hip arthroplasty is an elevated-risk procedure, and his RCRI of 1 (known CAD) gives a modest risk.
  4. Functional capacity: if ≥4 METs (climbing two flights of stairs, heavy housework, gardening), proceed without further testing — stress testing would not improve outcomes.

Stress testing is considered only if functional capacity is poor or unknown and the result would change management (whether or not surgery happens). Revascularization before noncardiac surgery is indicated only when it would be indicated anyway (CARP trial showed no benefit of routine prophylactic revascularization).

Continue aspirin (prior PCI), statin and his beta-blocker; do not start a new beta-blocker on the day of surgery.

Why not the others

  • (A) Coronary CT angiography — Coronary CT angiography does not reduce perioperative events in patients with good functional capacity and no symptoms.
  • (B) Invasive coronary angiography — Invasive angiography is not indicated without an independent indication for revascularization.
  • (C) Pharmacologic stress myocardial perfusion imaging — Stress testing in patients with good functional capacity does not improve perioperative outcomes.
  • (E) Transthoracic echocardiography — Echocardiography is reserved for unexplained dyspnea, suspected significant valve disease or HF with a change in status.
🎯 Educational objective

Before elevated-risk noncardiac surgery, patients with functional capacity ≥4 METs and no active cardiac conditions can proceed without further cardiac testing.

CV-173.topic: Obstructive sleep apnea and resistant hypertension
CV-173.stem_html:
A 56-year-old man is evaluated for blood pressure that remains elevated despite chlorthalidone, 25 mg daily, amlodipine, 10 mg daily, and losartan, 100 mg daily. Pharmacy records confirm adherence. He avoids NSAIDs, decongestants and alcohol. His wife reports that he snores loudly and sometimes stops breathing during sleep. He falls asleep while watching television and once while driving.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 156/94 mm Hg (home average 152/92 mm Hg), and pulse rate is 78/min. BMI is 36 kg/m². Neck circumference is 47 cm (18.5 in). Examination is otherwise normal.

Potassium3.9 mEq/L
Creatinine1.0 mg/dL
Aldosterone-to-renin ratio6 (ng/dL)/(ng/mL/h) with suppressed aldosterone
Thyroid-stimulating hormone2.0 µU/mL
CV-173.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next diagnostic step?

choices.B: CT angiography of the renal arteries

CV-173.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Obstructive sleep apnea and resistant hypertension

He has resistant hypertension (above goal on three drugs from different classes, including a diuretic, at optimal doses, with confirmed adherence and home readings). Primary aldosteronism — the most common secondary cause — has been screened and is unlikely.

Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is present in up to 60%–80% of patients with resistant hypertension. His loud snoring, witnessed apneas, daytime sleepiness, obesity and large neck make it very likely. Use STOP-BANG to estimate pretest probability, then polysomnography (or home sleep apnea testing in uncomplicated cases).

Intermittent hypoxia and arousals raise sympathetic tone and aldosterone, causing nocturnal and daytime hypertension (often a non-dipping pattern). CPAP lowers blood pressure modestly (2–5 mm Hg) and improves sleepiness and driving safety. Next drug for resistant hypertension: spironolactone (PATHWAY-2).

Why not the others

  • (A) Adrenal vein sampling — Adrenal vein sampling localizes aldosterone excess after primary aldosteronism is confirmed; his screening is negative.
  • (B) CT angiography of the renal arteries — Renal artery imaging is for suspected renovascular disease (abrupt onset, flash pulmonary edema, abdominal bruit, AKI with RAAS blockade); his clinical picture points to OSA.
  • (C) Plasma free metanephrines — He has no paroxysmal headaches, palpitations or sweating to suggest pheochromocytoma.
  • (E) Serum cortisol after 1-mg dexamethasone — He has no cushingoid features.
🎯 Educational objective

Screen patients with resistant hypertension and symptoms of obstructive sleep apnea with polysomnography; OSA is the most common comorbid condition in resistant hypertension.

CV-174.stem_html:
A 42-year-old woman is evaluated for 6 months of episodic pounding headaches, palpitations, sweating and tremor lasting 10 to 20 minutes, several times a week. During two episodes, her home blood pressure was 210/120 mm Hg. Between episodes her blood pressure is mildly elevated. She has lost 3 kg (6.6 lb). She takes no medications, supplements or stimulants.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 152/96 mm Hg and pulse rate is 104/min. She is thin and anxious. There are no café-au-lait spots or neurofibromas. Thyroid examination is normal.

Fasting glucose118 mg/dL
Thyroid-stimulating hormone1.9 µU/mL
Potassium4.1 mEq/L
CV-174.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial diagnostic test?
CV-174.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Pheochromocytoma screening

The classic triad of episodic headache, palpitations and sweating with paroxysmal hypertension strongly suggests pheochromocytoma (or paraganglioma). Weight loss and impaired fasting glucose fit catecholamine excess.

Biochemical diagnosis comes first, then imaging:

  1. Plasma free metanephrines (drawn supine after 30 minutes of rest) or 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines — metanephrines are produced continuously inside the tumor, so they are sensitive even between episodes (sensitivity ~97%–99%)
  2. If clearly elevated (>3–4× ULN): CT or MRI of the abdomen and pelvis
  3. Functional imaging (⁶⁸Ga-DOTATATE PET, MIBG) for metastatic or extra-adrenal disease
  4. Genetic testing for all patients (about 30%–40% have germline variants: MEN2, VHL, NF1, SDH)

Preoperative management: alpha-blockade first (phenoxybenzamine or doxazosin) for 10–14 days, then a beta-blocker if needed, plus volume and salt loading — never a beta-blocker first (unopposed alpha stimulation → hypertensive crisis).

Why not the others

  • (A) 123I-MIBG scintigraphy — MIBG imaging localizes tumors after biochemical confirmation, mainly for metastatic or extra-adrenal disease.
  • (B) CT of the adrenal glands — Imaging before biochemical confirmation leads to adrenal incidentalomas and misdiagnosis.
  • (D) Serum catecholamines during an episode — Catecholamines are released episodically and have short half-lives; random levels are less sensitive than metanephrines.
  • (E) Urinary vanillylmandelic acid — VMA has poor sensitivity and is no longer recommended.
🎯 Educational objective

Screen for pheochromocytoma with plasma free metanephrines (or 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines) before any imaging.
