CV-175.stem_html:
A 72-year-old man is evaluated after renal artery duplex ultrasonography, obtained because of an abdominal bruit, showed 70%–80% stenosis of the left renal artery. He has hypertension, hyperlipidemia, coronary artery disease and peripheral artery disease. He smokes. He has had no episodes of pulmonary edema. Medications are amlodipine, 10 mg daily, chlorthalidone, 25 mg daily, losartan, 100 mg daily, aspirin and atorvastatin, 80 mg daily.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 132/78 mm Hg (home average 128/76 mm Hg) and pulse rate is 66/min. An abdominal bruit is heard.

Creatinine1.3 mg/dL (1.2–1.3 mg/dL over the past 2 years)
Potassium4.4 mEq/L
Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio60 mg/g
Kidney sizes on ultrasonographyright 11.2 cmleft 10.0 cm
CV-175.lead: In addition to smoking cessation, which of the following is the most appropriate management?
CV-175.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis

Atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis (RAS) is common in older patients with diffuse atherosclerosis. Randomized trials (ASTRAL, CORAL) showed that renal artery stenting added to optimal medical therapy does not reduce cardiovascular events, kidney failure or death — and carries procedural risks (atheroemboli, dissection, contrast injury).

Management is intensive medical therapy: ACE inhibitor or ARB (safe and beneficial in unilateral RAS; monitor creatinine), other antihypertensives as needed, high-intensity statin, antiplatelet therapy and smoking cessation. His blood pressure and kidney function are stable.

Consider revascularization in atherosclerotic RAS only for
Recurrent "flash" pulmonary edema or unstable angina from RAS
Rapidly progressive kidney failure from bilateral or solitary-kidney stenosis
Truly resistant hypertension despite optimal therapy

Fibromuscular dysplasia (younger women, "string of beads") is different — angioplasty without stenting is effective.

Why not the others

  • (B) Renal angiography with stent placement — Stenting did not improve outcomes over medical therapy in CORAL and ASTRAL; he has no high-risk features.
  • (C) Stop losartan — ARBs are appropriate in unilateral RAS when creatinine is stable; stopping one would worsen blood pressure and albuminuria.
  • (D) Surgical renal artery bypass — Surgical bypass carries higher risk and has no proven benefit in stable patients.
  • (E) Switch losartan to hydralazine — Hydralazine is less effective, causes reflex tachycardia and fluid retention, and loses the kidney and cardiovascular benefits of RAAS blockade.
🎯 Educational objective

Treat stable atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis with optimal medical therapy (including RAAS blockade and statin); reserve revascularization for flash pulmonary edema, rapidly declining kidney function or truly refractory hypertension.

CV-176.stem_html:
A 61-year-old man with resistant hypertension started spironolactone, 50 mg daily, 5 months ago, and his blood pressure is now at goal. He reports tender swelling under both nipples for 2 months and decreased libido. Other medications are amlodipine, chlorthalidone and lisinopril. He does not drink alcohol or use other medications or supplements.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 126/76 mm Hg. There is bilateral, tender, rubbery subareolar breast tissue about 3 cm in diameter, without masses, skin changes or nipple discharge. Testicular examination is normal.

Potassium4.7 mEq/L
ALT22 U/L
Thyroid-stimulating hormone1.8 µU/mL
CV-176.lead: Which of the following mechanisms best explains his breast enlargement?

choices.A: Activation of estrogen receptors by the parent drug
choices.D: Increased hepatic production of sex hormone–binding globulin only

CV-176.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Spironolactone-induced gynecomastia

Spironolactone is a nonselective steroid mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist that also:

  • Blocks androgen receptors (antiandrogen) — the main cause of gynecomastia, breast tenderness, decreased libido and erectile dysfunction
  • Reduces testosterone synthesis and increases the conversion of testosterone to estradiol, raising the estrogen-to-androgen ratio
  • Acts on progesterone receptors (menstrual irregularity in women)

Gynecomastia is dose-related (about 10% at 25 mg; more at ≥50 mg).

Management: switch to eplerenone — a selective mineralocorticoid antagonist with much less affinity for androgen and progesterone receptors, so gynecomastia is rare. (Eplerenone is less potent, so a higher equivalent dose is used; it has CYP3A4 interactions.) Finerenone is another nonsteroidal, selective option for diabetic CKD and HFpEF.

Why not the others

  • (A) Activation of estrogen receptors by the parent drug — Spironolactone does not act as an estrogen receptor agonist.
  • (C) Elevated prolactin from dopamine blockade — Hyperprolactinemia from dopamine antagonists (antipsychotics, metoclopramide) causes gynecomastia, but spironolactone is not a dopamine antagonist.
  • (D) Increased hepatic production of sex hormone–binding globulin only — SHBG changes are not the main mechanism of spironolactone-induced gynecomastia.
  • (E) Inhibition of 5-alpha reductase — 5-alpha reductase inhibitors (finasteride, dutasteride) can cause gynecomastia, but this is not spironolactone's mechanism.
🎯 Educational objective

Spironolactone causes gynecomastia mainly through androgen receptor antagonism; switching to the selective mineralocorticoid antagonist eplerenone avoids it.

CV-177.topic: Blood pressure in acute ischemic stroke
CV-177.stem_html:
A 68-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 75 minutes after the sudden onset of right arm and face weakness and difficulty speaking. She has hypertension and takes amlodipine. She takes no anticoagulants.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 198/108 mm Hg on two measurements, pulse rate is 82/min and regular, and glucose by fingerstick is 132 mg/dL. She has expressive aphasia, right facial droop and right arm weakness (NIH Stroke Scale score 9).

Noncontrast CT of the head shows no hemorrhage. CT angiography shows no large-vessel occlusion. She meets all other criteria for intravenous thrombolysis.
CV-177.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Give sublingual nifedipine, then give thrombolysis
choices.B: Give thrombolysis without lowering blood pressure
choices.C: Lower blood pressure over 24 hours, then reconsider thrombolysis
choices.D: Lower blood pressure to below 140/90 mm Hg, then give thrombolysis
choices.E: Lower blood pressure to below 185/110 mm Hg, then give thrombolysis

CV-177.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Blood pressure in acute ischemic stroke

In acute ischemic stroke, the brain's ischemic penumbra depends on perfusion pressure, so blood pressure is usually allowed to stay high — except when thrombolysis is planned, because high pressure increases the risk of hemorrhagic transformation.

Situation (AHA/ASA 2019 acute stroke guideline) BP target
Before IV thrombolysis (alteplase or tenecteplase) <185/110 mm Hg
During and 24 h after thrombolysis <180/105 mm Hg
No thrombolysis or thrombectomy Treat only if >220/120 mm Hg (lower by about 15% in 24 h)

Use IV labetalol, nicardipine or clevidipine. If BP cannot be kept below 185/110 mm Hg, do not give thrombolysis. Every minute counts — "time is brain" — so BP control must be rapid, not delayed for hours.

After thrombectomy with successful recanalization, aggressive BP lowering to <140 mm Hg systolic was harmful (ENCHANTED2/MT, OPTIMAL-BP); keep <180/105.

Why not the others

  • (A) Give sublingual nifedipine, then give thrombolysis — Sublingual nifedipine causes abrupt, uncontrolled drops in pressure and is contraindicated.
  • (B) Give thrombolysis without lowering blood pressure — Giving thrombolysis with blood pressure above 185/110 mm Hg increases the risk of intracranial hemorrhage.
  • (C) Lower blood pressure over 24 hours, then reconsider thrombolysis — Delaying thrombolysis by hours reduces its benefit; blood pressure should be lowered quickly to the threshold and treatment given.
  • (D) Lower blood pressure to below 140/90 mm Hg, then give thrombolysis — Excessive lowering reduces penumbral perfusion and is not recommended.
🎯 Educational objective

Before intravenous thrombolysis for acute ischemic stroke, lower blood pressure to <185/110 mm Hg with IV labetalol, nicardipine or clevidipine, then maintain <180/105 mm Hg for 24 hours.

CV-178.stem_html:
A 38-year-old woman is evaluated for 1 year of progressive exertional dyspnea and occasional palpitations. She has no other medical history.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 112/70 mm Hg and pulse rate is 76/min and regular. There is a right ventricular heave. A grade 2/6 midsystolic murmur is heard at the left upper sternal border. The second heart sound is widely split, and the split does not vary with respiration. There is no clubbing or cyanosis.

Electrocardiogram shows sinus rhythm, right axis deviation and an rsR′ pattern in lead V1 with a QRS duration of 0.10 second. Chest radiograph shows an enlarged right heart and prominent pulmonary arteries.
CV-178.lead: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
CV-178.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Atrial septal defect

A secundum atrial septal defect (the most common ASD, in the fossa ovalis) often goes unnoticed until adulthood. Left-to-right shunting at the atrial level volume-overloads the right atrium, right ventricle and pulmonary arteries.

Classic findings:

  • Wide, fixed splitting of S₂ — the shunt equalizes respiratory changes in RV filling, so pulmonic closure is always delayed
  • Pulmonic flow murmur (left upper sternal border) — from increased flow across a normal pulmonic valve, not across the defect itself
  • RV heave; sometimes a tricuspid diastolic flow rumble
  • ECG: incomplete RBBB (rsR′ in V1) with right axis deviation
  • Late complications: atrial arrhythmias, pulmonary hypertension, paradoxical embolism, RV failure

Closure (percutaneous device for secundum defects) is indicated for RV enlargement with a significant shunt (Qp:Qs ≥1.5), as long as pulmonary vascular resistance is not severely elevated.

Defect ECG axis Note
Secundum ASD Right Device closure
Primum ASD Left Cleft mitral valve; surgery
Sinus venosus ASD Right (ectopic atrial rhythm) Anomalous pulmonary veins; surgery

Why not the others

  • (A) Ostium primum atrial septal defect — Primum ASD typically shows left axis deviation and often a cleft mitral valve with mitral regurgitation.
  • (B) Patent ductus arteriosus — PDA causes a continuous "machinery" murmur at the left infraclavicular area with left-heart volume overload.
  • (C) Pulmonic valve stenosis — Pulmonic stenosis causes an ejection click and a widely split S₂ that still varies with respiration, without pulmonary plethora.
  • (E) Ventricular septal defect — A VSD causes a harsh holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border and left-heart volume overload.
🎯 Educational objective

Recognize secundum ASD by fixed splitting of S₂, a pulmonic flow murmur, RV enlargement, and incomplete RBBB with right axis deviation.

CV-179.topic: Patent foramen ovale and cryptogenic stroke
CV-179.stem_html:
A 44-year-old man is evaluated 3 weeks after an ischemic stroke that caused left hand weakness, now resolved. MRI showed a single cortical infarct in the right middle cerebral artery territory. He does not smoke and has no hypertension, diabetes or hyperlipidemia.

Evaluation showed no large-artery stenosis on CT angiography, normal left ventricular function, no atrial fibrillation on 30 days of ambulatory monitoring, and no hypercoagulable disorder. Transesophageal echocardiography with agitated saline shows a patent foramen ovale with a large right-to-left shunt (>20 microbubbles) and an atrial septal aneurysm. His RoPE score is 8. He takes aspirin and atorvastatin.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg and pulse rate is 68/min. Neurologic examination is normal.
CV-179.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate management to prevent recurrent stroke?
CV-179.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Patent foramen ovale and cryptogenic stroke

He has an embolic stroke of undetermined source with no other cause after a thorough workup, and a PFO with high-risk features (large shunt, atrial septal aneurysm). The RoPE score (young age, no vascular risk factors, cortical infarct) of 8 indicates the PFO is very likely the cause (attributable fraction ~84%).

Three randomized trials (CLOSE, REDUCE, RESPECT) showed that PFO closure plus antiplatelet therapy reduced recurrent stroke compared with antiplatelet therapy alone in patients aged 18–60. The 2020 AAN advisory, 2021 AHA/ASA secondary prevention guideline and SCAI guideline support closure (after shared decision-making) in this group, especially with high-risk anatomy.

Complications of closure: atrial fibrillation (usually transient, early), device thrombus or erosion (rare).

Closure is not recommended for migraine alone, for patients older than 60 (data limited), or when another stroke mechanism is present.

Why not the others

  • (A) Aspirin alone — Antiplatelet therapy alone had a higher recurrence rate than closure plus antiplatelet therapy in high-risk PFO.
  • (B) Lifelong apixaban — DOACs have not been shown superior to aspirin for PFO-associated stroke and carry more bleeding over decades.
  • (C) Lifelong warfarin — Long-term warfarin carries bleeding risk and has not proved better than closure.
  • (D) No antithrombotic therapy — Withholding antithrombotic therapy after an ischemic stroke is inappropriate.
🎯 Educational objective

In patients aged 18–60 with an embolic stroke and no other cause, PFO closure plus antiplatelet therapy reduces recurrence, especially with a large shunt or atrial septal aneurysm.

CV-180.stem_html:
A 24-year-old man is evaluated for hypertension discovered at a college sports physical. He has occasional headaches and leg fatigue when running. He takes no medications or supplements and does not use stimulants.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 164/88 mm Hg in the right arm, 160/86 mm Hg in the left arm and 112/70 mm Hg in the legs. Femoral pulses are weak and delayed compared with the radial pulses. A grade 2/6 systolic murmur is heard over the left infrascapular area of the back, and an early systolic ejection click is heard at the apex.

Electrocardiogram shows left ventricular hypertrophy. Chest radiograph shows notching of the inferior borders of the posterior ribs and an indentation of the descending aorta.

Potassium4.2 mEq/L
Creatinine0.9 mg/dL
CV-180.lead: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.B: Fibromuscular dysplasia of the renal arteries

CV-180.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Coarctation of the aorta

Coarctation of the aorta is a narrowing of the descending aorta, usually just distal to the left subclavian artery. In adults it presents as hypertension in the arms with lower pressure and weak, delayed pulses in the legs.

Key findings:

  • Arm–leg BP gradient (>20 mm Hg) and brachial–femoral pulse delay
  • Systolic murmur over the back (across the coarctation) and continuous murmurs from collateral intercostal arteries
  • Rib notching (erosion by enlarged intercostal collaterals) and the "figure 3" sign on chest radiograph
  • Bicuspid aortic valve in about 50%–70% (the ejection click here); also intracranial (berry) aneurysms; Turner syndrome in women

Confirm with CT or MR angiography. Treat with stent or surgical repair when the gradient is significant (≥20 mm Hg, or less with collaterals). Lifelong follow-up is needed for recoarctation, aneurysm and persistent hypertension.

Why not the others

  • (B) Fibromuscular dysplasia of the renal arteries — Renal artery FMD causes hypertension without an arm–leg pressure gradient, rib notching or a murmur over the back.
  • (C) Pheochromocytoma — Pheochromocytoma causes paroxysmal hypertension with headache, sweating and palpitations, not a fixed arm–leg gradient.
  • (D) Primary aldosteronism — Primary aldosteronism causes hypertension (often with hypokalemia) but not unequal upper and lower extremity pressures.
  • (E) Takayasu arteritis — Takayasu arteritis typically affects young women and causes arm (subclavian) pulse deficits and arm–arm pressure differences, with systemic inflammation.
🎯 Educational objective

Suspect coarctation of the aorta in young adults with hypertension, an arm–leg blood pressure gradient, delayed femoral pulses and rib notching; look for an associated bicuspid aortic valve.

CV-181.stem_html:
A 30-year-old woman with a bileaflet mechanical mitral valve, placed 5 years ago for rheumatic mitral stenosis, calls her cardiologist because a home pregnancy test is positive. Her last menstrual period was 5 weeks ago. She takes warfarin, 7.5 mg daily, which has kept her INR between 2.5 and 3.5. She wishes to continue the pregnancy.

On examination at the visit, blood pressure is 108/66 mm Hg and pulse rate is 82/min. Crisp mechanical valve clicks are heard.

Echocardiogram shows a normally functioning mitral prosthesis.
CV-181.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate anticoagulation management for the first trimester?
CV-181.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Mechanical heart valve in pregnancy

Mechanical valves in pregnancy carry a high risk of valve thrombosis (pregnancy is hypercoagulable) and of fetal harm from warfarin. Warfarin crosses the placenta; exposure in weeks 6–12 causes warfarin embryopathy (nasal hypoplasia, stippled epiphyses), and the risk is dose-dependent.

Warfarin dose First trimester (weeks 6–12) — 2020 ACC/AHA, 2025 ESC
≤5 mg/day Continuing warfarin is reasonable (lowest valve thrombosis risk) after counseling
>5 mg/day Switch to dose-adjusted LMWH twice daily (target anti-Xa peak about 0.8–1.2 U/mL, check troughs) or continuous IV UFH (aPTT ≥2× control)

She takes 7.5 mg/day, so switch to therapeutic, dose-adjusted LMWH with weekly anti-Xa monitoring (doses must rise as pregnancy progresses). Warfarin may be resumed in the second and third trimesters, then switch to IV UFH before planned delivery. Pregnancy should be managed by a pregnancy heart team at an experienced center.

Why not the others

  • (A) Apixaban — DOACs are contraindicated with mechanical valves and are not recommended in pregnancy.
  • (B) Aspirin alone — Aspirin alone provides inadequate protection against mechanical valve thrombosis.
  • (C) Continue warfarin, 7.5 mg daily — At doses above 5 mg/day, warfarin carries a substantially higher risk of embryopathy and fetal loss.
  • (E) Prophylactic-dose low-molecular-weight heparin — Fixed prophylactic LMWH doses lead to valve thrombosis; LMWH must be therapeutic and adjusted to anti-Xa levels.
🎯 Educational objective

In pregnant women with mechanical valves who need more than 5 mg/day of warfarin, switch to dose-adjusted LMWH (anti-Xa monitoring) or IV UFH during weeks 6–12.

CV-182.stem_html:
A 67-year-old man is referred for preoperative evaluation before elective total knee arthroplasty. Ten weeks ago he underwent elective PCI with a drug-eluting stent in the right coronary artery for stable angina refractory to medical therapy. He now has no chest pain. Medications are aspirin, clopidogrel, metoprolol, atorvastatin and lisinopril. The orthopedic surgeon requires clopidogrel to be stopped before surgery. His knee pain is moderate and controlled with acetaminophen and physical therapy.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 128/76 mm Hg and pulse rate is 60/min. Examination is otherwise normal.
CV-182.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation?

choices.A: Postpone surgery until at least 6 months after PCI
choices.B: Proceed with surgery now after stopping aspirin and clopidogrel for 7 days
choices.C: Proceed with surgery now after stopping clopidogrel, with heparin bridging
choices.D: Proceed with surgery now while continuing aspirin and clopidogrel
choices.E: Replace clopidogrel with warfarin for the perioperative period

CV-182.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Elective surgery after drug-eluting stent

Noncardiac surgery soon after a drug-eluting stent (DES) raises the risk of stent thrombosis and MI, especially if antiplatelet therapy must be interrupted — surgery creates a prothrombotic, inflammatory state.

2024 AHA/ACC perioperative guideline:

After PCI with DES Elective noncardiac surgery
Stable CAD (elective PCI) Delay ≥6 months (≥3 months may be considered if the risk of further delay exceeds stent risk)
ACS Delay ≥12 months (≥6 months may be considered if needed)
Balloon angioplasty without stent ≥14 days

His knee surgery is truly elective and his pain is controlled, so the safest choice is to wait until 6 months after PCI. If surgery cannot wait and the P2Y12 inhibitor must stop, continue aspirin throughout, stop clopidogrel 5 days before, and restart within 24–48 hours after surgery.

Why not the others

  • (B) Proceed with surgery now after stopping aspirin and clopidogrel for 7 days — Stopping both antiplatelet drugs 10 weeks after DES implantation markedly increases the risk of stent thrombosis.
  • (C) Proceed with surgery now after stopping clopidogrel, with heparin bridging — Heparin bridging does not protect against stent thrombosis (it is not an antiplatelet agent) and increases bleeding.
  • (D) Proceed with surgery now while continuing aspirin and clopidogrel — Dual antiplatelet therapy during joint replacement increases bleeding, and the surgeon has already said clopidogrel must stop; delaying elective surgery is safer.
  • (E) Replace clopidogrel with warfarin for the perioperative period — Warfarin does not prevent stent thrombosis.
🎯 Educational objective

Delay elective noncardiac surgery for at least 6 months after drug-eluting stent placement for stable coronary disease (12 months after ACS); continue aspirin if surgery cannot wait.

CV-001.stem_html:
A 49-year-old man comes to the office to review his blood pressure log. Three months ago his office blood pressure was 158/96 mm Hg. Since then he has cut back on salt, walks 30 minutes most days and has lost 2 kg (4.4 lb). His validated home cuff now shows an average of 156/98 mm Hg over the last 2 weeks. He has no symptoms. He does not have diabetes and does not smoke. His father had a myocardial infarction at age 61.

Blood pressure in the office today is 154/97 mm Hg in both arms; pulse rate is 74/min. BMI is 29 kg/m². Cardiac examination is normal and there is no edema.

Sodium140 mEq/L
Potassium4.3 mEq/L
Creatinine0.9 mg/dL
Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio12 mg/g
LDL cholesterol128 mg/dL
CV-001.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Continue lifestyle changes and recheck blood pressure in 6 months
choices.B: Start a single-pill combination of an angiotensin receptor blocker and amlodipine

CV-001.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Essential hypertension

This man has confirmed stage 2 hypertension (home average ≥140/90 mm Hg) that persists despite 3 months of lifestyle change. His goal is <130/80 mm Hg.

When blood pressure is ≥140/90 mm Hg (or more than about 20/10 mm Hg above goal), one drug is rarely enough. Current US guidance recommends starting two first-line drugs from different classes at the same time, preferably as a single-pill combination. Two half-doses lower pressure more than one full dose, cause fewer dose-related side effects, and one pill improves adherence.

The first-line classes are thiazide-type diuretics, ACE inhibitors or ARBs, and dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers. An ARB + amlodipine pill is a standard choice; ACE inhibitor or ARB + thiazide is equally acceptable.

Office BP Plan
130–139 / 80–89 Lifestyle; add one drug if CVD, diabetes, CKD or high 10-year risk
≥140 / 90 Lifestyle plus two first-line drugs, ideally one pill
≥180 / 120 with organ damage Hypertensive emergency → hospital, IV therapy

Why not the others

  • (A) Continue lifestyle changes and recheck blood pressure in 6 months — He has already tried lifestyle change for 3 months and remains far above goal. Waiting 6 more months leaves stage 2 hypertension untreated.
  • (C) Start atenolol — Beta-blockers are not first-line for uncomplicated hypertension. They prevent fewer strokes than the first-line classes; use them when there is another indication (angina, prior MI, HFrEF, rate control).
  • (D) Start hydralazine — Hydralazine is a late add-on (resistant hypertension, pregnancy, HFrEF with nitrate). It causes reflex tachycardia and fluid retention when used alone.
  • (E) Start lisinopril plus losartan — ACE inhibitor + ARB together (dual RAAS blockade) raises the risk of hyperkalemia and acute kidney injury without cardiovascular benefit. Never combine them.
🧠 Mnemonic

"A-C-D" — the three first-line classes: ACE inhibitor/ARB, Calcium channel blocker (dihydropyridine), Diuretic (thiazide-type). Stage 2 → pick two of the three.

🎓 ABIM pearl

Confirm office readings with home or ambulatory monitoring before diagnosing hypertension. Office-only elevation is white-coat hypertension; normal office but high home readings is masked hypertension, which carries the same risk as sustained hypertension.

🎯 Educational objective

For confirmed stage 2 hypertension (≥140/90 mm Hg), start two first-line antihypertensives from different classes, preferably as a single-pill combination, and target <130/80 mm Hg.

CV-002.stem_html:
A 61-year-old woman comes to the office for a routine visit. She ran out of her amlodipine and chlorthalidone 8 days ago and did not refill them. She feels well. She has no headache, chest pain, dyspnea, visual change or weakness.

Blood pressure is 194/112 mm Hg, rechecked after 10 minutes of quiet rest at 190/110 mm Hg; pulse rate is 78/min. She is alert and oriented. Fundoscopic examination shows mild arteriolar narrowing without hemorrhages, exudates or papilledema. Heart and lung examination is normal, and neurologic examination is nonfocal.

Creatinine1.0 mg/dL (baseline 1.0 mg/dL)
Urinalysisno blood or protein
ECGsinus rhythm; left ventricular hypertrophy by voltage (unchanged from 1 year ago)
CV-002.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.B: Give intravenous labetalol in the emergency department
choices.C: Give oral clonidine every hour until blood pressure is below 140/90 mm Hg
choices.D: Obtain a noncontrast CT scan of the head
choices.E: Restart her home medications and recheck blood pressure within 1 week

CV-002.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Severe asymptomatic hypertension

This is severe asymptomatic hypertension (formerly "hypertensive urgency"): blood pressure ≥180/110–120 mm Hg without acute target-organ damage. Her fundi, kidneys, ECG and neurologic examination show no acute injury. The cause is obvious — she stopped her medicines.

The danger in this situation is lowering the pressure too fast. Chronic hypertension shifts cerebral and coronary autoregulation to the right. A sudden drop can cause stroke, myocardial ischemia or acute kidney injury. Short-term risk from the elevated pressure itself is low.

Correct care: restart (or intensify) oral therapy, aim to lower blood pressure gradually over days to weeks, and arrange close follow-up. ED referral and IV drugs are for hypertensive emergency, when organ damage is present.

Severe asymptomatic HTN Hypertensive emergency
Organ damage None acute Encephalopathy, stroke, ACS, pulmonary edema, AKI, dissection, retinal hemorrhage/papilledema
Setting Office / outpatient ICU
Drugs Oral IV (nicardipine, clevidipine, labetalol, esmolol)
Pace Over days–weeks ≤25% in the first hour (faster for dissection)

Why not the others

  • (A) Give immediate-release nifedipine sublingually now — Immediate-release nifedipine causes abrupt, unpredictable drops in pressure and has caused stroke and MI. It should not be used for this purpose.
  • (B) Give intravenous labetalol in the emergency department — IV antihypertensives are for hypertensive emergency. Using them without organ damage risks hypotension and hypoperfusion and adds no benefit.
  • (C) Give oral clonidine every hour until blood pressure is below 140/90 mm Hg — Rapid oral loading to a normal pressure within hours is the same error as IV therapy, and clonidine stacking causes rebound hypertension later.
  • (D) Obtain a noncontrast CT scan of the head — She has no neurologic symptoms or signs. Imaging is not needed without features of encephalopathy or stroke.
🎓 ABIM pearl

The number alone does not make an emergency — organ damage does. Look at the eyes, brain, heart, lungs and kidneys before you reach for an IV drug.

🎯 Educational objective

Severe hypertension without acute target-organ damage is treated with oral medication and gradual lowering over days to weeks with close outpatient follow-up, not with rapid or IV blood pressure reduction.

CV-003.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
CV-003.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Complete heart block

The strip shows third-degree (complete) AV block: P waves march at their own regular rate and wide QRS complexes march at a slower, independent rate — there is no relationship between them. Bedside clues fit: cannon a waves (atria contract against a closed tricuspid valve) and a variable S₁.

She has symptomatic complete heart block with syncope (Stokes-Adams attacks) and a wide escape rhythm, which means the block is below the AV node and the escape is unreliable. Once reversible causes are excluded, the treatment is a permanent pacemaker (Class 1). Her labs exclude hyperkalemia, hypothyroidism and acute MI, and lisinopril does not slow AV conduction.

Reversible causes to check before pacing
AV-nodal drugs: beta-blockers, nondihydropyridine CCBs, digoxin, amiodarone
Hyperkalemia
Acute inferior MI (often transient)
Lyme carditis (young patient, tick exposure)
Hypothyroidism, increased vagal tone, obstructive sleep apnea

Why not the others

  • (A) 30-day ambulatory event monitor — The diagnosis is already made on the strip. More monitoring only delays treatment of a rhythm that can cause sudden death.
  • (B) Oral theophylline — Theophylline is occasionally used for post-transplant bradycardia or as a temporary bridge. It is not a treatment for infranodal complete heart block.
  • (D) Stop lisinopril and observe — ACE inhibitors do not block the AV node. Stopping lisinopril would not correct complete heart block.
  • (E) Tilt-table testing — Tilt-table testing evaluates reflex (vasovagal) syncope. Her syncope is arrhythmic and already explained.
🧠 Mnemonic

Third-degree block: "P's and Q's don't agree" — atria and ventricles keep their own time.

🎓 ABIM pearl

A narrow escape (40–60/min) suggests block in the AV node (more stable). A wide escape (20–40/min) suggests infranodal block (His–Purkinje) — unstable, and atropine usually does not help.

🎯 Educational objective

Symptomatic complete heart block without a reversible cause is an indication for permanent pacemaker implantation.

CV-004.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate therapy to reduce her risk of stroke?

choices.D: No antithrombotic therapy because her pulse rate is controlled
choices.E: Warfarin with a target INR of 2.0–3.0

CV-004.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Atrial fibrillation — stroke prevention

The ECG shows atrial fibrillation: irregularly irregular R–R intervals and no discrete P waves.

Stroke risk in AF depends on the patient, not on the rhythm or rate. Her CHA₂DS₂-VASc score is 3 (age 65–74 = 1, hypertension = 1, female sex = 1). Anticoagulation is recommended when annual stroke risk is ≥2%, which corresponds to a score of ≥2 in men or ≥3 in women (female sex is a risk modifier — it counts only when other factors are present).

For eligible patients, a direct oral anticoagulant (DOAC) is preferred over warfarin: equal or better stroke prevention, about half the intracranial hemorrhage, no INR monitoring. DOACs are not used with a mechanical valve or moderate–severe rheumatic mitral stenosis — warfarin is the drug there.

CHA₂DS₂-VASc Points
CHF or LV dysfunction 1
Hypertension 1
Age ≥75 2
Diabetes 1
Stroke / TIA / thromboembolism 2
Vascular disease (MI, PAD, aortic plaque) 1
Age 65–74 1
Sex category (female) 1

Why not the others

  • (B) Aspirin — Aspirin gives little stroke protection in AF and bleeds almost as much as a DOAC. It is not recommended for stroke prevention in AF.
  • (C) Aspirin plus clopidogrel — Dual antiplatelet therapy is inferior to anticoagulation for AF stroke prevention and carries similar bleeding risk.
  • (D) No antithrombotic therapy because her pulse rate is controlled — Rate control treats symptoms, not stroke risk. Stagnant flow in the left atrial appendage persists however well the rate is controlled.
  • (E) Warfarin with a target INR of 2.0–3.0 — Warfarin works, but DOACs are preferred because they cause less intracranial hemorrhage and need no INR monitoring. Warfarin is the right choice only for a mechanical valve or moderate–severe mitral stenosis.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Calculate HAS-BLED to find and fix modifiable bleeding risks (uncontrolled BP, NSAIDs, alcohol, labile INR) — not to withhold anticoagulation. A high bleeding score is rarely a reason to skip a DOAC.

🎯 Educational objective

In atrial fibrillation, anticoagulate when CHA₂DS₂-VASc is ≥2 in men or ≥3 in women, and prefer a DOAC over warfarin unless the patient has a mechanical valve or moderate–severe mitral stenosis.

CV-005.stem_html:
An 82-year-old man is evaluated for 4 months of breathlessness when he climbs one flight of stairs. Last week he felt lightheaded and had to sit down while carrying groceries. He has hypertension and hyperlipidemia. He lives independently, drives and walks his dog daily.

Blood pressure is 134/78 mm Hg and pulse rate is 70/min. There is a grade 3/6 late-peaking crescendo–decrescendo systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border that radiates to both carotids. The aortic component of S₂ is soft. Carotid upstrokes are delayed and weak.

Echocardiogram — aortic valve area0.7 cm²
Echocardiogram — mean gradient48 mm Hg
Echocardiogram — peak aortic jet velocity4.6 m/s
Echocardiogram — LV ejection fraction60%
CV-005.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Balloon aortic valvuloplasty as definitive therapy
choices.C: Start a beta-blocker for exertional symptoms

CV-005.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Aortic stenosis

He has severe aortic stenosis (AVA ≤1.0 cm², mean gradient ≥40 mm Hg, peak velocity ≥4.0 m/s) and he is symptomatic (exertional dyspnea and presyncope). Once symptoms appear, average survival without valve replacement is only a few years, and sudden death becomes a real risk. Aortic valve replacement is indicated (Class 1).

No medicine changes the natural history of AS. The question is only which replacement. At age >80, transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) is generally preferred over surgery when anatomy is suitable; for patients <65 with long life expectancy, surgical AVR is usually favored; between those ages, it is a shared decision by the heart team.

Classic symptoms of severe AS Rough survival without AVR
Angina ~5 years
Syncope ~3 years
Heart failure ~2 years

Why not the others

  • (A) Balloon aortic valvuloplasty as definitive therapy — Balloon valvuloplasty gives only temporary relief (restenosis within months). It is a bridge, not definitive therapy.
  • (B) Repeat echocardiography in 12 months — Watchful waiting with serial echo is for asymptomatic severe AS with normal LV function. Symptoms change the indication to valve replacement now.
  • (C) Start a beta-blocker for exertional symptoms — Beta-blockers do not relieve the obstruction and can worsen exertional symptoms by limiting the heart rate response.
  • (D) Start lisinopril to reduce afterload — Vasodilators can drop blood pressure sharply because cardiac output is fixed by the narrowed valve; they do not treat the obstruction.
🧠 Mnemonic

Symptoms of severe AS — "SAD": Syncope, Angina, Dyspnea. Any one of them with severe AS → replace the valve.

🎓 ABIM pearl

A soft or absent A₂ and late-peaking murmur mean severe AS. Murmur loudness is misleading — it falls when the LV fails.

🎯 Educational objective

Symptomatic severe aortic stenosis requires aortic valve replacement; in patients older than 80 years with suitable anatomy, transcatheter implantation is preferred.

CV-006.stem_html:
A 62-year-old man comes for follow-up 6 months after a non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction treated with a drug-eluting stent. He takes aspirin, ticagrelor, metoprolol succinate, lisinopril and atorvastatin 80 mg daily. He reports taking every dose and has no muscle pain. He walks 40 minutes daily and follows a Mediterranean diet.

Blood pressure is 124/76 mm Hg. Examination is normal.

Total cholesterol162 mg/dL
LDL cholesterol88 mg/dL (before the MI 156 mg/dL)
HDL cholesterol42 mg/dL
Triglycerides160 mg/dL
ALT28 U/L
Hemoglobin A1c5.6%
CV-006.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to reduce his cardiovascular risk?
CV-006.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Lipid management after myocardial infarction

He has clinical ASCVD with a recent ACS — very high risk. He is already on a maximally tolerated high-intensity statin, yet his LDL is still well above the 2026 ACC/AHA goal of <55 mg/dL for very-high-risk ASCVD.

The next step is a nonstatin drug with outcome data: ezetimibe first (cheap, oral, well tolerated; IMPROVE-IT showed fewer cardiovascular events after ACS). If LDL remains above threshold, add a PCSK9 inhibitor (or inclisiran/bempedoic acid in selected patients).

Lower LDL, longer, is better — every 39 mg/dL (1 mmol/L) reduction in LDL lowers major vascular events by about 20%.

Statin intensity Drug and daily dose LDL reduction
High Atorvastatin 40–80 mg, rosuvastatin 20–40 mg ≥50%
Moderate Atorvastatin 10–20, rosuvastatin 5–10, simvastatin 20–40 30%–49%

Why not the others

  • (B) Add fenofibrate — Fibrates lower triglycerides; his triglycerides are only mildly elevated and fibrates added to a statin have not reduced cardiovascular events.
  • (C) Add niacin — Niacin raises HDL but did not reduce events on top of a statin (AIM-HIGH, HPS2-THRIVE) and causes flushing, hyperglycemia and myopathy.
  • (D) Continue current therapy unchanged — His LDL is above the threshold for adding therapy in very-high-risk ASCVD. Accepting it leaves avoidable risk.
  • (E) Switch to rosuvastatin 5 mg daily — Rosuvastatin 5 mg is moderate intensity — a step down from atorvastatin 80 mg.
🎓 ABIM pearl

After ACS, check a lipid panel 4–12 weeks after starting or changing therapy to confirm response and adherence, then every 3–12 months.

🎯 Educational objective

In very-high-risk ASCVD with LDL ≥70 mg/dL despite a maximally tolerated statin, add ezetimibe and then a PCSK9 inhibitor if needed.

CV-007.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
CV-007.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Acute pericarditis

He meets the diagnosis of acute pericarditis (≥2 of 4): pleuritic, positional chest pain; a pericardial friction rub; diffuse concave ST elevation with PR depression; and a new pericardial effusion. Most cases in young adults are viral or idiopathic.

First-line therapy is a high-dose NSAID (or aspirin) plus colchicine. Colchicine roughly halves the recurrence rate and speeds symptom relief. Typical course: ibuprofen 600 mg three times daily for 1–2 weeks with a taper; colchicine 0.5 mg twice daily (once daily if <70 kg) for 3 months. Restrict strenuous exercise until symptoms and CRP resolve (at least 3 months for athletes).

Admit if any high-risk feature: fever >38 °C, subacute onset, large effusion or tamponade, failure of NSAIDs after 1 week, immunosuppression, trauma, oral anticoagulation, or myopericarditis (elevated troponin).

Why not the others

  • (A) Ibuprofen alone — An NSAID alone works but leaves about twice the recurrence risk compared with adding colchicine.
  • (C) Pericardiocentesis — The effusion is small and there is no tamponade. Pericardiocentesis is for tamponade or suspected bacterial/malignant effusion.
  • (D) Prednisone 1 mg/kg daily — Glucocorticoids as first-line therapy increase recurrences. Reserve them for NSAID contraindications, failure, or specific causes (autoimmune disease, pregnancy constraints).
  • (E) Urgent coronary angiography — Normal troponin, normal wall motion, diffuse (not territorial) ST elevation and PR depression point away from STEMI.
🎓 ABIM pearl

ECG tells pericarditis from STEMI: concave ST elevation in many territories, PR depression, no reciprocal ST depression (except aVR and V1), and no Q waves.

🎯 Educational objective

Treat acute idiopathic or viral pericarditis with a high-dose NSAID plus colchicine for 3 months; avoid first-line glucocorticoids because they increase recurrence.

CV-008.topic: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
CV-008.stem_html:
A 64-year-old man with ischemic cardiomyopathy comes for follow-up. He gets short of breath after walking about two blocks but has no dyspnea at rest, orthopnea or edema. Over the past 6 months his medicines were titrated to sacubitril–valsartan 97/103 mg twice daily, metoprolol succinate 200 mg daily, spironolactone 25 mg daily and furosemide 20 mg daily. He does not have diabetes.

Blood pressure is 112/70 mm Hg and pulse rate is 60/min, regular. Jugular venous pressure is normal and the lungs are clear. There is no edema. Echocardiography last month showed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 30%.

Sodium138 mEq/L
Potassium4.6 mEq/L
Creatinine1.3 mg/dL (eGFR 58 mL/min/1.73 m²)
Hemoglobin A1c5.7%
CV-008.lead: Which of the following drugs should be added to his regimen?
CV-008.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction

Guideline-directed therapy for HFrEF rests on four pillars, each of which lowers mortality: an ARNI (or ACE inhibitor/ARB), an evidence-based beta-blocker, a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist and an SGLT2 inhibitor. He is on three of the four.

Dapagliflozin or empagliflozin reduce cardiovascular death and heart-failure hospitalization by about 25% in HFrEF with or without diabetes (DAPA-HF, EMPEROR-Reduced). Benefit appears within weeks. They can be started down to an eGFR of about 20–25 mL/min/1.73 m², cause little hypotension, and slow kidney function decline.

Pillar Examples Watch for
ARNI (or ACEi/ARB) Sacubitril–valsartan Hypotension, K⁺, angioedema (36-h ACEi washout)
Beta-blocker Carvedilol, metoprolol succinate, bisoprolol Bradycardia, start low when euvolemic
MRA Spironolactone, eplerenone K⁺ >5.0, eGFR <30
SGLT2 inhibitor Dapagliflozin, empagliflozin Genital mycotic infection, euglycemic DKA, volume

Why not the others

  • (B) Digoxin — Digoxin reduces hospitalizations for symptoms but not mortality. It is added only when symptoms persist on full GDMT or for AF rate control.
  • (C) Diltiazem — Nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers are negative inotropes and worsen HFrEF. Avoid them.
  • (D) Hydralazine plus isosorbide dinitrate — Hydralazine–nitrate is added for self-identified Black patients with persistent NYHA III–IV symptoms on optimal therapy, or for patients who cannot take an ARNI/ACE inhibitor/ARB. He fits neither.
  • (E) Ivabradine — Ivabradine is for patients in sinus rhythm whose heart rate stays ≥70/min on a maximally tolerated beta-blocker. His pulse rate is 60/min.
🧠 Mnemonic

The four pillars: "Always Be My Shield" — ARNI, Beta-blocker, MRA, SGLT2 inhibitor.

🎓 ABIM pearl

He also meets criteria for a primary-prevention ICD: ischemic cardiomyopathy, EF ≤35%, NYHA II, ≥40 days after MI, on ≥3 months of GDMT, with >1-year expected survival.

🎯 Educational objective

Every patient with HFrEF should receive all four mortality-reducing drug classes — ARNI/ACE inhibitor/ARB, beta-blocker, MRA and an SGLT2 inhibitor — regardless of diabetes status.

📚 Read more in Wardology🏛️ HFrEF — reduced EF & the 4 pillars →

  2. McMurray JJV, et al. Dapagliflozin in patients with heart failure and reduced ejection fraction (DAPA-HF). N Engl J Med 2019;381:1995.

CV-009.stem_html:
A 52-year-old woman is evaluated during a follow-up visit for hypertension diagnosed 4 years ago. Her blood pressure has remained elevated despite adherence to amlodipine, 10 mg/d; lisinopril, 40 mg/d; and chlorthalidone, 25 mg/d. Home blood pressure readings average 152/94 mm Hg. She reports occasional muscle cramps. She does not drink alcohol or use NSAIDs.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 156/96 mm Hg and pulse rate is 72/min. BMI is 27. There is no abdominal bruit. The remainder of the examination is unremarkable.

Sodium143 mEq/L
Potassium3.2 mEq/L
Bicarbonate31 mEq/L
Creatinine0.8 mg/dL
CV-009.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnostic test to perform next?

choices.E: Plasma aldosterone concentration and plasma renin activity

CV-009.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Primary aldosteronism — screening

She has resistant hypertension (above goal on three drugs at full dose, one a diuretic) plus hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis. That trio points to primary aldosteronism, the most common curable cause of secondary hypertension (about 1 in 10 hypertensive patients, up to 1 in 5 with resistant hypertension).

Screen with a morning plasma aldosterone concentration (PAC) and plasma renin activity (PRA). A positive screen is a suppressed renin with a PAC ≥10–15 ng/dL (aldosterone-to-renin ratio >20–30). Most antihypertensives can be continued for screening; correct hypokalemia first, because low potassium lowers aldosterone and can produce a false-negative result.

Step Test
1. Screen PAC + PRA (ratio)
2. Confirm Oral salt loading or saline infusion (skip if K⁺ low, renin suppressed and PAC >20 ng/dL)
3. Subtype Adrenal CT, then adrenal vein sampling if surgery is being considered
4. Treat Unilateral → laparoscopic adrenalectomy; bilateral → spironolactone or eplerenone

Why not the others

  • (A) 24-hour urine metanephrines — Metanephrines screen for pheochromocytoma, which causes paroxysmal symptoms (headache, palpitations, sweating) and does not explain hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis.
  • (B) Adrenal-protocol CT scan — Imaging comes only after biochemical confirmation. Adrenal nodules are common and usually nonfunctioning, so CT first leads to false conclusions.
  • (C) Kidney artery duplex ultrasonography — Renovascular disease is possible in resistant hypertension, but the hypokalemia and alkalosis make aldosterone excess the first thing to test. There is also no bruit or rise in creatinine with the ACE inhibitor.
  • (D) Overnight 1-mg dexamethasone suppression test — The dexamethasone suppression test screens for cortisol excess. She has no cushingoid features.
🧠 Mnemonic

"Low K, high BP, think the A in RAA" — hypokalemia + hypertension = check Aldosterone and renin.

🎓 ABIM pearl

Current guidance (Endocrine Society 2025) urges screening for primary aldosteronism in all patients with hypertension, not only those with resistance or hypokalemia. Most patients with the disease have a normal potassium.

🎯 Educational objective

Screen for primary aldosteronism with a plasma aldosterone concentration and plasma renin activity in patients with resistant hypertension or hypertension with hypokalemia.

  2. 2025 AHA/ACC multisociety high blood pressure guideline. Hypertension 2025.

CV-010.stem_html:
A 31-year-old woman is evaluated for hypertension found at a routine visit 2 months ago and confirmed by home readings averaging 158/100 mm Hg. She has no symptoms. She has never smoked. She takes no medications, including oral contraceptives, and her family history is negative for hypertension.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 160/102 mm Hg in both arms and pulse rate is 68/min. BMI is 22. A systolic-diastolic bruit is heard in the right upper abdominal quadrant. The remainder of the examination is normal.

Potassium3.6 mEq/L
Creatinine0.7 mg/dL
Urinalysisnormal
TSH1.8 µU/mL
CV-010.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnostic test?
CV-010.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Renovascular hypertension — fibromuscular dysplasia

New, significant hypertension in a young woman without risk factors, with an abdominal bruit, is fibromuscular dysplasia (FMD) until proven otherwise. FMD is a nonatherosclerotic, noninflammatory disease of medium-sized arteries; the kidney and carotid arteries are most often affected, classically with a "string of beads" appearance in the mid-to-distal renal artery.

Image the renal arteries with CT angiography (or MR angiography; duplex ultrasonography in an experienced laboratory is acceptable). Catheter angiography is the reference standard and is usually done when intervention is planned.

Unlike atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis — where stenting rarely beats medical therapy — FMD responds well to percutaneous balloon angioplasty without stenting, and hypertension is often cured. Because FMD is a systemic arteriopathy, a one-time head-to-pelvis vascular imaging study looks for aneurysms and dissection elsewhere.

FMD Atherosclerotic RAS
Patient Woman, 15–50 y Older, smoker, diffuse atherosclerosis
Location Mid/distal renal artery Ostium/proximal
Treatment Angioplasty (no stent) Medical therapy (statin, antiplatelet, BP control)

Why not the others

  • (B) Kidney biopsy — Her urinalysis and kidney function are normal. Nothing suggests parenchymal kidney disease.
  • (C) Kidney scintigraphy with captopril — Captopril renography has poor sensitivity and specificity and is no longer recommended for diagnosing renovascular disease.
  • (D) Plasma metanephrines — Pheochromocytoma is rare and causes paroxysms; it does not produce an abdominal bruit.
  • (E) Polysomnography — Sleep apnea is a common cause of secondary hypertension, but she has a normal BMI and the bruit points to a vascular cause.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Clues to renovascular hypertension — onset <30 or >55 years, abrupt worsening of previously controlled BP, creatinine rise >30% after an ACE inhibitor/ARB, flash pulmonary edema, unexplained small kidney, or an abdominal bruit.

🎯 Educational objective

Suspect fibromuscular dysplasia in a young woman with new hypertension and an abdominal bruit, and confirm it with CT or MR angiography.

  2. 2025 AHA/ACC multisociety high blood pressure guideline. Hypertension 2025.

CV-011.stem_html:
A 46-year-old man is evaluated after three office visits over 2 months with elevated blood pressure. He has no symptoms and no medical history. He does not smoke. He exercises regularly.

His office readings were 148/92, 150/94 and 146/90 mm Hg. Home readings with a validated upper-arm device, taken twice daily for 1 week, average 122/76 mm Hg.

On physical examination today, blood pressure is 148/94 mm Hg and pulse rate is 84/min. BMI is 24. The remainder of the examination is normal. Basic metabolic panel, lipid levels and urinalysis are normal; 10-year ASCVD risk is 4%.
CV-011.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.B: Confirm with 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring
choices.E: Reassure him and stop all future blood pressure checks

CV-011.explain_html:
Correct answer: B White-coat hypertension

Office readings are high, home readings are normal: this pattern suggests white-coat hypertension. Before labeling and treating — or dismissing — him, confirm the pattern with the reference standard, 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM). Thresholds for hypertension on out-of-office testing are lower than in the office.

Measurement Hypertension threshold
Office ≥130/80
Home average ≥130/80
ABPM daytime (awake) ≥130/80
ABPM nighttime ≥110/65
ABPM 24-hour ≥125/75

If ABPM confirms white-coat hypertension, he does not need drug therapy, but he needs periodic out-of-office monitoring because about 1 in 5 people with this pattern develop sustained hypertension within a few years.

Why not the others

  • (A) Begin chlorthalidone — Treating white-coat hypertension causes hypotension at home and adds no proven benefit. Confirm the diagnosis first.
  • (C) Measure plasma aldosterone and renin — Secondary-hypertension testing is premature before the diagnosis of hypertension itself is confirmed.
  • (D) Obtain an echocardiogram — Echocardiography is not part of the routine evaluation of newly elevated blood pressure.
  • (E) Reassure him and stop all future blood pressure checks — White-coat hypertension carries a modestly higher risk of developing sustained hypertension. He needs ongoing out-of-office monitoring, not discharge from follow-up.
🎓 ABIM pearl

The mirror image — normal office, high home readings — is masked hypertension. It carries the same cardiovascular risk as sustained hypertension and is treated as such.

🎯 Educational objective

Confirm suspected white-coat hypertension with 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring before starting or withholding treatment.

CV-012.stem_html:
A 64-year-old man is evaluated for uncontrolled hypertension. He takes olmesartan, 40 mg/d; amlodipine, 10 mg/d; and chlorthalidone, 25 mg/d, and his pharmacy confirms on-time refills. Home readings average 148/88 mm Hg. He has type 2 diabetes treated with metformin. He does not take NSAIDs, decongestants or supplements. Polysomnography last year was normal.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 150/90 mm Hg and pulse rate is 70/min. BMI is 30. The remainder of the examination is unremarkable.

Potassium4.2 mEq/L
Creatinine1.0 mg/dL
eGFR78 mL/min/1.73 m²
Plasma aldosterone-to-renin ratio8 (not suggestive of primary aldosteronism)
CV-012.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
CV-012.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Resistant hypertension — fourth drug

He has true resistant hypertension: above goal on three drugs of different classes at maximal doses, including a diuretic, with adherence confirmed, white-coat effect excluded by home readings, and common secondary causes (sleep apnea, aldosteronism, interfering drugs) addressed.

The best fourth drug is a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist — spironolactone (25–50 mg/d). In the PATHWAY-2 trial it lowered blood pressure more than bisoprolol or doxazosin. Many patients with resistant hypertension have relative aldosterone excess and volume expansion even with normal screening.

Watch potassium and creatinine, especially with an ARB, diabetes or reduced eGFR. If spironolactone causes gynecomastia, switch to eplerenone. If potassium is a problem, amiloride is an alternative.

Why not the others

  • (A) Add clonidine — Clonidine causes sedation, dry mouth and rebound hypertension if doses are missed. It is a late option.
  • (B) Add hydralazine — Hydralazine causes reflex tachycardia and fluid retention and is reserved for later steps.
  • (C) Add lisinopril — Combining an ACE inhibitor with an ARB (dual RAAS blockade) raises the risk of hyperkalemia and AKI with no outcome benefit.
  • (E) Refer for renal denervation — Renal denervation is an option only after optimal medical therapy (including an MRA) fails or is not tolerated, in selected patients at experienced centers.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Before calling hypertension "resistant", rule out pseudoresistance — poor technique (small cuff), white-coat effect, nonadherence, inadequate doses, and interfering substances (NSAIDs, decongestants, stimulants, alcohol, licorice).

🎯 Educational objective

Add spironolactone as the fourth drug in true resistant hypertension.

CV-013.stem_html:
A 58-year-old woman is evaluated for a dry, tickling cough that started 6 weeks ago. She has no fever, wheezing, heartburn or postnasal drip. She does not smoke. Lisinopril was started 2 months ago for hypertension; her blood pressure is now controlled.

On physical examination, vital signs are normal. Oxygen saturation is 98% breathing ambient air. The oropharynx is clear and the lungs are clear. Chest radiograph is normal.
CV-013.lead: Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of her cough?

choices.A: Accumulation of bradykinin and substance P
choices.D: Increased angiotensin II activity in the bronchi

CV-013.explain_html:
Correct answer: A ACE inhibitor–induced cough

ACE is the same enzyme as kininase II. Blocking it raises angiotensin I and lowers angiotensin II, but it also stops the breakdown of bradykinin and substance P. These peptides accumulate in the airway, sensitize cough receptors and stimulate prostaglandin production — a dry cough in about 10% of patients (more often in women and people of East Asian descent).

The cough can start days to months after the first dose and usually resolves 1–4 weeks after stopping the drug (sometimes up to 3 months). The fix is to switch to an ARB, which blocks the angiotensin II receptor without affecting bradykinin, so cough is no more common than with placebo.

The same bradykinin mechanism causes ACE inhibitor angioedema. ARBs carry a much smaller risk, but most experts avoid them after ACE inhibitor angioedema.

Why not the others

  • (B) Acid reflux into the larynx — Reflux-related cough is possible, but she has no reflux symptoms and the cough started after lisinopril.
  • (C) Eosinophilic airway inflammation — Eosinophilic airway inflammation underlies cough-variant asthma and nonasthmatic eosinophilic bronchitis. The timing with lisinopril points to the drug.
  • (D) Increased angiotensin II activity in the bronchi — ACE inhibitors lower angiotensin II. Angiotensin II is not the cause of the cough.
  • (E) Mast cell degranulation by IgE — ACE inhibitor cough and angioedema are not IgE-mediated, which is also why antihistamines do not help.
🧠 Mnemonic

ACE inhibitors "K"eep the Kinins — bradykinin up → cough, angioedema. ARBs leave kinins alone.

🎯 Educational objective

ACE inhibitor cough results from accumulation of bradykinin and substance P; switching to an ARB resolves it.

CV-014.stem_html:
A 50-year-old Black man is evaluated for hypertension confirmed by home monitoring (average 138/86 mm Hg). He has no symptoms. He has no diabetes, kidney disease or heart failure. He has followed a low-sodium diet and exercised for 6 months. His 10-year ASCVD risk is 11%.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 140/88 mm Hg and pulse rate is 76/min. BMI is 28. The remainder of the examination is normal.

Potassium4.1 mEq/L
Creatinine1.0 mg/dL
Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio10 mg/g
CV-014.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial drug therapy?
CV-014.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Hypertension in a Black adult

His average blood pressure is in stage 1 range (130–139/80–89 mm Hg) but his 10-year ASCVD risk is ≥10% (the 2025 guideline uses a PREVENT 10-year risk ≥7.5%), so drug therapy is indicated on top of lifestyle change. Because he is close to goal, one drug is reasonable.

In Black adults without CKD or heart failure, a thiazide-type diuretic or a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker is preferred as initial therapy. In ALLHAT, ACE inhibitor monotherapy in Black patients produced less blood pressure lowering and more strokes and heart failure than chlorthalidone or amlodipine. ACE inhibitors and ARBs still work well in combination with these drugs, and they are preferred in anyone with albuminuric CKD or HFrEF, whatever their race.

Why not the others

  • (B) Doxazosin — Alpha-blockers are not first-line; the doxazosin arm of ALLHAT was stopped early for excess heart failure.
  • (C) Lisinopril — An ACE inhibitor is a first-line class, but as monotherapy in Black patients without CKD it is less effective and was linked to more stroke and angioedema in ALLHAT.
  • (D) Metoprolol succinate — Beta-blockers are not first-line for uncomplicated hypertension.
  • (E) Spironolactone — Spironolactone is the add-on for resistant hypertension, not initial therapy.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Angioedema from ACE inhibitors is 3–4 times more common in Black patients — another reason a CCB or thiazide comes first when monotherapy is chosen.

🎯 Educational objective

In Black adults with hypertension and no CKD or heart failure, start with a thiazide-type diuretic or a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker.

CV-015.topic: Intensive blood pressure targets — benefits and harms
CV-015.stem_html:
A 76-year-old man with hypertension, hyperlipidemia and stable coronary artery disease asks about his blood pressure goal. He lives independently, walks a mile daily and has no history of falls or orthostatic symptoms. He takes amlodipine, losartan, atorvastatin and aspirin.

On physical examination, seated blood pressure is 138/76 mm Hg and standing blood pressure is 134/74 mm Hg; pulse rate is 66/min. The remainder of the examination is normal. eGFR is 64 mL/min/1.73 m².

You discuss lowering his systolic blood pressure to less than 120 mm Hg, as in the SPRINT trial.
CV-015.lead: Compared with a target of less than 140 mm Hg, an intensive target is most likely to cause which of the following?

choices.A: An increase in acute kidney injury and electrolyte abnormalities
choices.E: More myocardial infarctions owing to diastolic hypotension

CV-015.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Intensive blood pressure targets — benefits and harms

In SPRINT (nondiabetic adults at high cardiovascular risk, including those ≥75 years), a systolic target <120 mm Hg versus <140 mm Hg reduced major cardiovascular events by about 25% and all-cause mortality by about 27%. The benefit was at least as large in the ≥75-year subgroup.

The cost: more hypotension, syncope, electrolyte abnormalities (hypokalemia, hyponatremia) and acute kidney injury (mostly reversible eGFR declines). Injurious falls were not increased, and intensive control reduced mild cognitive impairment.

For a fit, independent older adult like this man, guidelines recommend a target of <130/80 mm Hg, and lower if tolerated. Frailty, limited life expectancy or orthostatic hypotension call for individualized, less aggressive targets.

Why not the others

  • (B) An increase in all-cause mortality — Intensive treatment lowered all-cause mortality in SPRINT.
  • (C) An increase in injurious falls — Injurious falls were similar between groups, including in adults ≥75 years.
  • (D) Faster cognitive decline — Intensive control reduced the risk of mild cognitive impairment (SPRINT MIND); it did not speed cognitive decline.
  • (E) More myocardial infarctions owing to diastolic hypotension — The "J-curve" worry about low diastolic pressure was not borne out; myocardial infarction was not increased.
🎓 ABIM pearl

On the boards, "older" alone is not a reason for a looser blood pressure goal. Look for frailty, falls, orthostasis or limited life expectancy before relaxing the target.

🎯 Educational objective

Intensive systolic blood pressure lowering reduces cardiovascular events and mortality, including in fit older adults, at the cost of more acute kidney injury, electrolyte abnormalities, hypotension and syncope.

CV-016.stem_html:
A 55-year-old woman is evaluated for 2 months of substernal chest pressure that comes on when she climbs two flights of stairs and resolves within 5 minutes of rest. She has hypertension and hyperlipidemia. She does not smoke. Medications are lisinopril and rosuvastatin.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 132/78 mm Hg and pulse rate is 74/min. BMI is 26. Cardiac examination is normal. Resting ECG shows sinus rhythm with no ST-segment or T-wave abnormalities. She walks briskly every day.
CV-016.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnostic test?

choices.D: High-sensitivity troponin measurement now and in 3 hours
choices.E: No testing; begin aspirin and observe

CV-016.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Stable chest pain — initial testing

She has typical (cardiac) chest pain — substernal, provoked by exertion, relieved by rest — and is stable: the pattern has not changed, it is not occurring at rest, and the ECG is normal. Her pretest probability of obstructive coronary artery disease is intermediate.

The 2021 AHA/ACC chest pain guideline gives coronary CT angiography (CCTA) or stress testing equal (Class 1) weight for intermediate-risk stable chest pain. CCTA is favored in younger patients (<65 years) without known CAD who are not on optimal preventive therapy, because it shows both stenosis and nonobstructive plaque; stress imaging is favored in older patients with known CAD or heavy calcification. She can exercise and has a normal ECG, so an exercise ECG would also be acceptable.

Patient Preferred first test
Low risk, age <40 Often no test
Intermediate risk, <65 y, no known CAD CCTA (or stress test)
Known CAD, heavy calcium, older Stress imaging (echo, SPECT, PET, CMR)
Can exercise + interpretable ECG Exercise ECG acceptable
High-risk features or refractory symptoms Invasive angiography

Why not the others

  • (A) Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging — Stress CMR is an imaging option, but rest CMR without stress is not a test for coronary artery disease.
  • (B) Coronary angiography — Invasive angiography is for high-risk noninvasive results, refractory symptoms despite medical therapy, or acute coronary syndrome.
  • (D) High-sensitivity troponin measurement now and in 3 hours — Serial troponins are for suspected acute coronary syndrome. Her pain is stable and exertional, and she is seen in the office.
  • (E) No testing; begin aspirin and observe — Typical angina at intermediate risk merits testing to define coronary anatomy and guide therapy.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Three features of typical angina — substernal discomfort, provoked by exertion or emotion, relieved by rest or nitroglycerin. All three = typical; two = atypical; one or none = noncardiac.

🎯 Educational objective

For stable chest pain at intermediate risk in a patient younger than 65 years without known CAD, coronary CT angiography (or stress testing) is an appropriate first test.

CV-017.stem_html:
A 67-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 1 hour after onset of crushing chest pain and diaphoresis. Sublingual nitroglycerin was given by paramedics, and he became lightheaded.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 82/50 mm Hg, pulse rate is 58/min, and respiration rate is 18/min. Oxygen saturation is 96% breathing ambient air. Jugular venous pressure is elevated, and it rises with inspiration. Lungs are clear. ECG shows 3-mm ST-segment elevation in leads II, III and aVF, with ST elevation of 1 mm in lead V4R. The cardiac catheterization laboratory has been activated.
CV-017.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
CV-017.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Right ventricular infarction

Inferior STEMI + hypotension, elevated JVP and clear lungs = right ventricular infarction (seen in up to 40% of inferior STEMIs, usually with proximal right coronary artery occlusion). ST elevation in V4R confirms it. Kussmaul sign (JVP rising with inspiration) can occur.

The infarcted RV cannot pump blood forward, so left ventricular filling depends on preload. Nitrates, diuretics and morphine lower preload and can cause profound hypotension — exactly what happened after his nitroglycerin.

Treat with: IV isotonic fluids to raise preload (watch for overload), avoid nitrates and diuretics, maintain AV synchrony (pace if heart block), inotropes such as dobutamine if hypotension persists, and — most important — emergency reperfusion with primary PCI.

Why not the others

  • (A) Intravenous furosemide — Diuretics reduce preload and worsen hypotension in RV infarction. His lungs are clear; he is not volume overloaded on the left.
  • (B) Intravenous metoprolol — Beta-blockers are contraindicated in hypotension, bradycardia and shock.
  • (C) Intravenous morphine — Morphine is a venodilator, lowers preload and may delay antiplatelet absorption.
  • (E) Repeat sublingual nitroglycerin — More nitroglycerin would further drop preload. Nitrates are contraindicated in RV infarction.
🧠 Mnemonic

RV infarct triad: "Hypotension, high JVP, clear lungs." Treatment: fluids in, nitrates out.

🎯 Educational objective

Treat hypotension from right ventricular infarction with intravenous fluids and urgent reperfusion while avoiding nitrates, diuretics and other preload-reducing drugs.

CV-018.stem_html:
A 63-year-old woman is admitted from the emergency department with 4 hours of intermittent substernal chest pressure at rest. She has type 2 diabetes and hypertension. Her pain resolved after sublingual nitroglycerin, and she is now pain-free.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 138/80 mm Hg, pulse rate is 82/min, and respiration rate is 16/min. Oxygen saturation is 97% breathing ambient air. Lungs are clear and there is no murmur or edema. ECG shows 1-mm horizontal ST-segment depression in leads V4 through V6.

High-sensitivity troponin T at arrival48 ng/L (reference <14)
High-sensitivity troponin T at 2 hours112 ng/L
Creatinine0.9 mg/dL
CV-018.lead: In addition to aspirin, anticoagulation and high-intensity statin therapy, which of the following is the most appropriate management?
CV-018.explain_html:
Correct answer: A NSTEMI — timing of invasive strategy

She has an NSTEMI: rest angina, ST depression and a rising troponin. She is now stable — no ongoing pain, no hemodynamic or electrical instability, no heart failure.

Patients with NSTE-ACS and high-risk features — rising troponin consistent with MI, dynamic ST changes, or a GRACE score >140 — benefit from an early invasive strategy within 24 hours. Others at intermediate risk can have angiography during the hospitalization (within 24–72 hours).

Immediate (<2 h) angiography is reserved for very-high-risk features: refractory angina, hemodynamic instability or cardiogenic shock, acute heart failure, life-threatening arrhythmias, or mechanical complications.

Risk Timing
Very high (shock, refractory pain, VT/VF, acute HF) Immediate, <2 h
High (NSTEMI by troponin, dynamic ST changes, GRACE >140) Early, <24 h
Lower risk During admission or ischemia-guided

Why not the others

  • (B) Coronary CT angiography — CCTA is for low-to-intermediate risk chest pain without confirmed MI. Her diagnosis is established; she needs invasive angiography with possible revascularization.
  • (C) Emergency coronary angiography within 2 hours — She is pain-free and stable; none of the very-high-risk criteria for immediate angiography is present.
  • (D) Exercise stress test before discharge — Stress testing is for low-risk patients after MI is ruled out. She has an NSTEMI with dynamic ECG changes.
  • (E) Fibrinolytic therapy — Fibrinolysis is harmful in NSTE-ACS; it benefits only ST-elevation MI when PCI is not available in time.
🎯 Educational objective

In NSTEMI with high-risk features but no very-high-risk features, perform coronary angiography within 24 hours.

CV-019.topic: Antithrombotic therapy after PCI in atrial fibrillation
CV-019.stem_html:
A 72-year-old man underwent PCI with a drug-eluting stent to the left anterior descending artery 2 days ago for NSTEMI. He has persistent atrial fibrillation, hypertension and diabetes; his CHA₂DS₂-VASc score is 4 and his HAS-BLED score is 2. Before admission he took apixaban. During the procedure he received aspirin and a loading dose of clopidogrel. He has no history of bleeding.

Vital signs and examination are normal. Creatinine is 1.1 mg/dL and hemoglobin is 13.4 g/dL.
CV-019.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate antithrombotic regimen at discharge?

choices.A: Apixaban and clopidogrel, with aspirin stopped at discharge or within 1 week
choices.B: Apixaban, aspirin and clopidogrel for 12 months

CV-019.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Antithrombotic therapy after PCI in atrial fibrillation

After PCI, a patient with AF needs two different protections: an anticoagulant against stroke and a P2Y₁₂ inhibitor against stent thrombosis. Triple therapy (anticoagulant + aspirin + P2Y₁₂ inhibitor) roughly doubles major bleeding without preventing more ischemic events.

The default strategy (AUGUSTUS, ENTRUST, PIONEER, RE-DUAL): DOAC + clopidogrel, giving aspirin only peri-procedurally (up to 1 week; up to 30 days if thrombotic risk is very high). Continue dual therapy for 12 months after ACS (6 months after elective PCI), then anticoagulant alone.

Component Choice
Anticoagulant DOAC (apixaban had the least bleeding) over warfarin
P2Y₁₂ inhibitor Clopidogrel (not ticagrelor or prasugrel)
Aspirin Stop at discharge or ≤1 week (≤30 days if high thrombotic risk)
After 12 months DOAC alone

Why not the others

  • (B) Apixaban, aspirin and clopidogrel for 12 months — Prolonged triple therapy markedly increases bleeding. Aspirin should be stopped early.
  • (C) Aspirin and clopidogrel; stop apixaban — Dual antiplatelet therapy does not protect against AF-related stroke; with a CHA₂DS₂-VASc score of 4 he needs anticoagulation.
  • (D) Aspirin and ticagrelor plus apixaban — Potent P2Y₁₂ inhibitors (ticagrelor, prasugrel) combined with an anticoagulant and aspirin cause excessive bleeding.
  • (E) Warfarin, aspirin and clopidogrel — DOACs cause less bleeding than warfarin in this setting, and the triple combination is the problem.
🎓 ABIM pearl

"Drop the aspirin, keep the DOAC, use clopidogrel." Three drugs = three times the trouble.

🎯 Educational objective

After PCI in a patient with atrial fibrillation, use a DOAC plus clopidogrel and stop aspirin at discharge or within 1–4 weeks.

CV-020.topic: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction
CV-020.stem_html:
A 74-year-old woman is evaluated in follow-up 2 weeks after hospitalization for acute decompensated heart failure. She now has dyspnea only when walking up a hill. She has hypertension, obesity and type 2 diabetes. Medications are furosemide, 20 mg/d; amlodipine; losartan; and metformin.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 128/72 mm Hg and pulse rate is 74/min. BMI is 35. Jugular venous pressure is normal. Lungs are clear. There is trace ankle edema.

Echocardiogram shows a left ventricular ejection fraction of 60%, left ventricular hypertrophy, grade 2 diastolic dysfunction and an enlarged left atrium. There is no valve disease. eGFR is 58 mL/min/1.73 m².
CV-020.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate addition to her treatment?

choices.E: Sacubitril-valsartan in place of losartan as the first step

CV-020.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction

She has HFpEF — heart failure symptoms with LVEF ≥50% and evidence of structural heart disease and raised filling pressures — and the classic phenotype: older, female, hypertensive, obese and diabetic.

SGLT2 inhibitors (empagliflozin, dapagliflozin) are the first disease-modifying drugs for HFpEF. In EMPEROR-Preserved and DELIVER they reduced the composite of heart failure hospitalization or cardiovascular death by about 20%, driven by fewer hospitalizations. They are recommended (Class 2a) for all patients with HFpEF, with or without diabetes, and they also protect the kidney.

The rest of HFpEF care: diuretics for congestion, treating hypertension and AF, weight loss (semaglutide or tirzepatide improve symptoms in obese HFpEF), exercise training, and — in selected patients, particularly at the lower end of the EF range — a mineralocorticoid antagonist (spironolactone or finerenone) or an ARNI.

Why not the others

  • (A) Digoxin — Digoxin does not improve outcomes in HFpEF and has a narrow therapeutic window in older adults with reduced kidney function.
  • (C) Isosorbide dinitrate — Nitrates reduced activity levels in HFpEF (NEAT-HFpEF) and are not recommended.
  • (D) Ivabradine — Ivabradine is used in HFrEF with sinus rhythm and heart rate ≥70/min despite beta-blockade. It has no role in HFpEF.
  • (E) Sacubitril-valsartan in place of losartan as the first step — Sacubitril-valsartan has only a weak (Class 2b) recommendation in HFpEF, mainly at the lower end of the ejection fraction range. SGLT2 inhibitors have stronger evidence and come first.
🎯 Educational objective

Add an SGLT2 inhibitor to diuretic therapy in patients with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction to reduce heart failure hospitalization.

CV-021.topic: Acute decompensated heart failure — diuretic dosing
CV-021.stem_html:
A 69-year-old man is admitted with 1 week of progressive dyspnea, orthopnea and leg swelling. He has HFrEF (LVEF 30%) and takes furosemide, 40 mg orally twice daily, along with carvedilol, sacubitril-valsartan, spironolactone and dapagliflozin.

On physical examination, blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg, pulse rate is 88/min, and respiration rate is 22/min. Oxygen saturation is 93% breathing ambient air. He is warm to the touch. Jugular venous pressure is 14 cm H₂O. There are bibasilar crackles and 3+ pitting edema to the knees.

Sodium136 mEq/L
Potassium4.4 mEq/L
Creatinine1.3 mg/dL (baseline 1.2 mg/dL)
CV-021.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial diuretic regimen?
CV-021.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Acute decompensated heart failure — diuretic dosing

He is "warm and wet" — congested but well perfused. The treatment is IV loop diuretics, and the dose matters.

Gut edema reduces oral absorption, so switch to IV. Loop diuretics have a threshold: below a certain dose the kidney excretes almost no extra sodium. In DOSE, a high-dose strategy — IV furosemide at 2.5 times the total daily oral dose — relieved congestion faster than a low dose, with only small, transient creatinine changes and no worse outcomes. His total daily oral dose is 80 mg, so the starting IV dose is about 200 mg/d (for example, 80–100 mg IV twice daily). Bolus versus continuous infusion made no difference.

Check urine output and spot urine sodium 2 hours after the dose: urine sodium <50–70 mEq/L or urine output <100–150 mL/h in the first 6 hours means the dose is too low — double it. If loop diuretics alone fail, add a thiazide (metolazone or chlorothiazide) or acetazolamide for sequential nephron blockade.

Why not the others

  • (A) Furosemide, 40 mg intravenously once daily — IV furosemide 40 mg/d is a lower total dose than his home dose and is likely to fall below the natriuretic threshold.
  • (B) Furosemide, 40 mg orally twice daily — Continuing his outpatient oral dose has already failed; poor absorption and underdosing explain the decompensation.
  • (D) Hydrochlorothiazide, 25 mg orally once daily — A thiazide alone is too weak; thiazides are added to loop diuretics for resistance, not used as initial monotherapy in ADHF.
  • (E) Tolvaptan, 15 mg orally once daily — Tolvaptan corrects hyponatremia but did not improve outcomes in ADHF (EVEREST); he is not hyponatremic.
🎓 ABIM pearl

A small rise in creatinine during decongestion ("permissive" worsening kidney function) is not a reason to stop diuresis if the patient is still congested. Persistent congestion is what predicts poor outcomes.

🎯 Educational objective

Treat congestion in ADHF with intravenous loop diuretics at a total daily dose of about 2–2.5 times the home oral dose, and titrate by urine output and urine sodium.
