HE-015.stem_html:
A 24-year-old woman is evaluated before a planned wisdom-tooth extraction because of a history of bleeding. She has had heavy menstrual periods since menarche, needing to change pads every hour on heavy days. She had prolonged bleeding after a tonsillectomy at age 8. She bruises easily and has frequent nosebleeds. Her mother also has heavy menses. She takes no medications.

Examination is normal except for a few small bruises.

Hemoglobin11.4 g/dL
MCV76 fL
Platelet count228,000/µL
PTnormal
aPTTnormal to mildly prolonged (36 s; reference 25–35 s)
HE-015.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next diagnostic test?

choices.C: Mixing study for a lupus anticoagulant
choices.E: Von Willebrand factor antigen, activity (ristocetin cofactor or GPIb binding) and factor VIII activity

HE-015.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Von Willebrand disease

Mucocutaneous bleeding — menorrhagia since menarche, epistaxis, easy bruising, bleeding after tonsillectomy — with a family history, normal platelets, normal PT and normal or slightly prolonged aPTT → von Willebrand disease (VWD), the most common inherited bleeding disorder (~1% of people; usually type 1, autosomal dominant).

VWF does two jobs: platelet adhesion (bridges platelets to collagen via GPIb) and carrying factor VIII (protects it from clearance) — which is why the aPTT may be slightly prolonged.

Initial panel: VWF antigen, VWF activity (ristocetin cofactor or GPIbM assay), factor VIII activity. VWF levels rise with stress, estrogen, pregnancy and inflammation — repeat if borderline. Blood type O has lower VWF levels.

Treatment: desmopressin (DDAVP) releases stored VWF (type 1), VWF-containing concentrates for major surgery or nonresponders, and tranexamic acid for mucosal bleeding and menorrhagia (plus hormonal therapy). Treat her iron deficiency.

Why not the others

  • (A) Bone marrow biopsy — Bone marrow biopsy has no role in evaluating an inherited bleeding disorder with normal blood counts.
  • (B) Factor IX activity — Hemophilia B (factor IX deficiency) is X-linked, presents in males with joint and muscle bleeds and a prolonged aPTT.
  • (C) Mixing study for a lupus anticoagulant — A lupus anticoagulant prolongs the aPTT in vitro but causes thrombosis, not bleeding.
  • (D) Platelet function analyzer only — The PFA-100 is neither sensitive nor specific enough to diagnose or exclude VWD.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Platelet-type bleeding (mucosal, petechiae, immediate bleeding) → VWD or platelet disorders. Factor-type bleeding (joints, muscles, delayed bleeding) → hemophilia.

🎯 Educational objective

Evaluate lifelong mucocutaneous bleeding with VWF antigen, VWF activity and factor VIII activity to diagnose von Willebrand disease.

ID-001.stem_html:
A 32-year-old man comes to the office with 3 days of fever, productive cough and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. He has no medical problems, takes no medications and has not taken antibiotics in the past year. He has no drug allergies. He does not smoke or drink alcohol heavily.

Temperature is 38.6 °C (101.5 °F), blood pressure is 124/76 mm Hg, pulse rate is 98/min, respiration rate is 20/min and oxygen saturation is 97% breathing ambient air. Crackles and bronchial breath sounds are heard at the right base. He is alert and drinking fluids well.

Chest radiograph shows right lower lobe consolidation. Blood urea nitrogen is 12 mg/dL.
ID-001.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

choices.D: Hospital admission for intravenous ceftriaxone and azithromycin

ID-001.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Community-acquired pneumonia — outpatient

He has community-acquired pneumonia with CURB-65 = 0 (no confusion, BUN <20, RR <30, BP normal, age <65) → treat at home.

For an outpatient without comorbidities or MRSA/Pseudomonas risk factors, ATS/IDSA recommends high-dose amoxicillin (1 g three times daily), which covers Streptococcus pneumoniae, the most common and most lethal bacterial cause. Doxycycline is an alternative. A macrolide alone is used only where pneumococcal macrolide resistance is <25%, which is not true in most of the US.

Outpatient CAP Regimen (5 days minimum, until stable)
No comorbidities Amoxicillin 1 g TID, or doxycycline, or macrolide (if local resistance <25%)
Comorbidities (heart, lung, liver, kidney disease, diabetes, alcohol use disorder, cancer, asplenia) Amoxicillin–clavulanate or a cephalosporin plus macrolide or doxycycline, or a respiratory fluoroquinolone alone

Why not the others

  • (B) Amoxicillin–clavulanate plus azithromycin — Combination therapy is for outpatients with comorbidities. He has none.
  • (C) Azithromycin — Macrolide monotherapy fails against resistant pneumococci; US resistance rates are well above 25%.
  • (D) Hospital admission for intravenous ceftriaxone and azithromycin — CURB-65 of 0 and normal oxygenation support outpatient care.
  • (E) Levofloxacin — Respiratory fluoroquinolones are reserved for patients with comorbidities or beta-lactam allergy because of tendon rupture, aortic aneurysm, QT prolongation, C. difficile and resistance concerns.
🧠 Mnemonic

CURB-65: Confusion, Urea (BUN) >19 mg/dL, Respiratory rate ≥30, BP <90 systolic or ≤60 diastolic, age ≥65. 0–1 → home; 2 → consider admission; ≥3 → hospital, think ICU.

🎓 ABIM pearl

Treat for at least 5 days and until afebrile for 48–72 hours with stable vital signs. A follow-up chest film is not routinely needed if he recovers.

🎯 Educational objective

Treat outpatient community-acquired pneumonia in a healthy adult without risk factors with high-dose amoxicillin (or doxycycline); reserve fluoroquinolones and combination therapy for patients with comorbidities.

ID-002.stem_html:
A 27-year-old woman comes to the office with 2 days of painful urination, urgency and frequency. She has no fever, chills, flank pain, vaginal discharge or itching. Her last menstrual period was 2 weeks ago and a urine pregnancy test is negative. She had one similar episode 3 years ago. She has no drug allergies.

Temperature is 36.9 °C (98.4 °F). There is mild suprapubic tenderness and no costovertebral angle tenderness.

Urine dipstick is positive for leukocyte esterase and nitrite.
ID-002.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

choices.E: No antibiotic until urine culture results are available

ID-002.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Acute uncomplicated cystitis

Dysuria and frequency without vaginal symptoms in a nonpregnant woman has a >90% probability of acute uncomplicated cystitis. No culture is needed before treatment for a typical first or infrequent episode.

First-line choices (IDSA) are agents with low resistance and little collateral damage to gut flora:

First-line Course
Nitrofurantoin monohydrate/macrocrystals 100 mg BID 5 days
Trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole DS BID 3 days (if local resistance <20%)
Fosfomycin 3 g single dose
Pivmecillinam 3–5 days

Nitrofurantoin reaches high concentrations only in urine, so do not use it for pyelonephritis or when creatinine clearance is very low.

Why not the others

  • (A) Amoxicillin for 7 days — E. coli resistance to amoxicillin is high; aminopenicillins alone are not recommended for empiric cystitis therapy.
  • (B) Ceftriaxone intramuscularly once — Parenteral ceftriaxone is unnecessary for lower-tract infection in an outpatient who can take oral medication.
  • (C) Ciprofloxacin for 3 days — Fluoroquinolones work but are reserved for pyelonephritis or when first-line agents cannot be used, because of serious adverse effects and resistance.
  • (E) No antibiotic until urine culture results are available — Waiting for culture delays relief. Cultures are for recurrent, complicated or atypical cases, or suspected pyelonephritis.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Fever, flank pain or CVA tenderness → pyelonephritis: get a urine culture and use a fluoroquinolone or TMP-SMX (if susceptible), often after one IV dose of ceftriaxone.

🎯 Educational objective

Treat acute uncomplicated cystitis empirically with nitrofurantoin for 5 days (or TMP-SMX, fosfomycin, or pivmecillinam); reserve fluoroquinolones for pyelonephritis.

ID-003.stem_html:
A 52-year-old man comes for a routine health visit. He feels well. He has no chronic medical conditions, does not smoke and takes no medications. He received a tetanus–diphtheria–pertussis (Tdap) vaccine 5 years ago and an influenza vaccine this fall. He has never received a pneumococcal vaccine.

Examination is normal.
ID-003.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate pneumococcal vaccination for this patient?

choices.A: 15-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV15) now and no further doses
choices.C: A single dose of 20-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV20) now
choices.E: PPSV23 now and PCV20 in 1 year

ID-003.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Adult pneumococcal vaccination

Since late 2024, CDC recommends pneumococcal vaccination for all adults aged 50 years and older (and for younger adults with risk conditions), regardless of health.

For adults who have never received a conjugate vaccine, give one dose of PCV20 or PCV21 — that completes the series. Alternatively, give PCV15 followed by PPSV23 one year later.

Conjugate vaccines link the polysaccharide to a protein carrier, which recruits T-cell help and produces memory and better immunogenicity than plain polysaccharide vaccines.

Why not the others

  • (A) 15-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV15) now and no further doses — PCV15 must be followed by PPSV23 (usually ≥1 year later) to complete the series.
  • (B) 23-valent pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine (PPSV23) now — PPSV23 alone is no longer recommended as the first or only vaccine; it gives weaker, shorter immunity than conjugate vaccines.
  • (D) No pneumococcal vaccine until age 65 — The age threshold for routine vaccination was lowered from 65 to 50 years.
  • (E) PPSV23 now and PCV20 in 1 year — Starting with PPSV23 is the outdated sequence; when both are needed, the conjugate vaccine goes first.
🧠 Mnemonic

"Twenty at fifty" — PCV20 (or PCV21) once at 50+ and you are done.

🎓 ABIM pearl

He is also due for recombinant zoster vaccine (2 doses, 2–6 months apart) — recommended for all adults ≥50, even with a prior shingles episode.

🎯 Educational objective

All adults aged 50 years or older who have not received a pneumococcal conjugate vaccine should get a single dose of PCV20 or PCV21 (or PCV15 followed by PPSV23).

ID-004.stem_html:
A 68-year-old man is scheduled for extraction of a fractured molar next week. Four years ago he had a bioprosthetic aortic valve replacement for aortic stenosis. He has hypertension and takes lisinopril and aspirin. He has no drug allergies and no history of endocarditis.

Examination shows a soft systolic ejection murmur at the right upper sternal border. Echocardiography 6 months ago showed a normally functioning prosthetic valve.
ID-004.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation before the procedure?

choices.A: Amoxicillin 2 g orally 30–60 minutes before the procedure
choices.B: Amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily for 7 days after the procedure
choices.C: Clindamycin 600 mg orally before the procedure

ID-004.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Infective endocarditis prophylaxis

Antibiotic prophylaxis before dental work is now limited to patients at highest risk of a bad outcome from endocarditis, and only for procedures that manipulate the gingiva or periapical region or perforate the oral mucosa (extractions qualify).

Prosthetic valves of any type (including bioprosthetic and transcatheter valves, and valve repairs with prosthetic material) are a highest-risk condition. The regimen is a single dose of amoxicillin 2 g orally 30–60 minutes before the procedure.

Highest-risk conditions (prophylaxis for dental procedures)
Prosthetic valve or prosthetic material used in valve repair
Previous infective endocarditis
Unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart disease; repaired CHD with residual shunt or defect near prosthetic material
Cardiac transplant with valvulopathy

Why not the others

  • (B) Amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily for 7 days after the procedure — Prophylaxis is a single dose before the procedure; a postprocedure course adds adverse effects without benefit.
  • (C) Clindamycin 600 mg orally before the procedure — Clindamycin is no longer recommended for penicillin-allergic patients because it causes more C. difficile infection; azithromycin, clarithromycin or doxycycline are used instead.
  • (D) Intravenous vancomycin before the procedure — IV vancomycin is unnecessary for an outpatient dental procedure in a patient without penicillin allergy.
  • (E) No antibiotic prophylaxis — A prosthetic valve is one of the few conditions where prophylaxis is still recommended.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Prophylaxis is not recommended for GI or GU procedures (colonoscopy, cystoscopy) in any of these patients, or for mitral valve prolapse, bicuspid aortic valve or native valve regurgitation alone. Good oral hygiene prevents far more endocarditis than antibiotics.

🎯 Educational objective

Give a single preprocedure dose of amoxicillin 2 g before dental procedures involving the gingiva in patients with prosthetic valves, prior endocarditis, or certain congenital heart disease.

ID-005.stem_html:
A 45-year-old woman comes to the office with 2 days of a painful, red, swollen area on her left lower leg. She has no injury, recent travel or prolonged immobility. She has hypertension. She has no drug allergies.

Temperature is 37.7 °C (99.9 °F), blood pressure is 132/80 mm Hg and pulse rate is 88/min. There is a 10 × 8 cm warm, tender, poorly demarcated area of erythema on the anterior shin with no fluctuance, drainage, crepitus or bullae. Point-of-care ultrasound shows subcutaneous edema without a fluid collection. Scaling and maceration are present between the toes of the left foot.
ID-005.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
ID-005.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Nonpurulent cellulitis

This is nonpurulent cellulitis — spreading erythema, warmth and tenderness without pus or an abscess. The usual cause is beta-hemolytic streptococci (group A and others) entering through broken skin — here interdigital tinea pedis.

Treat mild nonpurulent cellulitis with an oral agent active against streptococci: cephalexin, dicloxacillin, penicillin V or amoxicillin, typically for 5–6 days, extended if not improving. Elevate the leg — it speeds resolution.

Nonpurulent (cellulitis/erysipelas) Purulent (abscess, furuncle)
Main organism Streptococci S. aureus (often MRSA)
Key treatment Beta-lactam (cephalexin) Incision and drainage ± TMP-SMX or doxycycline

Why not the others

  • (B) Hospital admission for intravenous vancomycin — She has no systemic toxicity, hypotension or rapidly spreading infection. IV therapy and MRSA coverage are for moderate–severe or purulent infection.
  • (C) Incision and drainage — There is no abscess to drain on examination or ultrasound.
  • (D) Topical mupirocin — Topical antibiotics treat impetigo; they do not reach dermal and subcutaneous infection.
  • (E) Trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole — TMP-SMX has unreliable activity against streptococci; it is used for purulent infections where MRSA is likely.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Prevent recurrence by treating tinea pedis, edema and venous insufficiency. Bilateral "cellulitis" is almost always something else — usually stasis dermatitis.

🎯 Educational objective

Treat mild nonpurulent cellulitis with an oral antistreptococcal beta-lactam such as cephalexin; reserve MRSA-active drugs for purulent infections and drainage for abscesses.

ID-006.stem_html:
A 27-year-old man comes to the office asking about ways to prevent HIV infection. He has sex with men, has had four male partners in the past 6 months and uses condoms inconsistently. He was treated for rectal gonorrhea 3 months ago. He has no symptoms.

Examination is normal.

HIV-1/2 antigen/antibody testnegative
Creatinine0.9 mg/dL
eGFR

90 mL/min/1.73 m²

HBsAgnegative; anti-HBs positive (vaccinated)
ID-006.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.D: Counsel on condom use and retest for HIV in 1 year
choices.E: Repeat HIV testing in 3 months before deciding on prophylaxis

ID-006.explain_html:
Correct answer: A HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis

He is at substantial risk of HIV — men who have sex with men with condomless anal sex and a recent bacterial STI. The USPSTF gives a Grade A recommendation to offer pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) to such patients.

PrEP options:

  • Daily oral emtricitabine–tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (F/TDF) — all populations; ~99% effective for sexual exposure when taken consistently.
  • Daily emtricitabine–tenofovir alafenamide (F/TAF) — not for receptive vaginal sex.
  • Injectable cabotegravir every 2 months, or lenacapavir every 6 months (approved 2025).

Before starting: confirm a negative HIV test (ideally antigen/antibody plus RNA if recent exposure), check creatinine (TDF requires eGFR ≥60) and hepatitis B status (stopping tenofovir can flare HBV). Follow up every 3 months with HIV and STI testing.

Why not the others

  • (B) Begin post-exposure prophylaxis for 28 days — PEP is for a single high-risk exposure within the last 72 hours. He has ongoing risk, which calls for PrEP.
  • (C) Begin three-drug antiretroviral therapy — Treatment-dose ART is for people with HIV. He tested negative.
  • (D) Counsel on condom use and retest for HIV in 1 year — Counseling alone leaves him at high ongoing risk; PrEP is strongly recommended in addition to condoms.
  • (E) Repeat HIV testing in 3 months before deciding on prophylaxis — Delaying PrEP leaves him exposed. Start now, with HIV testing every 3 months.
🎯 Educational objective

Offer HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis to people at substantial risk of HIV after confirming a negative HIV test and adequate kidney function.

ID-007.topic: New HIV diagnosis — opportunistic infection prophylaxis
ID-007.stem_html:
A 38-year-old woman was diagnosed with HIV infection 1 week ago after testing during an emergency department visit. She has had fatigue and a 4-kg (8.8-lb) weight loss. She has no cough, headache or visual symptoms.

On physical examination, vital signs are normal. Oral thrush is present. There is no lymphadenopathy.

CD4 cell count140/µL
HIV RNA210,000 copies/mL
Toxoplasma IgGnegative
HBsAgnegative
Interferon-γ release assaynegative
Chest radiographnormal
ID-007.lead: In addition to starting antiretroviral therapy, which of the following is the most appropriate prophylaxis?

choices.C: No prophylaxis until the CD4 count result is repeated

ID-007.explain_html:
Correct answer: D New HIV diagnosis — opportunistic infection prophylaxis

With a CD4 count <200/µL (or oral candidiasis, or CD4 <14%), she needs Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP) prophylaxis. The drug of choice is trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (one double-strength or single-strength tablet daily). It also protects against toxoplasmosis when the CD4 is <100/µL and Toxoplasma IgG is positive.

Start ART as soon as possible — ideally within days of diagnosis — for everyone with HIV, regardless of CD4 count. Exceptions where ART is briefly delayed: cryptococcal meningitis (wait 4–6 weeks) and TB meningitis, because of IRIS risk.

CD4 (cells/µL) Prophylaxis
<200 (or thrush) PJP — TMP-SMX
<100 + Toxoplasma IgG+ Toxoplasma — TMP-SMX (DS)
<50 MAC — not needed if ART is started promptly

Stop PJP prophylaxis when the CD4 count is >200/µL for ≥3 months on ART.

Why not the others

  • (A) Azithromycin weekly — Primary MAC prophylaxis is no longer recommended for patients who start ART immediately, and it is used only when the CD4 count is <50/µL.
  • (B) Fluconazole daily — Primary fluconazole prophylaxis for candidiasis or cryptococcus is not recommended; treat thrush, but do not give long-term prophylaxis.
  • (C) No prophylaxis until the CD4 count result is repeated — The CD4 count is clearly <200/µL and she has thrush; prophylaxis should start now.
  • (E) Valganciclovir daily — CMV prophylaxis is not recommended; monitor for retinitis when CD4 is <50/µL.
🎯 Educational objective

Start trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for PJP prophylaxis in patients with HIV and a CD4 count below 200/µL or oral candidiasis, and start ART promptly.

ID-008.stem_html:
A 24-year-old man is evaluated for 6 days of fever, sore throat, diffuse muscle aches and a rash. He had condomless sex with a new male partner 3 weeks ago.

On physical examination, temperature is 38.6 °C (101.5 °F). There is a diffuse maculopapular rash on the trunk, shallow oral ulcers, pharyngeal erythema without exudates and diffuse lymphadenopathy.

Leukocyte count3,200/µL with 18% atypical lymphocytes
Platelet count118,000/µL
ALT96 U/L
Heterophile antibody (monospot)negative
Rapid streptococcal antigennegative
ID-008.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnostic test?

choices.B: Epstein-Barr virus viral capsid antigen IgM
choices.D: HIV-1/2 antigen/antibody immunoassay and HIV-1 RNA

ID-008.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Acute HIV infection

Fever, pharyngitis, mucocutaneous ulcers, rash, lymphadenopathy, cytopenias and mild hepatitis 2–4 weeks after a high-risk exposure = acute retroviral syndrome until proven otherwise. A negative monospot makes EBV less likely.

During acute infection, antibodies may not yet be detectable. The fourth-generation HIV-1/2 antigen/antibody assay detects p24 antigen about 2 weeks after infection. Because the result may still be negative very early, also send an HIV-1 RNA (viral load) — in acute HIV it is usually very high (>100,000 copies/mL).

Diagnosing acute HIV matters: viral load and transmission risk are highest now, and starting ART immediately limits the viral reservoir.

Test Window period
HIV RNA ~10 days
4th-gen Ag/Ab (p24) ~18–45 days
Antibody-only Up to 90 days

Why not the others

  • (A) CD4 cell count — The CD4 count is not a diagnostic test for HIV and can drop transiently in acute infection.
  • (B) Epstein-Barr virus viral capsid antigen IgM — EBV is possible, but mucocutaneous ulcers, a recent high-risk exposure and a negative monospot make acute HIV the priority; missing it has major consequences.
  • (C) HIV-1 antibody–only rapid test — Antibody-only tests can be negative for weeks to months in acute infection.
  • (E) Rapid plasma reagin — Secondary syphilis can cause rash and lymphadenopathy and should also be tested, but it does not explain oral ulcers with this acute febrile picture.
🎯 Educational objective

When acute HIV infection is suspected, test with a fourth-generation antigen/antibody assay plus HIV-1 RNA.

ID-009.stem_html:
A 44-year-old man is evaluated after routine screening during a visit for HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis. He has no symptoms. He has had several male partners in the past year. His last syphilis test, 3 years ago, was negative. He has no penicillin allergy.

Examination shows no rash, chancre, lymphadenopathy or neurologic abnormalities, including no visual or hearing changes.

Rapid plasma reagin (RPR)reactive (titer 1:32)
Treponemal antibodyreactive
HIV-1/2 antigen/antibodynegative
ID-009.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

choices.A: Benzathine penicillin G, 2.4 million units intramuscularly once
choices.B: Benzathine penicillin G, 2.4 million units intramuscularly weekly for 3 weeks
choices.C: Doxycycline, 100 mg twice daily for 7 days
choices.D: Intravenous aqueous penicillin G for 14 days

ID-009.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Latent syphilis

He has latent syphilis (positive nontreponemal and treponemal tests, no signs or symptoms). Because his last negative test was more than 1 year ago, the infection cannot be dated: he has latent syphilis of unknown duration, which is treated as late latent.

Stage Treatment
Primary, secondary, early latent (<1 y) Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM once
Late latent or unknown duration Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM weekly × 3
Neurosyphilis, ocular, otic IV aqueous penicillin G 18–24 MU/d × 10–14 days

Follow nontreponemal titers at 6, 12 and 24 months; a fourfold decline (e.g., 1:32 → 1:8) indicates response. The treponemal test usually stays positive for life.

Why not the others

  • (A) Benzathine penicillin G, 2.4 million units intramuscularly once — A single dose is for early syphilis (infection acquired within 1 year), which cannot be documented here.
  • (C) Doxycycline, 100 mg twice daily for 7 days — Doxycycline is an alternative only for penicillin allergy, and for late latent syphilis the course is 28 days.
  • (D) Intravenous aqueous penicillin G for 14 days — IV penicillin is for neurosyphilis or ocular/otic syphilis. He has no neurologic findings.
  • (E) Lumbar puncture before treatment — Lumbar puncture is indicated only for neurologic, ocular or otic signs, or treatment failure — not for asymptomatic latent syphilis, even with HIV.
🎓 ABIM pearl

The Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction — fever, myalgias and headache within 24 hours of treatment, most common in early syphilis — is treated with antipyretics and is not a penicillin allergy.

🎯 Educational objective

Treat late latent syphilis or latent syphilis of unknown duration with three weekly intramuscular doses of benzathine penicillin G.

ID-010.stem_html:
A 22-year-old man is evaluated for 3 days of dysuria and purulent urethral discharge. He has had two female partners in the past month. He has no allergies.

On physical examination, there is a yellow urethral discharge. The testes are nontender. There is no rash or joint swelling.

Gram stain of the discharge shows gram-negative intracellular diplococci. Nucleic acid amplification testing for Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis is pending, along with HIV and syphilis testing.
ID-010.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

choices.C: Ceftriaxone, 250 mg intramuscularly plus azithromycin, 1 g orally once
choices.D: Ceftriaxone, 500 mg intramuscularly once, plus doxycycline, 100 mg twice daily for 7 days

ID-010.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Uncomplicated gonococcal urethritis

Gram-negative intracellular diplococci in urethral discharge confirm gonococcal urethritis.

CDC 2020–2021 recommendations:

  • Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM once (1 g if weight ≥150 kg). The dose was raised because of rising MICs.
  • If chlamydia has not been excluded, add doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days. Doxycycline replaced azithromycin as the preferred chlamydia treatment (better for rectal infection; less macrolide resistance pressure).
  • Treat partners (expedited partner therapy where legal), test for HIV and syphilis, and retest at 3 months.

Why not the others

  • (A) Azithromycin, 2 g orally once — Azithromycin monotherapy is not recommended because of rising gonococcal macrolide resistance.
  • (B) Cefixime, 400 mg orally once alone — Oral cefixime is an alternative only if ceftriaxone is unavailable, and chlamydia would still need treatment.
  • (C) Ceftriaxone, 250 mg intramuscularly plus azithromycin, 1 g orally once — This was the older regimen (ceftriaxone 250 mg + azithromycin). The current recommendation is a higher ceftriaxone dose and doxycycline for chlamydia.
  • (E) Ciprofloxacin, 500 mg orally once — Fluoroquinolones have not been recommended for gonorrhea since 2007 because of widespread resistance.
🎯 Educational objective

Treat uncomplicated gonorrhea with ceftriaxone 500 mg intramuscularly once, plus doxycycline for 7 days if chlamydia has not been excluded.

ID-011.stem_html:
A 34-year-old woman who emigrated from the Philippines 2 years ago is evaluated after a positive interferon-γ release assay (IGRA) on routine testing before starting work as a nurse. She has no cough, fever, night sweats or weight loss. She has no medical problems and takes no medications. She is not pregnant.

Examination is normal.

Interferon-γ release assaypositive
Chest radiographnormal
HIV antigen/antibodynegative
ALT18 U/L
ID-011.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.B: No treatment because she received BCG vaccine as a child
choices.E: Sputum acid-fast bacilli smears and cultures, then four-drug therapy

ID-011.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Latent tuberculosis infection

A positive IGRA with no symptoms and a normal chest radiograph = latent TB infection (LTBI). She was born in a high-incidence country and arrived recently (the first 5 years carry the highest reactivation risk), so treatment is strongly recommended.

Preferred regimens are short rifamycin-based, with better completion and less hepatotoxicity than isoniazid:

Regimen Duration
Rifampin daily 4 months (4R)
Isoniazid + rifapentine weekly 3 months (3HP)
Isoniazid + rifampin daily 3 months (3HR)
Isoniazid daily 6–9 months (alternative)

Rifamycins have many drug interactions (oral contraceptives, warfarin, DOACs, antiretrovirals) — check before prescribing, and counsel about backup contraception.

Why not the others

  • (A) Isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol — Four-drug therapy is for active TB disease. She has no symptoms and a normal chest radiograph.
  • (B) No treatment because she received BCG vaccine as a child — IGRA is not affected by BCG vaccination (unlike the tuberculin skin test), so a positive IGRA indicates true infection.
  • (C) Repeat IGRA in 1 year — A positive IGRA does not need repeating; she needs treatment.
  • (E) Sputum acid-fast bacilli smears and cultures, then four-drug therapy — Sputum testing is for patients with symptoms or abnormal chest imaging.
🎯 Educational objective

Treat latent tuberculosis infection with a short rifamycin-based regimen, such as 4 months of daily rifampin, after excluding active disease.

ID-012.stem_html:
A 46-year-old man from Connecticut is evaluated in July for 5 days of fatigue, mild headache and a rash on his thigh. He hikes regularly but does not recall a tick bite.

On physical examination, temperature is 37.8 °C (100.0 °F). There is a 12-cm, round, erythematous patch on his right thigh with central clearing. There is no facial weakness, meningismus or joint swelling. Heart rate is regular at 76/min.
ID-012.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.A: Doxycycline, 100 mg twice daily for 10 days
choices.C: Lyme serology, and treat if positive

ID-012.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Early Lyme disease

An expanding annular rash ≥5 cm, often with central clearing ("bull's-eye"), after outdoor exposure in an endemic area in summer is erythema migrans — diagnostic of early localized Lyme disease. Most patients do not remember the tick bite.

Do not test. Serology is often negative in early disease (antibodies take 2–4 weeks) — the rash is the diagnosis. Treat clinically with doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 10 days (amoxicillin or cefuroxime for 14 days are alternatives, e.g., in pregnancy).

Lyme manifestation Treatment
Erythema migrans Oral doxycycline 10 d
Facial palsy, carditis (PR <300 ms) Oral doxycycline 14–21 d
Meningitis Oral doxycycline or IV ceftriaxone 14–21 d
High-degree AV block IV ceftriaxone + temporary pacing
Arthritis Oral doxycycline 28 d

Why not the others

  • (B) Intravenous ceftriaxone for 14 days — IV ceftriaxone is reserved for severe disseminated disease (high-degree heart block, some neurologic disease).
  • (C) Lyme serology, and treat if positive — Serologic testing is insensitive in early Lyme disease and not recommended when erythema migrans is present.
  • (D) Single 200-mg dose of doxycycline — A single dose of doxycycline is used as prophylaxis within 72 hours of removing an engorged Ixodes tick, not to treat established infection.
  • (E) Topical corticosteroid cream — Erythema migrans is an infection, not dermatitis; steroids would delay treatment.
🎯 Educational objective

Diagnose early Lyme disease clinically by erythema migrans and treat with oral doxycycline for 10 days without serologic testing.

ID-013.stem_html:
A 36-year-old man is evaluated for 3 days of fever, chills, headache and myalgias. He returned 10 days ago from a 3-week trip to visit family in Nigeria. He did not take malaria prophylaxis because he grew up there.

On physical examination, temperature is 39.4 °C (102.9 °F), blood pressure is 118/70 mm Hg, and pulse rate is 112/min. He is alert. There is mild scleral icterus and splenomegaly. There is no rash or meningismus.

Hemoglobin11.2 g/dL
Platelet count62,000/µL
Total bilirubin2.4 mg/dL
Creatinine1.0 mg/dL
Glucose96 mg/dL
ID-013.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnostic test?

choices.E: Thick and thin peripheral blood smears

ID-013.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Malaria in a returning traveler

Fever in a traveler returning from sub-Saharan Africa is malaria until proven otherwise. Plasmodium falciparum can become life-threatening within hours. "Visiting friends and relatives" travelers who skip prophylaxis are at the highest risk — immunity acquired in childhood fades after a few years away.

Thrombocytopenia, hyperbilirubinemia (hemolysis) and splenomegaly support the diagnosis.

The test of choice is thick and thin peripheral blood smears (thick = detection; thin = species and percent parasitemia) — plus a rapid antigen test if available. If negative, repeat every 12–24 hours for a total of three sets.

Severe malaria (parasitemia ≥5%, altered mental status, shock, AKI, acidosis, hypoglycemia, severe anemia, ARDS) is treated with IV artesunate.

Why not the others

  • (A) Blood cultures only — Blood cultures are appropriate to rule out typhoid and bacteremia, but they will not diagnose malaria, the most urgent consideration.
  • (B) Dengue NS1 antigen — Dengue is possible after travel to the tropics, but the incubation and setting (West Africa, splenomegaly, hemolysis) make malaria the priority; dengue does not exclude the need for smears.
  • (C) Serologic testing for malaria — Malaria serology reflects past exposure and is not useful for acute diagnosis.
  • (D) Stool ova and parasites — Stool testing is for diarrheal illness or eosinophilia, not for acute febrile illness with hemolysis.
🎯 Educational objective

Evaluate fever in a traveler returning from a malaria-endemic area with thick and thin blood smears (and a rapid antigen test), repeated up to three times if negative.

ID-014.stem_html:
A 61-year-old man with type 2 diabetes is hospitalized with fever. Two of two blood culture sets grow methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus. He has a tender, erythematous peripheral IV site in his left forearm from a hospitalization 1 week ago; the catheter was removed. He has no prosthetic valves or devices.

On physical examination, temperature is 38.6 °C (101.5 °F), blood pressure is 126/74 mm Hg, and pulse rate is 98/min. There is no heart murmur. The remainder of the examination is normal.

He is treated with IV vancomycin, and transthoracic echocardiogram is normal.
ID-014.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Change to intravenous cefazolin, repeat blood cultures and obtain transesophageal echocardiography
choices.B: Change to oral dicloxacillin and discharge
choices.C: Change to oral linezolid for 14 days

ID-014.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia

S. aureus bacteremia is never a contaminant and carries 20–30% mortality. The care bundle improves survival:

  1. Switch to a β-lactam for MSSA — cefazolin or nafcillin/oxacillin. β-lactams are more effective than vancomycin against MSSA.
  2. Repeat blood cultures every 24–48 hours until negative.
  3. Echocardiography in all patients — TEE for most, because TTE misses many vegetations. A negative TTE does not exclude endocarditis.
  4. Remove the source (catheter — done) and look for metastatic foci (spine, joints, abscesses).
  5. Infectious disease consultation — lowers mortality.

Duration: uncomplicated (no endocarditis or implants, cultures negative within 72 h, fever resolved by 72 h, no metastatic infection) → ≥14 days from first negative culture. Otherwise 4–6 weeks. Selected stable patients can step down to oral therapy (SABATO).

Why not the others

  • (B) Change to oral dicloxacillin and discharge — Oral dicloxacillin has poor bioavailability, and the evaluation (repeat cultures, TEE) is incomplete.
  • (C) Change to oral linezolid for 14 days — Linezolid is not first-line for MSSA, and an oral switch is premature before cultures clear and endocarditis is excluded.
  • (D) Continue vancomycin and add gentamicin — Gentamicin adds nephrotoxicity without benefit in native-valve S. aureus infection.
  • (E) Continue vancomycin for 5 days — Five days is far too short; even uncomplicated S. aureus bacteremia needs at least 14 days.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Grows S. aureus in blood? Think "TEE, ID, β-lactam, repeat cultures."

🎯 Educational objective

Treat MSSA bacteremia with an antistaphylococcal β-lactam, document clearance with repeat blood cultures and obtain transesophageal echocardiography.

ID-015.stem_html:
A 66-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department with 12 hours of fever, severe headache and confusion. She has no recent travel, head trauma or neurosurgery. She is not immunocompromised and has no drug allergies.

On physical examination, temperature is 39.2 °C (102.6 °F), blood pressure is 128/72 mm Hg, and pulse rate is 112/min. She is lethargic and disoriented, with nuchal rigidity. There is no papilledema and no focal neurologic deficit. There is no rash.

Blood cultures have been drawn. Head CT without contrast is normal.
ID-015.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate empiric treatment, given before lumbar puncture results are available?
ID-015.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Bacterial meningitis — empiric therapy

Fever, headache, neck stiffness and altered mental status = acute bacterial meningitis until proven otherwise. Do not delay antibiotics for lumbar puncture or imaging.

Empiric therapy by age:

Patient Likely organisms Empiric regimen
2–50 y S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis Vancomycin + ceftriaxone
>50 y, alcohol use, immunocompromised, pregnant Above + Listeria Vancomycin + ceftriaxone + ampicillin
Post-neurosurgery, shunt, penetrating trauma Staphylococci, gram-negative bacilli (incl. Pseudomonas) Vancomycin + cefepime/ceftazidime/meropenem

Dexamethasone (0.15 mg/kg every 6 h for 4 days), given just before or with the first antibiotic dose, reduces death and hearing loss in pneumococcal meningitis. Stop it if the organism is not S. pneumoniae.

Add acyclovir if HSV encephalitis is suspected (behavioral changes, seizures, temporal lobe findings).

Why not the others

  • (A) Acyclovir alone — Acyclovir treats HSV encephalitis but does not cover bacterial meningitis.
  • (B) Ceftriaxone alone — Ceftriaxone alone misses penicillin-resistant pneumococci (vancomycin) and Listeria (ampicillin).
  • (C) Ceftriaxone and vancomycin — She is over 50, so ampicillin for Listeria is needed; dexamethasone should also be given with the first dose.
  • (E) Meropenem alone — Meropenem does cover Listeria, but monotherapy misses highly penicillin-resistant pneumococci and it is not a standard first-line choice.
🎯 Educational objective

Treat suspected bacterial meningitis in adults older than 50 years with vancomycin, ceftriaxone and ampicillin, plus dexamethasone with the first antibiotic dose.

ID-016.stem_html:
A 28-year-old woman is evaluated for 2 days of fever, right flank pain, dysuria and urinary frequency. She has nausea but can keep down fluids and pills. She is not pregnant. She has had no recent antibiotics or hospitalizations. Local fluoroquinolone resistance among E. coli is 6%.

On physical examination, temperature is 38.5 °C (101.3 °F), blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg, and pulse rate is 98/min. There is right costovertebral angle tenderness.

Leukocyte count12,800/µL
Creatinine0.8 mg/dL
Urine pregnancy testnegative
Urinalysispositive leukocyte esterase and nitrite; many leukocytes and WBC casts
Urine culturepending
ID-016.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

choices.A: Ciprofloxacin, 500 mg orally twice daily for 7 days
choices.D: Nitrofurantoin, 100 mg orally twice daily for 7 days

ID-016.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Acute pyelonephritis — outpatient

Fever, flank pain, CVA tenderness and pyuria with WBC casts = acute uncomplicated pyelonephritis. She is not pregnant, not septic, and can take oral medication, so she can be treated as an outpatient.

Choose a drug that reaches kidney tissue:

  • Ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily for 7 days (or levofloxacin 750 mg daily for 5–7 days) when local fluoroquinolone resistance is ≤10%.
  • TMP-SMX twice daily for 14 days if the organism is known to be susceptible.
  • If resistance is >10% or unknown, give a single IV dose of ceftriaxone (or an aminoglycoside) before oral therapy.

Always send a urine culture and adjust therapy to the results.

Why not the others

  • (B) Fosfomycin, 3 g orally once — Fosfomycin does not achieve adequate kidney tissue levels and is used only for cystitis.
  • (C) Hospitalization for intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam — Inpatient care is for sepsis, inability to take oral therapy, pregnancy, obstruction or failed outpatient treatment. Piperacillin-tazobactam is unnecessarily broad.
  • (D) Nitrofurantoin, 100 mg orally twice daily for 7 days — Nitrofurantoin concentrates in the bladder only; it does not treat kidney infection.
  • (E) Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for 3 days — Three days is the cystitis course. TMP-SMX for pyelonephritis requires 14 days and known susceptibility.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Nitrofurantoin and fosfomycin are "bladder-only" drugs — never for pyelonephritis, prostatitis or bacteremia.

🎯 Educational objective

Treat uncomplicated outpatient pyelonephritis with an oral fluoroquinolone for 5–7 days when local resistance is 10% or less, and avoid nitrofurantoin and fosfomycin.

ID-017.stem_html:
An 84-year-old woman who lives in a nursing home is evaluated because a urine culture sent during a routine monthly assessment grew more than 100,000 CFU/mL of Escherichia coli. She has mild dementia and chronic urinary incontinence that is unchanged. She has no fever, dysuria, new urgency, flank pain or change in mental status. She is not scheduled for any procedures.

On physical examination, temperature is 36.8 °C (98.2 °F). Vital signs are normal. She is at her cognitive baseline. There is no suprapubic or flank tenderness.

Urinalysis shows moderate leukocyte esterase and 20 leukocytes/hpf.
ID-017.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
ID-017.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Asymptomatic bacteriuria

This is asymptomatic bacteriuria (ASB) — bacteria in the urine without symptoms or signs of UTI. Pyuria does not change this: it is common with ASB and is not an indication for treatment.

ASB affects up to 50% of women in nursing homes. Treating it does not reduce symptomatic UTI or mortality, but it does cause adverse drug events, C. difficile infection and resistant organisms.

Screen and treat ASB only in:

  • Pregnancy
  • Before urologic procedures with mucosal trauma (e.g., TURP)

Do not treat it in older adults, people with diabetes, catheters, spinal cord injury, or kidney transplant recipients beyond the first month. Nonspecific changes (falls, mild confusion) without other signs should prompt a search for other causes, not reflexive antibiotics.

Why not the others

  • (A) Cephalexin for 7 days — Antibiotics for ASB cause harm without benefit.
  • (B) Nitrofurantoin for 5 days — Treating ASB with any antibiotic, including nitrofurantoin, is not indicated.
  • (D) Prophylactic daily trimethoprim — Prophylaxis promotes resistance and is not indicated for ASB.
  • (E) Repeat urine culture in 1 week — Surveillance cultures in asymptomatic patients should not be done; this culture should not have been sent.
🎯 Educational objective

Do not screen for or treat asymptomatic bacteriuria (with or without pyuria) except in pregnancy and before urologic procedures that breach the mucosa.

ID-018.stem_html:
A 62-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and peripheral neuropathy is evaluated for an ulcer under his left first metatarsal head that has been present for 6 weeks. It drains a small amount of fluid. He has no fever or pain.

On physical examination, temperature is 37.0 °C (98.6 °F). There is a 2-cm deep ulcer with minimal surrounding erythema. A sterile metal probe touches bone through the ulcer base. Pedal pulses are palpable.

Leukocyte count8,600/µL
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate92 mm/h
Plain radiograph of the footno cortical erosion or periosteal reaction
ID-018.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next diagnostic test?

choices.E: Superficial swab culture of the ulcer

ID-018.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Diabetic foot osteomyelitis

A chronic diabetic foot ulcer with a positive probe-to-bone test and an ESR >70 mm/h strongly suggests osteomyelitis. Plain radiographs are often normal early: bone changes take 2–3 weeks to appear (30–50% bone loss is needed).

MRI is the most accurate imaging test (high sensitivity and specificity, shows abscesses and extent for surgical planning). The diagnostic gold standard is bone biopsy (percutaneous or surgical) for culture and histology — it guides targeted antibiotics.

Treatment: debridement or resection of infected bone where needed, plus pathogen-directed antibiotics (typically 6 weeks without resection; shorter if all infected bone is removed), offloading and glucose control.

Why not the others

  • (A) Bone scintigraphy (three-phase bone scan) — Three-phase bone scans are sensitive but not specific — neuropathic (Charcot) joints and soft tissue infection also cause uptake.
  • (B) CT of the foot — CT shows cortical destruction and sequestra but is less sensitive than MRI for early osteomyelitis and marrow edema.
  • (D) Repeat plain radiograph in 6 months — Waiting delays diagnosis and treatment of an active bone infection.
  • (E) Superficial swab culture of the ulcer — Superficial swabs grow colonizers and correlate poorly with bone pathogens; they should not guide therapy.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Probe-to-bone + ESR >70 in a diabetic foot ulcer — treat as osteomyelitis until MRI or biopsy says otherwise.

🎯 Educational objective

Evaluate suspected diabetic foot osteomyelitis (positive probe-to-bone, high ESR) with MRI when plain radiographs are normal, and obtain bone biopsy for culture.

ID-019.stem_html:
A 54-year-old man with type 2 diabetes is brought to the emergency department with 1 day of severe left thigh pain that began after a minor scrape while gardening. The pain is much worse than the appearance of his skin.

On physical examination, temperature is 38.9 °C (102.0 °F), blood pressure is 92/56 mm Hg, and pulse rate is 124/min. The left thigh has a poorly demarcated area of erythema with tense edema extending beyond the redness, dusky violaceous patches and two hemorrhagic bullae. There is crepitus on palpation. Sensation over the area is reduced.

Leukocyte count24,800/µL
Sodium128 mEq/L
Creatinine2.1 mg/dL
Creatine kinase1,850 U/L
Lactate4.6 mmol/L
ID-019.lead: In addition to fluid resuscitation and broad-spectrum antibiotics, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: CT of the thigh before deciding on surgery

ID-019.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Necrotizing soft tissue infection

Pain out of proportion to the skin findings, edema beyond the erythema, bullae, skin discoloration, anesthesia, crepitus (gas) and septic shock = necrotizing soft tissue infection (necrotizing fasciitis).

This is a surgical emergency. The key determinant of survival is time to surgical debridement. Imaging should never delay surgery when the clinical diagnosis is clear. The diagnosis is confirmed at operation (gray, necrotic fascia; "dishwater" fluid; fascia separates easily from muscle — the "finger test").

Empiric antibiotics: vancomycin (or linezolid) + piperacillin-tazobactam (or a carbapenem) + clindamycin. Clindamycin suppresses toxin production by streptococci and clostridia.

Types: polymicrobial (type I) — diabetes, perineum (Fournier gangrene); monomicrobial (type II) — group A Streptococcus, sometimes S. aureus.

Why not the others

  • (A) CT of the thigh before deciding on surgery — CT can support the diagnosis in unclear cases, but with crepitus and septic shock it only delays definitive surgery.
  • (C) Hyperbaric oxygen therapy — Hyperbaric oxygen has no proven benefit and must never delay debridement.
  • (D) Intravenous immune globulin — IVIG is sometimes used for streptococcal toxic shock syndrome, but it is adjunctive and unproven; it is not the priority.
  • (E) MRI of the thigh — MRI takes too long and should not delay surgery in an unstable patient.
🧠 Mnemonic

Necrotizing infection red flags — "Pain > skin, gas, shock, bullae." Operate, don't image.

🎯 Educational objective

Suspected necrotizing fasciitis requires emergency surgical exploration and debridement plus broad-spectrum antibiotics with clindamycin; imaging must not delay surgery.

ID-020.stem_html:
A 52-year-old woman comes for a routine health maintenance visit. She had chickenpox as a child. She had an episode of shingles on her left chest 2 years ago that resolved. She has rheumatoid arthritis treated with methotrexate and low-dose prednisone, and her rheumatologist plans to start tofacitinib.

Examination is normal.
ID-020.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation regarding herpes zoster vaccination?

choices.B: No vaccine because she already had shingles
choices.C: Recombinant zoster vaccine only after she turns 60 years old
choices.D: Recombinant zoster vaccine, two doses 2–6 months apart

ID-020.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Herpes zoster vaccination

The recombinant zoster vaccine (RZV, Shingrix) is recommended for:

  • All adults ≥50 years — two doses, 2–6 months apart
  • Adults ≥19 years who are or will be immunocompromised (e.g., JAK inhibitors, biologics, transplant, HIV) — doses can be given 1–2 months apart

RZV is >90% effective and is not live, so it is safe with immunosuppression. A history of shingles is not a reason to skip it — recurrence occurs; give the vaccine once the rash has resolved. People do not need varicella serology before vaccination.

JAK inhibitors such as tofacitinib markedly increase zoster risk, so vaccination before starting is ideal.

Why not the others

  • (A) Live attenuated zoster vaccine once — The live zoster vaccine is no longer available in the United States and was contraindicated in immunosuppression.
  • (B) No vaccine because she already had shingles — Previous zoster does not prevent recurrence; vaccination is still recommended.
  • (C) Recombinant zoster vaccine only after she turns 60 years old — She is already 52, and her immunosuppression would justify vaccination even at a younger age.
  • (E) Varicella-zoster immune globulin — VZIG is passive post-exposure prophylaxis for susceptible high-risk people exposed to varicella, not routine prevention.
🎯 Educational objective

Give two doses of recombinant zoster vaccine to all adults aged 50 years or older and to immunocompromised adults aged 19 years or older, including those with prior shingles.

ID-021.stem_html:
A 71-year-old woman with COPD is hospitalized in January with 4 days of fever, myalgias, cough and worsening dyspnea. She received the influenza vaccine this season.

On physical examination, temperature is 38.7 °C (101.7 °F), blood pressure is 126/74 mm Hg, pulse rate is 104/min, and respiration rate is 24/min. Oxygen saturation is 89% breathing ambient air. There are scattered wheezes. Chest radiograph shows no infiltrate.

Nasopharyngeal PCR is positive for influenza A.
ID-021.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

choices.C: No antiviral therapy because she was vaccinated
choices.D: No antiviral therapy because symptoms began more than 48 hours ago

ID-021.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Influenza in a hospitalized patient

All hospitalized patients with influenza should receive antiviral therapy as soon as possible, regardless of symptom duration or vaccination status. The 48-hour window applies to healthy outpatients; in hospitalized and high-risk patients, treatment even after 48 hours reduces complications and mortality.

Oral oseltamivir (75 mg twice daily for 5 days; adjust for kidney function) is the drug of choice. Baloxavir is an option for uncomplicated outpatient influenza but is not recommended as monotherapy in hospitalized patients.

Also treat on presentation — regardless of 48 hours — anyone at high risk: age ≥65, pregnancy, chronic lung/heart/kidney/liver disease, diabetes, immunosuppression, obesity (BMI ≥40), nursing home residents.

Watch for secondary bacterial pneumonia (S. aureus, S. pneumoniae), especially if she improves then worsens.

Why not the others

  • (A) Amantadine — Adamantanes are not recommended because nearly all circulating influenza A strains are resistant.
  • (B) Intravenous zanamivir — IV zanamivir is not available as a standard option and is reserved for special circumstances (e.g., unable to absorb oral drug, resistant virus).
  • (C) No antiviral therapy because she was vaccinated — Vaccine failures occur; vaccination does not reduce the indication for treatment.
  • (D) No antiviral therapy because symptoms began more than 48 hours ago — The 48-hour rule does not apply to hospitalized patients; benefit persists beyond 48 hours.
🎯 Educational objective

Treat every hospitalized patient with influenza with oseltamivir as soon as possible, regardless of symptom duration or vaccination status.

ID-022.stem_html:
A 68-year-old man is evaluated on hospital day 7 after admission for a hip fracture repair. He has a new fever, productive cough and increasing oxygen requirement. He received IV cefazolin perioperatively and IV piperacillin-tazobactam for a urinary infection 3 days ago (completed). He is not receiving mechanical ventilation. Local data show that 15% of S. aureus isolates in the hospital are methicillin-resistant.

On physical examination, temperature is 38.8 °C (101.8 °F), blood pressure is 118/68 mm Hg, pulse rate is 106/min, and respiration rate is 24/min. Oxygen saturation is 90% on 4 L/min nasal cannula. Crackles are heard at the right base.

Chest radiograph shows a new right lower lobe consolidation. Sputum culture and an MRSA nasal PCR are sent.
ID-022.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate empiric antibiotic regimen?
ID-022.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Hospital-acquired pneumonia

Pneumonia ≥48 hours after admission is hospital-acquired pneumonia (HAP). Typical pathogens include Pseudomonas aeruginosa, other gram-negative bacilli and S. aureus (including MRSA).

The IDSA/ATS approach:

  • Antipseudomonal coverage for everyone: piperacillin-tazobactam, cefepime, levofloxacin, imipenem or meropenem.
  • Add MRSA coverage (vancomycin or linezolid) if IV antibiotics in the past 90 days, MRSA prevalence >20% or unknown, or high mortality risk (septic shock, ventilation). He received IV antibiotics 3 days ago.
  • Two antipseudomonal agents only if high mortality risk or structural lung disease.

De-escalate at 48–72 hours: a negative MRSA nasal PCR (high negative predictive value) allows vancomycin to be stopped. Treat for 7 days.

Why not the others

  • (A) Ampicillin-sulbactam alone — Ampicillin-sulbactam covers neither Pseudomonas nor MRSA.
  • (C) Ceftriaxone and azithromycin — Ceftriaxone and azithromycin are CAP therapy and do not cover Pseudomonas or MRSA.
  • (D) Levofloxacin alone — Levofloxacin covers Pseudomonas but not MRSA, and he has a risk factor for MRSA (recent IV antibiotics).
  • (E) Vancomycin alone — Vancomycin alone misses gram-negative pathogens, including Pseudomonas.
🎯 Educational objective

Treat hospital-acquired pneumonia empirically with an antipseudomonal β-lactam, and add MRSA coverage when there are risk factors such as intravenous antibiotics in the previous 90 days.

MS-001.stem_html:
A randomized controlled trial enrolls 8,000 adults with atrial fibrillation who cannot take anticoagulants. Patients are assigned to a new drug or placebo and followed for 5 years. The primary outcome is stroke.

Group Patients Strokes at 5 years
New drug 4,000 240 (6%)
Placebo 4,000 400 (10%)
MS-001.lead: How many patients must be treated with the new drug for 5 years to prevent one stroke?
MS-001.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Number needed to treat

Number needed to treat (NNT) = 1 ÷ absolute risk reduction (ARR).

  • Control event rate (CER) = 10% = 0.10
  • Experimental event rate (EER) = 6% = 0.06
  • ARR = CER − EER = 0.10 − 0.06 = 0.04
  • NNT = 1 / 0.04 = 25

Treating 25 patients for 5 years prevents one stroke. The relative risk reduction (RRR) is (0.10 − 0.06) / 0.10 = 40% — a bigger-sounding number that hides how often the event happens.

Measure Formula Here
Absolute risk reduction CER − EER 4%
Relative risk EER / CER 0.6
Relative risk reduction 1 − RR 40%
NNT 1 / ARR 25

Why not the others

  • (A) 4 — "4" confuses the ARR (4%) with the NNT.
  • (B) 10 — "10" is the placebo event rate expressed as a percentage, not the NNT.
  • (D) 40 — "40" is the relative risk reduction (40%), not the NNT.
  • (E) 60 — "60" reflects the relative risk (0.6) and is not an NNT.
🧠 Mnemonic

"Absolutely flip it" — NNT is the reciprocal of the absolute (not relative) risk reduction. Always round up to the next whole patient.

🎓 ABIM pearl

The same formula gives the number needed to harm (NNH): 1 ÷ absolute risk increase of an adverse event. Compare NNT with NNH when weighing a therapy.

🎯 Educational objective

Number needed to treat equals 1 divided by the absolute risk reduction; relative risk reduction overstates benefit when baseline risk is low.

MS-002.stem_html:
A new blood test for colorectal cancer has a sensitivity of 90% and a specificity of 90%. It is used to screen an average-risk population of 10,000 adults in which the prevalence of colorectal cancer is 1%.

A 58-year-old man in this population has a positive test result.
MS-002.lead: Which of the following is closest to the probability that he has colorectal cancer?
MS-002.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Predictive value and prevalence

Build a 2 × 2 table for 10,000 people with 1% prevalence:

Cancer (100) No cancer (9,900)
Test + 90 (TP) 990 (FP) 1,080
Test − 10 (FN) 8,910 (TN) 8,920
  • True positives = 90% × 100 = 90
  • False positives = 10% × 9,900 = 990
  • Positive predictive value (PPV) = TP / all positives = 90 / 1,080 ≈ 8%

Sensitivity and specificity are properties of the test. PPV and NPV depend on prevalence. When a disease is rare, even a good test produces mostly false positives. This is why screening tests are followed by a confirmatory test (here, colonoscopy).

Prevalence ↑ PPV ↑ NPV ↓
Prevalence ↓ PPV ↓ NPV ↑

Why not the others

  • (B) 50% — Fifty percent would require the true and false positives to be equal, which needs a much higher prevalence.
  • (C) 82% — This value has no basis in the calculation.
  • (D) 90% — Ninety percent is the sensitivity — the probability of a positive test in someone with cancer — not the probability of cancer after a positive test.
  • (E) 99% — Ninety-nine percent approximates the negative predictive value (8,910 / 8,920 ≈ 99.9%).
🧠 Mnemonic

SnNout, SpPin — a Sensitive test, when Negative, rules out; a Specific test, when Positive, rules in (but only if the disease is not too rare).

🎯 Educational objective

Positive predictive value depends on disease prevalence; in a low-prevalence population, most positive results are false positives even with a sensitive and specific test.

MS-003.stem_html: A new imaging test detects pancreatic cancer at an earlier stage than symptoms do. In an observational study, patients whose cancer was found by screening lived an average of 3.5 years from diagnosis, compared with 1.5 years for patients diagnosed after symptoms appeared. Age at death was the same in both groups.
MS-003.lead: Which of the following best explains the difference in survival?
MS-003.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Lead-time bias in screening

Lead-time bias: screening finds a disease earlier in its course, so survival measured from diagnosis looks longer — even if death occurs at the same time. Patients simply know about their cancer longer.

The tell-tale sign: survival from diagnosis improves, but age at death (or disease-specific mortality) does not.

Bias What happens Fix
Lead-time Earlier diagnosis inflates survival time Compare mortality rates, not survival from diagnosis
Length-time Screening picks up slow-growing, less aggressive tumors (long preclinical phase) Randomized trials
Overdiagnosis Detects cancers that would never cause symptoms or death Randomized trials; long follow-up
Healthy-volunteer (selection) People who choose screening are healthier Randomization

The only reliable proof that screening works is a randomized trial showing reduced disease-specific (ideally all-cause) mortality.

Why not the others

  • (A) Confounding by smoking status — Confounding could distort survival, but identical age at death with longer survival from diagnosis is the signature of lead time.
  • (C) Length-time bias — Length-time bias reflects detection of slower-growing tumors; it would make screen-detected patients live longer, not die at the same age.
  • (D) Overdiagnosis — Overdiagnosis detects cancers that would never cause death; here everyone died of the disease at the same age.
  • (E) The screening test reduces mortality — If screening reduced mortality, screened patients would die later.
🎯 Educational objective

Lead-time bias makes survival from diagnosis appear longer with screening without changing the time of death; screening benefit must be shown by reduced mortality in randomized trials.

MS-004.stem_html: A 74-year-old man is hospitalized with cellulitis. He has a documented penicillin allergy with anaphylaxis. Because of an order entry error, he receives one dose of piperacillin-tazobactam. Within minutes he develops hives and wheezing; he is treated promptly with epinephrine and recovers fully within 2 hours. He asks the resident what happened.
MS-004.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

choices.A: Advise him that he should talk to a lawyer
choices.B: Explain that he received an antibiotic he is allergic to because of an error, apologize, describe what is being done to prevent a recurrence, and report the event
choices.C: Tell him he had a reaction to an antibiotic, without mentioning the error, to avoid upsetting him
choices.D: Tell him the nurse made the error
choices.E: Wait until the hospital's risk management office completes its review before saying anything

MS-004.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Disclosure of a medical error

Physicians have an ethical duty to disclose errors that cause harm or could cause harm (ACP Ethics Manual, AMA Code). Effective disclosure includes:

  1. What happened — in plain language, promptly (as soon as the patient is stable)
  2. An apology — expression of regret ("I'm sorry this happened")
  3. Why it happened, to the extent known, without speculation or blame
  4. What it means for the patient and how consequences are being managed
  5. What will be done to prevent recurrence
  6. Report through the institution's safety system (and involve risk management, but do not let it delay disclosure)

Honest disclosure supports trust and is associated with fewer malpractice claims, not more. Many states have "apology laws" that make expressions of sympathy inadmissible.

Patient safety culture focuses on systems (e.g., allergy alerts, order sets) rather than individual blame.

Why not the others

  • (A) Advise him that he should talk to a lawyer — Advising legal action is not the physician's role and undermines the therapeutic relationship.
  • (C) Tell him he had a reaction to an antibiotic, without mentioning the error, to avoid upsetting him — Withholding the cause of the reaction is deceptive and violates the duty of honesty.
  • (D) Tell him the nurse made the error — Blaming an individual is inappropriate; errors usually reflect system failures, and the full analysis is not complete.
  • (E) Wait until the hospital's risk management office completes its review before saying anything — Risk management can help, but disclosure to the patient should not be delayed for an internal review.
🎯 Educational objective

Disclose medical errors promptly and honestly, including what happened, an apology, the consequences and how recurrence will be prevented, and report them through the institution's safety system.

MS-005.stem_html:
An 82-year-old woman with advanced dementia is hospitalized with aspiration pneumonia and is now unable to communicate. Two years ago, while she had capacity, she completed an advance directive stating that if she became unable to recognize her family she would not want feeding tubes, mechanical ventilation or CPR, and she named her son as her health care power of attorney.

Her son agrees with comfort-focused care. Her daughter, who lives out of state and has just arrived, insists that "everything be done", including a feeding tube and intubation if needed.
MS-005.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

choices.A: Ask the hospital ethics committee to make the decision
choices.B: Follow the daughter's wishes because she is requesting more treatment
choices.C: Follow the son's decisions, consistent with the patient's advance directive, while supporting and communicating with the daughter
choices.D: Obtain a court-appointed guardian before making any decisions
choices.E: Place a feeding tube until the family reaches agreement

MS-005.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Surrogate decision-making

When a patient lacks capacity, decisions follow a clear order:

  1. The patient's own expressed wishes — advance directive (living will) or prior clear statements
  2. The designated health care proxy (durable power of attorney for health care)
  3. If none, a surrogate by state hierarchy (usually spouse → adult children → parents → siblings)

Surrogates apply substituted judgment — what the patient would choose — not their own preferences. Only when the patient's wishes are unknown does the best-interest standard apply.

Here, the patient's written wishes and her chosen proxy agree. The daughter's disagreement does not override them. The team should meet with the family, explain the patient's wishes, acknowledge the daughter's grief, offer palliative care support, and consider ethics consultation to help mediate — but the decision follows the patient's directive.

Why not the others

  • (A) Ask the hospital ethics committee to make the decision — Ethics committees advise and mediate; they do not replace a valid proxy's decisions.
  • (B) Follow the daughter's wishes because she is requesting more treatment — Requests for more treatment do not override the patient's documented wishes or her designated proxy.
  • (D) Obtain a court-appointed guardian before making any decisions — Guardianship is needed only when there is no valid proxy or the proxy is acting against the patient's interests.
  • (E) Place a feeding tube until the family reaches agreement — Placing a feeding tube against the patient's directive violates her autonomy, and feeding tubes do not improve survival or prevent aspiration in advanced dementia.
🎯 Educational objective

When a patient lacks capacity, follow her advance directive and her designated health care proxy, who should use substituted judgment; other family members cannot override them.

MS-005.plain: An 82-year-old woman with advanced dementia is hospitalized with aspiration pneumonia and is now unable to communicate. Two years ago, while she had capacity, she completed an advance directive stating that if she became unable to recognize her family she would not want feeding tubes, mechanical ventilation or CPR, and she named her son as her health care power of attorney. Her son agrees with comfort-focused care. Her daughter, who lives out of state and has just arrived, insists that "everything be done", including a feeding tube and intubation if needed. Which of the following is the most
MS-005.search: an 82-year-old woman with advanced dementia is hospitalized with aspiration pneumonia and is now unable to communicate. two years ago, while she had capacity, she completed an advance directive stating that if she became unable to recognize her family she would not want feeding tubes, mechanical ventilation or cpr, and she named her son as her health care power of attorney. her son agrees with comfort-focused care. her daughter, who lives out of state and has just arrived, insists that "everything be done", including a feeding tube and intubation if needed. correct answer: c surrogate decision-making when a patient lacks capacity, decisions follow a clear order: the patient's own expressed wishes — advance directive (living will) or prior clear statements the designated health care proxy (durable power of attorney for health care) if none, a surrogate by state hierarchy (usually spouse → adult children → parents → siblings) surrogates apply substituted judgment — what the patient would choose — not their own preferences. only when the patient's wishes are unknown does the best-interest standard apply. here, the patient's written wishes and her chosen proxy agree . the daughter's disagreement does not override them. the team should meet with the family , explain the patient's wishes, acknowledge the daughter's grief, offer palliative care support, and consider ethics consultation to help mediate — but the decision follows the patient's directive. why not the others (a) ask the hospital ethics committee to make the decision — ethics committees advise and mediate; they do not replace a valid proxy's decisions. (b) follow the daughter's wishes because she is requesting more treatment — requests for more treatment do not override the patient's documented wishes or her designated proxy. (d) obtain a court-appointed guardian before making any decisions — guardianship is needed only when there is no valid proxy or the proxy is acting against the patient's interests. (e) place a feeding tube until the family reaches agreement — placing a feeding tube against the patient's directive violates her autonomy, and feeding tubes do not improve survival or prevent aspiration in advanced dementia. 🎯 educational objective when a patient lacks capacity, follow her advance directive and her designated health care proxy, who should use substituted judgment; other family members cannot override them. 📚 read more in wardology ⚖️ ethics — capacity, surrogates & errors → 🕊️ goals of care & pronouncing death → references sulmasy ls, bledsoe ta. american college of physicians ethics manual, 7th ed. ann intern med 2019;170:s1. american geriatrics society. feeding tubes in advanced dementia position statement. j am geriatr soc 2014;62:1590.  surrogate decision-making

NE-001.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate first step in management?
NE-001.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Hyperkalemia with ECG changes

The strip shows tall, peaked T waves, flattened P waves and a widened QRS — hyperkalemia with ECG changes, a medical emergency that can deteriorate to sine-wave rhythm, ventricular fibrillation or asystole without warning.

Treat in three steps, and the first is always to protect the heart:

Step Drugs Onset
1. Stabilize the membrane IV calcium gluconate 3 g (or calcium chloride 1 g via central line); repeat if ECG unchanged 1–3 min, lasts 30–60 min
2. Shift K⁺ into cells Regular insulin 10 units IV + dextrose (if glucose <250); nebulized albuterol 10–20 mg 15–30 min
3. Remove K⁺ from the body Loop diuretic (if making urine), potassium binder (SZC, patiromer), dialysis if refractory or anuric Hours

Calcium does not lower potassium — it restores the gap between resting and threshold potential so the heart cannot fire chaotically. Then stop spironolactone and lisinopril and look for the cause.

Why not the others

  • (A) Emergency hemodialysis — Dialysis is the definitive removal therapy for refractory hyperkalemia or kidney failure; it comes after membrane stabilization and shifting.
  • (C) Intravenous furosemide — Loop diuretics help remove potassium if he is making urine, but they act slowly and do not protect the heart.
  • (D) Intravenous regular insulin with dextrose — Insulin–dextrose is essential and comes right after calcium; it lowers potassium in 15–30 minutes but does not protect the myocardium immediately.
  • (E) Sodium zirconium cyclosilicate orally — Binders take hours to work and are for potassium removal after stabilization.
🧠 Mnemonic

"C-BIG-K-Drop": Calcium, Beta-agonist, Insulin + Glucose, Kayexalate/binders, Diuretics/dialysis.

🎓 ABIM pearl

In patients on digoxin with hyperkalemia, calcium is still given when ECG changes are present; the "stone heart" fear is not supported by modern data.

🎯 Educational objective

Hyperkalemia with ECG changes is treated first with intravenous calcium to stabilize the cardiac membrane, then insulin–dextrose and albuterol to shift potassium, and finally measures to remove potassium.

NE-002.stem_html:
A 44-year-old man comes to the office after passing his third calcium oxalate kidney stone in 4 years. To prevent stones he has stopped eating dairy products. He drinks about 1.2 L of fluid daily and eats fast food several times a week. He has hypertension and takes no medications.

Blood pressure is 142/88 mm Hg. Examination is normal.

Calcium (serum)9.6 mg/dL
Parathyroid hormone38 pg/mL
Uric acid (serum)5.8 mg/dL
24-hour urine — volume1.3 L
24-hour urine — calcium340 mg (normal <300 mg)
24-hour urine — oxalate38 mg (normal <45 mg)
24-hour urine — citrate620 mg (normal >450 mg)
24-hour urine — sodium230 mEq
24-hour urine — uric acid610 mg (normal <800 mg)
NE-002.lead: In addition to increasing fluid intake, which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation?

choices.C: Start chlorthalidone and reduce dietary sodium

NE-002.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Recurrent calcium nephrolithiasis

His 24-hour urine shows idiopathic hypercalciuria (normal serum calcium and PTH) with low urine volume and high sodium intake — the drivers of his calcium stones.

The plan:

  • Fluids to make >2.5 L of urine per day (the single most effective measure).
  • Thiazide diuretic (chlorthalidone, indapamide or hydrochlorothiazide): increases distal calcium reabsorption → lowers urine calcium and stone recurrence. It also treats his hypertension.
  • Low sodium diet: sodium drags calcium into urine; a high-salt diet blunts the thiazide effect.
  • Normal dietary calcium (1000–1200 mg/day) and moderate animal protein.

Why not the others

  • (A) Continue avoiding dairy products — A low-calcium diet increases stones: less calcium in the gut leaves more free oxalate to be absorbed, raising urine oxalate. It also harms bone.
  • (B) Start allopurinol — Allopurinol is for calcium stones with hyperuricosuria (and normal urine calcium) or for uric acid stones. His urine uric acid is normal.
  • (D) Start potassium citrate — Potassium citrate is for hypocitraturia (or uric acid stones). His citrate is normal; it is also an add-on to offset thiazide-induced hypokalemia.
  • (E) Start vitamin C 1000 mg daily — Vitamin C is metabolized to oxalate and increases calcium oxalate stone risk.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Every first stone needs serum calcium and a stone analysis; recurrent stones (or a first stone in a high-risk patient) need a 24-hour urine to pick targeted therapy.

🎯 Educational objective

Recurrent calcium stones with idiopathic hypercalciuria are prevented with high fluid intake, a thiazide diuretic, sodium restriction and a normal-calcium diet.

NE-003.stem_html:
A 64-year-old man comes to the office with 1 year of a weak urinary stream, hesitancy, a feeling of incomplete emptying and getting up three times a night to urinate. The symptoms bother him and he wants treatment. He has no dysuria, hematuria, fever, back pain or weight loss. He takes no medications.

Blood pressure is 134/82 mm Hg. The abdomen is soft without a palpable bladder. Digital rectal examination shows a smooth, symmetric, nontender, mildly enlarged prostate (estimated 30 g) without nodules.

Urinalysisno blood, leukocytes or glucose
Creatinine0.9 mg/dL
Post-void residual (bladder scan)60 mL
International Prostate Symptom Score17 (moderate)
NE-003.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?
NE-003.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Benign prostatic hyperplasia

He has bothersome lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) from benign prostatic hyperplasia, with a normal urinalysis, normal creatinine and a small post-void residual.

First-line medical therapy is an α₁-blocker (tamsulosin, alfuzosin, silodosin, doxazosin, terazosin). Blocking α₁ receptors in prostatic and bladder-neck smooth muscle relaxes the outlet and improves symptoms within days, regardless of prostate size.

Drug Works on Onset Use
α₁-blocker Dynamic (muscle tone) Days First line for bothersome LUTS
5α-reductase inhibitor Static (gland size) 6–12 months; shrinks gland ~20%–30% Prostate >30–40 g; reduces retention and surgery risk
PDE-5 inhibitor (tadalafil) Smooth muscle Weeks LUTS with erectile dysfunction
Antimuscarinic / β₃-agonist Bladder overactivity Weeks Persistent storage symptoms, PVR <250–300 mL

Why not the others

  • (A) Finasteride — 5α-reductase inhibitors take months to work and are reserved for larger prostates (>30–40 g), often combined with an α-blocker.
  • (B) Oxybutynin — Antimuscarinic drugs treat bladder overactivity; alone they are not first-line for obstructive BPH symptoms and can precipitate urinary retention.
  • (C) Prostate biopsy — A smooth, symmetric prostate without nodules and no PSA indication does not call for biopsy.
  • (E) Transurethral resection of the prostate — Surgery is for symptoms that fail medical therapy or for complications (retention, recurrent infection, stones, hematuria, upper-tract damage).
🎓 ABIM pearl

Warn patients starting tamsulosin about orthostatic dizziness and intraoperative floppy iris syndrome — tell the eye surgeon before cataract surgery.

🎯 Educational objective

An α₁-blocker such as tamsulosin is first-line therapy for bothersome LUTS due to BPH; 5α-reductase inhibitors are added for larger prostates.
