RH-013.stem_html:
A 68-year-old man with rheumatoid arthritis is evaluated for 2 days of a hot, swollen, very painful right knee. He cannot bear weight. He takes methotrexate and adalimumab. He has had no trauma.

On physical examination, temperature is 38.3 °C (100.9 °F), blood pressure is 128/76 mm Hg, and pulse rate is 102/min. The right knee is warm, red and has a large effusion; any movement causes severe pain. Other joints show no active synovitis.

Leukocyte count14,200/µL
C-reactive protein186 mg/L
Serum urate7.8 mg/dL
RH-013.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Arthrocentesis with synovial fluid cell count, Gram stain, culture and crystal analysis
choices.C: Increase methotrexate for an RA flare

RH-013.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Septic arthritis

An acute hot, swollen joint is septic arthritis until proven otherwise. He has major risk factors: RA (damaged joints), immunosuppression (TNF inhibitor, methotrexate), and older age. Septic arthritis destroys cartilage within days and has a mortality of up to 10%.

Arthrocentesis is the single most important test — do it before antibiotics:

  • Synovial WBC >50,000/µL (often >100,000) with >90% neutrophils suggests infection (lower in immunosuppressed patients).
  • Gram stain and culture (and blood cultures).
  • Crystal analysis — but crystals do not exclude infection; gout and sepsis can coexist.

His serum urate is irrelevant to the decision: it can be high without gout and normal during a gout flare.

Then start empiric IV antibiotics (vancomycin ± ceftriaxone depending on Gram stain) and arrange joint drainage (needle, arthroscopic or open).

Why not the others

  • (B) Begin colchicine for presumed gout — Treating presumed gout without aspirating risks missing a septic joint; a high urate does not establish gout.
  • (C) Increase methotrexate for an RA flare — A single acutely inflamed joint with fever in an immunosuppressed patient is not a typical RA flare and must be aspirated first.
  • (D) Intra-articular glucocorticoid injection — Injecting glucocorticoids into an infected joint is dangerous; infection must be excluded first.
  • (E) MRI of the knee — MRI can show effusion and osteomyelitis, but it cannot distinguish infection from crystals, and it delays the essential test.
🎯 Educational objective

Aspirate an acute hot joint for cell count, Gram stain, culture and crystals before starting treatment, because septic arthritis must be excluded.

RH-014.stem_html:
A 76-year-old woman is evaluated on postoperative day 3 after a hip replacement for acute pain and swelling of her right wrist. She has hypothyroidism and osteoarthritis.

On physical examination, temperature is 37.9 °C (100.2 °F). The right wrist is warm, swollen and tender, with limited motion.

Wrist radiograph shows a linear calcification of the triangular fibrocartilage. Arthrocentesis is performed.

Synovial fluid leukocyte count22,000/µL (80% neutrophils)
Synovial fluid Gram stainno organisms (culture pending)
Polarized microscopyrhomboid-shaped, weakly positively birefringent crystals
RH-014.lead: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
RH-014.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Calcium pyrophosphate deposition (pseudogout)

Acute CPP crystal arthritis (pseudogout): an older patient with an acutely inflamed wrist or knee, often triggered by surgery or acute illness, with chondrocalcinosis on radiographs and rhomboid, weakly positively birefringent crystals (blue when parallel to the compensator).

Gout (monosodium urate) CPPD
Crystal shape Needle Rhomboid
Birefringence Strongly negative (yellow when parallel) Weakly positive (blue when parallel)
Typical joints 1st MTP, ankle, knee Knee, wrist
Radiograph Punched-out erosions with overhanging edges Chondrocalcinosis

In patients <60 or with polyarticular disease, look for associated metabolic disorders: hemochromatosis, hyperparathyroidism, hypomagnesemia, hypophosphatasia ("the 4 Hs").

Treat with joint aspiration, intra-articular glucocorticoids (once infection is excluded), NSAIDs or colchicine.

Why not the others

  • (B) Gout — Gout crystals are needle-shaped and strongly negatively birefringent.
  • (C) Osteoarthritis flare — Osteoarthritis causes a noninflammatory effusion (WBC <2,000/µL) without crystals.
  • (D) Reactive arthritis — Reactive arthritis is an asymmetric oligoarthritis of the lower limbs after GI or GU infection, without crystals.
  • (E) Rheumatoid arthritis — RA is a symmetric polyarthritis of the small joints; it does not cause a monoarthritis with CPP crystals.
🧠 Mnemonic

"P for Pseudogout, Positive and Parallelogram (rhomboid)." Gout = Needles, Negative.

🎯 Educational objective

Diagnose acute CPP crystal arthritis by rhomboid, weakly positively birefringent crystals in synovial fluid, often with chondrocalcinosis on radiographs.

RH-015.stem_html:
A 66-year-old woman is evaluated for 2 years of right knee pain that is worse with walking and stairs and better with rest. Morning stiffness lasts less than 15 minutes. She has hypertension and stage 3a chronic kidney disease (eGFR 52 mL/min/1.73 m²). Acetaminophen has not helped.

On physical examination, BMI is 32. There is bony enlargement and crepitus of the right knee with a small cool effusion. There is no warmth or erythema.

Radiographs show medial joint space narrowing and osteophytes.
RH-015.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

choices.E: Topical diclofenac and an exercise and weight-loss program

RH-015.explain_html:
Correct answer: E Knee osteoarthritis

Activity-related knee pain, brief morning stiffness, bony enlargement, crepitus and medial joint space narrowing in an older adult = knee osteoarthritis.

The core treatments (ACR 2019) are exercise (strengthening, aerobic, tai chi) and weight loss (≥5–10% of body weight improves pain and function), plus self-management education.

For drug therapy, topical NSAIDs are recommended first for the knee — they work nearly as well as oral NSAIDs with far less systemic exposure. They are the best choice in older adults and those with CKD, hypertension or GI risk, where oral NSAIDs are risky. Intra-articular glucocorticoid injections give short-term relief for flares. Total knee replacement is for end-stage disease when conservative care fails.

Why not the others

  • (A) Arthroscopic débridement — Arthroscopic débridement and lavage do not help degenerative knee osteoarthritis and are not recommended.
  • (B) Intra-articular hyaluronic acid injection — Hyaluronic acid injections have little benefit over placebo and are conditionally recommended against.
  • (C) Oral glucosamine and chondroitin — Glucosamine and chondroitin are no better than placebo and are not recommended.
  • (D) Oral tramadol — Tramadol has modest benefit with risks of dependence, falls and serotonin syndrome; it is conditionally recommended only when other options fail.
🎯 Educational objective

Treat knee osteoarthritis with exercise, weight loss and topical NSAIDs, particularly in older adults or patients with chronic kidney disease.

RH-016.stem_html: A 52-year-old man of Han Chinese descent is evaluated after his third gout flare in a year. He has tophi on both elbows. He has hypertension and chronic kidney disease (eGFR 48 mL/min/1.73 m²). His serum urate is 9.4 mg/dL. You plan to start urate-lowering therapy.
RH-016.lead: Which of the following should be done before starting allopurinol?
RH-016.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Allopurinol hypersensitivity — HLA-B*58:01

Allopurinol hypersensitivity syndrome — including DRESS and SJS/TEN — is rare but carries a mortality of up to 25%. The strongest risk factor is HLA-B*58:01, which is common in people of Han Chinese, Korean, Thai and African descent. CKD and starting at high doses also raise the risk.

ACR 2020 recommends testing for HLA-B*58:01 before starting allopurinol in patients of Southeast Asian (e.g., Han Chinese, Korean, Thai) or African American descent. If positive, choose febuxostat instead.

Other allopurinol rules:

  • Start low (≤100 mg/d; ≤50 mg/d in CKD stage 4+) and titrate to serum urate <6 mg/dL — higher doses are fine in CKD once titrated slowly.
  • Give anti-inflammatory prophylaxis (colchicine, NSAID or low-dose prednisone) for 3–6 months when starting.

Why not the others

  • (A) 24-hour urine uric acid — A 24-hour urine uric acid is rarely needed and does not affect the safety of allopurinol.
  • (C) Liver biopsy — Liver biopsy has no role in starting urate-lowering therapy.
  • (D) No testing is needed — His ancestry calls for HLA-B*58:01 testing to avoid a potentially fatal reaction.
  • (E) Thiopurine methyltransferase (TPMT) activity — TPMT testing is done before azathioprine or mercaptopurine. It matters for allopurinol only because allopurinol interacts with those drugs.
🎯 Educational objective

Test for HLA-B*58:01 before starting allopurinol in patients of Southeast Asian or African American descent to reduce the risk of severe hypersensitivity.

RH-017.stem_html:
A 72-year-old woman is evaluated for 6 weeks of aching and stiffness of both shoulders and hips, worst in the morning for about 2 hours. She has trouble getting out of bed and combing her hair. She has no headache, jaw pain with chewing, scalp tenderness or visual symptoms.

On physical examination, there is reduced active range of motion of both shoulders because of pain; passive motion is better. Strength is normal when tested despite the pain. There is no synovitis of the hands. Temporal arteries are normal.

Erythrocyte sedimentation rate64 mm/h
C-reactive protein38 mg/L
Creatine kinasenormal
Rheumatoid factor and anti-CCPnegative
TSHnormal
RH-017.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

choices.E: Temporal artery biopsy before any treatment

RH-017.explain_html:
Correct answer: C Polymyalgia rheumatica

An older adult with bilateral shoulder and hip girdle aching and morning stiffness, raised inflammatory markers, normal CK and no features of another disease → polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR).

PMR responds dramatically to low-dose glucocorticoids: prednisone 12.5–25 mg/d (EULAR/ACR 2015). Improvement within days is so typical that a poor response should make you question the diagnosis. Taper slowly over at least 1 year to the lowest effective dose. Add methotrexate (or tocilizumab) for relapses or high risk of glucocorticoid toxicity.

About 15–20% of PMR patients have giant cell arteritis — always ask about headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness and vision. If present, high-dose prednisone (40–60 mg) is needed. She has none.

Why not the others

  • (A) Methotrexate alone — Methotrexate is a glucocorticoid-sparing add-on, not initial monotherapy.
  • (B) Naproxen alone — NSAIDs may help briefly but are inadequate for PMR and add GI and kidney risk in older adults.
  • (D) Prednisone, 60 mg/d — High-dose prednisone is for giant cell arteritis. Uncomplicated PMR responds to low doses, and higher doses cause more toxicity.
  • (E) Temporal artery biopsy before any treatment — Temporal artery biopsy is for suspected GCA. She has no cranial or visual symptoms.
🎯 Educational objective

Treat polymyalgia rheumatica with low-dose prednisone (12.5–25 mg/d) and screen for symptoms of giant cell arteritis.

RH-018.stem_html:
A 54-year-old man is evaluated for 3 months of chronic sinus congestion with bloody nasal discharge, ear fullness, cough and, over the past week, hemoptysis. Two courses of antibiotics did not help.

On physical examination, temperature is 37.9 °C (100.2 °F), blood pressure is 152/90 mm Hg. There are nasal crusts and a saddle-nose deformity is developing. There is palpable purpura on the lower legs.

Creatinine2.4 mg/dL (1.0 mg/dL 2 months ago)
Urinalysis2+ protein; dysmorphic erythrocytes and red cell casts
Chest CTmultiple bilateral cavitating nodules
RH-018.lead: Which of the following is the most likely to be positive?

choices.E: Perinuclear ANCA (p-ANCA) with anti-myeloperoxidase antibodies and eosinophilia

RH-018.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Granulomatosis with polyangiitis

The triad of upper airway (sinusitis, nasal crusting, saddle nose, otitis), lower airway (cavitating nodules, hemoptysis) and kidney disease (rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with red cell casts) = granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA), a small-vessel ANCA-associated vasculitis.

About 90% of patients with active, generalized GPA are c-ANCA / anti–PR3 positive. Confirm with biopsy of an affected site when feasible (kidney biopsy shows pauci-immune necrotizing crescentic GN).

Disease ANCA Clues
GPA c-ANCA, PR3 ENT + lung nodules + kidney, granulomas
Microscopic polyangiitis p-ANCA, MPO Lung hemorrhage + kidney, no ENT or granulomas
EGPA p-ANCA, MPO (~40%) Asthma + eosinophilia, neuropathy
Anti-GBM disease ANCA− (sometimes +), anti-GBM+ Lung hemorrhage + kidney, linear IgG

Induction for organ-threatening disease: glucocorticoids + rituximab (or cyclophosphamide); avacopan allows lower steroid doses.

Why not the others

  • (A) Antinuclear antibodies with low complement — Lupus causes immune-complex GN with low complement; ENT destruction and cavitating nodules are not features.
  • (B) Anti–glomerular basement membrane antibodies — Anti-GBM disease causes pulmonary hemorrhage and GN, but not sinus disease or cavitating nodules.
  • (C) Cryoglobulins with hepatitis C viremia — Cryoglobulinemic vasculitis causes purpura and GN but not destructive ENT disease or lung cavities.
  • (E) Perinuclear ANCA (p-ANCA) with anti-myeloperoxidase antibodies and eosinophilia — p-ANCA/MPO with eosinophilia points to EGPA, which presents with asthma and eosinophilia rather than destructive sinus disease.
🎯 Educational objective

Recognize granulomatosis with polyangiitis by upper and lower airway disease plus glomerulonephritis and confirm with c-ANCA/anti–PR3 testing and biopsy.

Two courses of antibiotics did not help. On physical examination, temperature is 37.9 °C (100.2 °F), blood pressure is 152/90 mm Hg. There are nasal crusts and a saddle-nose deformity is developing. There is palpable purpura on the lower legs. Which of the following is the most likely to be positive?
RH-018.search: a 54-year-old man is evaluated for 3 months of chronic sinus congestion with bloody nasal discharge, ear fullness, cough and, over the past week, hemoptysis. two courses of antibiotics did not help. on physical examination, temperature is 37.9 °c (100.2 °f), blood pressure is 152/90 mm hg. there are nasal crusts and a saddle-nose deformity is developing. there is palpable purpura on the lower legs. creatinine 2.4 mg/dl (1.0 mg/dl 2 months ago) urinalysis 2+ protein; dysmorphic erythrocytes and red cell casts chest ct multiple bilateral cavitating nodules correct answer: d granulomatosis with polyangiitis the triad of upper airway (sinusitis, nasal crusting, saddle nose, otitis), lower airway (cavitating nodules, hemoptysis) and kidney disease (rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with red cell casts) = granulomatosis with polyangiitis (gpa) , a small-vessel anca-associated vasculitis. about 90% of patients with active, generalized gpa are c-anca / anti–pr3 positive . confirm with biopsy of an affected site when feasible (kidney biopsy shows pauci-immune necrotizing crescentic gn). disease anca clues gpa c-anca, pr3 ent + lung nodules + kidney, granulomas microscopic polyangiitis p-anca, mpo lung hemorrhage + kidney, no ent or granulomas egpa p-anca, mpo (~40%) asthma + eosinophilia , neuropathy anti-gbm disease anca− (sometimes +), anti-gbm+ lung hemorrhage + kidney, linear igg induction for organ-threatening disease: glucocorticoids + rituximab (or cyclophosphamide); avacopan allows lower steroid doses. why not the others (a) antinuclear antibodies with low complement — lupus causes immune-complex gn with low complement; ent destruction and cavitating nodules are not features. (b) anti–glomerular basement membrane antibodies — anti-gbm disease causes pulmonary hemorrhage and gn, but not sinus disease or cavitating nodules. (c) cryoglobulins with hepatitis c viremia — cryoglobulinemic vasculitis causes purpura and gn but not destructive ent disease or lung cavities. (e) perinuclear anca (p-anca) with anti-myeloperoxidase antibodies and eosinophilia — p-anca/mpo with eosinophilia points to egpa, which presents with asthma and eosinophilia rather than destructive sinus disease. 🎯 educational objective recognize granulomatosis with polyangiitis by upper and lower airway disease plus glomerulonephritis and confirm with c-anca/anti–pr3 testing and biopsy. 📚 read more in wardology 🩸 small- & medium-vessel vasculitis → 🧫 glomerular disease — nephritic & nephrotic → references chung sa, et al. 2021 acr/vasculitis foundation guideline for the management of anca-associated vasculitis. arthritis rheumatol 2021;73:1366.  granulomatosis with polyangiitis

RH-019.stem_html:
A 45-year-old woman with seropositive rheumatoid arthritis has persistent synovitis of the hands and wrists despite 6 months of methotrexate, 20 mg/wk. Her rheumatologist plans to add a TNF inhibitor. She was born in Mexico and moved to the United States at age 20. She has no symptoms of infection.

Examination shows synovitis of several MCP joints.
RH-019.lead: Which of the following tests must be performed before starting the TNF inhibitor?

choices.D: Interferon-γ release assay (or tuberculin skin test) and hepatitis B serologies

RH-019.explain_html:
Correct answer: D Screening before TNF inhibitor therapy

TNF inhibitors (infliximab, adalimumab, etanercept, golimumab, certolizumab) impair granuloma maintenance and markedly increase the risk of reactivation of latent tuberculosis — often extrapulmonary or disseminated. They can also reactivate hepatitis B.

Before any biologic or JAK inhibitor, screen for:

  • Latent TB — IGRA (preferred if BCG vaccinated) or tuberculin skin test, ± chest radiograph. If positive, start LTBI treatment ≥1 month before the biologic.
  • Hepatitis B — HBsAg, anti-HBc (and anti-HBs); hepatitis C antibody.
  • Update vaccinations (non-live vaccines can be given at any time; live vaccines must be given before starting).

Other cautions with TNF inhibitors: avoid in decompensated heart failure (NYHA III–IV) and demyelinating disease.

Why not the others

  • (A) Antinuclear antibody titer — ANA is not required before TNF inhibitors. They can induce drug-related ANA positivity and lupus-like syndromes, but baseline ANA does not change management.
  • (B) Bone density scan — Bone density testing is important with long-term glucocorticoids but is not a prerequisite for TNF inhibitors.
  • (C) Echocardiography — Echocardiography is not routine; TNF inhibitors are avoided in known moderate-to-severe heart failure, which is assessed clinically.
  • (E) Pulmonary function tests — Pulmonary function tests are not required before TNF inhibitors.
🎯 Educational objective

Screen for latent tuberculosis and hepatitis B before starting a TNF inhibitor or other biologic therapy.

RH-020.stem_html:
A 58-year-old man who works as a plumber is evaluated for 3 days of painful swelling over the back of his right elbow. He scraped his elbow on a pipe a week ago.

On physical examination, temperature is 37.9 °C (100.2 °F). There is a fluctuant, warm, red, tender swelling over the olecranon process with a small healing abrasion. Elbow flexion and extension are full and painless except at the extremes when the swelling is compressed.
RH-020.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Aspiration of the bursa with cell count, Gram stain, culture and crystal analysis

RH-020.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Septic olecranon bursitis

Superficial olecranon bursitis sits over the joint, not in it: the elbow moves freely through most of its range. Septic arthritis, by contrast, makes any movement extremely painful.

Warmth, erythema, tenderness, fever and a skin break suggest septic bursitis, almost always S. aureus from skin trauma. Aspirate the bursa (approaching from the side, not through inflamed skin) for:

  • Cell count (septic usually >2,000–5,000/µL, often much higher, neutrophil-predominant)
  • Gram stain and culture
  • Crystals (gout is a common cause of olecranon bursitis)

Treat septic bursitis with antistaphylococcal antibiotics (e.g., cephalexin, or doxycycline/TMP-SMX if MRSA risk), repeat aspiration as needed; surgery only for failure.

Aseptic (traumatic) bursitis — chronic leaning ("student's elbow"), no warmth — is treated with compression, padding and avoiding pressure.

Why not the others

  • (B) Elbow arthrocentesis through the joint — The elbow joint itself is not involved (full painless motion); passing a needle through an infected bursa into the joint risks seeding it.
  • (C) Intrabursal glucocorticoid injection — Glucocorticoid injection is contraindicated until infection is excluded and is generally avoided in olecranon bursitis because of infection and skin atrophy risk.
  • (D) MRI of the elbow — The diagnosis is clinical and confirmed by aspiration; MRI is unnecessary.
  • (E) Surgical bursectomy — Bursectomy is reserved for refractory or recurrent septic bursitis.
🎓 ABIM pearl

Other bursitis to know for the CERT exam — prepatellar ("housemaid's knee," septic risk like olecranon), trochanteric (greater trochanteric pain syndrome, lateral hip pain lying on that side), pes anserine (medial knee below the joint line in obese women with knee OA).

🎯 Educational objective

Aspirate a warm, red olecranon bursa for cell count, Gram stain, culture and crystals to distinguish septic from crystal-induced or traumatic bursitis.

RH-021.stem_html:
A 52-year-old woman is evaluated for 4 months of numbness and tingling in her right hand that wakes her at night; she shakes her hand to relieve it. Symptoms involve the thumb, index and middle fingers. She has hypothyroidism and type 2 diabetes. She works as a data entry clerk.

On physical examination, there is reduced sensation over the palmar aspect of the first three fingers, sparing the thenar eminence. Tapping over the volar wrist reproduces tingling in these fingers, and holding the wrists in full flexion for 60 seconds does the same. There is mild weakness of thumb abduction; there is no thenar atrophy. Sensation over the little finger and the dorsum of the hand is normal.
RH-021.lead: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
RH-021.explain_html:
Correct answer: B Carpal tunnel syndrome

Carpal tunnel syndrome — compression of the median nerve at the wrist — is the most common entrapment neuropathy. The picture: nocturnal paresthesias of the thumb, index, middle (and radial half of ring) fingers, relief by shaking the hand ("flick sign"), positive Tinel (tapping) and Phalen (wrist flexion) signs, and later weakness of thumb abduction and thenar atrophy.

Sparing of the thenar eminence is a key localizing clue: the palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve leaves above the carpal tunnel, so it is spared at the wrist but affected in more proximal lesions.

Risk factors: diabetes, hypothyroidism, pregnancy, RA, obesity, amyloidosis, acromegaly, repetitive wrist use.

Treat with nocturnal neutral wrist splinting, glucocorticoid injection, and surgical release for severe or persistent disease (thenar atrophy, EMG denervation). EMG/nerve conduction confirm the diagnosis and severity when surgery is considered.

Why not the others

  • (A) C6 cervical radiculopathy — C6 radiculopathy causes neck pain radiating down the arm, numbness of the thumb and index finger including the dorsum, and reduced biceps/brachioradialis reflexes.
  • (C) Cubital tunnel syndrome — Cubital tunnel syndrome (ulnar nerve at the elbow) causes numbness of the little and ring fingers and weakness of the intrinsic hand muscles.
  • (D) De Quervain tenosynovitis — De Quervain tenosynovitis causes pain (not numbness) over the radial styloid with a positive Finkelstein test.
  • (E) Thoracic outlet syndrome — Thoracic outlet syndrome usually affects the lower trunk (C8–T1), causing ulnar-sided symptoms, and is worsened by arm elevation.
🎯 Educational objective

Recognize carpal tunnel syndrome by nocturnal paresthesias in the median nerve distribution, positive Tinel and Phalen signs and sparing of the thenar eminence sensation.

RH-022.stem_html:
A 42-year-old woman is evaluated for 1 year of widespread pain above and below the waist on both sides of her body, fatigue, unrefreshing sleep and difficulty concentrating. Pain medicines, including ibuprofen and an opioid prescribed by an urgent care clinic, have not helped.

On physical examination, vital signs are normal. There is diffuse soft tissue tenderness. Joints show no swelling or synovitis. Strength and reflexes are normal.

Complete blood countnormal
ESR and C-reactive proteinnormal
TSHnormal
Creatine kinasenormal
RH-022.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?

choices.A: Graded aerobic exercise program and patient education
choices.E: Referral for trigger-point injections every month

RH-022.explain_html:
Correct answer: A Fibromyalgia

Chronic widespread pain for ≥3 months with fatigue, unrefreshing sleep and cognitive symptoms ("fibro fog"), normal examination apart from tenderness, and normal laboratory tests fits fibromyalgia (ACR 2016 criteria). It is a disorder of central pain processing (nociplastic pain), not inflammation or tissue damage.

The best-supported first-line treatments are nonpharmacologic: patient education, graded aerobic exercise (the most effective single intervention), cognitive behavioral therapy and sleep hygiene.

If drug therapy is needed, use agents that act on central pain pathways: low-dose amitriptyline (at bedtime), duloxetine or milnacipran (SNRIs), or pregabalin.

Avoid opioids — they do not help and may worsen pain sensitivity (opioid-induced hyperalgesia). NSAIDs and glucocorticoids do not work because there is no inflammation.

Why not the others

  • (B) Hydroxychloroquine — Hydroxychloroquine treats lupus and RA, not fibromyalgia.
  • (C) Long-acting opioid — Opioids are ineffective in fibromyalgia and carry risks of dependence and hyperalgesia.
  • (D) Prednisone, 10 mg/d — There is no inflammation; glucocorticoids do not help and cause harm.
  • (E) Referral for trigger-point injections every month — Trigger-point injections have limited evidence and are not a first-line treatment.
🎯 Educational objective

Treat fibromyalgia first with patient education and graded aerobic exercise, adding duloxetine, pregabalin or low-dose amitriptyline if needed, and avoid opioids.
